text:
HARTFORD, CT — State officials are assessing their options after yet another attempt by the Trump administration to block Connecticut from developing new energy sources through the Revolution Wind project.

This week, the Trump administration asked a federal court for permission to rescind its past approval of Revolution Wind. Revolution Wind is a 704-megawatt offshore wind project approximately 15 nautical miles southeast of Point Judith, Rhode Island. The 65-turbine project began construction in 2023, and the final turbine was completed in September. The project is expected to reach full commercial operation later this year, and it is expected to deliver enough electricity to the New England grid to power 350,000 homes, equivalent to about 2.5% of the region’s electricity supply.

“Revolution Wind is a fully permitted, fully constructed offshore wind farm, built by union labor, that is already providing clean, affordable, reliable energy to Connecticut and the region,” Lamont said. “The Trump administration says it wants federal permitting reform legislation to accelerate energy projects and lower costs for ratepayers, but this action by the Department of Justice is completely contrary to that goal.”

Lamont said any meaningful agreement must be built on a fundamental principle: ratepayers, developers, and investors need certainty that projects can move forward when they comply with federal and state laws and regulations, and that permits already granted will be honored.

“That certainty is essential to building the affordable, reliable energy infrastructure our nation needs, including projects already in the pipeline,” he said.

Lamont said Connecticut would take “appropriate steps as needed” and that his office was in communication with Ørsted, the project’s developer, and Attorney General William Tong’s office.

Tong said the action by the administration made no sense.

“We sued to get Revolution Wind back online, and we will not hesitate to return to court again to protect Connecticut jobs and our access to clean, renewable, affordable power,” he said

Acting DEEP Commissioner Emma Cimino noted that Revolution Wind was already supplying energy to the grid, and that the project would save New England ratepayers a half-billion dollars in electricity market costs each year. Public benefits savings also would total about $150 million to $200 million over the life of the 20-year contract, she said.

“Revolution Wind also adds much-needed reliability to our grid, which is particularly important as we head into the cold winter months when heating usage is high and wind energy typically performs strongly,” she said. “Any actions to impede or delay this progress are not in the best interest of Connecticut residents.”

Connecticut’s senior senator, Democrat Richard Blumenthal, called Trump’s opposition to Revolution Wind and other clean energy projects “unhinged and unwarranted.”

“While Trump’s war of choice with Iran drives fuel costs sky high for Americans, he’s also waging war on offshore wind projects including New England’s Revolution Wind,” Blumenthal said. “If there’s one lesson from Trump’s mindless warmongering, it’s that we need to break our dependence on foreign imports of fossil fuels and embrace alternate sources of energy.”

Revolution Wind is expected to meet about 5% of Connecticut’s overall electricity demand, officials said.

text:
The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has approved Colorado’s request for primary enforcement authority (“primacy”) over Underground Injection Control (UIC) Class VI wells.

Starting November 12, 2026, the Colorado Energy and Carbon Management Commission (ECMC) will assume full jurisdiction over permitting, site characterization, environmental monitoring, and long-term well closures.

The state program incorporates strict groundwater protection rules alongside long-term site stewardship funded via Colorado’s Geologic Storage Stewardship Enterprise (HB25-1165).

The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has formally granted Colorado primary regulatory authority over Underground Injection Control (UIC) Class VI injection wells, transferring direct oversight of permanent deep geological carbon storage to state regulators.

The final rule, published by the EPA on October 13, 2026, takes effect on November 12, 2026. Beginning on that date, the Colorado Energy and Carbon Management Commission (ECMC) will assume sole responsibility for reviewing applications, issuing permits, monitoring operational performance, and enforcing compliance for Class VI carbon sequestration wells across state lands.

The transfer of authority follows a multi-year effort initiated after the Colorado General Assembly authorized the ECMC to pursue Class VI primacy in 2023. The state formally submitted its application in October 2025, demonstrating that its technical guidance, enforcement mechanics, and public engagement protocols meet or exceed federal Safe Drinking Water Act mandates.

Localizing Review Processes and Establishing Long-Term Stewardship

State officials emphasized that state-level primacy will accelerate review timelines by leveraging local geological expertise while maintaining stringent environmental safeguards.

Under ECMC oversight, Class VI permitting will follow a two-stage approval process: initial Commission approval of a project’s Class VI Development Plan, followed by a secondary verification review before issuing a formal Authorization to Inject.

Project developers must demonstrate site integrity across target storage formations and caprock seals, provide financial assurance for emergency responses and well plugging, and undergo mandatory public comment periods.

Relevant: Colorado And Wyoming Sign Agreement On Cross-Border CO2 Storage

“Having Class VI oversight in Colorado will allow fast decisions about permitting underground carbon storage to be made by Colorado experts who understand our geology, communities and environment,” said Governor Jared Polis.

To manage post-operational liabilities, long-term care for sequestered carbon will be financed through the state’s Geologic Storage Stewardship Enterprise, authorized under House Bill HB25-1165, which collects fees directly from Class VI injection operators.

The EPA will maintain federal oversight of the state program and retain direct permitting authority for Class VI injection activities on Tribal lands.

text:
Increased Incentive Level Reflects Connecticut’s Continuing Commitment to Clean Air and Helping Residents Afford Cleaner Transportation Options With Lower Lifetime Maintenance Costs

(HARTFORD) — The Connecticut Department of Energy and Environmental Protection (DEEP) announced today that the standard incentive level for the popular Connecticut Hydrogen and Electric Vehicle Purchase Rebate (CHEAPR) program will be changing effective October 15, 2026. The CHEAPR program offers incentives to Connecticut residents who purchase or lease an eligible new or used battery electric (BEV) or plug-in hybrid electric (PHEV) vehicle from a licensed Connecticut automobile dealership or original equipment manufacturer.

Effective October 15th, DEEP is increasing the standard incentive for new battery electric vehicles from $1,000 to $1,500. Demand for CHEAPR rebates skyrocketed in 2025 during the lead up to the loss of the federal tax credit on October 1, 2025, and as a result, DEEP reduced the amount of the standard rebate. Since the expiration of the federal tax credit, CHEAPR rebates have dropped by 50%. The drop in the number of CHEAPR rebates is the result of several factors including the impact of tariffs on manufacturing costs and product availability. Returning the standard rebate back to $1,500 can help consumers by addressing part of the gap created by policy changes by the federal government. Affordability remains top of mind for the Lamont Administration and with high gasoline prices , CHEAPR incentives can make cleaner, more affordable transportation choices available by reducing the upfront costs of BEVs.

The Rebate+ incentives, which provide additional incentives for prequalified low- and moderate-income families to consider a new or used electric vehicle, will remain at current levels while DEEP considers other program improvements. There remains significant interest in Rebate+ with demand slightly ahead of last year. DEEP will continue to monitor demand for this popular program, and work with the CHEAPR board and the Connecticut General Assembly to ensure the program continues to support Connecticut drivers.

“With gasoline and diesel prices at all-time highs, it’s more important than ever that the CHEAPR program continue to meet Connecticut drivers where they are,” said DEEP Acting Commissioner Emma Cimino. “Connecticut’s CHEAPR rebate remains a popular incentive that has helped almost 28,000 drivers get behind the wheel of an EV and benefit from lower fuel and lifetime maintenance costs.”

EVs can be CHEAPR over the long term

Cars and trucks cost us more than their up-front purchase price. These costs are called the “total cost of ownership” or “TCO” and many factors go into determining their impact. TCO includes upfront costs such as purchase price, taxes and registration fees; recurring costs such as fuel, maintenance, repairs and insurance; and end of ownership costs that reflect depreciation in the resale value of the vehicle.

While BEVs may not be right for everyone, if you tend to purchase used vehicles and hold on to them for a while, then a BEV will likely cost you less over the long run. BEVs are inherently more efficient than internal combustion vehicles because more energy goes to moving the vehicle and less is wasted as heat, and electricity is usually less expensive than gasoline when used as a transportation fuel (e.g., at Connecticut’s retail electric rate and assuming average efficiency of 3.5kWh, fueling with electricity is equivalent to paying about $2.66/gallon). EVs require less maintenance (no oil changes, water pumps, timing belts, etc.), and their brakes last longer because BEVs use regenerative braking technologies.

About CHEAPR

CHEAPR provides a cash rebate at the Point-of-Sale (POS) to Connecticut residents who purchase or lease a new eligible vehicle costing up to $50,000 from a licensed Connecticut new car dealer. DEEP launched the CHEAPR program in May of 2015 and since that time has issued over $50 million in rebates to Connecticut residents who have purchased or leased almost 28,000 new or used electric vehicles. Since the beginning of the year, CHEAPR has issued incentives for over 2,700 new EVs, including over 520 for Rebate+.

Incentive levels fall into two buckets: “Standard” and “Rebate +.” All Connecticut licensed drivers are eligible for the standard incentive. To be eligible for Rebate +, a Connecticut licensed driver must be pre-qualified and either meet income thresholds, participate in an identified list of income qualified programs, or reside in either a distressed municipality or an environmental justice (EJ) community. The Rebate + incentive is awarded in the form of a voucher, so applicants must pre-apply to ensure eligibility.

As of October 15, 2026, the Standard incentive for a new battery electric vehicle will be $1,500. The Rebate + incentive for a new battery electric vehicle will be unchanged at $3,000. As this award is issued in addition to and stackable with the Standard incentive, the new total incentive will be $4,500. The Rebate + incentive for a new plug-in hybrid vehicle will be unchanged at $1,500 and is awarded in addition to the Standard incentive, for a total incentive of $2,000. With uncertainty and added expense caused by tariffs, changes in federal policy, and auto manufacturers cancelling their investments in new technology, new electric vehicles remain out of reach for many moderate-income residents, the Rebate+ program also offers incentives for used battery electric and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles. These voucher-based incentives also remain unchanged at $5,000 and $3,000, respectively. Keep in mind that Rebate+ requires pre-approval to ensure eligibility.

About Connecticut’s Air Quality

There are over 2.7 million vehicles registered in Connecticut. Cars and trucks account for almost 70% of smog-forming emissions in Connecticut and almost 35% of our climate pollution. Air quality in Connecticut exceeded the federal health-based standards for ozone (smog) on 17 days in 2026, 22 days in 2025 and 23 days in 2024. Individuals in sensitive groups, including children, the elderly and those with pre-existing health conditions, who are exposed to unhealthy levels of air pollution are at an increased risk of developing respiratory symptoms and may experience shortness of breath or difficulty breathing. Children and people with asthma or other lung disease are most at risk for experiencing these symptoms. People experiencing severe symptoms are more likely to miss work or school and seek medical treatment.

Helping to put cleaner vehicles on our roads is one of the most effective means to combat air pollution and the associated poor health outcomes while also pushing back on federal cuts to health care and weakened fuel efficiency and emissions standards. CHEAPR helps fill the gap left by the federal government and will remain an important tool to help Connecticut consumers overcome the higher sticker price on a vehicle that will save them money on fuel and maintenance while having a more positive impact on our air quality.

DEEP monitors, tracks, and forecasts daily air quality levels across Connecticut for ozone from May 1st through September 30th each year and for fine particulate matter (PM2.5) each day of the year. On April 30, 2024, DEEP began informing Connecticut’s regulated community and the general public of the ozone season via the State of Connecticut E-mail list serve and posting air quality forecasts on the DEEP webpage.

For more information visit the CHEAPR Website .

text:
Support CleanTechnica's work through a Substack subscription, on Patreon, or on Stripe. Help us produce all of the high-quality, original content we publish week after week despite the challenges of content-scraping AI, antisocial media, inflation, and other hurdles.

In-road wireless EV charging systems are the kiss of death for gas and diesel fuel. They enable EV drivers to recharge without stopping or exiting their vehicle, saving time and improving personal security, too. That’s a next-level convenience no gas-powered vehicle can top. While much of the activity around in-road charging is still in the R&D stage, the leading global automaker Honda is among the electrification stakeholders ready to take it to the next level.

Wireless EV Charging Is Coming For Your Fossil Fuels

The public EV charging station network has made significant progress in the US over the past several years. The early days were plagued by long stretches of road with few or no charging stations in sight, lack of connectivity, and unplanned down times. Now the gaps are filling and reliability has improved to the point where more EV-curious drivers are confident about switching to an EV.

Still, the next big thing would be a system that enables drivers to charge up seamlessly while in motion. That may seem somewhat futuristic, and it is. However, the technology pieces are in place. Emedded, wireless charging systems offer aesthetic benefits and are potentially more tamper-proof and durable than conventional charging stations.

Stationary wireless systems began to surface in the early 2000’s, and now in-road charging systems have begun to emerge at the demonstration stage. Back in 2023, CleanTechnica recapped the state of affairs at the demonstration phase, with Germany and Sweden in the running alongside the Pennsylvania Turnpike, Detroit, Michigan, and the state of Indiana here in the US.

In 2024 the field advanced another degree when the US-based wireless EV charging startup InductEV hooked up with ENRX of Norway in a Memorandum of Understanding aimed at establishing higher-level global standards for wireless charging.

“The motivation for the MOU appears to be noise from the robotaxi field, which is fixing on a lower-level charge,” CleanTechnica reported. At the time, Tesla’s Robotaxi division was lobbying for a lower-level charge for its Cybercabs. In contrast, InductEV and ENRX are among the wireless stakeholders pushing for a higher-level standard, needed to eliminate range anxiety over longer distances than a typical robotaxi service would cover.

Who Will Win The Wireless Charging Standard Race?

Readers, if you have any updates on the Cybercab wireless charging situation, drop a note in the comment thread. In the meantime, the US Department of Energy has already weighed in on the topic.

“High-power, in-road, dynamic wireless charging could increase the cost effectiveness and utility of EVs by increasing their range while enabling the use of smaller, cheaper batteries and reducing the charging demand at the fleet’s central facility,” the Energy Department observes in an undated web page.

“This could reduce the cost of charging hardware and distribution system upgrades as well as the cost of operations and increase vehicle utilization and return on investment,” the agency emphasizes.

More Dynamic Charging For The US…

High-level or not, Florida has also joined the ranks of wireless-forward stakeholders. In 2024 the state announced plans to integrate a wireless in-road charging system with the construction of a new highway.

The announcement is significant because it marks the first time a new highway has been designed with wireless EV charging. Previous efforts have involved retrofitting stretches of roadway. “Operational rather than experimental, the in-road charging section of the 125 mile long SR 516 will encompass just over 4 miles,” CleanTechnica reported in 2024.

The project is also significant because Florida has become one of the strongest markets for EV adoption in the US, and the new wireless system indicates that state transportation planners are planning on more to come. The new 125-mile highway will link busy Lake and Orange counties, providing EV drivers with a new option for charging up along four miles of the roadway.

…And Now Comes Honda

Evidently we ain’t seen nothing yet, because now Honda has jumped into the wireless EV charging pool. The news is of particular interest considering that Honda is among the leading automakers that still considers hydrogen fuel cell EVs a viable path to zero emission transportation.

The latest news from Honda doesn’t necessarily mean that the automaker has thrown in the fuel cell towel, but it does signify a shift in attention towards battery-powered EVs. On October 5, Honda recapped its wireless charging plans, which the company has been developing under its Honda R&D Co. subsidiary in collaboration with Taisei Corporation and Taisei Rotec Corporation. In a long form press statement, Honda described the foundational technology for a “magnetic coupling wireless power transfer road system,” enabling EVs to recharge while in motion.

“The system combines proprietary technology of each company: a Honda high-power-density power receiver/transmitter units compatible with DC power distribution; a Taisei high-response DC power supply system; and Taisei Rotec technology for embedding equipment in roads,” Honda explained.

“With these technologies, the system achieves high-power wireless power transfer (WPT) and excellent ease of installation in road pavement, envisioning applications for a wide range of mobility products, from passenger EVs to large commercial EVs,” the automaker added for emphasis.

Don’t get too excited just yet. So far the collaboration has reached the validation testing stage, and the three partners have set the period beginning April 1 of 2027 for an initial demonstration of the new system on public roads. With a focus on trucks and other large commercial vehicles, the in-ground system will be designed for durability under heavy loads.

Wait, Where’s Honda?

Honda further emphasizes that the initial focus will be on logistics and transportation, where it anticipates higher highest returns, so don’t expect to find a wireless-equipped electric sedan or SUV at your local Honda dealer any time soon.

For that matter, over the summer Honda announced that its only 100% battery EV in the North America market, the Prologue, will sail into the black hole of automotive history once inventories are exhausted in 2027.

Still, the wireless EV charging venture indicates that Honda has battery EVs in its sights, at least elsewhere around the globe if not here in the US. In May, for example, Honda reaffirmed its long term electrification plans. Among other developments, the automaker announced that its Xcelerator Ventures branch has put up stakes in the UK battery startup Nexeon, which itself is a stragic partner with the Korean firm SKC.

And of course, there’s always the hybrid EV strategy, which US automakers have adopted hand over fist. Last week Honda joined the scramble, announcing plans to introduce 15 hybrid EV models in the North American market within the next three years.

text:
Washington, D.C. – The National Association of Manufacturers, joined by members of its Council of Manufacturing Associations, Conference of State Manufacturers Associations and other leading manufacturing and business organizations, sent a coalition letter urging Congress to swiftly pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. Representing businesses across the country and industries throughout the manufacturing economy, the coalition called on lawmakers to advance the bipartisan permitting deal to reduce costly delays, provide greater certainty for investment and make it easier to build and expand manufacturing operations in America.

The full letter can be read below. The list of 100+ signers can be found here.

—-

Dear Majority Leader Thune and Minority Leader Schumer,

The undersigned organizations, members of the NAM’s Council of Manufacturing Associations and Conference of State Manufacturers Associations and other aligned manufacturing and business organizations, represent businesses, manufacturers, and energy producers that employ millions of Americans in every industrial sector and in every state, as well as U.S. territories and Puerto Rico. We write in strong and unified support for S. 5653, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act and respectfully urge you to bring it to the Senate floor for immediate consideration.

Our organizations applaud the hard work that the bipartisan negotiators have done to find practical solutions to the challenges our industry faces in permitting projects to expand and grow manufacturing. It is a testament to our democracy that leaders from both parties can come together to seek common ground and address the major challenges that are facing our industry in the United States. Reforming our permitting processes will make it easier and more cost-efficient for manufacturers to get shovels in the ground on job-creating projects.

Finalizing and passing S. 5653, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, is an historic opportunity to deliver long-overdue reforms to our nation’s permitting process while maintaining America’s commitment to environmental stewardship. Manufacturers cannot afford inaction.

Our nation’s broken permitting system affects projects in every industry and of every energy source, directly contributing to the rising cost of electricity to homeowners and businesses. Right now, in the United States, it takes 80% longer to get a permit authorized for a manufacturing facility than it does in any other free market economy.

Permitting delays cost manufacturers at least $8 billion every year. That’s money not being spent on hiring new workers, expanding shop floors, or going back into the local economy. Manufacturers are ready to build in America; we just need the certainty and a modernized permitting process to make it happen.

Should the Senate pass this critical legislation, we would call on the House to move expeditiously to consider the bipartisan comprehensive agreement and deliver this manufacturing win to the American people.

Now is the time for action. Manufacturers are ready to build, and modernized permitting will help us race to the future. Thank you for your leadership and dedication to supporting manufacturers in the United States.

text:
Dive Brief:

If all U.S. electric utilities were to achieve a 4% system peak reduction utilizing residential virtual power plants, the resource could help reduce bill increases for average households by more than half over the next five years, according to a report from The Brattle Group.

The 4% target is already being achieved by the top 10% of utility demand response programs, the report noted. If U.S. utilities scaled their programs to that level, “nationwide residential VPP capability would more than triple, from 10 GW to 35 GW,” Brattle said.

Scaling VPP capacity can be done with resources in place today, the report noted. A “substantial pool of flexible capacity already exists” in connected thermostats, electric vehicles and batteries, Brattle said.

Dive Insight:

Brattle’s analysis of residential VPP potential comes at a time of rising bills and economic anxiety across the U.S.

The average U.S. residential electricity rate increased 33% between 2019 and 2025, in nominal terms, Brattle analysts said. Growth has recently outpaced inflation, and the increased cost of power systems equipment is a “major driver,” the report said. “Recent doubling of natural gas-fired generation capacity costs is an acute near-term concern.”

Affordability “has become one of the most pressing challenges facing the industry, at the same time that utilities are confronting sharply higher costs for new infrastructure,” Brattle Principal Ryan Hledik said in a statement. “Our analysis shows that there is a significant amount of untapped flexible capacity already sitting in customers’ homes.”

If utilities achieved 4% peak demand reduction, the report estimates it would more than triple nationwide residential VPP capacity from approximately 10 GW to 35 GW. The additional 25 GW of residential demand flexibility “could generate $4 billion to $7 billion annually in financial benefits for US households,” the firm said. Those benefits include approximately $1.8 billion to $5.5 billion benefiting all ratepayers and another $1.9 billion paid directly to participating customers.

Brattle pointed to “improved enrollment” as a way for utilities to access the “latent DR potential” needed to reach 35 GW of residential VPP capacity. OEM-led enrollment strategies can help utilities expand VPPs, the report noted, by leveraging capabilities built into customers’ existing devices.

“If utilities and technology providers can activate that capacity at scale, VPPs can provide a meaningful source of near-term bill relief while also helping meet emerging system needs,” Hledik said.

Brattle’s analysis follows a March report in which the firm’s showed increased utilization of the existing U.S. electric grid could save consumers more than $100 billion over the next decade.

BAAJA would also speed the federal permitting process by altering the National Environmental Policy Act. Groups like the Sierra Club have criticized aspects of BAAJA, saying it "weakens environmental laws," while the legislation received strong support from other groups like the Citizens' Climate Lobby.

Fossil generation's exposure to global risk

Fossil fuel project cancellations have also declined at the same time that clean energy cancellations have increased, said EDF's report. Fossil fuel project cancellations dropped in 2024 and have remained low through the first half of 2026, the report said. Clean energy project cancellations have increased since 2022, and nearly 5% of a planned 281.7 GW of deployment was canceled in 2025.

One contributing factor is the Trump administration's policy of issuing emergency orders for coal plants to continue operating past previously set retirement dates, and funding new coal plants and retrofits, EDF said.

EDF's report noted that the cost of fossil fuel generation is more exposed to geopolitical risk, citing an Energy Innovation analysis from June which found that a spike in coal and gas prices like the one the U.S. saw in 2022 would "push up electricity costs $40.5 billion per year under a fossil fuel-heavy scenario."

"If utilities and developers respond to power demand primarily with new fossil generation, consumers could face higher costs from turbine supply constraints, rising capital costs, and fuel price volatility," EDF said.

In terms of the impacts of the Iran war and associated ongoing fuel crisis, Villagrana noted that these factors have so far "put more pressure on gasoline and diesel prices than on U.S. natural gas prices, so we anticipate limited immediate impacts on power development decisions."

"But a prolonged crisis highlights the risks of investing in fossil fuel power plants that depend on volatile fuel prices for decades," Villagrana said. "Wind and solar don't require fuel purchases, helping protect consumers from price swings and providing greater long-term cost certainty."

text:
Two new factsheets released by Oil Change International and Friends of the Earth U.S. analyze updated data from OCI’s open-access Public Finance for Energy Database (energyfinance.org), which has been updated with 2025 data alongside the release of this report. It tracks financial flows to fossil fuels and clean energy from G20 bilateral development finance institutions (DFIs) and export credit agencies (ECAs), and the multilateral development banks (MDBs).

Tipping the Scales: G20 & MDB clean energy finance overtakes fossil fuel finance

Download Tipping the Scales: G20 & MDB Energy Finance

This factsheet assesses the trends across G20 ECA, DFIs and MDBs. Overall, it finds that between 2023 and 2025:

Public finance for fossil fuels averaged at least USD 36.3 billion a year, compared to $52.7 billion for clean energy during the same time period. For the first time in our dataset, the three-year average for clean energy exceeds the fossil fuel average. Still, clean energy finance is nowhere near the scale needed to deliver a globally just transition that keeps temperatures below 1.5 degrees Celsius of warming, nor is it flowing to where it is most needed.

49% of all clean energy finance flowed to high-income countries based on World Bank classifications, followed by 28% to upper-middle-income countries. Less than 2% of clean energy finance flowed to low-income countries.

88% of all clean energy finance was provided as loans, while some Global South countries are already facing worst-in-history debt-levels. Less than 1% flowed as grants.

Exporting Climate Chaos: How much are G20 ECAs financing fossil fuels?

Download Exporting Climate Chaos: ECA Factsheet

This factsheet assesses the trends across G20 ECAs. Overall, it finds that between 2023 and 2025:

ECAs provided an annual average of USD 26.2 billion in fossil fuel finance. This is 64% of all their energy finance, and almost three times more than their clean energy support, which averaged just $9.8 billion annually during this same period. ECAs are going against the broader positive trend, which is that of overall G20 and MDB clean energy finance overtaking fossil fuel finance.

ECAs provided 72% of all G20 ECA, development finance institution (DFI), and multilateral development bank (MDB) fossil fuel finance. This makes ECAs the biggest fossil fuel financiers across international public finance institutions.

ECAs provided an annual average of $26 billion for oil and gas – over 99% of ECA support for fossil fuels.

text:
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

Dive Brief:

Changes to the federal policy landscape and rapid load growth projections have led utilities and developers to recalibrate toward deploying traditional dispatchable resources like natural gas, resulting in clean power growth slowing from its 2024 peak, while fossil capacity — if dispatched as projected — “could reach a market share not seen since the early 2010s,” the Environmental Defense Fund said in a report released Tuesday.

However, the deployment of gas-fired generation faces headwinds, including turbine shortages and the potential for natural gas price volatility, which could drive up the Levelized Cost of Energy for gas plants, the report noted.

“Rising gas turbine costs and supply shortages are already making new gas plants more expensive and slower to build, prompting some developers to consider clean power alternatives that can often come online faster and at a lower cost,” David Villagrana, EDF’s lead counsel for clean energy tax solutions, said in an email to Utility Dive.

Dive Insight:

While clean energy “continues to account for the largest share of planned U.S. power sector development,” EDF said planned development has slowed while fossil fuel deployments have caught up. “Based on capacity factors, planned natural gas project capacity is now comparable to that for solar and wind,” the report said.

An Oct. 8 Wood Mackenzie analysis found that investment in gas generation capacity is entering “a supply deficit cycle through the late 2030s, driven by data centre load growth, a dynamic that keeps thermal capital costs elevated and reinforces the long-term economic case for renewables and storage.”

Federal policy changes like coal industry subsidies, repealed greenhouse gas regulations, the rollback of clean energy tax credits and barriers for permitting new clean energy are increasingly incentivizing utilities and developers to pursue fossil fuel generation, the report said.

For that reason, Villagrana said, it’s “difficult to predict how much the market will shift,” even as developers encounter barriers to deploying new gas.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which was introduced in the Senate Sept. 30, would prevent the revocation or suspension of previously issued federal permits for energy projects, and create a right for projects to sue over a pattern of “disparate” federal treatment based on project type.

Villagrana said EDF “is still reviewing the bill and working with modelers, partners and colleagues to understand its impact.”

BAAJA would also speed the federal permitting process by altering the National Environmental Policy Act. Groups like the Sierra Club have criticized aspects of BAAJA, saying it “weakens environmental laws,” while the legislation received strong support from other groups like the Citizens’ Climate Lobby.

Fossil generation’s exposure to global risk

Fossil fuel project cancellations have also declined at the same time that clean energy cancellations have increased, said EDF’s report. Fossil fuel project cancellations dropped in 2024 and have remained low through the first half of 2026, the report said. Clean energy project cancellations have increased since 2022, and nearly 5% of a planned 281.7 GW of deployment was canceled in 2025.

One contributing factor is the Trump administration’s policy of issuing emergency orders for coal plants to continue operating past previously set retirement dates, and funding new coal plants and retrofits, EDF said.

EDF’s report noted that the cost of fossil fuel generation is more exposed to geopolitical risk, citing an Energy Innovation analysis from June which found that a spike in coal and gas prices like the one the U.S. saw in 2022 would “push up electricity costs $40.5 billion per year under a fossil fuel-heavy scenario.”

“If utilities and developers respond to power demand primarily with new fossil generation, consumers could face higher costs from turbine supply constraints, rising capital costs, and fuel price volatility,” EDF said.

In terms of the impacts of the Iran war and associated ongoing fuel crisis, Villagrana noted that these factors have so far “put more pressure on gasoline and diesel prices than on U.S. natural gas prices, so we anticipate limited immediate impacts on power development decisions.”

title: Michigan communities invest millions in their rivers. Will it bring returns?
description:
Grand Rapids is working to restore rapids to the Grand River downtown.
The state announced earlier this month it’s investing $89 million to clean up the Detroit, Kalamazoo and other rivers.
Even when the economic impact is not calculated, administrators say river restoration projects can be a worthwhile investment.

Stivers said some people see the White River as a secret and they want to keep it that way.
text:
On a recent sunny fall morning, a couple dozen people paddled in bright-colored kayaks past factories, a docked freighter and miniature mountains of industrial materials on southeast Michigan’s Lower Rouge River.

“This is really exciting to have this many people out here kayaking the Rouge because, when I was a kid, the Rouge was so dirty they told you, ‘Don’t touch it,’” said Sally Petrella, watershed ecologist with Friends of the Rouge, which organized the paddling event.

The river was once so polluted it famously caught on fire. Petrella told attendees it has “a long way to go,” but restoration efforts have made it “safe enough for you to be out here paddling.”

Communities across the state are pumping hundreds of millions of dollars into rivers like the Rouge, hoping for both environmental and economic returns.

Battle Creek has pitched a project to renaturalize part of the Kalamazoo River that runs over concrete. Grand Rapids is working to restore rapids to the Grand River downtown. A state park is being built around Flint’s riverfront. The state announced earlier this month it’s investing $89 million to clean up the Detroit, Kalamazoo and other rivers.

Backers envision more riverside development bringing tourists to kayak, fish and otherwise enjoy cleaner waterways that are more hospitable to native plants and animals.

Economic impact studies aren’t always completed for such projects, but many point to a 2007 Brookings Institution study that predicted a $3 return for every $1 invested in waterway restoration. A study on the Huron River in 2017 found the river produced $53.5 million in economic activity annually, while a 2023 White River study pegged its economic impact at $20 million.

“We’ve actually done studies in Muskegon that have showed a 6-to-1 return on investment,” said Alan Steinman, a professor at Grand Valley State University’s Annis Water Resources Institute and a co-author of the Michigan Blue Economy report. “The number is less important than the concept that, ’Oh my God, these properties really do have inherent value, cultural value and economic value that had none associated with (them) prior to the restoration effort.”

Kris Martin, an urban planner with Battle Creek Unlimited, the firm helping to look into whether part of the Kalamazoo river should be renaturalized, said removing the aging concrete channel would make the river “a greater amenity to the downtown.”

“Right now, it’s not accessible for the public at all,” he said. “And it’s quite dangerous.”

Martin said costs for the project will depend on the path forward but are expected to be “in the millions.” An economic cost-benefit analysis is expected to be a component in the next report released by the US Army Corps of Engineers.

For the Flint state park project, an economic analysis is not currently planned, because it would cost money, but project spending includes $30.2 million plus a $41 million endowment for future operations and maintenance.

As for Grand Rapids, the project is estimated to cost at least $19 million. Economic impact for the project as it stands today has not been publicized.

Even when the economic impact is not calculated, administrators say river restoration projects can be a worthwhile investment.

Starting in the mid-2000s, the Traverse City area began what has been deemed the largest dam removal project in Michigan’s history. Three dams along the Boardman River were taken out to reconnect coldwater streams and restore fish habitat. The project cost more than $27 million.

Conservation Resource Alliance — which served as the project manager and financial administrator for the effort — said it doesn’t actually know what the economic benefits have been.

“It’s something that’s really hard to quantify and would take a lot of time and investment from the partner collective that removed those dams to do so,” said Gavin MacDonald, communications manager for Conservation Resource Alliance.

But MacDonald said that, anecdotally, the payoff is that the dam removals restored a more free-flowing river that benefits fish and people.

“The river is now navigable, so you can paddle large stretches of the Boardman River,” MacDonald said. “It’s made it more accessible for the people that live in the region and the people that visit to explore and be more connected with nature.”

Sometimes the payoff is known.

For decades, prime downtown waterfront property in Detroit included vacant buildings and abandoned lots. The area has now been transformed to a nationally recognized waterfront that includes greenways and parks, more than eight miles of trails, places to get a drink and go sledding. About $2 billion in public and private dollars have been invested into the project so far and the Detroit Riverfront Conservancy says visitors spend $82 million a year.

The Huron River’s water trail was designated a part of the National Water Trail System in 2015. Elizabeth Riggs, deputy director at the Huron River Watershed Council at the time, had a hunch that the water trail and other restoration work benefitted the river, but she wanted proof.

“I and others working on the campaign were keen on trying to tell that story of (the river) in dollar terms — which is, as we know, a good way to tell a story — to try to reach as many people as possible, and to help convince decision-makers to invest in rivers and protecting them and restoring them,” she said.

The watershed council commissioned a study, published in 2017 by Grand Valley State University, to evaluate the economic impact of the Huron River. Researchers found that the river and its water trail were estimated to generate $53.5 million in economic output annually and that the river provided $150 million a year in economic value services through recreation, flood reduction, harboring rare organisms and more.

In 2023, Grand Valley State University also published an economic assessment of the White River. The river is located in west Michigan and runs through the Huron-Manistee National Forests. It’s fed by coldwater streams and can support salmon and trout.

The study found that nearly 70,000 visitors came to the White River in a year and that the river’s total economic impact was valued at $20 million.

“It’s a good number to know,” said John Stivers, secretary of the White River Watershed Partnership.

But he said that, when it comes to the White River, it’s a little complicated.

The river was designated as a Country-Scenic River by the Michigan Natural Resources Commission in 1975. Development on certain stretches need to go through a Natural Rivers Zoning Review Board, he said, and the river is further protected because it runs through national forest land.

Stivers said some people see the White River as a secret and they want to keep it that way.

“There are a lot of people that love it the way it is and aren’t really too interested in turning it into a high economic engine,” he said. “It’s a balance.”

text:
Roberto Baldwin

Within each EV is a battery pack.

Within those packs are modules. Within those modules are cells. These individual pieces are the heart of any battery pack. When an automaker talks about its chemistry, it's talking about cells. Whether pouch-shaped or prismatic (which resemble large AA batteries), this is where EVs get their energy.

Coesia, a company based in Bologna, Italy, wants that energy to be ready to go at all times. Coesia, the parent company of over 20 companies with locations around the globe, is in the business of building machines and facilitating automation. The core idea is to deliver a complete solution to customers.

For battery cell manufacturing, that solution allows battery makers to produce cells in short order. As demand for battery packs grows from EVs, ESS (energy storage systems), and other devices, one of Coesia's subsidiaries, GD, offers increased production speed that conforms to the extremely tight tolerances needed for today’s battery production.

GD is able to do this by working on winder and stacker technology that takes up one-quarter the space of those already available. When Coesia started, it created machines that were as quick as the larger units on the market. That meant that a battery manufacturer could now have four of these machines instead of one, increasing cell production by a factor of four with the same facility footprint.

It's not just faster; Coesia had to make sure the quality met the standards of its customers, realizing there's no point in going fast if the output is subpar. The company has a decades-long history of machine automation in other markets.

Coesia entered the market by looking at the production of batteries and decided to target the bottleneck of cell assembly. Currently there are six Coesia companies working on the lithium-ion manufacturing value chain.

Currently, Coesia offers stacking, winding, and cell assembly products. It's also working on processes for both the upstream and downstream of battery manufacturing. The value to customers would be to create an ecosystem that works within the Coesia system. Having full control of the dataset will give Coesia and its customers insights into a production line. That increased level of data shared by a Coesia ecosystem, with help from AI, could help optimize the line to increase yield and quality. Something that's far more difficult when integrating machines and data from multiple vendors.

Overview

Last updated: October 14, 2026

Donald Trump promised to cut Americans’ energy bills in half within a year of taking office. He has done the opposite at every turn. Since his first day back in office, Trump has used the full power of the federal government to rig our energy system for Big Oil, coal barons, and his wealthy donors. He has killed cheap, clean energy projects, forced aging coal plants slated to retire to stay open on customers’ dime, rolled back standards that save drivers money at the pump, and canceled or clawed back billions meant to lower household bills. None of this is an accident. Every one of these choices shows up on a family’s utility bill or at the pump.

Evergreen Action is keeping the receipts. Our Trump’s Energy Price Hike series documents each action his administration takes that drives up what Americans are paying for energy, including what Trump did, who gets stuck with the bill, and who stands to benefit from Trump’s policy moves. This page collects every entry from our series in one place, starting with the most recent actions and going back to the first day of Trump’s second term. Read them together, and the pattern is impossible to miss. Trump’s plan was always intended to govern for his fossil fuel allies, not for working families. The agenda he sold to the American people, one built on a promise to cut energy costs in half, was a lie from the start.

title: Building an energy system that delivers for all - GOV.UK
authors: Department for Energy Security and Net Zero
description:
And look I often say, if you have a blank piece of paper, and you can design the energy system, would you design the system we have now?
The privatisation of the energy system changed more than the ownership of individual assets.
We have inherited an energy system that is too exposed to volatile global markets.
But of course, of course, the number one test for reforming our energy system must be whether it benefits people.
But this cannot be a substitute for the big changes we need to deliver in the energy system to drive down energy costs for good.
text:
Good afternoon.

It is a pleasure to be here and I would like to say a huge thank you to Energy UK for bringing us all together.

You have heard today about the choices facing our energy system.

And I want to spend our time together talking about what it will take to build its future and the partnership between government and industry that will make this possible.

That starts with recognising what the people in this room do. You keep the country powered. You invest in our infrastructure, develop our people and build the projects on which our future depends.

You know what it takes to turn ambition into investment and investment into something people can see around them.

And you continued to do that through years of economic and political uncertainty.

So I just wanted to start by saying thank you to each and every one of you for everything you have done to get us to this point – and for the work I hope we will do together in the months and years ahead.

And that work begins with our ambition as a government to deliver a 10-year plan for national renewal.

One that unlocks growth in every single postcode.

Reindustrialises parts of the country that have been held back.

And ensures that people have the basics to live well.

In a Britain that is confident, that is forward-looking and that is hopeful.

And energy has an absolutely vital role to play in that.

An everyday essential that we all rely on.

But one that is increasingly unaffordable for too many families and too many businesses.

In a system that is simply not working for them as consumers.

Now look I know that this is not a reality that any of us can be happy with – and it is one we are absolutely determined to turn around as a government.

And we have taken the next steps for the drive for homegrown clean power.

We all know that one of the reasons we are seeing rising prices is because we are uniquely exposed to volatile global fossil fuel markets.

Which means that conflicts miles away in Ukraine and now the Middle East reverberate deeply in people’s pockets.

That’s why our ambition to deliver homegrown clean power is so important and is why we set it out when we came into government.

Now I know there are a few raised eyebrows, but look the point wasn’t just about the target itself, but the confidence and momentum it would create in the system.

And what we have delivered in partnership in just 2 years in pursuit of this mission has been incredibly impressive.

£100 billion of private investment in clean power unlocked.

Enough clean power consented to power over 20 million homes.

189 terawatt hours of clean power delivered last year.

And over the course of 2025, almost two-thirds of Britain’s electricity generation came from clean power.

Huge progress – and we will continue to play our part to sustain this momentum.

But we know the public doesn’t measure the success of our energy system in gigawatts.

They measure it in bills and whether they can live comfortably.

And by these measures, the framework within which you are being asked to deliver is not working.

That is not a criticism of the businesses that have invested, built and innovated within it.

It is a recognition that even the best companies cannot compensate for a system that lacks sufficient coordination and long-term direction.

That is failing in its purpose of providing this essential good to the British people at a reasonable cost.

So let’s be clear with how we got here.

And look I often say, if you have a blank piece of paper, and you can design the energy system, would you design the system we have now? Probably not.

So I think it is important we are honest about where Britain went wrong.

The privatisation of the energy system changed more than the ownership of individual assets.

Generation, transmission, distribution and retail were separated into different parts of the system.

And those reforms changed the state’s relationship with the energy system.

Government moved away from direct ownership and coordination.

Responsibility was carved up, and farmed out across companies, regulators, network operators and public bodies.

And when responsibility fragments, accountability weakens.

Successive governments recognised that markets alone could not make every decision the country required.

So, they introduced targets, created new regulation, new frameworks.

And the cumulative effect of all these interventions was that central government and regulators ended up micromanaging the system, often with imperfect information.

The result was neither free market, nor public direction. It was a system in which industry was often asked to deliver without the infrastructure, certainty or joined-up decision-making it needed.

And crucially, the state never really left the energy system.

Because it can’t.

The idea that the state could be absent from providing a service as critical as energy was fundamentally flawed from the outset.

The state cannot – it cannot - relinquish responsibility for keeping the lights on.

For protecting consumers.

For maintaining national security.

Or for preparing the system for the future.

So government returned through regulation, subsidy, contracts, targets and interventions.

But it never resolved the fundamental question of how to make our energy system work for the families and businesses it is there to serve.

And we are now living with the consequences of that.

We have inherited an energy system that is too exposed to volatile global markets.

We have projects ready to invest and businesses ready to expand, but can’t secure timely connections.

We have renewable power available in a system that still pays generators to turn down their output because the network cannot always use or move that power efficiently.

And we have families who want lower bills, but who are locked out from accessing cheaper electricity because they cannot upgrade their homes.

When energy suppliers failed during the last energy crisis, 4 million households were affected and customers were left carrying £2.7 billion in costs.

And look, these are not isolated problems.

They show what happens when the system as a whole lacks sufficient coherence and accountability.

A system can have ambitious targets.

It can have willing investors.

It can have viable projects.

But if the networks cannot connect them, those ambitions remain on paper.

If people do not see and feel the benefits of them, the system loses the confidence of the public.

So the answer cannot simply be another layer of targets.

That is why piecemeal reform is no longer enough.

Stronger consumer protection matters. Of course it does.

A more powerful and effective Ofgem matters. Of course it does. And we’re driving forwards with those reforms.

But our ambition must be greater than making another adjustment to the model that we have.

Our task is to make the whole system work coherently in the interest of the consumers that we serve.

Now that requires us to be clear about the choices that are in front of us.

There are some choices that will make sense for the state to step in.

There are some choices where competition, private investment and innovation have a vital role to play.

And there are those that should sit closer to communities, giving people the freedom and opportunity to shape the energy future of their places.

But the choice is not a binary between state or market.

That is a false choice.

Many countries around the world, with far lower electricity prices than ours, combine public ownership with vibrant markets.

So the real question is: who is best placed to do what?

Where should government set the strategic direction and establish firm rules?

Where should businesses have the operational freedom to compete, to innovate and deliver?

And where should communities have the power to lead, participate and benefit?

The purpose of reform should be to accelerate delivery, not to pause it.

To give investors greater certainty, not less.

And to replace accumulated uncertainty with clear responsibilities, freedom and accountability for the system to deliver.

And this is precisely the purpose of Great British Energy.

Giving the state the ability to do more than regulate industry and its decisions again.

Instead, creating the capability to invest directly.

Develop projects, build partnerships and take a longer view.

Entering parts of the market where the strategic value is high, even when the immediate commercial incentives aren’t obvious.

Ensuring that more of the value created by Britain’s natural resources is retained for the benefit of the British people.

Ensuring the public have a direct stake in the energy assets that will shape our economic future.

And we can already see what practical public investment means.

Take the Sizewell C nuclear power station for example. My department is the primary public shareholder, alongside private consortium partners.

Taxpayers will see up to £18 billion in net consumer benefits and we’ll reduce overall electricity system costs by roughly £2 billion per year compared to other routes to net zero.

Lower costs.

Good jobs, buoyant supply chains, greater security.

Great British Energy working alongside private investors.

Building capability in technologies and supply chains where Britain has a strategic interest.

And helping shape markets rather than merely responding to them.

The same principle underpins Great British Grid that the Prime Minister announced at conference.

We cannot, we cannot deliver cheaper power if viable projects remain stuck in a queue.

We cannot electrify industry if businesses cannot get the connections they need.

And we cannot build a more secure energy system if generation, networks and demand are planned as separate challenges.

Great British Grid is about acknowledging what industry has been telling us - projects cannot be delivered at the required scale unless network planning, connections and investment are treated as a strategic national priority.

Great British Grid will provide additional public investment and dedicated leadership, working alongside existing network operators and private investors.

It will enable the vital grid upgrades needed after decades of underinvestment, helping to reduce constraint costs and meet rising electricity demand.

This is the shift that we want to see from fragmentation to coordination.

But of course, of course, the number one test for reforming our energy system must be whether it benefits people. And that is the ultimate test we will apply in everything we do as a department.

Whether families and businesses can afford the energy they use.

Now there are short-term reliefs that we must provide to give people some breathing room. And we know that and we understand that particularly in the current context.

That’s why one of the first thing’s the Prime Minister did when he came into office was to cut VAT on energy bills, building on the £150 off the costs of energy bills that we did in the Budget last year.

And the expansion of the £150 Warm Home Discount to over 6 million families.

So we know we need to do our part to give people breathing room.

But this cannot be a substitute for the big changes we need to deliver in the energy system to drive down energy costs for good. And we are very clear as a government this is our responsibility and this is the moment we must grip this.

Now I have given you a top-down view as you will expect.

But I am really clear these reforms cannot simply be mandated from Whitehall.

They will be delivered hand in hand with the people, places and communities that must see the benefits.

When communities host the infrastructure that powers Britain’s future, they should share fairly in the rewards.

Places shouldn’t host the transition. They should have a stake in it.

So we will back local energy, support greater community participation and put a fairer relationship between clean-energy infrastructure and the communities hosting it.

Through Great British Energy, which will support over 1,000 community and local energy projects by 2030.

We will pave the way for communities to own more of the renewable energy projects built in their area and share more directly in the benefits of the clean power transition.

And vitally we will put our communities at the centre of delivering the Warm Homes Plan.

Devolving funding so regional and local government can play a critical role in co-ordinating and accelerating the pace of home and building upgrades that we absolutely need to see over the course of the next decade.

So that we can insulate, solar, clean heat and smart technology street by street, state by state, community by community.

So that people can directly benefit from the drive towards electrification.

There’s a lot of work that I know we need to do together.

There will be those who say you should slow down.

That the answer is to build less.

To reform less.

To relinquish control.

To blindly place our faith in the established way of doing things.

But I believe that we must seize the opportunity of this moment as we must make this transition.

And to do that, we’ve got to be ambitious.

And we can only do that with clear strategic direction from government.

With certainty, opportunity and autonomy for industry in the right parts of the system.

And a stronger voice for communities.

The need for the energy transition is real and urgent. And for those that question that, I simply say look at the summer we’ve just had. Record heatwaves, droughts, wildfires. They are an indication that climate change is there and we have got to do our part to respond to it.

And in this transition which is accelerating every day in the UK and all around the world.

The UK’s net zero economy now generates around £105 billion in Gross Value Added and supports 1.1 million full-time equivalent jobs, spanning energy, manufacturing, construction, engineering and professional services.

Oil and gas will of course remain part of our energy mix for decades to come.

And we will bring these vital communities with us as we move towards mass electrification and renewable power.

Because the UK must be a leader for making the transition work for all people.

And all of you here today are world leaders.

You are the backbone of the energy system that we must build and of the future economy that we must build.

So what we do and what that looks like, we must do in partnership. And that brings some questions, what do we want the end goal to look like?

More control over the sources of our power, the level of our bills, the infrastructure that forms the bones of our economy?

Or less?

Do we want more certainty for businesses to invest? Or do we want less?

Or remaining overexposed every time a crisis overseas shakes fossil fuel markets, is that the reality that we want? Or less?

These are the big questions that we’ll be asking all of you and of ourselves.

But for me we are really clear there’s an absolute imperative for government to grip this.

There is an absolute imperative for the state to provide direction.

To build public capability.

To invest where the national interest demands it.

And to create the conditions in which we collectively make to ensure businesses can invest, can build the infrastructure that we need, and can get us to an energy system that does the very simple job of ensuring this essential good – not a luxury – a basic that everyone needs, is provided to people at a cost that is affordable.

And look, the commitment that you have from me is, from my department and from all of government is to do everything that we can to work in partnership to get there. We will play our part because the stakes are far too high.

But I hope you are all willing to go on this journey with us.

And to work in partnership to deliver the energy future that I believe we can.

Thank you.

title: EU's methane rules face one-year delay, sparking environmental backlash | Euronews
description:
The European Commission proposed on Wednesday a one-year delay for importers to show compliance with EU methane rules, giving companies until May 2029 to prove that their supplies meet equivalent EU standards.
Under the Commission proposal, importers of oil, gas and coal from outside the EU have more time to comply with the bloc’s methane rules.
The EU methane law requires fossil fuel importers to provide information on emissions associated with production.
Jack Corscadden, senior Campaigner at Environmental Investigation Agency, said there was no demonstrable link between the implementation of the EU methane rules and the current energy supply challenges.
Esther Bollendorff, fossil free program manager at the NGO Climate Action Network Europe, said that delaying the EU methane rules made no economic or strategic sense.
text:
The European Commission proposed on Wednesday a one-year delay for importers to show compliance with EU methane rules, giving companies until May 2029 to prove that their supplies meet equivalent EU standards.

The proposal follows pressure from industry and governments concerned about compliance costs and energy security, but falls short of calls from some EU countries for a three-year delay.

Environmental groups condemned the move, arguing that the methane rules pose no threat to Europe's energy security and that the current supply crisis stems instead from the US-Israeli war against Iran, which has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

Under the Commission proposal, importers of oil, gas and coal from outside the EU have more time to comply with the bloc’s methane rules. Originally, importers were expected to demonstrate by January 2027 that their suppliers had systems in place to monitor and report methane emissions equivalent to those required under EU law.

Under the proposed changes, the requirement would start applying in 2028, with the first report and proof of compliance due by 31 May 2029, covering supplies from the previous year.

EU governments and industry have pushed for a delay amid turmoil in energy markets, while climate campaigners accuse Brussels of weakening a recently adopted law without tackling the underlying causes of the crisis.

EU countries adopted methane rules in May 2024, introducing requirements to measure, report and verify emissions from the energy sector as part of efforts to curb one of the most potent greenhouse gases.

But the latest energy crisis, which has driven up prices and threatened diesel and gas supplies, has fuelled concerns that the rules could aggravate shortages.

French President Emmanuel Macron recently joined industry calls to delay the requirements, which were due to take effect in early 2027.

"It is also important not to weaken European production capacities while preparing for long-term supply difficulties," Macron said in a letter to the Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

The United States, the EU's largest supplier of liquefied natural gas (LNG), has also repeatedly complained about the impact of the rules on American energy companies.

Suspending penalties

The Commission had already offered significant flexibility, including a three-year suspension of certain penalties, in a concession to industry. But it had stopped short of formally postponing the compliance deadline.

The EU methane law requires fossil fuel importers to provide information on emissions associated with production.

In practice, importers may need to collect reliable data from producers operating thousands of kilometres away, at the other end of a complex supply chain.

Importers argue that they still face legal uncertainty despite the proposed suspension of penalties, and have called for more time and clearer obligations.

Environmental groups, however, warn that even a limited delay could pave the way for further concessions, while doing little to improve Europe's energy security.

They also argue that reopening the legislation risks penalising companies and producing countries that have already invested in monitoring and reporting systems, while undermining confidence in EU rules.

Jack Corscadden, senior Campaigner at Environmental Investigation Agency, said there was no demonstrable link between the implementation of the EU methane rules and the current energy supply challenges.

“After a summer of record-breaking heatwaves and wildfires, the Commission is failing European citizens by delaying this vital piece of climate legislation to appease fossil fuel producers and exporters," Corscadden said.

Esther Bollendorff, fossil free program manager at the NGO Climate Action Network Europe, said that delaying the EU methane rules made no economic or strategic sense.

"At a time of yet another energy price crisis and tensions on the gas market, methane mitigation could unlock over 40 billion cubic meters of gas from the EU’s main fossil fuel suppliers - more than half the volume of US LNG imported by the EU in 2025," Bollendorff said.
