title: El Paso and New Mexico set ambitious climate goals. Their plans didn't account for massive ...
description:
A few months later, just across the state line in Texas, El Paso city officials adopted their own such plan with a similar ambition.
Twenty miles away in El Paso, construction is underway on another massive data center, this one built by Meta Platforms.
New Mexico state Rep. Sarah Silva, a Democrat, represents the community of Chaparral, directly across the state line from Meta’s data center site in Northeast El Paso.
Comparatively, the region spanning El Paso County and neighboring Hudspeth County released 8.4 million tons of greenhouse gases in 2019.
The Meta power plant in El Paso could release up to 1.3 million tons of climate emissions every year, according to an estimate calculated by El Paso Matters based on El Paso Electric regulatory filings and the Environmental Protection Agency’s emissions factors.
text:
This article is co-published with ProPublica and The Texas Tribune as part of an initiative to report on local control of government.

Last December, New Mexico officials celebrated publication of a plan to address climate change, designed to dramatically reduce the state’s greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. A few months later, just across the state line in Texas, El Paso city officials adopted their own such plan with a similar ambition.

Each report cost millions of dollars to draft, but neither one took into account how the construction of data centers could upend climate goals in both places.

Work is underway in Doña Ana County in southern New Mexico on one of the largest data center developments in the country: Project Jupiter, built by Austin-based Oracle. Twenty miles away in El Paso, construction is underway on another massive data center, this one built by Meta Platforms.

A third, larger data center project is planned less than a 30-minute drive from the Meta site, on the Fort Bliss Army post in East El Paso.

The data centers are “going to undo a lot of the very expensive and very meaningful work a lot of people are doing,” New Mexico state climatologist Dave DuBois told El Paso Matters.

The sites are among a wave of data centers under construction across the country, driven by the rapidly escalating demand for artificial intelligence services like Claude and ChatGPT. Such projects have drawn intense scrutiny in recent months, as residents and elected officials have questioned their impact on communities’ water supplies, household electric bills and air quality. Texas alone has 596 data centers that are either in operation or planned across Texas as of early September, according to research by The Texas Tribune.

But the projects located in this population center of 1.2 million, which encompasses El Paso and parts of southern New Mexico, are particularly notable because of their combined scope. When fully built out, the three data centers, each with its own power plant, will release millions of tons of greenhouse gas emissions, equivalent to the planet-warming emissions released by more than 2 million cars in a year.

They will also release air pollutants like particulate matter and nitrogen oxides, which directly affect local air quality and human health. The Meta and Project Jupiter data centers are expected to release these kinds of pollutants at relatively low levels, according to paperwork submitted to state regulators.

But even a small increase in air pollution can still negatively impact communities close to and downwind of the data center sites, said Shaolei Ren, a professor of electrical and computer engineering at the University of California, Riverside.

“The health impacts can be significant for local communities,” Ren said.

Because Project Jupiter, Meta and the Fort Bliss data centers are in two different states, and because there is no single federal regulation governing climate change or emissions, regulators have largely considered the projects’ impacts separately.

“We’ve never had a national climate law passed by Congress,” said Ari Peskoe, director of the Electricity Law Initiative at Harvard Law School. “And so what we’ve had in this country are primarily state and local efforts.”

The result is that officials in one state have little say over a project happening minutes away from them.

Texas and New Mexico also take different approaches to dealing with climate change. New Mexico has codified greenhouse gas reduction targets into state law; Texas has not.

New Mexico state Rep. Sarah Silva, a Democrat, represents the community of Chaparral, directly across the state line from Meta’s data center site in Northeast El Paso. Her state has the power to regulate air quality and impose noise requirements, but only in New Mexico, not at a Texas construction site, even if it’s only a few hundred yards away.

Likewise, residents living in West El Paso across the state line from Project Jupiter have no say in the project despite sharing an aquifer that crosses the state boundary. Emissions do not remain within the state where they originate, Silva said.

“This is why we need federal regulation,” she said. “How do we knit something together that makes sense for our region when actually this is the job of the federal government?”

Though they profess a desire to mitigate the impacts of climate change, local governments in El Paso and Doña Ana counties green-lit these projects in a part of the country seeing rapidly rising temperatures. The counties offered Meta and Project Jupiter tax incentives in exchange for corporate investment in their communities, job creation and, hopefully, the ability to attract more technology companies to the region.

State officials have also provided incentives. More than a decade ago, Texas legislators approved a data center sales tax break, which exempts the facilities from paying sales tax on equipment they purchase, a decision that could now cost the state $3.2 billion in revenue over the next two years, according to The Texas Tribune.

New Mexico lawmakers declined to advance a bill creating a similar tax break for data centers in 2021. But in 2025, they passed an unrelated law allowing large facilities such as Project Jupiter to generate their own electricity using natural gas. The law exempts these private power systems, known as microgrids, from renewable energy requirements, even as New Mexico requires electric utilities to source 50% of the power they sell from clean energy by 2030.

The power plants that keep data centers running typically produce large amounts of emissions like carbon dioxide and methane that drive global climate change over time. Combined, the plants proposed for Project Jupiter and Meta’s data center could emit up to 10 million tons of planet-warming emissions annually.

Comparatively, the region spanning El Paso County and neighboring Hudspeth County released 8.4 million tons of greenhouse gases in 2019. (The Army has shared scant information about the Fort Bliss data center, so it’s not clear what level of emissions the facility will produce.)

“This does add to our greenhouse gas emissions in a massive way,” said Gunnar Schade, an associate professor of atmospheric sciences at Texas A&M University. “This is a huge source.”

An unprecedented amount of energy

Silva, the New Mexico representative, was initially supportive of Project Jupiter, in part seeing it as an opportunity to create long-term jobs. Last year, she voted in favor of a bill that included an amendment — tacked on by state Sen. Michael Padilla, a Democrat from Albuquerque — that allows facilities like Project Jupiter, which aren’t connected to the local power grid, a 20-year exemption from clean energy laws, allowing them to generate all their electricity with fossil fuels.

“We worked this bill pretty much the entire session, but it did not quite get done. So, we found a piece of legislation that was very similar,” Padilla said in an interview last year. “That’s the legislative process. You have to be very creative to get your work done.”

But Silva soon soured on the project out of concern that it won’t employ enough local workers and because it won’t rely on zero-emission renewable energy. Oracle has said the data center will have 750 full-time employees when it’s up and running. The company told Doña Ana County officials in early September that nearly 3,700 people had worked at the site during construction up to that point.

Silva and other state lawmakers have said they voted for Padilla’s bill without realizing the broader implications for a data center project in the southern part of the state.

“State regulators, state legislators, I think, were so caught off guard at the speed at which these hyperscale data centers showed up in all of our communities almost simultaneously,” Silva said. “I would support a moratorium.”

The amount of energy Project Jupiter needs is unprecedented in the region: The data center will receive electricity from an on-site power plant made up of fuel cells built by a company called Bloom Energy. Bloom has said the plant will have the ability to produce up to 2.45 gigawatts of electricity — enough to power around 1.5 million homes and more than El Paso Electric has ever supplied to its 465,000 residential and commercial customers in far West Texas and southern New Mexico at one time, according to the utility’s corporate reports.

New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham, a Democrat, has specifically lauded Oracle’s promise to use fuel cells for electricity instead of natural gas turbines, which would have used more water and produced more air pollution.

However, an air permit — a state-granted license that authorizes industrial facilities to emit a predetermined amount of pollution — would allow the fuel cells to produce up to 8.8 million tons of greenhouse gas emissions per year. Lujan Grisham didn’t address questions from El Paso Matters about the impact of these additional climate emissions.

The Meta power plant in El Paso could release up to 1.3 million tons of climate emissions every year, according to an estimate calculated by El Paso Matters based on El Paso Electric regulatory filings and the Environmental Protection Agency’s emissions factors. Nancy Seidman, a senior adviser with the Regulatory Assistance Project, a nonprofit that advocates for clean energy, backed up that assessment.

“Regulators should weigh all emissions and other impacts like water usage, noise and local air pollution, which can affect public health, when they make decisions about data center projects,” Seidman wrote in an email to El Paso Matters. “This is particularly important when projects are phased over time, so that an accurate account can be made of the total, holistic impacts.”

The data center planned for Fort Bliss is expected to use 3 gigawatts of electricity that would likely be supplied by natural gas turbines, according to officials with the Department of Defense, who shared details with reporters during a briefing in April. The Army has issued few other details about the project because it is still in “exclusive negotiations” with the developer, Carlyle Group, a large publicly traded private equity firm.

Carlyle Group did not respond to a request for comment.

“These are cities in terms of their electricity consumption,” Peskoe, of Harvard Law School, said of AI hyperscale data center campuses such as Oracle’s and Meta’s. The facilities are cropping up so fast that “the pace of this and the scale of this — I think there’s no real parallel, at least for 50, 60, 70 years, but probably ever for the U.S. power industry.”

Facilities in New Mexico seeking a state air permit are required by law to disclose estimated amounts of air pollutants and greenhouse gas emissions the project will release. And the state Environment Department has spent months evaluating Project Jupiter’s air permit application, which was submitted in April. A spokesperson for the environmental department didn’t respond to emailed questions.

By contrast, the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality only requires project developers to disclose information about pollutants that affect local air quality, and not about greenhouse gas emissions, which are what contribute to climate change.

So when El Paso Electric sought an air permit last fall for the Meta data center’s natural gas power plant, the utility didn’t have to share estimated greenhouse gas emissions. The Texas commission approved the permit 20 days after it was filed, following an expedited review.

Meta directed questions about its data center’s power plant to El Paso Electric. The electric company declined to share estimates of the plant’s greenhouse gas emissions but said in a statement that the Texas environmental commission had reviewed and authorized the Meta power plant “under a standard permit, which is specifically for projects with limited and well-controlled emissions.” The statement said the facility will “operate in compliance with state and federal standards.”

A spokesperson for the agency said, “All standard permits have gone through formal notice and comment procedures and have been adopted by the commission in a public meeting.”

These plants will be releasing large amounts of greenhouse gases even as climate change has become increasingly evident in the El Paso metro area, which sits where Texas’ westernmost boundary meets New Mexico and northern Mexico. El Paso’s temperatures have risen faster than those of almost any other city in the United States since 1970, according to Climate Central, a nonprofit that quantifies climate shifts throughout the United States. Drought driven by climate change has amplified the impact of wind storms that fill the air in El Paso with hazardous dust in the spring and summertime.

This year has been the hottest on record in El Paso through the first nine months of 2026, according to the National Weather Service. Similar records have been set across the state line in New Mexico.

“If we started to do these kinds of things — having big data centers with natural-gas-fired turbines — it’s kind of like bringing back a lot of the retired plants that were more dirty, like coal,” said DuBois, the New Mexico state climatologist.

Fernando Berjano, the city of El Paso’s climate coordinator, wouldn’t comment specifically on effects resulting from the data centers in the region, but he said the kinds of power plants tied to them produce greenhouse gases that will make it harder for the city to meet its climate goals, as well as produce air pollutants.

If emissions increase in the El Paso area, “that has an impact on air quality, that has an impact on pollution,” Berjano said, “which is something that we all know is not good.”

The road ahead for data centers

Although construction is underway on the Project Jupiter and Meta data centers, regulatory hurdles remain for both facilities. The public hearing on the Project Jupiter air permit was scheduled to begin Sept. 14, but the New Mexico Supreme Court delayed it when opponents filed lawsuits challenging the state’s approval process and the facility’s use of groundwater.

The state Supreme Court last month lifted the stay. New Mexico more recently appointed an examiner to preside over the hearing that would authorize the facility’s emissions. Other legal challenges are making their way through the court system.

In Texas, El Paso Electric is still waiting for the state’s Public Utility Commission to approve construction of the power plant planned next to Meta’s data center, a decision that could come later this year.

Officials with both Project Jupiter and Meta have said they are taking steps to help mitigate the climate effects of their projects and plan to develop clean energy projects elsewhere to create new electricity sources and offset the greenhouse gases their data center power plants will release. Oracle also maintains that its emissions will be lower than what it sought in its air permit application and that it plans to get to net zero greenhouse emissions by 2031.

“Oracle is committed to building Project Jupiter responsibly and incorporating community feedback into our planning,” the company said in a statement.

The road ahead for data centers is unclear. Even once-supportive officials have softened or changed course: Last year, Lujan Grisham, New Mexico’s governor, said Project Jupiter “reaffirms New Mexico’s leadership in global trade, advanced manufacturing, and digital infrastructure.” In Texas, Gov. Greg Abbott at one point called his state “the epicenter of AI development.”

Now, amid growing opposition to Project Jupiter, Lujan Grisham recently said she takes seriously residents’ concerns about the data center “and expects any data center operating in New Mexico to meet the state’s rigorous environmental standards and use water responsibly.”

This summer, Abbott called on the Texas Public Utility Commission to ensure the projects pay for their own infrastructure and don’t lead to higher electricity costs for residents. He also recommended the state Legislature pass a number of regulations related to data centers next year, many concerning water and electricity usage, and recently told the Texas Water Development Board to penalize data centers that do not report their water usage.

Abbott’s new edicts do not address air pollution or climate change, nor the effects that a data center project in one state can have on another.

Texas Democratic state Rep. Joe Moody, whose district includes much of West and Northeast El Paso, near two of the data center projects, said Abbott’s proposals will likely shape the Texas Legislature’s debate over data-center-related policies next year but called them just a starting point.

“In the governor’s directives, we’re not talking about local control and local autonomy to make decisions on these projects,” he said. “And I do think that that’s a whole other lane of conversation that we’re going to get into next session.”

These Midterm Races Will Decide Data Centers’ Political Fate

text:
Richardson Electronics is partnering with ComEd to expand manufacturing of battery energy storage systems in Illinois and install its first onsite battery energy storage system demonstration project.

Richardson, based in La Fox, is building the largest commercial battery storage system in Illinois. As part of this, Richardson is installing a 5-MWh research and development demonstration project, supported through the ComEd interconnection process. The planned expansion will help scale the development and distribution of these products.

“For generations, manufacturing has been part of northern Illinois’ identity, and Richardson’s announcement demonstrates how that sector continues to shape our region’s economic future,” ComEd President and CEO Gil Quiniones said. “ComEd is committed to supporting business growth by making the grid investments needed to deliver industry-leading reliability at rates that are well below the average commercial and industrial rates for the top 20 largest metropolitan areas.”

This initiative is a critical step toward scaling locally made battery energy storage solutions that strengthen grid reliability, support renewable energy integration, and store energy for use during periods of high demand.

“Richardson Electronics has a long history of solving complex power and energy challenges through innovation and U.S.-based manufacturing,” Greg Peloquin, executive vice president and general manager of Power & Microwave Technologies and Green Energy Solutions groups, said. “Our advanced energy storage solutions will help customers manage energy more efficiently while supporting a more reliable and resilient grid. We value ComEd’s collaboration in bringing this onsite demonstration project to life.”

The project is supported by the Reimagining Energy and Vehicles in Illinois, or REV Illinois, program. REV is helping Richardson Electronics strengthen its La Fox operations, advance energy technology manufacturing and support continued economic growth in Illinois.

“As demand for reliable and affordable energy increases, Illinois has an opportunity not only to deploy new technologies, but to manufacture them,” Illinois Economic Development Corporation President and CEO Christy George said. “Richardson Electronics’ expansion demonstrates how Illinois’ manufacturing expertise can drive growth in emerging industries like battery storage while helping strengthen the energy infrastructure that supports our economy.”

Battery energy storage systems can charge when electricity is available and discharge when it is needed. This helps customers manage energy use and supports a more flexible electric system.

ComEd is supporting the project through its customer interconnection process and engineering studies. The company’s work includes helping prepare the site for the demonstration system and guiding Richardson through any potential system upgrade needs.

Projects like these are also eligible to apply for ComEd’s Distributed Generation Rebate Program, which recently hit a $350 million milestone.

ComEd is a unit of Chicago-based Exelon Corporation. ComEd provides power to more than 4.2 million customers across northern Illinois.

title: We Examined Who Actually Supported Repealing the Roadless Rule. The Results Tell a ...
authors: Will Pattiz, More Than Just Parks
description:
So was the North Dakota Petroleum Council, advocating for the removal of forest protections in a federal rulemaking concerning roadless national forest lands.
These disagreements reveal how deeply the Roadless Rule intersects with local politics, resource development, water supplies, wildlife management, and public land access.
The Roadless Rule has survived 25 years of political challenges because Americans have consistently recognized the value of preserving these places.
We’ve published our complete investigation into the Roadless Rule docket, including the organizational breakdowns, underlying numbers, methodology, and downloadable data.
Read Our Full Roadless Rule Docket Investigation Thanks to everyone who helped defend these forests.
text:
Nearly everyone wanted the Roadless Rule saved. We wanted to know who didn’t.

As we documented in our analysis of the federal docket, first published September 28 and updated with the final comment counts following the October 6 deadline, more than 99% of the nearly 1.2 million comments, letters, and signatures submitted on the Trump administration’s proposal to repeal the Roadless Rule opposed it.

The public’s position was overwhelming. But buried in that enormous record was another story we thought deserved a closer look.

Who, exactly, wanted the Roadless Rule gone?

Which businesses, industries, organizations, and government officials were pushing to eliminate protections for some of America’s last great undeveloped national forests? And what did they stand to gain?

We examined the formal positions of 454 organizations and government bodies that weighed in on the proposal. Just 95 supported repeal.

When we started looking at who those 95 were, a revealing picture emerged.

Upgrade to Paid

Follow the Industries

Of the 95 organizations and government bodies supporting repeal, 42 were industry and trade groups. Another 32 were counties, cities, towns, or local districts.

Together, those two categories accounted for nearly four out of every five organizations and government bodies calling for the Roadless Rule’s elimination.

The industry figures were particularly striking. Of 49 industry and trade groups that submitted positions, 42 supported rescission, just five opposed it, and two took mixed positions.

Here’s a sampling of the organizations that wanted the protections gone.

Timber and logging: American Forest Resource Council, Associated Oregon Loggers, Associated California Loggers, Montana Wood Products Association, and Forest Resources Association.

Mining and energy: National Mining Association, Alaska Miners Association, Western Energy Alliance, American Exploration & Mining Association, and North Dakota Petroleum Council.

Ranching and grazing: Oregon Cattlemen’s Association, Nevada Cattlemen’s Association, Montana Stockgrowers Association, and Wyoming Farm Bureau Federation.

Motorized recreation: Motorcycle Industry Council, International Snowmobile Manufacturers Association, and BlueRibbon Coalition.

Other interests: Alaska Bankers Association, National Federation of Independent Business, and Pacific Legal Foundation.

Several individual businesses also supported repeal, including Southport Lumber, Grande Portage Resources, Vizsla Copper, and Mountain Capital Partners, a ski resort operator.

The Alaska Bankers Association was among the more surprising names to appear in our findings. So was the North Dakota Petroleum Council, advocating for the removal of forest protections in a federal rulemaking concerning roadless national forest lands.

Many of these organizations have an obvious interest in loosening restrictions on road construction, logging, mining access, or other industrial activity.

The administration has framed its proposal as a way to improve forest management, reduce wildfire risks, and give local land managers greater flexibility. Those arguments appeared repeatedly among the groups supporting repeal.

Yet the Roadless Rule already allows exceptions for certain emergency situations and forest management activities.

Interestingly, even the International Association of Fire Chiefs declined to endorse wholesale repeal, recommending amendments to the existing rule instead.

We’ve documented these organizations and linked their filings in our full docket analysis.

The Government Officials Who Wanted It Gone

Industry groups were joined by a collection of county governments, state officials, and local districts that also wanted the Roadless Rule eliminated.

Of the 54 counties, cities, towns, and districts that submitted positions, 32 supported repeal, 21 opposed it, and one took a mixed position.

Among the more noteworthy findings:

Oregon: Baker, Harney, Jackson, Douglas, and Union counties supported rescission, even as the State of Oregon formally opposed it.

California: Siskiyou and Modoc counties supported repeal, while the state government opposed it.

Alaska, Utah, and Nevada: All three state governments filed in support of eliminating the rule.

Wyoming: The Wyoming Game and Fish Department explicitly supported full rescission, a particularly interesting position from an agency responsible for managing wildlife.

National Association of Counties: The national organization representing county governments supported repeal.

Meanwhile, cities including Asheville, North Carolina, and Walla Walla, Washington, called for keeping the protections. Salt Lake City’s mayor, public utilities director, and fire chief jointly urged the Forest Service to withdraw its proposed repeal.

Even Montana’s elected officials submitted competing letters, with groups of legislators taking opposing positions.

These disagreements reveal how deeply the Roadless Rule intersects with local politics, resource development, water supplies, wildlife management, and public land access.

But the central question remains. Should local economic and political interests be able to overturn national protections established for forests that belong to all Americans?

Who Was on the Other Side?

Here’s where the findings become especially striking.

While the majority of industry and trade groups favored repeal, the organizations representing conservation, tribal interests, scientific research, and much of the outdoor recreation community overwhelmingly called for keeping the Roadless Rule.

Consider these numbers:

Conservation organizations: 151 opposed repeal. Zero supported it. They included Earthjustice, the Sierra Club, National Audubon Society, National Wildlife Federation, and The Wilderness Society.

Tribes and tribal organizations: 31 opposed repeal. Zero supported it. Among them were the All Pueblo Council of Governors, Cowlitz Indian Tribe, Organized Village of Kake, and Affiliated Tribes of Northwest Indians. Three other filings took mixed positions.

Scientists and research institutions: 17 opposed repeal. Zero supported it. The American Fisheries Society, Society for Conservation Biology North America, and multiple chapters of The Wildlife Society were among those defending the rule.

Hunting, fishing, and recreation organizations: 85 opposed repeal, compared with 13 supporting it. Trout Unlimited, Outdoor Alliance, Appalachian Trail Conservancy, and American Mountain Guides Association all called for keeping the protections.

And then there were the businesses.

Patagonia, Black Diamond Equipment, REI, and Nantahala Outdoor Center were among the outdoor companies defending the rule.

So were some potentially less obvious organizations, including the Alaska Trollers Association, Alaska Longline Fishermen’s Association, New Hampshire Brewers Association, Business for Montana’s Outdoors, and Visit Big Sky.

These organizations represent an enormous range of interests, from protecting ancestral homelands and wildlife habitat to preserving clean drinking water, fisheries, and the outdoor recreation economy.

Their participation underscores just how broad the constituency for intact national forests has become.

The Numbers Behind the Million-Plus Comments

The organizational filings tell a fascinating story, but the broader public record is even more overwhelming.

Our final analysis counted 1,197,510 comments, letters, and signatures submitted during the 2026 comment period.

Of those:

1,190,695 opposed repeal.

2,137 supported repeal.

4,678 took mixed positions or stated none.

These figures include individually posted comments, letters submitted together in large collections, and petition signatures. They represent entries in the record rather than unique people. Even after removing all the duplicates we could identify, more than one million entries remained, although some people may still be counted more than once.

We uncovered several other remarkable findings.

104,719 comments were one of a kind, matching no other comment in the docket. Of those, 100,926 supported keeping the rule, compared with just 1,565 supporting repeal.

99.8% of form-letter copies that took a clear position supported keeping the rule. Just 452 of the 271,840 copies favored rescission.

Not a single bundled submission we counted supported repeal. Of the 807,446 letters and signatures contained in bundled files, 807,428 were associated with submissions calling for the rule to remain in place. The remaining 18 were associated with submissions stating no position.

Wildlife and habitat appeared in 85% of individually posted comments containing text. Drinking water and watersheds appeared in 78%, recreation in 57%, logging and timber in 48%, and wildfire in 44%. These figures count mentions, including repeated form letters, rather than distinct arguments.

The scale of the organizing effort was extraordinary.

We traced 845,443 comments, letters, and signatures to 49 named organizations, representing approximately 71% of everything counted in the 2026 record.

Earthjustice – 174,660

Natural Resources Defense Council –165,797

National Audubon Society – 74,726

Outdoor Alliance – 67,221

Sierra Club – 51,021

The Wilderness Society – 47,545.

Those totals include form letters and bundled submissions.

We’re enormously grateful to all these organizations and to everyone who took the time to stand up for these forests.

We’re also proud that this community was part of that effort through our Roadless Rule map and comment builder, created with the Sierra Club, and PLAN, our Public Lands Action Network.

Our analysis identified at least 1,823 comments written using our tools, including 1,657 that were one of a kind.

That’s a meaningful contribution from this community, and we’re deeply grateful to everyone who participated.

So What Does This Tell Us?

The public has given the Forest Service an extraordinary record to consider.

More than 99% of the comments, letters, and signatures counted opposed repeal. The overwhelming majority of conservation organizations, tribal governments, scientific institutions, and hunting, fishing, and recreation groups called for keeping the protections.

On the other side, the organizations advocating for repeal were heavily concentrated among extractive industries, trade associations, and local governments seeking greater flexibility over how national forests are managed.

That’s a revealing picture of the interests behind the effort to dismantle one of America’s most important forest protections.

The Roadless Rule has survived 25 years of political challenges because Americans have consistently recognized the value of preserving these places. They provide clean water, wildlife habitat, outstanding recreation, and something increasingly difficult to find in this country: vast forests that haven’t been carved apart by roads and industrial development.

The Forest Service now has to decide what to do with the record before it.

Public comments aren’t votes, and the agency’s final decision remains ahead. But the public has made its position abundantly clear.

We’ve published our complete investigation into the Roadless Rule docket, including the organizational breakdowns, underlying numbers, methodology, and downloadable data. We encourage you to explore it and see for yourself who stood on each side.

Read Our Full Roadless Rule Docket Investigation

Thanks to everyone who helped defend these forests. We’ll continue following the administration’s next steps and keep you informed.

Until next time,

Will

text:
In a significant move for domestic renewable fuel markets, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has released a proposed rule to fully reallocate 100 percent of the renewable fuel volumes waived through recent 2025 Small Refinery Exemptions (SREs).

The draft rule directly addresses the agency’s August 31 decisions, which granted hardship exemptions to 29 small refineries under the Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS). Those waivers exceeded initial agency projections, exempting an additional 770 million Renewable Identification Numbers (RINs) worth of renewable fuels from compliance obligations. Under the newly released proposal, the EPA is moving to ensure that every gallon of that exempted volume is restored to future blending obligations rather than lost from the marketplace.

The EPA is soliciting public feedback on two specific reallocation pathways:

Two-Year Phase-In: Dividing the 770 million RINs equally between the 2026 and 2027 compliance years, adding approximately 385 million RINs to each year’s Renewable Volume Obligation (RVO).

Single-Year Roll-In: Reallocating the entire 770 million RIN obligation directly into the 2027 compliance year.

The reallocation plan has drawn strong support across the agricultural sector, including the American Farm Bureau Federation, the Renewable Fuels Association, and Growth Energy. Farm leaders emphasized that recovering these waived volumes protects demand for grain and oilseed feedstocks—specifically corn and soybean oil—which directly supports commodity prices, livestock feed co-products like distillers grains, and the broader farm economy.

Agricultural economists noted that when refinery exemptions go unaddressed, they effectively erode the statutory baseline for domestic biofuels. Restoring the full 770 million gallons back into future blending pools signals certainty to commercial processors and provides a vital demand floor for Midwestern and Southern row-crop producers facing tighter margins.

The public comment period for the EPA’s proposed reallocation framework will remain open through December 4.

text:
Historically, U.S. mine tailings have been treated as waste to be disposed of, not as a potential resource. That view is changing. The U.S. Department of the Interior now considers mine waste “one promising domestic source of critical minerals,” and federal agencies are moving to ease recovery of critical minerals from tailings while encouraging remediation.

This post examines the federal framework for recovering critical minerals from mine waste, the regulatory and financial barriers that have historically inhibited the sector, and the funding opportunities available to companies seeking to turn tailings into profit.

Domestic Potential

The United States imports essentially 100% of 13 critical minerals and more than 50% of another 20 critical mineral commodities essential to national defense, advanced manufacturing, energy infrastructure, and emerging technologies. China dominates extraction and processing of many of these materials.

Domestic tailings could help close that gap. A preliminary analysis by the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) National Energy Technology Laboratory and the Idaho National Laboratory estimates that approximately 13,904 million metric tons of tailings across 189 major sites contain significant concentrations of rare earth elements, cobalt, gallium, germanium, indium, and platinum-group elements. For example, abandoned lead and zinc mines in Oklahoma have left behind waste rich in zinc and germanium. Researchers have also identified tellurium, which is vital for defense applications, in copper tailings at a Utah mine. Industry is already pursuing these opportunities: some mining companies estimate they could produce up to 800 million pounds of copper annually as soon as 2027 by leaching the metal from waste piles once considered worthless.

Reprocessing also offers environmental benefits. Legacy tailings sites can be sources of acid mine drainage, heavy-metal leaching, and dust. Reprocessing can remediate those conditions while recovering minerals.

The Current Political and Regulatory Framework

Fragmented regulation of domestic mining has historically impeded the expansion of the processing capacity needed to extract critical minerals from tailings. In recent years, Congress and the Executive Branch have taken a series of steps to address those barriers.

The Energy Act of 2020 created the first comprehensive statutory framework for federal critical minerals programs, including research on recovery from secondary and unconventional sources. The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act of 2021 then funded several programs explicitly targeting mine waste sites.

The Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023 amended the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) to impose presumptive deadlines of one year for environmental assessments (EAs) and two years for environmental impact statements (EISs). The Act also allows agencies to rely on existing EAs and categorical exclusions for certain projects, which may include tailings recovery at previously permitted or remediation sites. That same year, the Federal Permitting Improvement Steering Council proposed prioritizing critical mineral projects for FAST-41 coordinated review, which offers a single coordinating agency, a predictable timetable, and a public permit tracking dashboard.

On March 20, 2025, President Trump issued Executive Order (EO) 14241, which directs federal agencies to expedite permitting for domestic mineral projects and prioritize federal lands for mining and processing, delegates Defense Production Act (DPA) authorities to support domestic mineral production, and broadens the definition of “minerals” to include copper, zinc, uranium, potash, and gold.

In July 2025, Congress enacted the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), which made some of the most sweeping changes to federal mineral-resource policy in more than a generation.

Later that month, the Department of the Interior (DOI) issued Secretarial Order (SO) 3436, which defines mine waste broadly to include waste piles, coal refuse, tailings, and discharges on federal, state, tribal, and private lands. The Order directs DOI bureaus and offices to review and, where appropriate, amend regulations and streamline processes to encourage private-sector recovery of critical minerals from mine waste. Implementation will determine how much these reforms benefit the domestic mining industry.

Regulatory and Market Barriers

Tailings reprocessing does not fit neatly into existing regulatory categories. Depending on the site, regulators may treat a project as mining, waste management, remediation, or a hybrid, creating uncertainty about which rules apply and which agencies have jurisdiction.

The legal status of minerals in tailings under the General Mining Law of 1872 is also uncertain, including whether developers can claim tailings as minerals or whether tailings are waste governed by other frameworks, and what royalties apply on federal land. Some sites also face title disputes among surface owners, mineral estate holders, and the federal government.

Environmental liability has been a significant barrier to private investment in legacy tailings recovery. Because the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (CERCLA or Superfund) imposes strict, joint, and several liability, a party that disturbs contamination can become a potentially responsible party even if it did not cause the original pollution and its work improves site conditions. In some cases, cleanup liability could exceed recovery revenue by orders of magnitude.

State permits for water discharges, air emissions, and residual tailings add further layers of review. Permitting a new mine in the U.S. typically takes seven to ten years, compared with two to three years in Canada and one to two years in Australia. The practical effect of recent NEPA reforms on complex mining projects remains to be seen.

Funding and Government Program Opportunities

Several federal funding streams support these projects. A 2022 presidential determination under Title III of the Defense Production Act (DPA) made “by-product and co-product production at existing mining, mine waste reclamation, and other industrial facilities” eligible for support, and the Department of War has since made several hundred million dollars in DPA funding available, including for recovery from secondary sources. DOE’s new Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation has also announced plans to issue nearly $1 billion in funding opportunities, including $275 million for “Mines and Metals Capacity Expansion,” $80 million for “Mine of the Future,” and $134 million for a “Rare Earth Elements Demonstration Facility.” On September 30, 2026, DOE announced $29.5 million in awards to 17 U.S. National Laboratory projects to accelerate the development of innovative technologies that expand and improve domestic mining capabilities.

Tax incentives are less certain. Inflation Reduction Act production tax credits mainly target primary production and recycling. The OBBBA phases out parts of the tax credit framework for critical minerals processing and advanced manufacturing and eliminates or accelerates the phase-out of key demand-side incentives, including under Sections 45X and 30D. Some policy proposals would extend Section 45X credits to minerals recovered from secondary sources.

Certain projects may qualify for Superfund cost recovery or brownfield redevelopment funding if they demonstrably improve site conditions. Several states also offer tax credits, infrastructure investment, workforce training support, or expedited review for critical mineral projects. Layering these incentives with federal support could make some otherwise marginal projects viable.

Looking Ahead

Ultimately, the main obstacles to recovering critical minerals from mine tailings are regulatory uncertainty, economic risk, and institutional frameworks designed for conventional mining. Federal policy has rarely been more favorable to these projects, but success will still turn on site-specific economics, careful management of environmental and mineral-title risks, and strategic use of the reclamation, defense, and energy funding now available.

Our team is tracking regulatory developments in this space and can help stakeholders navigate federal funding opportunities, regulatory challenges, and the evolving permitting landscape for critical minerals projects.

authors: Alejandra Martinez, Alex Ford, Texas Tribune, www.houstonpublicmedia.org, alex-ford-texas-tribune
description:

A University of Texas/Texas Politics Project poll released in August found that 57% of Texas voters opposed building a data center in their community.

text:
In recent weeks, Gov. Greg Abbott and Attorney General Ken Paxton have adopted increasingly tough rhetoric against data centers, promising to crack down on hundreds of facilities that failed to disclose required information about their water use over the past five years.

But the law that Texas political leaders are invoking carries a maximum fine of just $500 — a potentially negligible penalty that's just a blip for large companies.

Data centers use millions of gallons of water a year to run their facilities and cool their servers. Under state law, facilities that fail to complete required water-use surveys can be charged with a Class C misdemeanor, punishable by up to a $500 fine, and barred from certain state funding and environmental permits.

But some experts say those consequences have significant limitations, raising questions about whether the state has the tools to force compliance from an industry expanding rapidly across Texas.

State officials don't know whether misdemeanor penalties have been issued against data centers, and the facilities aren't eligible for state funding. Increasing fines for Class C misdemeanors in the Water Code would require state legislation. Lawmakers do not convene in Austin for the 2027 legislative session until January.

"The governor is like, ‘Let’s enforce the laws on the books that weren’t being enforced.' That’s not much in the way of incentive," said Kathryn Guerra, who leads a watchdog campaign at the environmental nonprofit Public Citizen. "If those are the laws that we already have and nobody’s enforcing them, the data centers know."

Abbott's office defended its enforcement crackdown by saying that the water board, along with other agencies including the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality, the Electric Reliability Council of Texas and the Public Utility Commission of Texas, will work together.

"No other state agency will approve data centers until the Public Utility Commission, ERCOT, and the Water Development Board have the information they need to make informed decisions," said Andrew Mahaleris, Abbott's press secretary.

Mahaleris added that the governor has recommended that data centers pay for their own electric infrastructure, use less water-intensive cooling technologies and add power generation to the state's power grid.

Cameron Poursoltan, the director of energy policy at Texas for the Data Center Coalition, said the organization, which represents many data center operators, supports annual water reporting because state and regional planners need accurate data to build a water plan that meets the needs of all Texans.

The state already requires large water users, including data centers, to complete annual water use surveys. The Texas Water Development Board, the state agency tasked with overseeing the state's water planning process and financing water projects, uses responses to assess the current demand and to plan for water needs 50 years into the future.

But data centers have largely ignored the surveys. Or some argue they haven't received them.

Last year, 329 data centers were surveyed. Only about 30% responded. One lawmaker described the response rate as "pretty pathetic" at a legislative hearing this summer, despite the requirement being written into state law.

Some data center operators have defended the low response rate, saying they have not received a survey.

"Data centers take water stewardship extremely seriously," Poursoltan said. He added that the organization has worked with TWDB to resolve "significant contact information and data discrepancies that contributed to the TWDB Water Use Survey's initial lower response rate."

Tracking data centers in Texas

The survey has long been the state's only way to track how much water the rapidly expanding data center industry uses. Another effort to collect the information by the PUC this year has been voluntary and also had a low response rate.

Now, amid growing scrutiny of data centers and their demands on Texas' dwindling water supply, Abbott and Paxton are asking state agencies to enforce the existing law. The enforcement push comes as both Republicans face competitive elections and opposition to data center development grows.

A University of Texas/Texas Politics Project poll released in August found that 57% of Texas voters opposed building a data center in their community. Republicans remained closely divided, with 45% supporting while 43% opposed local data center construction. Meanwhile, 75% of registered Texas Democrats oppose data centers.

The water board, which collects the surveys to help plan the state's water needs, has historically had little ability to enforce the requirement. Abbott has directed the agency to notify local prosecutors about noncompliant facilities, while Paxton has launched an investigation. But the board says it has no authority to prosecute violations itself, and state officials don't know if fines have been issued against data centers.

The state's next steps could reveal how much leverage officials actually have. The water board is required to update Abbott's office by Oct. 14 on the progress of its enforcement efforts.

"We will continue working with state leaders to ensure our industry’s growth in Texas is responsible, transparent, and responsive to the communities where our members operate," Poursoltan said in an email.

What enforcement looks like

Abbott has directed the water board to notify county and district attorneys about facilities that fail to comply, leaving local officials to determine whether to pursue criminal cases.

Historically, the board relied on local law enforcement to ask for the list of noncompliant water users. Experts say this would put the onus on law enforcement to identify a crime, without knowing about the crime.

Ryan Kellus Turner, executive director of the Texas Municipal Courts Education Center, which provides legal resources and professional training for municipal judges, said the violations haven't generated significant discussion among court officials.

While the attorney general is investigating, Paxton does not have independent authority to prosecute local criminal cases, unless requested or appointed by a district or county attorney, according to the Texas Government Code. Paxton's office did not respond to questions about the limits of the law or what penalties it believes it can pursue. Shortly after Abbott's directive to the board, Paxton launched an investigation into hundreds of data center developments in several Texas counties "to ensure that they are transparent about their water usage and fully compliant with the law," he said in a press release.

"Texas law contains well over a thousand state-law fine-only offenses, many enacted over time to address particular regulatory or public policy concerns," Turner said. He added that the Legislature could increase fines as it did so in other cases where penalties can reach thousands of dollars.

The financial threats against data centers may also be limited. Perry Fowler, executive director at the Texas Water Infrastructure Network, which supports water infrastructure projects and policy, said data centers generally are not eligible for state funding that officials have threatened to withhold.

The water board serves as the state’s financial bank for water projects by providing grants and loans to cities, counties, river authorities, water districts, local water supply corporations and rural utility districts.

"There's nothing the board can withhold from them," Fowler said, so the threat of losing that money is less meaningful as opposed to a municipal utility that didn't fill out the survey and wanted dollars for water supply projects.

The permitting restrictions are also lower than they may sound. The state can withhold certain permits or permit renewals, but the law does not allow the state to revoke or suspend permits already issued to operating or planned data centers for failing to submit the survey, according to Ryan Vice, director of external relations at the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality.

That could leave some operating facilities facing little immediate consequences for failing to report their water use.

"Because permits are needed before operation and TWDB survey applies to sites that are already operating, barring permits might not adequately penalize a site for survey noncompliance until the site comes up for permit renewal or amendment," said Margaret Cook, vice president of Water and Community Resilience & Sustainability at the Houston Advanced Research Center.

Adrian Shelley, the executive director of Public Citizen, said the governor's directive is only meaningful if "it leads to a facility being prevented from opening or being shut down if it is already operating."

Hundreds of facilities haven't reported water usage

The Texas Water Board's surveys offer a limited picture of the industry's water use, in part because so few data centers have responded.

The survey is sent by mail to thousands of municipal public water systems and industrial facilities, including operating data centers.

The survey captures annual water volume used and basic facility details, including whether the facility self‑supplies or purchases water, the source of that water like surface water or groundwater, and whether it has on‑site power generation. It does not collect information on the type of technology data centers use to cool down their very hot servers. That technology is traditionally the biggest use of water for facilities.

The water board survey targets operating facilities that use more than 10 million gallons per year, which it considers "a significant industrial user."

Those that receive the survey are required by law to complete it. If an entity does not, the punishment includes ineligibility for state water funding, possible criminal charges with a maximum penalty of $500, and withholding certain environmental permits.

Accurate data collection is vital, the water board says on its website, because it helps in assessing current water supply and ensuring there is enough water to provide in areas with limited water and growing populations.

The water survey only goes out to data centers that were operating in that given year.

When the board surveyed 22 data centers in 2023, nearly a third of them responded. The next year, 67 data centers were surveyed and 28% submitted the survey. And last year, 329 data centers were surveyed and nearly 30% submitted responses.

Records obtained by The Texas Tribune covering 2020 through 2025 identified 334 unique data center facilities. Of those, 101 facilities — about a third — submitted at least once, and 233 facilities never submitted a requested survey.

While more data centers are being surveyed each year, overall compliance remains low, driven mainly by new facilities. Of the 329 facilities TWDB surveyed in 2025, 267 are new to the agency's tracking, and only 22.5% of them responded.

The board has said it did not have sufficient data to incorporate data center water use into the projections for its 2027 state water plan.

However, the responses that did come in show the scale of the industry's current reported water use.

In 2023, seven data center facilities reported using more than 144 million gallons combined — the municipal consumption of a small Texas town with a population of roughly 4,000 to 5,000 residents. In 2024, the number of facilities that completed the survey nearly tripled and the reported water usage was more than four times higher, with 19 facilities using more than 660 million gallons a year.

Last year's results show that 97 facilities completed the survey, reporting a collective total of 1.4 billion gallons of water that year.

Those numbers reflect only the facilities that submitted surveys, not the industry’s total water consumption.

Meta, a data center company, has submitted the survey for its Fort Worth facility the past two years.

"Transparency is a key pillar of Meta’s water stewardship program and we completed the TWDB survey as required," said a Meta spokesperson in an email. The North Texas facility consumes on average 72 million gallons a year.

"We commend Gov. Abbott’s leadership on protecting water resources and promoting responsible data center development in Texas," the spokesperson added. "Our Texas data centers use water-efficient cooling that minimizes consumption, and we fund projects across the state that restore hundreds of millions of gallons annually as we work toward restoring more water than we consume by 2030."

With the next legislative session coming up in January, Guerra at Public Citizen said state agencies should take time to understand the industry’s water use and the limits of the current reporting system.

"If we don’t have a full picture, then how are we supposed to go into the legislative session and make meaningful laws to protect folks?" she said.

text:
Redwood Materials wants to help companies sidestep yearslong waits for electricity by building on-site energy systems with recycled electric vehicle batteries, according to CEO JB Straubel.

The battery recycling startup is expanding beyond collecting and processing old EV batteries. It's increasingly pitching itself as a way for AI data centers to get power faster, without waiting for new connections to America's backed-up electric grid.

"Connecting to the grid can take years," Straubel wrote in a blog post on Wednesday.

His solution is what the industry calls "behind-the-meter" energy systems, which operate without needing to connect to the grid. Redwood would combine second-life EV batteries with solar panels and other on-site power sources, allowing customers to generate and store electricity at their own facilities.

The company is already putting the idea into practice with Rivian. Redwood recycles used batteries from the EV maker and is installing energy storage systems at Rivian's manufacturing plants, building on a 10-megawatt-hour installation at the company's Illinois factory.

Redwood is also packaging the batteries with its own power electronics and software, turning what began as a recycling business into a broader energy offering.

The company launched its Redwood Energy division last year on the premise that EV batteries still have years of useful life after they're retired from cars. It has already built a large battery system for a Crusoe data center.

Straubel's latest post makes clear where Redwood sees its biggest opportunity.

"The underlying problem is speed to power," he wrote, referring to the AI-fueled race to secure electricity.

That marks another step in Redwood's evolution. Investors originally backed the company to recycle batteries. Now, it's increasingly selling something different: a faster way to bring power to energy-hungry AI data centers.

text:
CHICAGO — On a beautiful fall Saturday morning on the South Side of Chicago, the Life Center Church of God in Christ thrummed with excitement. The pews were packed with over a thousand people dressed in their best — including more than a hundred in black graduation caps and gowns.

Before praying, Pastor Torrey L. Barrett invited the crowd to ​“turn it up,” so people cheered, danced, and waved hats in the air.

Though the sun streaming in the stained-glass windows was bright, the scene was not what might typically come to mind when one thinks about a solar industry gathering.

Instead of discussions of policy and technology, this was all celebration, music, and joy. And the people in the church were overwhelmingly African American, whereas the solar industry workforce is predominantly white.

But solar was the reason for the celebration. The 548 Foundation was commemorating the fact that its solar industry training program has now served more people than the number in its name, and is on track to reach 700 graduates by the end of the year. Participants are largely from the South and West sides of Chicago, disproportionately lower-income and African American communities whose residents have largely been left out of the clean energy economy.

The foundation was the brainchild of A.J. Patton, who grew up in a public-housing unit numbered 548 in Terre Haute, Indiana. Patton said his commitment to community empowerment and energy justice was sparked by the year — 1999 — that his family spent boiling water on an electric stove for baths, since his mother couldn’t afford a $400 gas bill.

I first met Patton in 2019, soon after he cofounded the startup 548 Capital LLC with his childhood friend from that same housing development, Erica Johnson, who was by then working in construction risk management for New York City’s housing authority. Their goal was to leverage renewable and energy-efficiency incentives to create affordable housing in marginalized Chicago neighborhoods, without contributing to the gentrification and displacement that often coincides with outside investment.

I was struck by Patton’s bold confidence and the large scale of their plans. He had quit a promising career in investment banking to focus on 548, entering a Chicago affordable-housing scene notorious for bureaucracy, cronyism, and challenges like the dilapidated state of buildings in low-income communities.

At the graduation, Patton described his path after launching the startup.

Their company acquired and renovated a six-flat apartment building, and soon more properties followed. They were ​“cutting folks’ bills,” Patton explained, but the people ​“swinging the hammers” on the building upgrades and solar panel installations did not reflect the local residents. When he pressed contractors to hire a more diverse workforce, he said he heard things like, ​“You know your people, they ain’t on time, they ain’t safe.”

That, Patton said, was the genesis of the 548 Foundation, a nonprofit that has now hosted 51 three-month training sessions in solar installation and related electrical and carpentry work, as well as basic life and job skills.

The 548 Foundation began offering trainings through the state workforce-development program in 2023, said Patton, and now the foundation holds multiple sessions each year in Chicago and the suburbs of Aurora, Elgin, and Waukegan, home to large Latino immigrant and African American populations. Another Chicago session will begin this month.

Under the state program, students get a stipend along with support to help them overcome barriers like child care and car trouble. The programs feature not only technical instruction but basic skills from math to resume-writing. Wraparound services help trainees with mental health, housing, and other needs. Across Illinois, these offerings have been crucial to helping people not only acquire skills and certifications but get and keep jobs, according to Patton and other workforce-development leaders.

In August 2024, I attended a job fair that 548 put on for their graduates. There, multiple solar employers did interviews that they said would promptly result in job offers, and instructors revealed some of the secrets to their success. They noted that the supportive services continue after graduation — trainees can keep coming back to 548 staff and affiliates for aid and advice. And the instructors work hard to prepare their charges for all the nuances of the job. For example, they role-play conflict mediation and start hands-on classes at 6 a.m., when work in the field often begins — so the participants can build routines around early-morning child care and other family responsibilities.

At the graduation, Patton touted the program’s results, and how it has dispelled stereotypes about Chicago’s Black communities.

“They said we didn’t want to work. Somehow, we have a 500-person waiting list to get in this program. Then they said we weren’t smart enough to learn this stuff. We have a 70% graduation rate, 700 graduates. Then they said the market wasn’t ready for us. Meanwhile, we have a 68% placement rate. Our students get jobs within 33 days of graduation. They’re averaging $68,000 a year. So while others are talking, we work. That’s what we do.”

He warned graduates to stay focused on their goals and careers despite such prejudice, as well as potential ​“distractions,” like friends who just want to party or long-lost relatives who suddenly appear to borrow money.

The cautionary notes soon dissolved into applause and music, as it was time for the diplomas. Instructors from different cohorts came to the pulpit to read the names of their trainees. Each graduate shook hands in a long receiving line including Patton and various elected officials, while people cheered loudly from the pews.

“I’m super proud of her!” enthused Natane Brown after dashing into the aisle to embrace her sister, Asia Bell.

After the ceremony the crowd spilled onto the sidewalk, where graduates were showered with flowers and balloons and posed for photos with family and friends.

Graduate Anthony Legorreta hoisted his young nephew in his arms as his relatives crowded. ​“This was most definitely a life-changing experience,” he said.

Fellow graduate Kelvin Davis said he loved the hands-on installation training, but sees himself ​“doing something toward desk work” in the solar industry – ​“not so much the physicality.”

“They were very open to whoever wants to learn. It’s an open door for the community,” said Davis of the program.

Graduate Mikah Allen doesn’t necessarily see himself working in solar at all. He prefers iron work and construction, and the links with trade union apprenticeships embedded in the training should help with that too. The state recently revamped the clean energy curriculum to prepare workers for a wider range of careers, given the current volatility of some clean energy industries.

At the graduation, Pastor Barrett described 548’s classes as part of the quest to build generational wealth in disenfranchised Black communities. He shared how his grandfather came to Chicago from the cotton fields of Mississippi with a third-grade education, and through a labor union job was able to buy a home and raise a family, including Barrett’s father, a renowned gospel singer, pastor, and civil rights activist.

“We come from neighborhoods that people write off,” Barrett said. ​“But you all have changed the trajectory not only of yourselves but of the community.” He predicted that ​“the next generation of contractors, the next generation of developers, the next generation of millionaires is sitting right in this room.”

At a time when discussion of the American solar industry often revolves around slashed federal incentives, troubled supply chains, and projects blocked by community opposition, the scene in the church that morning provided an inspiring and refreshing antidote. It was a reminder that even in the face of great challenges, clean energy can help improve not only the climate but individuals’ lives.
