description:
I’m really pleased to join you this afternoon as the new minister responsible for carbon capture, utilisation and storage.
The engineering expertise, project-delivery capability, offshore infrastructure and technical skills developed over decades in the North Sea are directly transferable to carbon capture, transport and storage.
Carbon capture offers a route to reduce their emissions while keeping production and skilled employment in Britain.
We are supporting the development of Acorn CCS, which is important to Scotland’s carbon capture infrastructure.
The government wants a strong carbon capture industry in Britain.
text:
Thank you, Olivia [Powis], for that introduction.

I’m really pleased to join you this afternoon as the new minister responsible for carbon capture, utilisation and storage.

In July, the Prime Minister asked me to continue in the department in a new role, as Olivia said, as Minister for Local Energy and Jobs. The idea behind this brief is simple.

Energy has always been a critical sector for our country – employing tens of thousands of people, driving and contributing to the country’s economy.

And with the country now firmly in the midst of the energy transition, my focus is on making sure that every single community feels the benefit and that people across the country can grab the opportunities of the transition with both hands.

What I say about this job is that it isn’t a job that deals in the abstract. This is about people and places. And that’s why it’s at the heart of the Prime Minister’s agenda for reindustrialisation.

This sector underpins so many communities in the UK and for decades, industrial decline has dismantled the people and places at the heart of it.

As we transition our economy from fossil fuels to clean homegrown power, we have to be clear what this is about…

…maintaining our independence, reducing our reliance on dictators and petrostates, rebuilding our industrial strength…

…creating good jobs and restoring opportunity in every part of the country.

And ultimately, building a world-leading British economy that is fit for the challenges of the future.

And I see CCUS playing a key role in that.

Your sector enables some of our most strategically important sectors, including cement, chemicals, refining and low-carbon power generation…

…to remain competitive in an increasingly carbon-constrained global economy.

It helps decarbonise existing industries, safeguard foundational sectors, and create the conditions for new low-carbon products and services to emerge.

The engineering expertise, project-delivery capability, offshore infrastructure and technical skills developed over decades in the North Sea are directly transferable to carbon capture, transport and storage.

From decarbonised cement to future low-carbon industrial products, CCUS is opening up opportunities across our industrial heartlands and ensuring they have a stake in the industries of the future.

At the same time, it creates new markets and supply chains, attracting private investment into our industrial heartlands.

CCUS is not just an industry in its own right. It is an enabler of wider industrial growth.

That is the central argument I want to make today.

Carbon capture is not an end in itself.

The pipelines, capture plants and storage sites – they matter.

But ultimately, they matter because of what they allow us to do, and the industries they enable.

To protect existing industries looking to decarbonise.

To make products in Britain that the world needs.

And, most importantly, to create good jobs and restore opportunity in communities right across the country.

That, in my mind, is the real prize before us.

When we talk about reindustrialisation, it can sometimes sound like quite an abstract idea.

A word that might be more comfortable and belong in an economic strategy or a government report.

But it describes and reflects the reality, the lived experience of millions of people in this country.

That too many places have been left behind for too long, with opportunities cut off and people moving away from their homes, or abroad, to find decent jobs.

Young people grow up in communities that they love.

Their families and friends are there.

Their roots are there.

But when it comes to the point of building a career, too often they feel they have little choice but to leave.

Not because they necessarily want to go, but because the secure jobs, training opportunities and well-paid careers are no longer available close to home.

And when that happens, a community does not simply lose one worker.

It loses skills. It loses spending power. It loses people who might have started businesses, raised families or contributed to local life.

Over time, that changes how a place sees itself.

Because meaningful work is about more than just a wage packet.

It gives people purpose, it gives people independence.

It allows them to plan for the future.

It gives families security, it gives young people something to aim for.

When generations of people see industries close, investment disappears and opportunities move elsewhere.

And the damage is not just economic.

It damages confidence. It weakens the sense that the future belongs to them.

It frays at the social fabric of a place.

We have seen this in the past in former mining communities.

We have seen it in our great manufacturing towns.

We have seen it in communities built around steel, around chemicals, oil and gas, and engineering.

I have the privilege of representing in parliament a shipbuilding community.

But I’m from the first generation in my family that didn’t work in the yards or the trades associated with them.

Why? Because the jobs just aren’t there anymore.

At the end of the 1950s, around 10,000 people in my community worked in shipyards.

Now that number is about to fall below 200.

And when the decline set in through the 1970s and through the 1980s, the new jobs that were promised materialised in the form of call centres and semiconductor manufacturers, but then most of them disappeared in the ‘90s and the noughties.

What the government is now focussed on is how we undo that damage.

These places powered this country.

They created Britain’s wealth.

They created the skills, the expertise and the industrial capacity on which our national success was built.

But too many were left without a serious plan when the industries around them declined.

Government stood back. Investment moved elsewhere. And people were told that this was simply the way that the economy worked.

This government does not accept that.

We have a responsibility to shape the economy.

To work with industry.

To invest strategically in the long-term and build the infrastructure businesses need.

And to ensure that economic change happens with communities, rather than happening to them.

That the places we are proud to call home can be given new life, designed by the people who know them best.

That is why, to my mind, reindustrialisation matters.

It is not about recreating the economy of the past.

It is about building the industries of the future in the places that have the skills, experience and ambition to lead them.

That thinking is at the heart of my job as Minister for Local Energy and Jobs.

The 2 parts of that title belong together.

Local energy.

And local jobs.

Because the clean energy transition will only succeed if people can see how it improves their lives.

If they see good jobs being created. If they see investment arriving in their communities. If local businesses win contracts.

If young people get apprenticeships. And if communities have a real stake in the economic change taking place around them.

My job is not simply to support projects. It is to ensure those projects support people and places.

That means strengthening local supply chains, enabling engineering firms to win new contracts, invest in new capabilities and grow for the long term.

It means making sure experienced workers know that the skills they have gained over decades will be needed in the industries we are building today.

And it means giving businesses confidence that Britain is serious about the infrastructure, skills and long-term certainty that industrial investment requires.

It also builds on strengths we already have.

That’s why CCUS is not only critical to achieving net zero.

It is central to this government’s reindustrialisation agenda.

And the clusters are proving that we can deliver it.

The most important thing about CCUS is not simply the carbon it captures. It is about what that infrastructure makes possible.

When we talk about pipelines and storage networks, we should also talk about the industries that can connect to them.

Cement works. Refineries. Chemical plants. Low-carbon power generation. Energy-from-waste facilities.

Take just one industry, cement.

The project at Padeswood is not simply carbon capture attached to a cement works. It will be the UK’s first carbon capture-enabled cement plant, securing the future of a vital foundation industry.

It is about protecting an important industrial site, the workers who depend on it and the supply chains built around it.

But it’s also about creating a new generation of low-carbon construction materials and positioning British businesses to serve future markets.

Or take refining and chemicals.

Carbon capture offers a route to reduce their emissions while keeping production and skilled employment in Britain.

The alternative cannot be to close British industry, import the same products from elsewhere and pretend the emissions have disappeared.

That would not be decarbonisation. It would be deindustrialisation by another name.

That is why I see CCUS not simply as environmental infrastructure, but as economic infrastructure.

And we are making great strides in building that infrastructure.

Working with industry, government has secured 5 Final Investment Decisions.

In the East Coast Cluster, the Northern Endurance Partnership and Net Zero Teesside Power are helping to build a new low-carbon industrial heartland, supporting around 3,000 jobs during construction while delivering secure, flexible low-carbon power.

In the North West and in North Wales, as part of HyNet, Liverpool Bay CCS is now supporting over 1,400 jobs.

In the same cluster, as I mentioned a moment ago, Padeswood is securing the future of a vital foundation industry.

And Protos will be the UK’s first carbon capture-enabled energy-from-waste facility, demonstrating British innovation in action.

These competitions will help maximise the use of infrastructure already under construction, attract further private investment, develop supply chains, and strengthen Teesside’s position as a leading hub for clean industrial growth.

Projects in the East Coast Cluster have announced over £2 billion of supply-chain contracts awarded to more than 260 UK suppliers to date.

They have also announced investment of over £1 million in local skills development, with 175 local young people in training.

That is what reindustrialisation looks like in practice.

Combined, Padeswood and Protos will support over 600 jobs.

The real value of a cluster is the ecosystem that can grow around it, and we are building the foundations of new industrial economies.

And this opportunity reaches beyond the first 2 clusters.

Two Teesside-based competitions are running this year to support expansion.

We will be setting out the next steps soon, so that industry has the clarity you need, taking into account the readiness of additional store capacity along the East Coast.

We are funding the development of CCUS infrastructure in the Humber region as part of the Viking cluster.

We are supporting the development of Acorn CCS, which is important to Scotland’s carbon capture infrastructure.

It will help strengthen industrial competitiveness, attract private capital, and ensure Scotland can play a leading role in the UK’s growing carbon-management industry.

Together, this industry and these projects are already supporting around 5,500 jobs in the UK.

And I want to hear from you. I want to hear from all of you.

To hear what is working, hear where the challenges are, and to support the work you are doing.

It begins with government and industry working together to maintain investor confidence, attract new investment and drive down costs as we deliver this first wave of projects.

At the same time, you have a part to play in this as well.

Showing how these projects create real economic growth, and support domestic supply chains, and, ultimately, provide value for money.

This is how the clean energy mission delivers not only decarbonisation, but reindustrialisation and economic growth.

And sets us up to be an economy that can resist the effects of wars and crises overseas that we do not control.

But it is no secret that we are operating in a challenging fiscal environment, and this government remains committed to meeting its fiscal rules.

So I owe you today to level with you, the next phase of the CCUS programme will be in the context of broader difficult decisions on funding.

We must ensure that public investment is targeted where it can deliver the greatest value, while continuing to build confidence in the long-term future of the sector.

That may mean making decisions about priorities, sequencing and pace, and recognising that progress will not always happen everywhere at once.

But this will also mean opportunity. As we move beyond first-of-a-kind projects, we are developing policies that offer industry and private investment greater leadership and flexibility: simplifying access to networks, enabling non-pipeline connections, and allowing international transfers of CO2.

And the Prime Minister has been clear that UK projects must deliver for UK plc and UK workers.

So as the CCUS sector grows, the requirement for government subsidy will need to reduce if it is to be sustainable for the long term.

But let me be totally clear, my overriding message to you today is that the government wants a strong CCUS sector in this country.

That it is an important sector for the UK’s future, and we will continue to engage closely with industry as we continue to deliver the programme.

That is why one of the first things I did after the reshuffle and taking this job was get a meeting in the diary with the CCSA.

And I will be out visiting the clusters soon.

And one thing I can do for you is make this transition more visible.

Showing off what this sector has already achieved, that the energy transition can deliver real opportunity for our communities and our country.

The government is in delivery mode, 2.5 years after the election.

And I want to see how this industry is boosting local economies, and I want people to know about those successes.

So please don’t be shy in coming forward and telling me about those successes.

The government wants a strong carbon capture industry in Britain.

To restore a sense of worth to our communities, to rebuild our industrial base, to lay the foundations for the future.

And behind every strategy document, investment decision, every statistic, is a person who is proud of their community and wants to build a decent life.

And we are serving them too.

So, my message today is a simple one.

Success will not be measured only by how much carbon we capture.

It will be measured by what we build, and the message we send as we do.

That the transition to clean energy is not a threat to British industry.

It can be the beginning of its renewal.

That is why this government is backing carbon capture and storage.

So, in closing, I want to thank you all for your work so far, and I’m looking forward to we all we can achieve together in the months and years ahead.

Thank you.

COLUMBUS, Ohio, Oct. 14, 2026 – American Electric Power (Nasdaq: AEP) plans to invest approximately $4 billion to advance a new 702-megawatt fuel cell generation project near Cheyenne, Wyoming, under a long-term 20-year power purchase agreement (PPA) with Google, marking a significant step in AEP’s strategy to serve growing demand from large-scale customers.

Under the PPA, Google will acquire power from Cheyenne Fuel Cell, LLC, which is approximately 92% owned and controlled by AEP, and nearly 8% owned by funds advised by Basalt Infrastructure Partners, LLP. AEP and its partners plan to start construction in 2026, and the facility is expected to be fully operational by the end of 2028.

“As power demand continues to grow, AEP is bringing together new technologies and strong partnerships to deliver reliable, innovative energy solutions quickly and at scale,” said Bill Fehrman, AEP chairman, president and chief executive officer. “This project demonstrates how we are creating new opportunities to meet evolving energy needs for customers both within and beyond our traditional service territory.”

AEP’s development and construction of this fuel cell generation facility is supporting Google's growing energy needs in the greater Cheyenne area. The planned facility uses advanced fuel cell technology developed by Bloom Energy that can be deployed rapidly and provide reliable, on-demand power to meet the needs of large-load customers. The technology generates electricity without combustion of natural gas, and the project includes plans to integrate carbon capture technology to deliver reliable, near-zero-emissions power. The project follows agreements reached between Google and Black Hills Corp., effective Sept. 30.

About AEP

American Electric Power (Nasdaq: AEP) is committed to improving our customers' lives with reliable, affordable power. We plan to invest $78 billion from 2026 through 2030 to enhance service for customers and support the growing energy needs of our communities. Our nearly 18,000 employees operate and maintain the nation's largest electric transmission system with 40,000 line miles, along with more than 252,000 miles of distribution lines to deliver energy to 5.6 million customers in 11 states. AEP also is one of the nation's largest electricity producers with approximately 33,000 megawatts of diverse owned and contracted generating capacity. We are focused on safety and operational excellence, creating value for our stakeholders and bringing opportunity to our service territory through economic development and community engagement. Our family of companies includes AEP Texas, Appalachian Power (in Virginia, West Virginia and Tennessee), Indiana Michigan Power, Kentucky Power, Ohio Power, Public Service Company of Oklahoma, and Southwestern Electric Power Company (in Arkansas, Louisiana, east Texas and the Texas Panhandle). AEP also owns AEP Energy, which provides innovative competitive energy solutions nationwide. AEP is headquartered in Columbus, Ohio. For more information, visit aep.com.

text:
U.S. Rep. Frank J. Mrvan has introduced federal legislation aimed at protecting Northwest Indiana residents and other American consumers from higher electricity costs resulting from orders that require aging power plants to remain operational or reopen after being permanently closed.

The legislation, known as the Utility Affordability and Transparency Act, was introduced October 2, 2026, as H.R. 10687. It seeks to prevent federal taxpayers and utility customers from bearing additional expenses associated with maintaining or reopening facilities that utility companies have determined are too expensive or no longer economical to operate.

The proposal comes as households throughout Northwest Indiana continue to face concerns about the affordability of electricity, natural gas and other essential services.

Under the legislation, the U.S. Department of Energy would be prohibited from issuing certain emergency orders that delay the scheduled retirement of power plants or require electricity generation from facilities that have already permanently closed.

The measure also would establish additional requirements for evaluating and publicly disclosing the financial costs associated with federal intervention in electricity generation decisions.

Mrvan, who represents Indiana’s 1st Congressional District, said consumers deserve greater accountability when government actions contribute to rising household utility costs.

“Northwest Indiana residents are struggling to make ends meet, and a major part of that burden is the cost of heating and cooling their homes,” Mrvan said. “Consumers deserve transparency about what is driving their utility costs and what can be done to lower them.”

A central provision of the legislation would require the Department of Energy to find alternatives to emergency orders that could reduce overall costs to consumers and electric utilities.

The department also would be required to publish reports detailing the estimated expenses associated with emergency orders affecting electricity generation.

Another provision would require affected utility companies to identify additional costs resulting from federal emergency orders on customers’ monthly electricity bills.

The requirement would give consumers a clearer understanding of whether a portion of their electricity charges resulted from federal decisions rather than ordinary utility operating expenses.

The proposed legislation follows an ongoing dispute between Northwest Indiana Public Service Co. (NIPSCO) and federal directives requiring coal-fired generating units to remain available for operation.

In June, Mrvan challenged a Department of Energy order affecting the R.M. Schahfer Generating Station in Wheatfield, Indiana. In a letter to federal officials, he cited approximately $11.5 million in estimated losses reported by NIPSCO following earlier emergency orders.

The Department of Energy has defended its actions, maintaining that keeping coal-fired generating facilities available is necessary to preserve electric grid reliability and reduce the possibility of power shortages and blackouts. Federal officials issued additional orders affecting Indiana generating stations in September.

The competing positions highlight a central question in the national energy debate: how to maintain a dependable electricity supply without imposing unnecessary financial burdens on customers.

Mrvan maintains that consumers should not be responsible for additional costs when federal decisions override planned power plant retirements.

“Hardworking families should not be forced to pay higher utility rates because the federal government is requiring energy companies to reopen or keep outdated coal-fired generating units operating beyond their planned retirement,” Mrvan said.

The congressman said greater transparency would help residents understand how government energy policies affect their monthly expenses.

The legislation would not immediately reduce electricity rates. Its proposed restrictions and disclosure requirements would first have to receive congressional approval and become law.

For Northwest Indiana residents, the issue carries particular significance as concerns continue over utility affordability and the financial impact of federal energy decisions.

Mrvan said the legislation is intended to establish accountability before additional expenses are imposed on consumers.

“Families deserve to know where government policies are increasing their bills, why those costs are being imposed, and what alternatives exist to lower them.”

The bill was introduced in the House of Representatives. Its ultimate consideration and potential amendment remain subject to further congressional action.

SWINDON, United Kingdom, October 14, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Sensata Technologies (NYSE: ST), today announced its brake force sensors are now enabling electromechanical braking (EMB) systems in leading electric vehicles. This milestone marks a significant step in the transition from traditional hydraulic braking to fully electric, brake-by-wire systems, as vehicle OEMs increasingly adopt architectures designed for electrification, autonomy, and software-defined control.

Electromechanical brakes represent a shift from hydraulic to electric actuation, requiring precise and continuous measurement of brake force to maintain safety, comfort, and performance. Sensata's brake force sensors are designed to provide that critical input, directly measuring clamping force within the brake caliper and enabling closed-loop control at each wheel.

Unlike conventional hydraulic and electro-hydraulic brake systems, which rely on pressure-based control, EMB systems depend on an accurate clamping force measurement to distinguish between braking scenarios such as gentle deceleration and emergency stops. Higher accuracy enables smoother, safer, and more responsive braking behavior across all driving conditions.

Sensata's Brake Force sensor integrates directly into the caliper, measuring clamping force in real time and transmitting data to the control unit at high frequency. This continuous feedback allows each wheel to operate as an independent, intelligently controlled system. The sensor builds on Sensata's Micro Strain Gauge (MSG) technology, proven in safety-critical braking applications for more than 25 years, and applies it in a new way to measure force directly rather than hydraulic pressure.

Key benefits of Sensata's Brake Force sensor include:

Precise EMB Control: Directly measures clamping force within the brake caliper, providing the real-time input required for precise electromechanical brake control.

Improved Braking Performance: Delivers high-accuracy force feedback to support responsive braking, consistency, and control across a wide range of driving conditions.

Simplified System Integration: Connects directly to the caliper control unit without additional connectors, helping reduce system complexity.

Compact, Lightweight Design: Supports integration into EMB architectures without adding unnecessary size or weight at the wheel end.

Functional Safety Support: Provides caliper-level force feedback to support the highest automotive functional safety requirements.

This approach enables OEMs to optimize braking performance at each wheel, improving vehicle dynamics, consistency, and safety. EMB architectures also simplify vehicle design by eliminating hydraulic components such as brake lines and fluid systems, reducing manufacturing complexity and maintenance requirements.

"Electromechanical braking represents a fundamental shift in vehicle architecture, requiring a new level of precision in sensing and control," said Markus Schwabe, Executive Vice President and President, Automotive, Sensata Technologies. "Our brake force sensing technology enables OEMs to achieve accurate, real-time control of braking force at each wheel, supporting the performance, comfort and safety requirements of next-generation EVs."

Sensata's patented force sensing design delivers high signal accuracy in a compact form factor, supporting consistent performance across the full range of braking scenarios. This includes low-force events such as gradual deceleration, where detection of the pad-to-disc contact point detection is critical for comfort, as well as high-force emergency braking conditions. This precise control of clamping force contributes to shorter stopping distances and more consistent braking behavior.

Adoption of EMB systems is accelerating as OEMs pursue simpler vehicle architectures, improved vehicle performance, and advanced functions such as centralized motion control and autonomous driving. Independent wheel control, faster response times, and elimination of brake drag can further improve vehicle efficiency and performance.

As electromechanical braking moves into mass production vehicles, accurate force sensing is becoming a critical part of safe, scalable brake-by-wire systems. Sensata's Brake Force sensors help OEMs accelerate adoption of these next-generation braking systems across EV platforms, supporting the industry's path toward zero road fatalities.

To learn more about Sensata's Brake Force sensor, visit sensata.com.

title: Africa needs an energy ladder
description:

They are different rungs of the same ladder, connecting energy access to economic opportunity and, ultimately, structural transformation.
It needs an energy ladder, and that ladder must ultimately lead towards greater productivity, economic transformation and industrialisation.

[5] Africa Minigrid Developers Association, 17 actions for minigrids to catalyze electrification in Sub-Saharan Africa: Mission 300 position paper (2026).
text:
Olamide Niyi-Afuye, chief executive of the Africa Minigrid Developers Association, argues that a connection is the first rung of Africa’s energy ladder, and that the climb has to continue into productive use and industry, with the minigrid sector able to connect 115 million people by 2030.

Writing after the UN General Assembly’s High-Level Week and Climate Week NYC, Olamide Niyi-Afuye, chief executive of the Africa Minigrid Developers Association (AMDA), sets out why a connection should be counted as “the first rung of the ladder, not necessarily the last”, and what it will take to move from energy access to industrialisation. The piece first appeared on AMDA’s website and is published here with thanks to AMDA.

I left New York after the UN General Assembly High-Level Week and Climate Week NYC with one thought that kept recurring across very different conversations: Africa’s energy challenge is evolving.

For many years, much of the global conversation has understandably focused on access. How do we connect the hundreds of millions of Africans who still live without electricity? How quickly can we reach communities that conventional grids may not reach swiftly and economically? What combination of technologies and financing can close that gap?

Those questions remain urgent. But increasingly, I believe we need to ask another question:

What happens after the power comes on?

Access alone is not the end goal. What matters is what reliable, quality power enables people and economies to achieve.

It means a small business can extend its operating hours, preserve its products, power its equipment and increase productivity. It means a hospital can reliably operate essential medical equipment, store vaccines safely and provide better patient care. It means students can study after sunset, access digital learning and pursue better educational outcomes without having to read in darkness. And in conflict-affected and remote areas, it means security and surveillance systems can operate more reliably, strengthening monitoring and response capabilities.

These are not simply benefits of electricity. They are the foundations of economic opportunity, stronger public services, human development and more resilient communities.

At the Third Roundtable on Powering the Renewable Energy Future at the United Nations, my closing message on behalf of the Africa Minigrid Developers Association (AMDA) was simple: we know the technology works. We know the demand exists. Increasingly, we also understand many of the policy and financing solutions required.

What we need now is scale: a transition from successful individual projects to replicable, commercially viable and bankable markets.

But scale cannot simply mean more connections. It must mean delivering power that is reliable, affordable and fit for purpose, while building an energy system capable of supporting Africa’s economic ambitions.

This requires us to look beyond the number of connections and ask harder questions. Are enterprises becoming more productive? Are health facilities delivering better services? Are students learning in better conditions? Are communities becoming more resilient? Can energy providers build sustainable businesses while serving customers who are often the most expensive to reach?

These are the outcomes that should increasingly shape how we design, finance and measure Africa’s energy transition.

The real measure of energy access is not just whether the lights come on. It is what becomes possible when they stay on.

That is the shift from electrification to productive energy access, and it must be central to how we think about scaling renewable energy across Africa.

Access is the first rung

Approximately 600 million Africans still lack access to electricity[1]. Distributed renewable energy solutions have become an increasingly important pathway to first-time access. According to ESMAP, they have connected 497 million people who might otherwise have waited years for a conventional grid connection[2]. Every one of those connections matters. For a household gaining electricity for the first time, the difference can be transformative.

But connecting people to electricity and powering their economic progress are two different, albeit connected, ambitions.

Electricity access exists on a continuum. For millions of households, power sufficient for lighting, communications and basic appliances represents a significant improvement in quality of life. Yet the power needed to light a home is not necessarily sufficient to refrigerate agricultural produce, operate irrigation systems, run milling equipment, weld metal, process raw materials or manufacture goods competitively.

This distinction is not an argument against basic access. It is an argument for what must follow.

The next phase of Africa’s energy transition must focus not only on who has electricity, but also on whether that electricity is reliable, affordable and sufficient to unlock greater economic opportunity.

That requires the right mix of technologies for different customers, productive activities and geographies. National grids, minigrids, distributed generation, energy storage and household energy solutions all have important roles to play. The objective is not to favour one technology over another, but to ensure that the energy infrastructure can evolve alongside the needs of the people and enterprises it serves.

An initial connection should therefore be celebrated for what it represents: a fundamental step towards inclusion and opportunity. But it should also be recognised for what it is: the first rung of the ladder, not necessarily the last.

The ladder must lead somewhere

This is where the conversation moves beyond electricity connections to Africa’s broader economic ambitions.

Africa does not need energy simply to consume more electricity. It needs energy that enables people to produce more, businesses to grow, industries to emerge and jobs to be created. The real value of electricity lies in the economic and social activity it makes possible.

Consider what reliable, quality power can unlock. Farmers can irrigate their land, reduce post-harvest losses and process produce closer to where it is grown. Small enterprises can operate machinery, extend production hours, improve product quality and serve larger markets. Hospitals can maintain cold chains and operate essential medical equipment more reliably. Students can study after dark and access digital learning. Communities, including those in conflict-affected areas, can benefit from more reliable security and surveillance infrastructure.

These outcomes matter because they turn electricity from a basic utility into an enabler of productivity, human development and economic resilience.

At a larger scale, reliable and competitively priced energy can help Africa process more of its agricultural products and minerals locally rather than exporting them primarily in their raw form. It can support light manufacturing, strengthen local value chains and help build competitive African industries capable of generating employment and retaining more economic value on the continent.

That is why the energy ladder must ultimately lead towards industrialisation, not stop at household connections.

This does not mean every rural electricity project must power a factory, or that every community should follow the same development pathway. It means energy systems should be designed to accommodate progression towards increasingly productive uses.

A household connection improves quality of life. Access to a productive-use appliance can increase a household’s income. Reliable power for a cluster of enterprises can transform a local economy. Agro-processing and light manufacturing can create jobs and retain value within communities. At scale, affordable and dependable electricity becomes part of the foundation for industrialisation.

Each step creates possibilities that the previous one alone could not fully deliver.

These are not competing objectives. They are different rungs of the same ladder, connecting energy access to economic opportunity and, ultimately, structural transformation.

The question for Africa’s energy sector is therefore not simply how quickly we can extend access. It is whether we are building energy systems that allow households, enterprises and entire economies to move up that ladder.

From connections to economic outcomes

This requires us to think differently about how we measure success. Our sector has historically focused on connections, systems deployed and megawatts installed. Those metrics remain important. But they tell us how far the infrastructure has reached, not what the infrastructure makes possible. The Benchmarking Africa’s Minigrids Report 2024[1] offers an important glimpse of that wider impact. The Powering Jobs Census 2022 estimates more than half a million direct DRE jobs globally, including approximately 374,000 direct DRE jobs across Africa[3]. The implication is clear: energy access is not only an infrastructure outcome.

But jobs created are only one measure of the value that electricity can generate. The larger question is what happens when reliable electricity becomes available to households, businesses, farmers and public institutions? What economic activity becomes possible as a result?

A connection is an output. Livelihoods enhanced, jobs created and healthcare improved are the outcomes.

The next generation of sector data needs to use the harmonised KPI framework[4] to speak the same language and answer harder questions: how much energy is being consumed, and how much of it productively; how many businesses, including agro-processors and productive-use appliance firms, have been created or expanded; how household and enterprise incomes have changed; and how many jobs are being supported, broken down by gender.

These questions move us closer to the reason we are building energy infrastructure in the first place.

Financing the rungs

Our financing architecture must evolve accordingly. One of my strongest reflections from New York was that capital exists, technology exists and demand certainly exists. The difficulty is connecting them on terms that reflect the economics of the markets we serve.

Distributed renewable energy developers carry risks that conventional infrastructure finance was not designed to absorb: currency exposure, early-stage demand risk, long development cycles, affordability constraints and, in some cases, even the cost of stimulating productive demand.

This is where catalytic capital must actually be catalytic. Patient capital can give developers the time needed to build viable portfolios. Access to local-currency financing can reduce the underlying currency mismatch between revenues and debt service, while foreign-exchange protection can manage residual currency risk where foreign-currency financing remains necessary. Guarantees can share risks that commercial lenders are not yet prepared to carry. Results-based financing can help bridge the gap between affordability and financial viability.

These are not simply different financing instruments. Together, they can create the conditions for commercial capital to follow. The scale of the opportunity makes this imperative. The minigrid sector alone has the potential to connect 115 million new people by 2030, requiring an estimated $28 billion to $46 billion in capital investment[5]. Simply providing conventional debt at marginally lower rates will not unlock that scale. Achieving the Mission 300 ambition will require a financing architecture capable of absorbing and sharing risks that commercial markets cannot yet price efficiently.

But there is another dimension. Electricity is an enabler, not the end goal.

Financing electricity infrastructure alone is insufficient. The businesses, equipment and productive assets that consume that power must also be financed. Otherwise, we risk building energy systems without building the economic activity that makes them sustainable. That means thinking about energy infrastructure and productive-use investment together. And as productive demand grows, the economics of the energy infrastructure itself improve.

Build systems that can grow

Africa’s energy deficit is far too significant, and its development ambitions too important, for the continent’s electrification future to be framed around a single technology. No single solution can meet the scale and diversity of Africa’s energy needs.

The electricity system that emerges across Africa will necessarily be diverse: national grids alongside interconnected and isolated minigrids, distributed generation, storage and household-level solutions, with the appropriate mix varying significantly between and within countries. The more consequential question is not which technology delivers electricity at the lowest cost or the fastest pace. It is how we build an electricity system that supports productive activity, enables businesses to grow, strengthens local value chains and drives industrialisation.

Ultimately, the measure of success must extend beyond the number of connections delivered to the economic opportunities created, the productivity unlocked and the lasting development value of electrification.

The objective is to build an electricity system capable of growing with Africa’s needs.

That means designing energy systems for progression. As demand grows, generation should be capable of expanding and evolving. Where appropriate, minigrids should be able to interconnect with national grids. Grid expansion should build on existing private investment in distributed renewable energy, rather than unnecessarily stranding viable infrastructure and capital. Consumers, too, should have pathways towards progressively higher levels of electricity consumption as their incomes, businesses and communities develop.

The system must be capable of climbing the ladder with them.

From projects to markets

This also changes the conversation about scale.

Africa does not simply need more successful projects. It needs functioning markets capable of producing successful projects repeatedly and at scale. That means predictable regulation, appropriate financing, transparent procurement, credible demand, stronger local institutions, investors with the confidence to invest at scale and developers capable of investing with confidence. It also means bringing governments, development finance institutions, philanthropy and industry together much earlier.

The private sector is increasingly at the table, and that is important. Developers understand where permitting becomes a bottleneck, where financing structures fail to match project economics, where regulations create unintended consequences, and where demand assumptions differ from what actually happens on the ground. That practical experience should help shape policies and DRE programmes, not simply implement them once the electricity architecture has already been designed.

This was central to my message at the United Nations: use the convening power of international institutions to turn proven solutions in individual countries into replicable, investable markets across Africa.

The next measure of success

We should never lose sight of the urgency of Africa’s electricity-access challenge.

Every household connected and every community receiving reliable power for the first time represents progress. But the first connection cannot be where ambition ends. The next phase of Africa’s energy transition must ask what happened because people were connected: whether businesses grew, farmers became more productive, communities attracted investment, incomes rose, new jobs emerged, local economies became more sophisticated, and people could consume progressively more electricity as their needs grew. At AMDA, our ambition, and that of our members, is therefore larger than deploying more minigrids. It is about creating the enabling conditions for distributed energy to become critical infrastructure for Africa’s prosperity.

Africa needs electricity access. But it also needs something beyond access.

It needs an energy ladder, and that ladder must ultimately lead towards greater productivity, economic transformation and industrialisation.

Access is the first rung. Our responsibility is to make sure Africans can keep climbing. Because the ultimate promise of Africa’s energy transition will not be measured only in panels installed, systems deployed, connections made, or megawatts generated.

It will be measured by what Africans are able to build, produce, and become once the power is on.

Sources

[1] Africa Minigrid Developers Association, Benchmarking Africa’s minigrids report (2024).

[2] World Bank, Access to electricity. In Tracking SDG 7: The energy progress report 2026 (2026).

[3] Power for All, Powering jobs census 2022: The energy access workforce (2022).

[4] Africa Minigrid Developers Association, Minigrid sector KPI framework (2026).

[5] Africa Minigrid Developers Association, 17 actions for minigrids to catalyze electrification in Sub-Saharan Africa: Mission 300 position paper (2026).

He trained in law, with an LLB from the University of Kent and an LLM from the University of Birmingham, and his career has taken him from William Bailey Solicitors and Wole Olanipekun & Co. to FMDQ Securities Exchange. Before joining AMDA he was Strategic Advisor at Mainstream Energy Solutions, where he managed major hydropower investments.

text:
In the past few months, Ford’s discontinued electric pickup, the F-150 Lightning, has seen a huge surge in sales.

The reason is simple: Those in the U.S. who want an electric pickup don’t have any cheaper options. There aren’t that many new electric pickup trucks, but the ones that do exist are pretty pricey. The GMC Sierra EV starts at $62,000. The Rivian R1T starts at over $70,000. The GMC Hummer EV Pickup starts at over $97,000. The Cybertruck is fugly and can’t even drive over some sand. The cheapest option? The Chevrolet Silverado EV starts at nearly $53,000, which isn’t horrible but reflects the new average cost of a new vehicle in 2026.

A Ford F-150 Lightning currently has an average used price of around $45,000 (depending on where you live, the year, and the condition, of course). But yeah, it’s a lot cheaper and it’s selling.

It’s apparently not that nobody wants an electric truck. Nobody wants an expensive electric truck. This sounds like good news for the Slate truck and Ford Fathom.

But for now, we got the Lightning.

What happened to the Ford F-150 Lightning if it’s so desirable?

Ford didn’t discontinue the Lightning because it sucked, that’s for sure. My colleague Dave McQuilling was a fan after he had the opportunity to test-drive one.

“Trucks are about utility and, for all of its faults, the F-150 Lightning provides more utility than pretty much any other truck. Which is why it’s a shame Ford has shelved it,” he wrote.

The Ford F-150 Lightning was discontinued in December 2025, largely due to the high cost of production. Ford didn’t really see a good profit margin. In fact, Ford lost tens of thousands of dollars on each Lightning built. To make up for this, Ford had to keep raising the price. Most American truck buyers were not willing to spend around $80,000.

Some would probably argue that the whole point of an American truck is to get s*** done for cheap. They’re meant to be a versatile workhorse that can tow, haul stuff around, and look badass in a driveway without costing a fortune. That’s the American dream. And that’s what really made electric pickup seem a bit silly when they first started coming out. Who wants a fancy shmancy electric pickup that’s nearly six figures?

Nine months into 2026, Ford has sold only 4,470 Lightnings, almost 80% fewer than it sold in the same period last year.

However, used Lightnings are now pretty affordable. According to Recurrent, used Lightnings only spend about 16 days on dealership lots. They’re selling fast.

As gas prices skyrocket, a used Lightning seems like a smart investment. It’s a capable truck without needing to fill a tank. Win-win, especially at this lower price point.

“When Ford was selling it brand new, the math was complicated,” said Jimmy Douglas, CEO of wholesale electric vehicle dealer Plug. “The Lightning is now 50% to 60% of the sticker price, and that is really a sweet spot; it’s an incredible truck for the money.”

Make way for the Ford Fathom at half the price

Of course, that excitement may dwindle once the Ford Fathom comes out. That $30,000 price point is nearly unheard of over here in the U.S., where we aren’t allowed to have cheap Chinese EVs. Ford CEO Jim Farley even said at one point that the company learned from the Lightning.

It was too big and the battery was too expensive.

“I think you’re going to see a product that really has a potential to change our industry,” Farley said in an interview with USA TODAY. “Not just be a successful product. Like any other OEM would give you a model name. But actually a project that is almost as revolutionary as the Model T was. Which ironically it’s a small electric pickup truck.”

The Ford Fathom is five years in the making. It will finally be out at the end of 2027. It’s still pretty far out, so there’s plenty of time for people to snatch up these Ford F-150 Lightning until then.

Several efforts to contain surging energy bills in California recently crossed the finish line in moves that stand to benefit Tesla (TSLA), Sunrun (RUN), Enphase (ENPH), and Alphabet (GOOGL) spinoff Renew Home, analysts say.

Gov. Gavin Newsom signed Senate Bills 905 and 913 — both from state Sen. Josh Becker — on Sept. 30. The new laws make way "for networks of community clean energy to become a bigger part of our power mix," said Laura Deehan, state director at the policy group Environment California, which backed the bills.

Such networks, known as virtual power plants in industry jargon, weave together idle electric car batteries, home battery systems, smart thermostats, and residential solar with the grid. VPPs use software to add up scattered energy storage; they can cushion spikes in demand, ward off peak fees, and create new ways for folks to earn cash from energy they store or generate.

SB 913 directs the California Public Utilities Commission and the California Independent System Operator to figure out how to integrate with home battery energy storage systems. The point is to pay residents and aggregators to send energy back to the grid when gas-fired peaker plants normally kick in.

SB 905 directs the CPUC to make utilities measure where existing grids can host more energy. It clears the way for regulators to later incentivize utilities to embrace lower-cost technologies such as VPPs over standard grid upgrades, wrote Canary Media. It also orders the CPUC to consider cutting the profits utilities can reap from lower-risk investments, like burying power lines.

"With these bills, VPPs can be built that don't require any action in the state budget," said Brad Heavner, executive director of the California Solar & Storage Association. "The utilities will be buying power from networks of batteries and heat pumps instead of power plants and long-distance power lines."

Newsom also signed SB 868, from state Sen. Scott Wiener, enabling Californians to use portable, plug-in solar panels to cut their energy bills. Utah and eight other states beat California to legalizing so-called balcony solar. New York could follow if Gov. Kathy Hochul signs a similar bill.

While many VPP efforts to date are demonstrations or otherwise limited in scope, total capacity in California is already close to multiple gigawatts. "A Tesla-Sunrun VPP dispatched 580MW of peak power to California's grid in a recent heatwave, and Tesla currently has over 1.3GW of residential capacity deployed under its own VPP in California alone," said Pete Tillotson, a senior analyst at Benchmark Minerals.

VPPs are typically used when energy demand is extremely high, according to Tillotson. "However, as they mature into a more established asset for grid operators, we will likely see capacities continue to increase across California and the country," he said.

These Clean Energy Players Benefit

Tillotson sees VPPs as an already viable method of protecting households from rising energy prices. "Enabling more residential capacity and crucially incentivizing its use as an asset will be critical in (VPP) development."

The likely beneficiaries of the new regulations include battery makers Tesla and Enphase, plus installers such as OC Solar, added Tillotson. He also sees upside for companies that lease solar systems and VPP software makers such as Renew Home.

"Sunrun will likely be the big beneficiary," said BloombergNEF analyst Cosmo van Steenis. "They already operate a VPP in California called CalReady and are launching another with Google, Tesla and PG&E." He added, "Batteries have already led to higher margins for the company, even amidst a rocky time for the residential solar industry, so more revenue streams in their largest market will likely help Sunrun."

Tesla Stock And The EV Angle

Tesla has been talking about linking EVs, home battery systems, and the grid for years now. The automaker expanded support for vehicle-to-home charging — "to power your home during power outages" — to its mass-market Model 3 and Model Y vehicles in October. While Tesla makes most of its money selling cars, its higher-margin energy business is posting stronger growth. Still, Tesla stock has shed more than 16% of its value this year. It's due to report Q2 earnings on Oct. 21.

Another automaker, GM (GM), said in June that it will make bi-directional charging standard. Doing so enables stored energy to flow from its plugged-in EVs during peak demand.

The broader push into electrics — which are effectively battery systems on wheels — comes as AI energy consumption and grid upgrades hammer ratepayers in some parts of the U.S., while the diesel squeeze hikes home heating bills in others. EV demand plunged in the states with the early end of tax incentives last year. Yet, hybrid and EV sales are rising again with gas prices as the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran squeezes global fuel supplies.

title: drilling does not equal more jobs: Why the link between production and employment has broken
description:
Concern over declining oil and gas jobs has been central to the debate over new drilling.
The link between production and employment is broken Even during the period defined by industry as a “supportive regulatory and fiscal environment”, employment within the oil and gas sector fell sharply.
Between 2013 and 20191, which included the introduction of the Conservative Government’s policy of “maximum economic recovery” (MER), UK net oil and gas production increased by 19% (with net gas production rising only 7% and net oil production by 29%)2.
Oil and gas historical production and projections were taken from the February 2026 NSTA production projections data.
Average annual trends in oil and gas production were calculated by averaging the year-on-year percentage change in production over the chosen time period.
text:
Concern over declining oil and gas jobs has been central to the debate over new drilling. Oil and gas workers have borne the brunt of a declining basin, an industry that has consistently prioritised shareholder profits over investment in the transition, and a total lack of transition planning from the Scottish Government and – until recently – the UK Government. There is still far to go for both, but the data is clear: the answer to a decline in oil and gas employment is not new drilling.

The link between production and employment is broken

Even during the period defined by industry as a “supportive regulatory and fiscal environment”, employment within the oil and gas sector fell sharply. Between 2013 and 20191, which included the introduction of the Conservative Government’s policy of “maximum economic recovery” (MER), UK net oil and gas production increased by 19% (with net gas production rising only 7% and net oil production by 29%)2. Despite these increases, the direct oil and gas workforce fell by 17%, and the combined direct and indirect workforce fell by 35%3.

"UK production increased by nearly 20% between 2013 and 2019 - but the wider O&G workforce fell by 35%"

These findings are supported by other independent analysis that showed although “for most of the basin's history, production and employment moved in lockstep...this link has now broken”.

This analysis also found that employment in Aberdeen’s oil and gas sector fell by 11% between 2014 and 2019, while production rose by a fifth. Output and jobs moved in the opposite direction during the one period when more oil was actually being produced.

When we take a broader look at the last decade we see that direct and indirect oil and gas jobs have halved, reducing from 247,400 jobs in 2014 to 115,000 in 2024.3 Oil and gas jobs are predicted to decline regardless of predicted levels of production.

The basin is still in decline

Under the industry-termed “supportive regulatory and fiscal environment”, production remained roughly flat (or rose modestly, depending on your starting-date assumption). But the basin is still in overall decline.

The North Sea is an ultra-mature basin where production has been falling for decades, with most of the oil and gas it once contained now already extracted. Since 1998, production has decreased annually by approximately 5% on average, and the North Sea Transition Authority forecasts an average annual decline of about 10% until 20504.

Despite the previous Government's efforts, modest production increases did not meaningfully meet UK demand. From 2010 to 2024, the Conservative Government handed out hundreds of new North Sea oil and gas licences across seven licensing rounds which so far have led to just 36 days of extra gas.

It is clear that efforts to squeeze additional drops from a dwindling basin did not stop thousands of job cuts or substantially increase domestic gas production to sufficiently meet demand. Workers need a plan for what comes next and it can’t be solely left up to industry. It is crucial that the Government supports oil and gas workers’ transition.

What is needed from Government

We cannot afford to leave the transition up to oil and gas companies, the vast majority of which have not planned to shift investment away from fossil fuels. Their plan is to extract as much profit out of the declining basin as they can before quitting.

If this Burnham Government is serious about rewiring the country and delivering growth to left-behind communities, it should start by rejecting new oil and gas projects like Rosebank and Jackdaw that will do next to nothing to stem the decline in North Sea jobs, and instead focus all of its efforts on investing in renewables and other industries that have a future – like offshore wind manufacturing. To approve new oil and gas now would be to kick the can down the road while sending contradictory messages to investors and drawing focus away from what is actually needed to create jobs.

The focus should then be on enabling the UK’s energy workforce to transfer into these jobs – focusing on the communities and regions most affected by oil and gas decline.

The UK’s oil capital, Aberdeen, has had a “disastrous decade”, and is now forecast to have the slowest growth of any UK city. But, with focused investment, and more municipal ownership of renewables projects, jobs and wealth can be brought back to this community and others like it.

‍

Methodology

Changes in oil and gas production and the workforce between 2013 and 2019 were calculated as the percentage change between the 2013 and 2019 figures. We chose 2013 as the start year to capture pre-policy change as a baseline. The end year, 2019, was chosen to avoid COVID's effect on employment in 2020.

Oil and gas historical production and projections were taken from the February 2026 NSTA production projections data.

Oil and gas direct and indirect workforce estimates were taken from the annual OEUK Workforce Insights reports (2017 to 2024) and the OEUK Economy and People report (2025).

Average annual trends in oil and gas production were calculated by averaging the year-on-year percentage change in production over the chosen time period.

Neuse River Resource Recovery Facility Bioenergy Recovery Project

Raleigh, N.C.

Award of Merit

Submitted by: Crowder Construction Co.

Owner: Raleigh Water

Lead Design Firm: Hazen and Sawyer

General Contractor: Crowder Construction Co.

Constructed at North Carolina’s largest wastewater treatment plant for the city of Raleigh, this $205.4-million project converts wastewater biosolids into renewable natural gas. It integrates thermal hydrolysis and anaerobic digestion, using high heat and pressure to increase biogas production, expand digester capacity and reduce biosolids volumes by about 50%. The resulting biosolids meet EPA Class A standards for unrestricted reuse, while biogas is upgraded to pipeline-quality renewable natural gas.

The team encountered poorly compacted soils and large subsurface boulders. Rather than install deeper foundations, crews preloaded the soils with material from a nearby city-owned borrow area and crushed excavated boulders for aggregate base.

Constructed within an active 75-million-gallon-per-day wastewater treatment facility, the project required careful sequencing and coordination to maintain uninterrupted treatment operations throughout construction. Tie-ins, shutdowns and process transitions were planned with plant staff to ensure continuous service and regulatory compliance.

The facility now supplies renewable natural gas to more than 70 GoRaleigh transit buses daily, making Raleigh the first municipality in North Carolina to fuel its transit fleet with gas produced from its own wastewater system. The project also reduces hauling and disposal needs while generating revenue from surplus gas sales.

text:
LANSING -- Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel has joined a coalition of 26 states, counties, and cities in filing a lawsuit against the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) challenging its final rule weakening corporate average fuel economy (CAFE) standards for new passenger cars and light trucks. Historically, NHTSA's standards have reduced consumer costs by improving fuel efficiency for vehicles, placed downward pressure on gas prices by reducing fuel consumption, protected the U.S. economy from global oil shocks, and reduced pollution from tailpipes and refineries. However, the final rule significantly weakens fuel economy standards and hurts both consumers and the environment.

In the lawsuit filed in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit, the coalition alleges that NHTSA's new rule is contrary to law and that NHTSA contravenes its mandate from Congress to set fuel economy standards at their "maximum feasible" level. Far from "maximum feasible," NHTSA's backsliding standards for the next five years require less efficiency than what the U.S. fleet actually achieved in 2021.

"Michigan knows better than most what is at stake when it comes to fuel economy and the future of the auto industry," said Attorney General Nessel. "The government should be encouraging automotive innovation that our workers, manufacturers and communities have helped drive for generations. This new rule leaves Michigan families more exposed than ever to the swings of global oil prices and I stand firmly with my colleagues in telling NHTSA it's time to follow the Congressional mandate."

In 1975, Congress enacted the Energy Policy and Conservation Act, which requires NHTSA to establish "maximum feasible" fuel economy standards for new vehicles that reflect technological feasibility, economic practicability, the effect of other motor vehicle standards of the government, and the need to conserve energy.

The final rule misinterprets NHTSA's statutory authority and improperly forces the agency to ignore the presence of millions of electric vehicles in the nation's existing fleet, leading to a flawed and dramatically distorted analysis of the "maximum feasible" fuel economy level that the auto industry can achieve. NHTSA's novel reinterpretation of the law renders the federal fuel economy program toothless, unable to protect consumers against rising gas prices or the ongoing global oil shock from President Trump's war.

In their lawsuit, the coalition alleges that NHTSA's final rule is arbitrary and capricious and violates the Administrative Procedure Act and the Energy Policy and Conservation Act.

In filing this lawsuit, Attorney General Nessel joins the attorneys general of Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, the District of Columbia, Hawai'i, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, and the City and County of San Francisco, as well as the City of Chicago, the City and County of Denver, and the City of New York.

name: EPA
title: The EPA Is About to Hand Oil and Gas Companies a Huge Methane-Related Gift
authors: Rachel Santarsiero, Jake Bittle, Naveena Sadasivam, Ari Berman, Sophie Hurwitz, Anna Merlan, Inae Oh, Alex Nguyen, Amy Littlefield
description:
The environmental agency was “within days,” he told them, of releasing the draft reconsideration of a major Biden-era oil and gas methane rule.
The oil and gas sector is one of the largest sources of methane emissions in the United States and is responsible for one-third of global methane emissions.
Previous regulations attempted to rein in those emissions, as well as other harmful air pollution emitted by oil and natural gas operations.
Now, with the EPA’s expected overhaul of Quad O, methane emissions can potentially be deregulated entirely.
And in April, Continental Resources, Chord Energy, and Kraken Oil & Gas Partners LLC wrote letters to the EPA asking the agency to allow operators to continue routine flaring.
text:
Last week, less than a month after rolling back power plant pollution standards, Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin addressed an audience of oil and gas executives at the New Mexico Oil and Gas Association’s annual meeting in Santa Fe. The environmental agency was “within days,” he told them, of releasing the draft reconsideration of a major Biden-era oil and gas methane rule. The new proposal would weaken regulations on oil and gas operators to allow for additional leaking, venting, and flaring—a move that could significantly raise emissions of the greenhouse gas super-pollutant.

Methane has 80 times more heat-trapping potential than carbon dioxide over a 20-year life span, and some scientists and policy experts say reducing the gas could help pull “the emergency brake” for climate change. The oil and gas sector is one of the largest sources of methane emissions in the United States and is responsible for one-third of global methane emissions. Previous regulations attempted to rein in those emissions, as well as other harmful air pollution emitted by oil and natural gas operations.

Zeldin said the new EPA measure would save taxpayers $45 billion. “Americans must be able to afford to heat their homes in the winter and fill up their car and drive to work,” Zeldin said in a press statement issued during the meeting. “They can’t do that when the people producing the energy are weighed down by unnecessary burdens. The Trump EPA is committed to fixing this so the US can reach its full energy potential.”

In line with advancing the Trump administration’s determination to “[unleash] American energy,” the revisions would significantly weaken pollution controls for older and leakier oil and gas wells. It would also rescind the agency’s Methane Super Emitter Program, a third-party monitoring system designed to report major leaks and blowouts on oil and gas wells, and ease regulations for other operation components that work in tandem to capture, destroy, or recover methane.

Some environmental advocates argue that the EPA’s proposed regulatory rollback reflects a coordinated industry wish list. “Lee Zeldin’s EPA is giving oil and gas corporations exactly what they’ve long wanted,” said Julia Kane, a researcher with oil and gas watchdog Fieldnotes, “a toothless methane standard they can use to pretend they’re well-regulated, all while they continue to knowingly leak and flare dangerous amounts of the heat-trapping gas.” The EPA did not respond to a request for comment by the time of publication.

According to a Fieldnotes report Kane published last month, industry communications, records obtained through the Freedom of Information Act, and statements from oil and gas executives revealed a coordinated industry strategy in which fossil fuel groups maneuvered behind the scenes to avoid regulatory accountability. Fieldnotes reached out to the named companies prior to publishing the report, and although several industry groups pushed back on Fieldnotes’ characterizations of their policy goals, none refuted the specific claims on which those characterizations were based.

The report also details how several oil and gas companies and trade associations worked with members of the second Trump administration’s EPA and congressional Republicans to eliminate the Waste Emissions Charge, the first direct fee the US government has ever used to penalize oil and gas producers for excess greenhouse gas emissions, and “eviscerate” the overarching methane regulatory program created by the Biden administration. The EPA met with oil and gas industry representatives at least three dozen times during President Donald Trump’s first year of his second term to discuss methane regulations, according to agency visitor logs.

Following the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act, the Biden administration proposed key revisions to preexisting methane rules that crucially altered how companies were required to estimate their methane pollution, including a rule targeting leaking, venting, and flaring. This rule, known as OOOOb/c or “Quad O,” which Zeldin is now proposing to gut, regulated methane emitted from new and existing oil and gas operations and imposed a ban on routine flaring. When the rule was finalized in 2024, oil and gas groups promptly sued, but the lawsuit has been temporarily halted.

Now, with the EPA’s expected overhaul of Quad O, methane emissions can potentially be deregulated entirely. According to reporting last week in E&E News, two sources briefed on the rule and granted anonymity said the agency’s move could likely “leave the door open for EPA to ultimately opt out of regulating methane from oil and gas operations.”

Fracking billionaire Harold Hamm—described by Trump as a longtime friend and “amazing man”—has helped pushed for this outcome. Hamm is the founder and longtime executive chairman of the Domestic Energy Producers Alliance (DEPA), which is the only oil and gas trade group to publicly support the EPA’s climate denial rationale in its February decision rescinding the 2009 endangerment finding, the landmark decision that allowed the agency to regulate greenhouse gases and link emissions to things like public health and human welfare. On the same day this action was taken, DEPA sent a letter to Zeldin encouraging the EPA to repeal or revise methane regulations dependent on the legal determination. In an internal newsletter, DEPA also argued that the EPA didn’t have the authority to regulate methane after the agency repealed the finding.

“Hamm has tremendous sway over Trump,” Kane told me. “If EPA’s proposal gives the agency the option to completely deregulate methane from the oil and gas industry, that’s likely Hamm’s influence.”

Other industry groups have taken a more subtle yet no less coordinated approach in pushing the administration to defang methane rules, according to Fieldnotes’ reporting. For example, a coalition led by the Independent Petroleum Association of America pushed the EPA to create a separate category for stripper wells—low-producing wells with disproportionately high methane emissions—to shield them from regulation. The American Petroleum Institute has been arguing since the Biden administration originally established the Super Emitter Program that companies should be notified of third-party monitoring plans ahead of time, allowing industry to avoid meaningful outside accountability. And in April, Continental Resources, Chord Energy, and Kraken Oil & Gas Partners LLC wrote letters to the EPA asking the agency to allow operators to continue routine flaring.

These standards are still in review at the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs, but Zeldin reassured his audience that the reconsideration would be published within days.

“The oil and gas industry says it’s a ‘good-faith’ partner eager to help craft regulations, but time and time again, it’s worked behind the scenes to delay and weaken them,” Kane said. “As a result, the United States today emits more methane from its oil and gas sector than any other country in the world.”
