text:
The uranium hexafluoride, which is enriched to 4.95% uranium-235, is currently held at "a US nuclear fuel facility outside the state of California", Bluecore Energy said, without giving details about the quantity of uranium involved.

The company is developing its first maritime nuclear energy system and conducting research and development on a non-fuelled maritime reactor module prototype. Unlike conventional nuclear power plants built around permanent land-based sites, Bluecore Energy says its systems are designed from the beginning for deployment on floating maritime platforms, an architecture that creates flexibility for where they can operate.

The initial 10 MWe system could power the equivalent of about 15,000 homes or scale to meet the power needs of a major port. Designed to be fuelled once for years of operation, the reactors can be paired together for scale to provide a new power source for ports, utilities, data centres, offshore infrastructure, and communities facing energy constraints.

The company recently announced a USD50 million seed financing and is also engaged in pre-application engagement with both the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission and US Coast Guard. In June, it received an Approval in Principle from the American Bureau of Shipping for its floating nuclear power plant design - the first such approval awarded to a US-designed floating nuclear power plant - and is now advancing several key workstreams in parallel.

"We've moved quickly since launching Bluecore Energy, but speed only matters if it is paired with rigour," said Kofi Asante, founder and CEO of Bluecore Energy. "We are putting the pieces in place across fuel, testing, engineering, safety, regulation and maritime classification at the same time. That is what it takes to turn this technology into a real system, and ultimately deliver reliable, zero-emission energy where it is needed most."

The company says that "securing the enriched uranium represents a tangible step beyond reactor design and non-fuelled hardware development and toward the physical fuel infrastructure required for future fueled testing".

Per Jander, a director on WMC's nuclear fuel team, said: "As a leading intermediary in the global nuclear fuel market, WMC is excited by the emergence of marine nuclear and proud to bring our expertise to a new generation of reactor developers like Bluecore Energy. Establishing a reliable nuclear fuel supply is a fundamental part of moving any reactor programme forward."

name: EVs
title: Electric Vehicle Subsidy U-Turn Leaves Factories and Workers Stranded
description:
This dramatic reduction in EV production illuminates a key economic reality.
For almost twenty years, American auto manufacturers knew that Washington was stimulating EV demand.
A broader regulatory regime consisted of stringent fuel-economy requirements and government support for domestic battery production.
US automakers clearly anticipated higher US EV demand than ultimately materialized.
Detroit must attempt to forecast consumer preferences, gas prices, battery costs, and the like in order to determine EV production.
text:
Nearly 1,000 plant workers near Kansas City find themselves on indefinite layoff. The reason for this, according to a union official? A gap of about 115,000 vehicles. General Motors had been on pace to produce about 150,000 Chevrolet Bolts before early 2027, buy now expect to only produce about 35,000 — a cut of 75 percent. Washington removing its $7,500 tax credit for EV purchases last September, and that federal policy change caused demand to fall sharply. GM plans on adding production of gasoline-powered automobiles at said plant, namely the Chevrolet Equinox and Buick Envision SUV, but this has yet to occur. This dramatic reduction in EV production illuminates a key economic reality. Lawmakers may introduce and eliminate tax credits or rewrite regulatory targets quickly, but manufacturers cannot retool production processes with nearly the same speed.

For almost twenty years, American auto manufacturers knew that Washington was stimulating EV demand. Beginning in 2008, a federal consumer credit worth $7,500 increased the expected return of producing and selling electric vehicles. A broader regulatory regime consisted of stringent fuel-economy requirements and government support for domestic battery production.

With federal policy in place, expected technological improvement, falling battery costs, and expanding consumer demand encouraged EV-specific investment. Market and governmental variables all contributed to this vision of the future in Detroit. While not the only cause, DC’s EV-related policies influenced decisions about what kinds of vehicle production will or ought to exist in five, ten, or twenty years.

Here, we find the economic rub. Capital becomes less and less malleable as it progresses through production: capital goods become increasingly specialized as resources are committed to the production of particular goods. Purchased iron may be directed into a handful of lines of production. Once the iron has been turned into a skillet or oven, it becomes harder to use in alternate lines of production. Good luck using that skillet as an engine block for a car.

Companies, then, have to choose their investments carefully. In 2020, GM announced a $27 billion investment plan in EVs for five years, a 35 percent increase in its plans from before the pandemic. In the month following the end of the EV credit last year, GM reported a “negative impact of $1.6 billion in its next quarter.”

GM could have used that $27 billion to finance myriad high-potential projects. Once GM started spending that money, though, the investment turned into particular things: specialized factory layouts, battery equipment, vehicle tooling, worker training, and logistical networks, just to name a few. The further down the production line resources moved, the less interchangeable they became. A battery-production line worth $100 million is not economically equivalent to $100 million of internal-combustion-engine production capacity simply because the accounting value is the same. They are not equally suitable for both types of production. If production plans have to change afterward, capital must be modified, combined with new capital, sold at a loss, or redirected as best as possible — and quite possibly to a lower-valued alternative, given the partial transformation of the resources already completed.

US automakers clearly anticipated higher US EV demand than ultimately materialized. In fact, through September of this year, US EV sales are down about 31 percent in 2026, accounting for only 6 percent of new-vehicle sales, after sitting at 8.5 percent in 2025. Hybrids, however, are up 23 percent, representing about 16 percent of the current US market.

Businesses can and frequently do misjudge consumers without any interference from the government. Per the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, 50 percent of small businesses fail within five years. Part of the EV adjustment is almost certainly a necessary market correction to overly optimistic forecasts that may have existed without government interference. EVs now constitute 23 percent of new-car sales in Europe, spurred by its own cocktail of regulatory incentives.

That said, entrepreneurs must take regime uncertainty into consideration if they hope to survive. Detroit must attempt to forecast consumer preferences, gas prices, battery costs, and the like in order to determine EV production. On top of that, it must develop an answer to the question: “what will Washington’s rules be in 10 years?”

This is an especially difficult task when even DC’s own goals are not necessarily implemented. Some two dozen states, cities, counties, and environmental groups are contesting the new fuel-economy rules issued on September 28. This creates a wonderfully terrible need to predict not only current regulations, but whether said rules will survive judicial review, the upcoming midterms, and a new Congress in January.

And so, we return to Kansas City. General Motors can stop its Chevrolet Bolt production much quicker than it can change the factories and capital equipment it’s dedicated to producing them. Expiring tax credits, ever-changing regulatory targets, and an uncertain court case can change circumstances and conditions in an instant. Meanwhile, factory floors, machinery, supply logistics, and worker skills cannot adapt at the same pace.

Industrial policy, then, has a greater influence than just redirecting money. It has the effect of changing expectations, then guiding investments, which in turn become physical capital with increasing specificity. Factories cannot be refitted and supply lines rerouted as quickly as pens can alter laws. Manipulation of expected returns manifests itself in real production decisions — and misallocation — of our scarce resources.

title: Data centers in Texas and New Mexico may upend climate goals - The Texas Tribune
authors: Diego Mendoza-Moyers, Paul Ratje, El Paso Matters, ProPublica, visuals  Paul Ratje, for The Texas Tribune

text:
Sign up for The Brief, The Texas Tribune’s daily newsletter that keeps readers up to speed on the most essential Texas news.

This article is co-published with El Paso Matters and ProPublica as part of an initiative to report on local control of government. Sign up to receive ProPublica’s biggest stories as soon as they’re published.

Last December, New Mexico officials celebrated publication of a plan to address climate change, designed to dramatically reduce the state’s greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. A few months later, just across the state line in Texas, El Paso city officials adopted their own such plan with a similar ambition.

Each report cost millions of dollars to draft, but neither one took into account how the construction of data centers could upend climate goals in both places.

Work is underway in Doña Ana County in southern New Mexico on one of the largest data center developments in the country: Project Jupiter, built by Austin-based Oracle. Twenty miles away in El Paso, construction is underway on another massive data center, this one built by Meta Platforms.

A third, larger data center project is planned less than a 30-minute drive from the Meta site, on the Fort Bliss Army post in east El Paso.

The data centers are “going to undo a lot of the very expensive and very meaningful work a lot of people are doing,” New Mexico state climatologist Dave DuBois told El Paso Matters.

The sites are among a wave of data centers under construction across the country, driven by the rapidly escalating demand for artificial intelligence services like Claude and ChatGPT. Such projects have drawn intense scrutiny in recent months, as residents and elected officials have questioned their impact on communities’ water supplies, household electric bills and air quality. Texas alone has 596 data centers that are either in operation or planned across Texas as of early September, according to research by The Texas Tribune.

But the projects located in this population center of 1.2 million, which encompasses El Paso and parts of southern New Mexico, are particularly notable because of their combined scope. When fully built out, the three data centers, each with its own power plant, will emit millions of tons of greenhouse gas emissions, equivalent to the planet-warming emissions released by more than two million cars in a year.

They will also release air pollutants like particulate matter and nitrogen oxides, which directly affect local air quality and human health. The Meta and Project Jupiter data centers are expected to release these kinds of pollutants at relatively low levels, according to paperwork submitted to state regulators. But even a small increase in air pollution can still negatively impact communities close to and downwind of the data center sites, said Shaolei Ren, a professor of electrical and computer engineering at University of California, Riverside.

“The health impacts can be significant for local communities,” Ren said.

Because Project Jupiter, Meta and the Fort Bliss data centers are in two different states, and because there is no single federal regulation governing climate change or emissions, regulators have largely considered the projects’ impacts separately.

“We’ve never had a national climate law passed by Congress,” said Ari Peskoe, director of the Electricity Law Initiative at Harvard Law School. “And so what we’ve had in this country are primarily state and local efforts.”

The result is that officials in one state have little say over a project happening minutes away from them.

Texas and New Mexico also take different approaches to dealing with climate change. New Mexico has codified greenhouse gas reduction targets into state law; Texas has not.

New Mexico state Rep. Sarah Silva, a Democrat, represents the community of Chaparral, directly across the state line from Meta’s data center site in northeast El Paso. Her state has the power to regulate air quality and impose noise requirements, but only in New Mexico, not at a Texas construction site, even if it’s only a few hundred yards away.

Likewise, residents living in west El Paso across the state line from Project Jupiter have no say in the project despite sharing an aquifer that crosses the state boundary. Emissions do not remain within the state where they originate, Silva said.

“This is why we need federal regulation,” said Silva. “How do we knit something together that makes sense for our region when actually this is the job of the federal government?”

Though they profess a desire to mitigate the impacts of climate change, local governments in El Paso and Doña Ana counties green-lit these projects in a part of the country seeing rapidly rising temperatures. The counties offered Meta and Project Jupiter tax incentives in exchange for corporate investment in their communities, job creation and, hopefully, the ability to attract more technology companies to the region.

State officials have also provided incentives. More than a decade ago, Texas legislators approved a data center sales tax break, which exempts the facilities from paying sales tax on equipment they purchase, a decision that could now cost the state $3.2 billion in revenue over the next two years, according to The Texas Tribune.

New Mexico lawmakers declined to advance a bill creating a similar tax break for data centers in 2021. But in 2025, they passed an unrelated law allowing large facilities such as Project Jupiter to generate their own electricity using natural gas. The law exempts these private power systems, known as microgrids, from renewable energy requirements, even as New Mexico requires electric utilities to source 50% of the power they sell from clean energy by 2030.

The power plants that keep data centers running typically produce large amounts of emissions like carbon dioxide and methane that drive global climate change over time. Combined, the plants proposed for Project Jupiter and Meta’s data center could emit up to 10 million tons of planet-warming emissions annually. Comparatively, the region spanning El Paso County and neighboring Hudspeth County released 8.4 million tons of greenhouse gases in 2019. (The Army has shared scant information about the Fort Bliss data center, so it’s not clear what level of emissions the facility will produce.)

“This does add to our greenhouse gas emissions in a massive way,” said Gunnar Schade, an associate professor of atmospheric sciences at Texas A&M University. “This is a huge source.”

An Unprecedented Amount of Energy

Silva, the New Mexico representative, was initially supportive of Project Jupiter, in part seeing it as an opportunity to create long-term jobs. Last year, she voted in favor of a bill that included an amendment — tacked on by state Sen. Michael Padilla, a Democrat from Albuquerque — that allows facilities like Project Jupiter, which aren’t connected to the local power grid, a 20-year exemption from clean energy laws, allowing them to generate all their electricity with fossil fuels.

“We worked this bill pretty much the entire session, but it did not quite get done. So, we found a piece of legislation that was very similar,” Padilla said in an interview last year. “That’s the legislative process. You have to be very creative to get your work done.”

But Silva soon soured on the project out of concern that it won’t employ enough local workers and because it won’t rely on zero-emission renewable energy. Oracle has said the data center will have 750 full-time employees when it’s up and running. The company told Doña Ana County officials in early September that nearly 3,700 people had worked at the site during construction up to that point.

Silva and other state lawmakers have said they voted for Padilla’s bill without realizing the broader implications for a data center project in the southern part of the state.

“State regulators, state legislators, I think, were so caught off guard at the speed at which these hyperscale data centers showed up in all of our communities almost simultaneously,” Silva said. “I would support a moratorium.”

The amount of energy Project Jupiter needs is unprecedented in the region: The data center will receive electricity from an on-site power plant made up of fuel cells built by a company called Bloom Energy. Bloom has said the plant will have the ability to produce up to 2.45 gigawatts of electricity — enough to power around 1.5 million homes and more than El Paso Electric has ever supplied to its 465,000 residential and commercial customers at one time, according to the utility’s corporate reports.

New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham, a Democrat, has specifically lauded Oracle’s promise to use fuel cells for electricity instead of natural gas turbines, which would have used more water and produced more air pollution. However, an air permit — a state-granted license that authorizes industrial facilities to emit a predetermined amount of pollution — would allow the fuel cells to produce up to 8.8 million tons of greenhouse gas emissions per year. Lujan Grisham didn’t address questions from El Paso Matters about the impact of these additional climate emissions.

The Meta power plant in El Paso could release up to 1.3 million tons of climate emissions every year, according to an estimate calculated by El Paso Matters based on El Paso Electric regulatory filings and the Environmental Protection Agency’s emissions factors. Nancy Seidman, a senior adviser with the Regulatory Assistance Project, a nonprofit that advocates for clean energy, also backed up that assessment.

“Regulators should weigh all emissions and other impacts like water usage, noise and local air pollution, which can affect public health, when they make decisions about data center projects,” Seidman wrote in an email to El Paso Matters. “This is particularly important when projects are phased over time, so that an accurate account can be made of the total, holistic impacts.”

The data center planned for Fort Bliss is expected to use 3 gigawatts of electricity that would likely be supplied by natural gas turbines, according to officials with the Department of Defense, who shared details with reporters during a briefing in April. The Army has issued few other details about the project because it is still in “exclusive negotiations” with the developer, Carlyle Group, a large publicly traded private equity firm.

Carlyle Group did not respond to a request for comment.

“These are cities in terms of their electricity consumption,” Peskoe, of Harvard Law School, said of AI hyperscale data center campuses such as Oracle’s and Meta’s. The facilities are cropping up so fast that “the pace of this and the scale of this — I think there’s no real parallel, at least for 50, 60, 70 years, but probably ever for the U.S. power industry.”

Facilities in New Mexico seeking a state air permit are required by law to disclose estimated amounts of air pollutants and greenhouse gas emissions the project will release. And the state Environment Department has spent months evaluating Project Jupiter’s air permit application, which was submitted in April. A spokesperson for the environmental department didn’t respond to emailed questions.

By contrast, the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality only requires project developers to disclose information about pollutants that affect local air quality, and not about greenhouse gas emissions, which are what contribute to climate change.

So when El Paso Electric sought an air permit last fall for the Meta data center’s natural gas power plant, the utility didn’t have to share estimated greenhouse gas emissions. The Texas commission approved the permit 20 days after it was filed, following an expedited review.

Meta directed questions about its data center’s power plant to El Paso Electric. The electric company declined to share estimates of the plant’s greenhouse gas emissions but said in a statement that the Texas environmental commission had reviewed and authorized the Meta power plant “under a standard permit, which is specifically for projects with limited and well-controlled emissions.” The statement said the facility will “operate in compliance with state and federal standards.”

A spokesperson for the agency said, “All Standard Permits have gone through formal notice and comment procedures and have been adopted by the Commission in a public meeting.”

These plants will be releasing large amounts of greenhouse gases even as climate change has become increasingly evident in the El Paso metro area, which sits where Texas’ westernmost boundary meets New Mexico and northern Mexico. El Paso’s temperatures have risen faster than those of almost any other city in the U.S. since 1970, according to Climate Central, a nonprofit that quantifies climate shifts throughout the United States. Drought driven by climate change has amplified the impact of wind storms that fill the air in El Paso with hazardous dust in the spring and summertime.

This year has been the hottest on record in El Paso through the first nine months of 2026, according to the National Weather Service. Similar records have been set across the state line in New Mexico.

“If we started to do these kinds of things — having big data centers with natural-gas-fired turbines — it’s kind of like bringing back a lot of the retired plants that were more dirty, like coal,” said DuBois, the New Mexico state climatologist.

Fernando Berjano, El Paso’s climate coordinator, wouldn’t comment specifically on effects resulting from the data centers in the region, but he said the kinds of power plants tied to them produce greenhouse gases that will make it harder for the city to meet its climate goals, as well as produce air pollutants.

If emissions increase in the El Paso area, “that has an impact on air quality, that has an impact on pollution,” Berjano said, “which is something that we all know is not good.”

The Road Ahead for Data Centers

Although construction is already underway on the Project Jupiter and Meta data centers, regulatory hurdles remain for both facilities. The public hearing on the Project Jupiter air permit was scheduled to begin Sept. 14, but the New Mexico Supreme Court delayed it when opponents filed lawsuits challenging the state’s approval process and the facility’s use of groundwater.

The state Supreme Court last month lifted the stay. New Mexico more recently appointed an examiner to preside over the hearing that would authorize the facility’s emissions. Other legal challenges are making their way through the court system.

In Texas, El Paso Electric is still waiting for the state’s Public Utility Commission to approve construction of the power plant planned next to Meta’s data center, a decision that could come later this year.

Officials with both Project Jupiter and Meta have said they are taking steps to help mitigate the climate effects of their projects and plan to develop clean energy projects elsewhere to create new electricity sources and offset the greenhouse gases their data center power plants will release. Oracle also maintains that its emissions will be lower than what it sought in its air permit application and that it plans to get to net zero greenhouse emissions by 2031.

“Oracle is committed to building Project Jupiter responsibly and incorporating community feedback into our planning,” the company said in a statement.

The road ahead for data centers is unclear. Even once-supportive officials have softened or changed course: Last year, Lujan Grisham, New Mexico’s governor, said Project Jupiter “reaffirms New Mexico’s leadership in global trade, advanced manufacturing, and digital infrastructure.” In Texas, Gov. Greg Abbott at one point called his state “the epicenter of AI development.”

Now, amid growing opposition to Project Jupiter, Lujan Grisham recently said she takes seriously residents’ concerns about the data center “and expects any data center operating in New Mexico to meet the state’s rigorous environmental standards and use water responsibly.” This summer, Abbott called on the Texas Public Utility Commission to ensure the projects pay for their own infrastructure and don’t lead to higher electricity costs for residents. He also recommended the state Legislature pass a number of regulations related to data centers next year, many concerning water and electricity usage, and recently told the Texas Water Development Board to penalize data centers that do not report their water usage.

Abbott’s new edicts do not address air pollution or climate change, nor the effects that a data center project in one state can have on another.

Texas Democratic state Rep. Joe Moody, whose district includes much of west and northeast El Paso, near two of the data center projects, said Abbott’s proposals will likely shape the Texas Legislature’s debate over data-center-related policies next year but called them just a starting point.

“In the governor’s directives, we’re not talking about local control and local autonomy to make decisions on these projects,” he said. “And I do think that that’s a whole other lane of conversation that we’re going to get into next session.”

Diego Mendoza-Moyers is a reporter covering energy and the environment at El Paso Matters. He can be reached at diegom@elpasomatters.org.

text:
Even before Massachusetts voters weigh in on a record-breaking nine ballot questions this November, the process for proposing initiative petitions for the 2028 ballot has begun. The Attorney General's Office has certified a slate of fourteen initiative petitions for the 2028 statewide ballot, several with significant implications for the business community. The Office declined to certify four others. Proponents of the certified petitions must now collect 74,574 signatures and file them with local election officials by November 18, 2026, and then with the Secretary of State by December 2, 2026. As outlined in our prior post (found here), proponents who meet this threshold face a second signature requirement if the Legislature does not adopt their proposal.

Notably, the Attorney General’s Office’s most recent review of initiative petitions for the 2028 ballot is not the only opportunity for proponents to raise potential petitions for 2028. Proponents have until August 4, 2027, to submit additional petitions to the Attorney General for certification as part of her office’s final review process of petitions for the 2028 ballot.

Below is a rundown of some of the currently certified initiatives most likely to garner attention heading into 2028.

Non-Ionizing Radiation Research Agency (26-01)

Petition 26-01 would create a new independent state agency, the Office of Research and Technology Optimization (ORTO), to study and make recommendations about non-ionizing radiation from power lines, cell towers, wireless networks, and digital devices under an “As Safe as Reasonable and Achievable” standard. ORTO would publish research, build a public map of radiation levels alongside anonymized health statistics, and offer fee-based testing to municipalities.

Personal Income Tax Reduction (26-02)

Petition 26-02, which was submitted by former candidate for governor Brian Shortsleeve, would phase down the state personal income tax rate on wages, salaries, interest, dividends, and most long-term capital gains from the current 5.00% to 4.00% over three years. The rate would drop to 4.67% for tax year 2029, 4.33% for tax year 2030, and 4.00% beginning in tax year 2031. If enacted, this measure would represent a meaningful reduction in individual tax rates and could influence decisions around executive compensation, business formation, and talent retention in the state. At the same time, the resulting reduction in state tax revenue would likely require corresponding cuts to state spending, which could adversely affect organizations that rely on state funding, programs, or contracts.

Data Center Regulation (26-08)

Petition 26-08 would impose significant new requirements on data center construction and expansion in Massachusetts. Under the proposal, no city or town could permit a new or expanded data center unless the operator secures a contract with its electricity supplier guaranteeing that (1) the supplier will not increase electricity costs for other customers due to the data center, and (2) the supplier will produce sufficient 100% renewable energy to meet the facility's needs without reducing renewable resources available to other customers. Data center operators would also be required to post financial guarantees covering all infrastructure-related costs in the event of a shutdown, capacity reduction, or contract violation. Proposed limitations on data center construction are the subject of vigorous discussion in legislatures across the country. A potential ballot question on this topic is worth particular attention because it could lead to sweeping reforms without the opportunity for amendment and compromise inherent in the legislative process.

Online Advertising Tax for Social Media Programs (26-09)

Petition 26-09 would impose a 1% tax on the sale of advertisements delivered via the internet to recipients accessing the internet from a device with a Massachusetts IP address. Revenue would be deposited into a new fund, administered by the Secretary of Education, subject to appropriation, to develop school-, home-, and community-based programs helping parents and educators promote the safe and healthy use of social media by elementary and high school students.

Clean Energy Tax Credit (26-10)

Petition 26-10 would create a state income tax credit for the purchase of an electric vehicle, energy storage system, heat pump, or solar power system, equal to the lesser of $25,000 or 50% of the purchase price. The credit claimed in any year would be capped at the taxpayer’s state income tax liability, but unused credits could be carried forward for up to ten years. The proposal could affect demand for clean energy products and installers, as well as state revenue.

Property Tax Caps (26-14 and 26-15)

Two versions of a property tax cap were certified. Petition 26-14 would cap each parcel's annual property tax at 102.5% of the prior year's amount; Petition 26-15 adds a mechanism allowing a city or town, by a two-thirds vote, to seek voter approval to override the cap for a single year. Existing Proposition 2½ limits growth in a municipality’s overall levy limit—generally 2.5% per year plus new growth and overrides, subject to a ceiling of 2.5% of total property value—but does not cap any individual tax bill, which can rise by more than 2.5% in a given year. The petitions would instead impose a parcel-level limit. Property owners and commercial real estate interests could see greater predictability in tax bills, while municipalities have raised concerns about the impact on local revenue and services.

Sales, Use, and Gasoline Tax Reductions (26-12 and 26-17)

Two petitions would reduce consumption-based taxes. Petition 26-12 would phase out the state gasoline tax, reducing the current $0.24 per gallon rate to $0.16 beginning January 1, 2029, to $0.08 beginning January 1, 2030, and to zero beginning January 1, 2031, subject to appropriation. Fuel retailers, distributors, transportation-dependent businesses, and consumers would be directly affected, as would transportation and infrastructure programs that rely on gasoline tax revenue.

Petition 26-17 would cut the state sales and use tax rate from 6.25% to 5.00%, with a corresponding reduction in the deposit rate required of out-of-state building contractors. A lower sales tax rate could affect retailers, consumers, and construction firms, as well as organizations that rely on state funding, given that the sales tax is a major source of state revenue.

Felony Larceny Threshold (26-16)

Petition 26-16 would make larceny of property valued at more than $250 a felony, punishable by up to five years in state prison, or by a fine of up to $25,000 and up to two years in jail. The proposal would also allow all property stolen within a 180-day period to be aggregated in determining its value, regardless of whether the thefts occur at the same or multiple establishments, or in the same or multiple counties. The measure is likely to draw significant attention from retailers and others focused on organized retail theft, as well as from criminal justice stakeholders.

Other Petitions

Other certified petitions would extend collective bargaining rights to state employees (26-05) and legislative employees (26-06), eliminate legislative stipends (26-11), and create a hardship license pathway for drivers with lifetime license revocations (26-18).

Key Takeaways

Potential opponents of any of the certified petitions should monitor signature-gathering efforts in the months ahead, because measures that collect sufficient signatures will proceed to the Legislature and, absent legislative action, to the ballot. Importantly, certification by the Attorney General and collection of signatures are not the final word on what appears on the ballot: petitions that meet the initial signature threshold can be, and frequently are, challenged before the Supreme Judicial Court on the ground that they fail to satisfy the constitutional requirements for inclusion on the ballot. Stakeholders on either side of a measure should consider early whether such a challenge may be warranted or should be anticipated, as these proceedings move quickly and can determine whether a question reaches voters at all.

text:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

Khaliel Moses – press@oilchange.org

Clean Energy Finance Overtakes Fossil Fuels for the First Time, but G20 Governments and Development Banks Still Fund Fossil Fuel Lock-In

New analysis released during World Bank and IMF Annual Meetings finds billions still flow to fossil fuels, while low-income countries receive just 2% of clean energy finance

14 October 2026 – As governments gather for the World Bank and IMF Annual Meetings, new research by Oil Change International and Friends of the Earth U.S. reveals that international public finance for clean energy from G20 countries and Multilateral Development Banks (MDBs) has surpassed fossil fuel finance for the first time.

The new factsheet, Tipping the Scales: Assessing G20 and MDB International Finance Institutions’ Energy Finance, finds that public finance for fossil fuels from G20 countries’ international finance institutions and MDBs averaged at least $36.3 billion a year between 2023 and 2025, compared to $52.7 billion for clean energy during the same time period. Still, clean energy finance is nowhere near the scale needed to deliver a globally just transition nor is it flowing to where it is most needed, with just 2% supporting low-income countries. Just a handful of countries are driving fossil fuel lock-in. Together, Canada, Japan, the United States and Italy made up 75% of all of the G20’s fossil fuel finance.

MDBs provided an average of $3.4 billion a year in direct support for fossil fuel projects, and many continue to back fossil fuels through channels that are harder to track. The World Bank has provided at least $19 billion in fossil fuel finance since the Paris Agreement in 2016, more than any other MDB.

In June 2026, the World Bank Group backtracked on its commitment to deliver 45% of its finance as climate finance. With the World Bank Annual Meetings underway, themed ‘Empowering people, Building Resilience,’ the data calls into question how the World Bank can support true resilience while continuing to invest in fossil fuels that not only wreck the climate, but also undermine energy security and affordability. This has seen taxpayer backed money prop up record-breaking profits of the fossil fuel industry while regular households face soaring energy bills. This factsheet demonstrates which actors need to step up their commitments and speed up the shift away from fossil fuels to protect their people from volatile energy prices.

The factsheet has been released alongside updated energy finance data on energyfinance.org, and a first-ever publicly available carbon capture and storage (CCS) and hydrogen subsidies database, which tracks $79 billion in government subsidies. We found that these projects offer a lifeline to the fossil fuel industry instead of funding a just energy transition.

Claire O’Manique, Public Finance Researcher at Oil Change International said:

“This new dataset represents a tipping point. Clean energy financing overtaking fossil fuel financing for the first time is an important milestone, but it doesn’t mean we can sit back and count our wins. A just transition will not happen at the scale required without governments actively steering it through redirecting and mobilising public finance. Wealthy Governments must move first and fastest to phase out fossil fuels at home and meet their climate finance obligations. We are running out of time. Without a fossil fuel phaseout and public finance being redirected to drive a just energy transition, we will continue to see escalating climate disasters that come at a huge human and economic cost such as the deadly glacial flood disaster in Nepal.”

Kate DeAngelis, Economic Policy Deputy Director at Friends of the Earth U.S. said: “Important progress is being made to move the world’s largest economies away from supporting fossil fuels and shift that financing toward renewable energy projects. Unfortunately, laggards, including the United States and Japan, are continuing to prop up the fossil fuel industry instead of helping countries transition to sustainable economies.”

text:
Last December, New Mexico officials celebrated publication of a plan to address climate change, designed to dramatically reduce the state’s greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. A few months later, just across the state line in Texas, El Paso city officials adopted their own such plan with a similar ambition.

Each report cost millions of dollars to draft, but neither one took into account how the construction of data centers could upend climate goals in both places.

Work is underway in Doña Ana County in southern New Mexico on one of the largest data center developments in the country: Project Jupiter, built by Austin-based Oracle. Twenty miles away in El Paso, construction is underway on another massive data center, this one built by Meta Platforms.

A third, larger data center project is planned less than a 30-minute drive from the Meta site, on the Fort Bliss Army post in east El Paso.

The data centers are “going to undo a lot of the very expensive and very meaningful work a lot of people are doing,” New Mexico state climatologist Dave DuBois told El Paso Matters.

The sites are among a wave of data centers under construction across the country, driven by the rapidly escalating demand for artificial intelligence services like Claude and ChatGPT. Such projects have drawn intense scrutiny in recent months, as residents and elected officials have questioned their impact on communities’ water supplies, household electric bills and air quality. Texas alone has 596 data centers that are either in operation or planned across Texas as of early September, according to research by The Texas Tribune.

But the projects located in this population center of 1.2 million, which encompasses El Paso and parts of southern New Mexico, are particularly notable because of their combined scope. When fully built out, the three data centers, each with its own power plant, will emit millions of tons of greenhouse gas emissions, equivalent to the planet-warming emissions released by more than two million cars in a year.

They will also release air pollutants like particulate matter and nitrogen oxides, which directly affect local air quality and human health. The Meta and Project Jupiter data centers are expected to release these kinds of pollutants at relatively low levels, according to paperwork submitted to state regulators. But even a small increase in air pollution can still negatively impact communities close to and downwind of the data center sites, said Shaolei Ren, a professor of electrical and computer engineering at University of California, Riverside.

“The health impacts can be significant for local communities,” Ren said.

Because Project Jupiter, Meta and the Fort Bliss data centers are in two different states, and because there is no single federal regulation governing climate change or emissions, regulators have largely considered the projects’ impacts separately.

“We’ve never had a national climate law passed by Congress,” said Ari Peskoe, director of the Electricity Law Initiative at Harvard Law School. “And so what we’ve had in this country are primarily state and local efforts.”

The result is that officials in one state have little say over a project happening minutes away from them.

Texas and New Mexico also take different approaches to dealing with climate change. New Mexico has codified greenhouse gas reduction targets into state law; Texas has not.

New Mexico state Rep. Sarah Silva, a Democrat, represents the community of Chaparral, directly across the state line from Meta’s data center site in northeast El Paso. Her state has the power to regulate air quality and impose noise requirements, but only in New Mexico, not at a Texas construction site, even if it’s only a few hundred yards away.

Likewise, residents living in west El Paso across the state line from Project Jupiter have no say in the project despite sharing an aquifer that crosses the state boundary. Emissions do not remain within the state where they originate, Silva said.

“This is why we need federal regulation,” said Silva. “How do we knit something together that makes sense for our region when actually this is the job of the federal government?”

Though they profess a desire to mitigate the impacts of climate change, local governments in El Paso and Doña Ana counties green-lit these projects in a part of the country seeing rapidly rising temperatures. The counties offered Meta and Project Jupiter tax incentives in exchange for corporate investment in their communities, job creation and, hopefully, the ability to attract more technology companies to the region.

State officials have also provided incentives. More than a decade ago, Texas legislators approved a data center sales tax break, which exempts the facilities from paying sales tax on equipment they purchase, a decision that could now cost the state $3.2 billion in revenue over the next two years, according to The Texas Tribune.

New Mexico lawmakers declined to advance a bill creating a similar tax break for data centers in 2021. But in 2025, they passed an unrelated law allowing large facilities such as Project Jupiter to generate their own electricity using natural gas. The law exempts these private power systems, known as microgrids, from renewable energy requirements, even as New Mexico requires electric utilities to source 50% of the power they sell from clean energy by 2030.

The power plants that keep data centers running typically produce large amounts of emissions like carbon dioxide and methane that drive global climate change over time. Combined, the plants proposed for Project Jupiter and Meta’s data center could emit up to 10 million tons of planet-warming emissions annually. Comparatively, the region spanning El Paso County and neighboring Hudspeth County released 8.4 million tons of greenhouse gases in 2019. (The Army has shared scant information about the Fort Bliss data center, so it’s not clear what level of emissions the facility will produce.)

“This does add to our greenhouse gas emissions in a massive way,” said Gunnar Schade, an associate professor of atmospheric sciences at Texas A&M University. “This is a huge source.”

An Unprecedented Amount of Energy

Silva, the New Mexico representative, was initially supportive of Project Jupiter, in part seeing it as an opportunity to create long-term jobs. Last year, she voted in favor of a bill that included an amendment — tacked on by state Sen. Michael Padilla, a Democrat from Albuquerque — that allows facilities like Project Jupiter, which aren’t connected to the local power grid, a 20-year exemption from clean energy laws, allowing them to generate all their electricity with fossil fuels.

“We worked this bill pretty much the entire session, but it did not quite get done. So, we found a piece of legislation that was very similar,” Padilla said in an interview last year. “That’s the legislative process. You have to be very creative to get your work done.”

But Silva soon soured on the project out of concern that it won’t employ enough local workers and because it won’t rely on zero-emission renewable energy. Oracle has said the data center will have 750 full-time employees when it’s up and running. The company told Doña Ana County officials in early September that nearly 3,700 people had worked at the site during construction up to that point.

Silva and other state lawmakers have said they voted for Padilla’s bill without realizing the broader implications for a data center project in the southern part of the state.

“State regulators, state legislators, I think, were so caught off guard at the speed at which these hyperscale data centers showed up in all of our communities almost simultaneously,” Silva said. “I would support a moratorium.”

The amount of energy Project Jupiter needs is unprecedented in the region: The data center will receive electricity from an on-site power plant made up of fuel cells built by a company called Bloom Energy. Bloom has said the plant will have the ability to produce up to 2.45 gigawatts of electricity — enough to power around 1.5 million homes and more than El Paso Electric has ever supplied to its 465,000 residential and commercial customers at one time, according to the utility’s corporate reports.

New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham, a Democrat, has specifically lauded Oracle’s promise to use fuel cells for electricity instead of natural gas turbines, which would have used more water and produced more air pollution. However, an air permit — a state-granted license that authorizes industrial facilities to emit a predetermined amount of pollution — would allow the fuel cells to produce up to 8.8 million tons of greenhouse gas emissions per year. Lujan Grisham didn’t address questions from El Paso Matters about the impact of these additional climate emissions.

The Meta power plant in El Paso could release up to 1.3 million tons of climate emissions every year, according to an estimate calculated by El Paso Matters based on El Paso Electric regulatory filings and the Environmental Protection Agency’s emissions factors. Nancy Seidman, a senior adviser with the Regulatory Assistance Project, a nonprofit that advocates for clean energy, also backed up that assessment.

“Regulators should weigh all emissions and other impacts like water usage, noise and local air pollution, which can affect public health, when they make decisions about data center projects,” Seidman wrote in an email to El Paso Matters. “This is particularly important when projects are phased over time, so that an accurate account can be made of the total, holistic impacts.”

The data center planned for Fort Bliss is expected to use 3 gigawatts of electricity that would likely be supplied by natural gas turbines, according to officials with the Department of Defense, who shared details with reporters during a briefing in April. The Army has issued few other details about the project because it is still in “exclusive negotiations” with the developer, Carlyle Group, a large publicly traded private equity firm.

Carlyle Group did not respond to a request for comment.

“These are cities in terms of their electricity consumption,” Peskoe, of Harvard Law School, said of AI hyperscale data center campuses such as Oracle’s and Meta’s. The facilities are cropping up so fast that “the pace of this and the scale of this — I think there’s no real parallel, at least for 50, 60, 70 years, but probably ever for the U.S. power industry.”

Facilities in New Mexico seeking a state air permit are required by law to disclose estimated amounts of air pollutants and greenhouse gas emissions the project will release. And the state Environment Department has spent months evaluating Project Jupiter’s air permit application, which was submitted in April. A spokesperson for the environmental department didn’t respond to emailed questions.

By contrast, the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality only requires project developers to disclose information about pollutants that affect local air quality, and not about greenhouse gas emissions, which are what contribute to climate change.

So when El Paso Electric sought an air permit last fall for the Meta data center’s natural gas power plant, the utility didn’t have to share estimated greenhouse gas emissions. The Texas commission approved the permit 20 days after it was filed, following an expedited review.

Meta directed questions about its data center’s power plant to El Paso Electric. The electric company declined to share estimates of the plant’s greenhouse gas emissions but said in a statement that the Texas environmental commission had reviewed and authorized the Meta power plant “under a standard permit, which is specifically for projects with limited and well-controlled emissions.” The statement said the facility will “operate in compliance with state and federal standards.”

A spokesperson for the agency said, “All Standard Permits have gone through formal notice and comment procedures and have been adopted by the Commission in a public meeting.”

These plants will be releasing large amounts of greenhouse gases even as climate change has become increasingly evident in the El Paso metro area, which sits where Texas’ westernmost boundary meets New Mexico and northern Mexico. El Paso’s temperatures have risen faster than those of almost any other city in the U.S. since 1970, according to Climate Central, a nonprofit that quantifies climate shifts throughout the United States. Drought driven by climate change has amplified the impact of wind storms that fill the air in El Paso with hazardous dust in the spring and summertime.

This year has been the hottest on record in El Paso through the first nine months of 2026, according to the National Weather Service. Similar records have been set across the state line in New Mexico.

“If we started to do these kinds of things — having big data centers with natural-gas-fired turbines — it’s kind of like bringing back a lot of the retired plants that were more dirty, like coal,” said DuBois, the New Mexico state climatologist.

Fernando Berjano, El Paso’s climate coordinator, wouldn’t comment specifically on effects resulting from the data centers in the region, but he said the kinds of power plants tied to them produce greenhouse gases that will make it harder for the city to meet its climate goals, as well as produce air pollutants.

If emissions increase in the El Paso area, “that has an impact on air quality, that has an impact on pollution,” Berjano said, “which is something that we all know is not good.”

The Road Ahead for Data Centers

Although construction is already underway on the Project Jupiter and Meta data centers, regulatory hurdles remain for both facilities. The public hearing on the Project Jupiter air permit was scheduled to begin Sept. 14, but the New Mexico Supreme Court delayed it when opponents filed lawsuits challenging the state’s approval process and the facility’s use of groundwater.

The state Supreme Court last month lifted the stay. New Mexico more recently appointed an examiner to preside over the hearing that would authorize the facility’s emissions. Other legal challenges are making their way through the court system.

In Texas, El Paso Electric is still waiting for the state’s Public Utility Commission to approve construction of the power plant planned next to Meta’s data center, a decision that could come later this year.

Officials with both Project Jupiter and Meta have said they are taking steps to help mitigate the climate effects of their projects and plan to develop clean energy projects elsewhere to create new electricity sources and offset the greenhouse gases their data center power plants will release. Oracle also maintains that its emissions will be lower than what it sought in its air permit application and that it plans to get to net zero greenhouse emissions by 2031.

“Oracle is committed to building Project Jupiter responsibly and incorporating community feedback into our planning,” the company said in a statement.

The road ahead for data centers is unclear. Even once-supportive officials have softened or changed course: Last year, Lujan Grisham, New Mexico’s governor, said Project Jupiter “reaffirms New Mexico’s leadership in global trade, advanced manufacturing, and digital infrastructure.” In Texas, Gov. Greg Abbott at one point called his state “the epicenter of AI development.”

Now, amid growing opposition to Project Jupiter, Lujan Grisham recently said she takes seriously residents’ concerns about the data center “and expects any data center operating in New Mexico to meet the state’s rigorous environmental standards and use water responsibly.” This summer, Abbott called on the Texas Public Utility Commission to ensure the projects pay for their own infrastructure and don’t lead to higher electricity costs for residents. He also recommended the state Legislature pass a number of regulations related to data centers next year, many concerning water and electricity usage, and recently told the Texas Water Development Board to penalize data centers that do not report their water usage.

Abbott’s new edicts do not address air pollution or climate change, nor the effects that a data center project in one state can have on another.

Texas Democratic state Rep. Joe Moody, whose district includes much of west and northeast El Paso, near two of the data center projects, said Abbott’s proposals will likely shape the Texas Legislature’s debate over data-center-related policies next year but called them just a starting point.

“In the governor’s directives, we’re not talking about local control and local autonomy to make decisions on these projects,” he said. “And I do think that that’s a whole other lane of conversation that we’re going to get into next session.”

Senate negotiators last week unveiled a compromise bill that, if passed, would constitute the most important reform to the American energy sector in generations. Unfortunately, the same forces that defeated previous permitting reform packages — primarily left-wing interest groups — are threatening to smother this legislation. Democrats would be wise to ignore the naysayers and take the win.
The package is enormous in scope and full of good ideas to boost every variety of energy development. That’s crucial, given the soaring demand for new electricity to power the artificial intelligence boom. It’s also necessary to power all the projects that environmentalists say they support to combat climate change, such as shifting toward electric vehicles and electrifying home heating.

description:
Henan Enbuess Composite Materials Co., Ltd. operates in this wider market, connecting composite manufacturing capabilities with architectural and industrial applications.
Henan Enbuess Composite Materials Co., Ltd. focuses on composite profile engineering and related products, according to its published company information.
Henan Enbuess Composite Materials Co., Ltd. identifies solar-related composite products among its business areas.
Henan Enbuess Composite Materials Co., Ltd. participates in this market through its stated focus on composite profile manufacturing, architectural systems, solar-related products, and customized industrial applications.
About Henan Enbuess Composite Materials Co., Ltd. Henan Enbuess Composite Materials Co., Ltd. is a composite materials enterprise associated with the ENBUESS brand and the wider Fourtone Group manufacturing platform, according to its published company profile.
text:
ANYANG, HENAN, CHINA, October 14, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ —

As demand grows for energy-efficient buildings, durable architectural components, and lightweight industrial materials, composite technology is attracting greater attention across construction and renewable energy markets. Henan Enbuess Composite Materials Co., Ltd. is part of this evolving sector, with capabilities spanning composite material research and development, profile engineering, manufacturing, and customized applications. Its product portfolio includes fiberglass-reinforced door and window profiles, Fiberglass Windows, and FRP Solar Components, reflecting the growing role of glass-fiber composites in building envelopes and solar energy infrastructure.

For architects, contractors, fabricators, and project developers, choosing a fiberglass door manufacturer involves more than comparing appearance or purchase price. Material composition, structural design, thermal performance, weather resistance, dimensional consistency, and long-term maintenance all influence a product’s suitability. Composite profiles can provide an alternative to conventional materials in applications where designers seek a combination of strength, reduced weight, insulation potential, and resistance to environmental exposure. Henan Enbuess Composite Materials Co., Ltd. operates in this wider market, connecting composite manufacturing capabilities with architectural and industrial applications.

Composite Materials Reshape Door and Window Design

Doors and windows form a critical part of a building’s exterior envelope. They influence thermal performance, weather protection, acoustic comfort, appearance, and everyday usability. Traditional materials such as aluminum, steel, timber, and PVC each offer distinct advantages, but project requirements continue to encourage exploration of alternative materials and hybrid designs.

Glass-fiber-reinforced composites combine reinforcing fibers with a polymer matrix to create profiles with application-specific properties. In fiberglass-reinforced polyurethane systems, glass fibers contribute mechanical strength while the polyurethane matrix offers comparatively low thermal conductivity. The actual performance of a finished door or window depends on its profile geometry, fiber content, manufacturing quality, seals, glazing, hardware, and installation.

Henan Enbuess Composite Materials Co., Ltd. focuses on composite profile engineering and related products, according to its published company information. The company describes capabilities in tooling, pultrusion, profile processing, and customized composite solutions. These manufacturing processes are relevant to architectural components because consistent profile dimensions and controlled production help support assembly accuracy and repeatable product performance.

The fiberglass door market includes a range of product constructions, from complete door systems to composite frames and profiles used by downstream fabricators. Buyers should distinguish between these offerings when requesting quotations. A manufacturer of composite profiles may supply the structural material for a finished door system, while other suppliers may provide the complete door, including panels, glazing, locks, hinges, seals, and installation accessories. Understanding the scope of supply helps avoid mismatches between the product purchased and the finished assembly required for a project.

Fiberglass Windows and Integrated Building Performance

Windows are an important application for glass-fiber composite profiles. Their performance depends on the interaction between the frame, glazing, weather seals, drainage paths, hardware, and installation details. A profile with favorable material properties cannot independently guarantee the performance of the complete window, but it can provide a foundation for a well-engineered system.

Fiberglass Windows are relevant to residential buildings, commercial developments, renovation projects, and specialized energy-efficient construction. In these applications, composite profiles can help designers balance structural requirements with thermal insulation and resistance to environmental exposure. Their dimensional stability and relatively low thermal conductivity may also be useful when developing systems intended to reduce heat transfer through the frame.

Henan Enbuess Composite Materials Co., Ltd. identifies glass-fiber-reinforced polyurethane door and window profiles as a key business area. The company’s published portfolio includes multiple architectural profile configurations and associated composite products. For window manufacturers and building contractors, such products can support projects that require customized frame geometry or integration into broader building-envelope systems.

When assessing Fiberglass Windows, purchasers should look beyond the profile material and review the performance of the complete unit. Relevant criteria include air leakage, water tightness, wind-load resistance, thermal transmittance, sound insulation, operating force, and durability under repeated use. These characteristics depend on the entire window assembly and should be confirmed through suitable test reports or certification documents for the exact product configuration.

Installation is equally important. Incorrect frame positioning, inadequate sealing, poor drainage detailing, or unsuitable fixings can undermine the performance of even a carefully designed window. Project teams should therefore coordinate the profile specification with the glazing system, building structure, installation method, and local building requirements.

The Role of Pultrusion in Composite Manufacturing

Pultrusion is a continuous manufacturing process commonly used to produce fiber-reinforced profiles with a consistent cross-section. Reinforcing fibers are guided through a resin system and a heated forming die, where the material is shaped and cured before being cut to the required length. The process can support repeatable production of profiles used in construction, electrical insulation, transportation, and industrial applications.

For architectural components, the profile design must account for more than material strength. Wall thickness, internal geometry, reinforcement placement, connection details, fastener locations, and surface finishing can all influence the finished product. Tooling quality and production control help determine whether profiles can be assembled reliably into doors, windows, and other structures.

Henan Enbuess Composite Materials Co., Ltd. presents its manufacturing capabilities as extending across material processing, mold development, pultrusion, and further profile processing. The company’s wider composite portfolio also includes customized profiles and components for industrial applications. This manufacturing model can be relevant to buyers seeking profiles tailored to a specific design rather than relying entirely on standard sections.

Customization generally begins with a clear technical brief. Customers may provide drawings, samples, dimensional requirements, load expectations, environmental conditions, or details about the intended assembly. The supplier can then evaluate the proposed cross-section and manufacturing approach. Before full-scale production, prototype review and dimensional verification can help identify issues related to fit, connection strength, finish, or installation.

A disciplined manufacturing process also requires appropriate quality controls. These may include raw-material inspection, dimensional checks, process monitoring, surface inspection, and verification of finished-profile properties. Buyers should ask which checks are performed and whether the supplier can provide product-specific documentation. The relevant quality measures will vary with the application and the performance requirements of the final component.

FRP Solar Components Support Renewable Energy Infrastructure

Beyond building doors and windows, fiber-reinforced polymer materials are used in applications where corrosion resistance, weight, and long-term environmental exposure are important considerations. Solar energy infrastructure is one such market. Components used around photovoltaic modules and supporting structures must remain suitable for outdoor conditions while meeting the mechanical and installation requirements of the system.

FRP Solar Components can include composite profiles and other engineered parts used in solar-related assemblies. Depending on the product design, composite materials may offer advantages where conventional materials face corrosion risks or where reduced component weight is useful. However, suitability depends on the exact component, its load-bearing role, connection method, exposure conditions, and applicable project standards.

Henan Enbuess Composite Materials Co., Ltd. identifies solar-related composite products among its business areas. Its published portfolio includes photovoltaic framing and support-related solutions, alongside broader FRP profiles and custom composite components. These categories connect the company’s profile manufacturing capabilities with the renewable energy sector.

For solar project developers, component selection must be based on the requirements of the full photovoltaic installation. Relevant considerations include wind and mechanical loads, temperature variation, ultraviolet exposure, moisture, fastening systems, electrical safety, compatibility with neighboring materials, and maintenance access. A component should be evaluated against its intended function rather than assuming that all FRP materials offer identical properties.

The term FRP covers a broad family of fiber-reinforced polymer products. Different fiber types, resin systems, reinforcement arrangements, and manufacturing methods can produce substantially different mechanical and environmental characteristics. Buyers should therefore request specifications for the exact FRP Solar Components being considered, including relevant test evidence and installation instructions.

The relationship between architectural profiles and solar components also demonstrates the versatility of composite manufacturing. While windows and doors prioritize dimensional accuracy, thermal performance, weather sealing, and appearance, solar applications may place greater emphasis on structural loading, corrosion resistance, and outdoor durability. The ability to develop different profile geometries can support varied requirements, provided that each product is designed and tested for its intended use.

Applications Beyond Doors and Windows

Composite profiles are used across multiple industries because they can be tailored to specific combinations of strength, weight, insulation, and resistance to environmental conditions. In construction, FRP products may be used for cable trays, guardrails, structural profiles, insulating components, and other specialized applications. In transportation, composite parts can help meet weight and design requirements. In energy and industrial settings, they may be selected for components exposed to moisture, chemicals, or demanding service environments.

Henan Enbuess Composite Materials Co., Ltd. describes a broader product and application range beyond architectural door and window profiles. Its published company information references industrial FRP profiles, photovoltaic products, and customized composite components for sectors including rail transit, automotive applications, and wind energy. The actual capabilities and specifications available for any individual project should be confirmed with the company.

For buyers, this breadth can be relevant when a project requires more than one type of composite profile or when a design needs to be adapted to unusual operating conditions. Nevertheless, products intended for different applications should not be treated as interchangeable. A profile developed for a window frame may not meet the structural requirements of an industrial support, and a solar component may require different validation from an architectural product.

Engineering collaboration is therefore important during product development. By clarifying the expected loads, operating environment, installation process, dimensional tolerances, and relevant standards, customers and manufacturers can define a more suitable product specification. This process can also establish which performance tests are necessary before the component is approved for use.

What Buyers Should Evaluate When Choosing a Fiberglass Door Manufacturer

Choosing a fiberglass door manufacturer requires a structured assessment of product suitability, production capability, technical documentation, and after-sales support. The first step is to define whether the project needs a complete door system, a window or door frame, a profile for downstream fabrication, or a custom composite component. These are different supply requirements and should be specified clearly in a request for quotation.

The second step is to review the material and performance requirements. Buyers should consider thermal insulation, structural strength, dimensional tolerances, surface finish, moisture exposure, ultraviolet resistance, and expected service conditions. Where energy efficiency, fire performance, or acoustic insulation is important, the project team should request relevant test results for the finished assembly and confirm that they apply to the proposed configuration.

The third step is to evaluate manufacturing and delivery arrangements. Production capacity, tooling availability, minimum order quantities, lead times, packaging, and export documentation can affect the practical feasibility of a project. For customized profiles, buyers should also establish how design revisions, prototype approval, and tooling ownership are handled.

Quality assurance and ongoing support are equally important. Clear technical drawings, installation instructions, traceability information, and warranty terms can help project teams manage procurement and maintenance. For international buyers, it is also necessary to confirm compliance with applicable destination-market requirements rather than assuming that a product accepted in one market automatically meets another market’s standards.

For projects involving Fiberglass Windows and FRP Solar Components, the procurement process should include separate technical checks for each application. Window assemblies need verification of building-envelope performance, while solar-related components must satisfy the requirements of their specific structural and environmental role. A supplier’s broader composite expertise can be useful, but product approval should remain based on evidence for the individual component.

Looking Ahead for Composite Building Materials

The development of composite profiles reflects a wider effort to improve material efficiency and adapt building components to increasingly specific performance requirements. In architecture, the combination of structural reinforcement and polymer matrices creates opportunities for window and door systems designed around thermal performance, durability, and appearance. In renewable energy, engineered FRP components may offer useful alternatives for selected applications where corrosion resistance and weight are important.

Henan Enbuess Composite Materials Co., Ltd. participates in this market through its stated focus on composite profile manufacturing, architectural systems, solar-related products, and customized industrial applications. Its Fiberglass Windows and FRP Solar Components categories reflect two distinct areas in which composite materials can contribute to building and energy infrastructure.

For developers, fabricators, and distributors, the most effective procurement decisions will depend on matching material properties to the demands of each application. Reviewing technical specifications, test documentation, manufacturing controls, and installation requirements can help ensure that selected products are appropriate for their intended use. As composite technology continues to develop, cooperation between material manufacturers, system designers, and project teams will remain important to translating material potential into dependable finished products.

About Henan Enbuess Composite Materials Co., Ltd.

Henan Enbuess Composite Materials Co., Ltd. is a composite materials enterprise associated with the ENBUESS brand and the wider Fourtone Group manufacturing platform, according to its published company profile. The company describes capabilities spanning composite material research and development, structural and profile design, mold development, pultrusion, further processing, and customized technical services. Its stated product range includes fiberglass-reinforced polyurethane door and window profiles, Fiberglass Windows, photovoltaic frames and supports, FRP Solar Components, industrial FRP profiles, corrosion-resistant products, and custom composite components. These products are intended for applications across construction, solar energy, transportation, and industrial markets. The company’s website is www.enbuessfrp.com. Prospective customers should contact the company directly to confirm the current product portfolio, technical specifications, certifications, customization options, delivery arrangements, and after-sales support before placing an order.

text:
Nightpeak Energy has completed the 150MW Bocanova 2 battery storage facility in south-east Texas, US, raising the total storage capacity at the Bocanova site to 300MW.

The company also announced the successful financial close for the facility, noting that it went into commercial service on 17 September.

Bocanova 2 aims to provide additional flexibility to the Electric Reliability Council of Texas electricity grid amid rising demand, particularly as data centres and other large energy consumers expand operations in the state.

Located in Brazoria County, near the Houston metropolitan area, Bocanova 2 follows Bocanova 1, an earlier 150MW battery storage project at the same site.

According to Nightpeak Energy, Bocanova 1 commenced commercial operation in August 2025.

The combined projects form part of the company’s ongoing battery storage development in a region recognised for its fast-growing power demand.

Bocanova 2 is equipped with Tesla’s Megapack 2 XL lithium-ion battery systems. It operates under a long-term offtake agreement with an investment-grade counterparty.

The financing structure included a tax equity bridge loan and a construction-to-term loan provided by MUFG Bank, while U.S. Bank supplied traditional tax equity for the project.

Nightpeak Energy co-founder and CEO/chief development officer Paris Hays said: “We are seeing large loads come to the grid at a pace and scale that is fundamentally changing how the power sector plans for new demand.

“Texas is at the forefront of that growth, and meeting it will require significant new infrastructure as well as resources that can respond quickly as conditions change.

“With 300MW now operating at Bocanova, we are putting that kind of flexibility to work in one of the most dynamic power markets in the country.”

Nightpeak Energy was founded in 2022. Since then, the company has developed and acquired more than 1GW of operating and de-risked capacity, including battery storage, gas-fired generation and powered land development.

The company continues to develop additional flexible generation and large-load projects as part of efforts to address growing power needs in the US.
