title: More than 760,000 solar panels are going up across 2,000 acres of the Mojave Desert off ...
description:
Solar panels have a big issue.
ContourGlobal, the London-based power producer building it, says Project Sterling will have more than 760,000 solar panels and more than 300 battery containers.
But Sterling’s the classic version, with a whole lot of panels spread across open desert.
Sterling’s battery system is rated at 360 megawatts and 1.4 gigawatt-hours.
Solar panels produce direct current, and Sterling’s panels are rated at 509 megawatts.
text:
Solar panels have a big issue. They stop making electricity when the sun goes down, but that’s right when people get home, turn on the TV, and crank up the air conditioning.

For this reason, the solar farm that’s just starting to go up in Arizona’s Mohave County is getting its own batteries. And I mean a lot of them. ContourGlobal, the London-based power producer building it, says Project Sterling will have more than 760,000 solar panels and more than 300 battery containers. Tesla’s already signed up to buy about 90% of what it makes.

Sterling’s site is just off old Route 66, on the stretch between Topock and Kingman. Here, a new 5.2-mile road, Polaris Road, is being built to connect the two. Lake Havasu City, the Arizona town that famously bought London Bridge, is about 20 miles to the south, so a London company setting up shop out there feels about right.

The whole project occupies more than 2,000 acres in the Mojave Desert. (Yes, the county spells it Mohave and the desert spells it Mojave. You get used to it. I almost am.) For comparison, Sterling’s more than 760,000 panels would top the 700,000 we wrote about, which sit on an old Soviet firing range in Germany. Solar’s turned up in odder spots around Arizona, like over an irrigation canal south of Phoenix. But Sterling’s the classic version, with a whole lot of panels spread across open desert.

Figures: ContourGlobal.

Tesla is buying about 1 terawatt-hour a year

Tesla’s deal is a power purchase agreement, which ContourGlobal announced back in July. A power purchase agreement is basically a long-term contract to buy a plant’s electricity at a price agreed up front. It lets a company like Tesla secure a lot of clean power without having to build or operate the plant itself. (Sorta Elon Musk’s whole thing, if you ask me.)

Under the deal, Tesla gets about 1 terawatt-hour a year, which ContourGlobal says is around 90% of what Sterling will produce. A terawatt-hour is a billion kilowatt-hours, and the kilowatt-hour is the unit on your power bill. Tesla also receives the renewable energy certificates that accompany that power, which are essentially receipts that let a company count the electricity as clean.

So where’s all that power going?

Sterling plugs into lines run by the Western Area Power Administration, the federal agency that sells the power from Hoover Dam, among other things. It also has firm rights to send power over the lines into California, and it’ll be pseudo-tied to California’s grid. A pseudo-tie basically lets a plant that’s physically in one grid operator’s territory act like part of another’s, so California’s grid operator can treat Sterling as one of its own plants. Trade publication pv magazine reported in July that the power’s meant for Tesla’s California operations.

ContourGlobal hasn’t said which Tesla sites will use it, what Tesla’s paying, or how many years the contract runs, and I couldn’t find anything from Tesla on it. This would probably be good to know, but I wouldn’t hold my breath for a price, either, since companies tend to keep those numbers to themselves. And if you’re Tesla, you apparently don’t like sharing data at all.

Antonio Cammisecra, ContourGlobal’s president and CEO, said in the company’s groundbreaking announcement that “our teams engineered the project around the specific needs of our customer.” ContourGlobal bought Sterling while it was still in development and reworked it to meet Tesla’s needs, so it’s basically a made-to-order power plant.

So how does a solar farm run for 16 hours a day?

Cammisecra also says Sterling will be able to deliver power for up to 16 hours a day. Basically, the panels handle the daylight, and the batteries handle the evening.

Sterling’s battery system is rated at 360 megawatts and 1.4 gigawatt-hours. If you’re wondering why a battery needs two ratings, think of megawatts as horsepower and gigawatt-hours as the size of the gas tank. One tells you how hard the battery can push, and the other tells you how long it can keep that up. Put it all together and Sterling’s batteries can run flat out for about four hours.

Add a long day of sunshine to about four hours of battery, and you can see how the company gets to 16. I’d guess 16 is a best-case number, though, since a December day in the Mojave is a lot shorter than a June one.

The batteries are lithium iron phosphate (LFP) with liquid cooling and built-in fire protection. LFP cells hold a little less energy than the nickel-heavy ones in a lot of EVs. They’re a lot less likely to catch fire, though, which you’d probably want if you’re parking more than 300 containers of them in the desert. As far as I can tell, neither of ContourGlobal’s announcements names a battery supplier. Tesla, the customer here, sells its own shipping-container-sized Megapack batteries to power companies, so I’m pretty curious whose cells end up inside.

Sterling is a 509-megawatt plant, or a 450-megawatt one

You’ll see Sterling described both ways. And they’re both right. Solar panels produce direct current, and Sterling’s panels are rated at 509 megawatts. The 450 is what the plant can actually send to the grid once inverters turn that into alternating current, the kind that comes out of your wall outlet.

The panel maker doesn’t seem to have been named either, so I can’t tell you how big each panel is. Divide 509 megawatts by 760,000 panels, though, and each one works out to somewhere around 670 watts.

The paperwork says construction started last year

ContourGlobal’s July announcement had one line that’s easy to skim past. It said work on Sterling had already started last year through “off-site physical work of significant nature,” including the purchase of major equipment.

I doubt that wording was an accident. The IRS uses almost the same phrase, “physical work of a significant nature,” as its test for when a solar project has officially started construction. For a plant that won’t be finished until 2028, that start date decides whether it can still claim the federal tax credits for wind and solar that Congress started phasing out last year. I couldn’t find anything from ContourGlobal on whether Sterling is claiming them.

If you’re planning a Route 66 road trip, the stretch between Topock and Kingman will probably be a little busier than usual for a while. ContourGlobal expects an average of about 400 people working on Sterling during construction, and it’s aiming to have the plant up and running in 2028.

text:
Cook Labor Government awards contract for Clean Energy Link - East project to WA based businesses

Project to create up to 600 local jobs and create local business opportunities

New figures show Western Power spent more than $1.3 billion in 2025-26 with local businesses

The utility worked with more than 290 local WA businesses, supporting local jobs

The Cook Labor Government is backing Western Australian jobs and local industry through a major contract award for Clean Energy Link - East (CEL - East), with WA-based businesses Acciona, GenusPlus, and UGL Engineering selected to deliver the project.

The project is expected to initially create 300 jobs, rising to 600 at the peak of construction.

Stage one of CEL - East includes new and upgraded transmission lines between Collie and Darkan to increase energy capacity from renewable energy zones in the eastern and south-eastern regions of the South West Interconnected System to WA homes and businesses.

The contracts will deliver critical infrastructure needed including:

a new 330kV terminal at Cordering;

expansion of Shotts and Muja terminals;

38km of 330kV transmission lines from Shotts to Cordering; and

54km of 330kV transmission lines from Muja to Cordering.

When complete CEL - East is expected to unlock approximately 2.3GW of renewable energy capacity, the equivalent power usage of around one million homes.

Together, CEL - East and CEL - North form one of the largest infrastructure, technology, and construction programs in WA's history, transforming the electricity network for the future and incorporating renewables to put downward pressure on power prices.

The contract award comes as new figures released for the first time today show Western Power spent more than $1.3 billion with local businesses in 2025-2026, up from $850 million the previous financial year.

More than 290 local Western Australian businesses supplied the materials, services, and skills needed to build and maintain our grid.

One example is Geographe Underground Services, a Bunbury-based civil works company, which has partnered with Western Power to deliver the Housing and Infrastructure Growth Program in the Mundijong West Industrial Area.

Through this work the company has been able to provide 40 local jobs and expand its capability in horizontal directional drilling enabling Western Power to install cabling to connect power in the Mundijong area.

This follows a direction issued to utilities by Energy and Decarbonisation Minister Amber-Jade Sanderson last December.

The direction ensures Government Trading Enterprises prioritise local businesses to ensure Western Australian workers benefit from the pipeline of work that will flow from major upgrades to the South West Interconnected System.

The Cook Labor Government directions have helped local small and medium businesses win the vast majority of Western Power's $1.5 billion annual spend, supporting local jobs right across WA.

Comments attributed to Premier Roger Cook:

"We're building a State of Energy in Western Australia, securing affordable, reliable, and lower carbon energy for WA households and businesses through renewables, backed by battery storage and flexible WA gas.

"Affordable, reliable, and lower carbon energy is critical to keeping our economy strong and remaining the best place in the world to get a secure and well-paid job.

"Affordable, reliable, and lower carbon energy will power jobs in defence, advanced manufacturing, and the downstream processing of our minerals, including in green iron.

"That includes investing in Clean Energy Link - East to secure local jobs and opportunities for WA businesses while building a stronger energy system.

"Having granted it Priority Project status, we are fast-tracking its delivery, supporting up to 600 local jobs and ensuring our grid is ready for when we get out of State-owned coal by 2030."

Comments attributed to Energy and Decarbonisation Minister Amber-Jade Sanderson:

"Clean Energy Link - East will deliver more affordable energy to WA households, while supporting local jobs and local businesses.

"The release of Western Power's local procurement figures for the first time shows that our plan is working - WA workers and WA businesses are delivering our clean energy transition.

"We have world class manufacturing capabilities here in WA, and that's why last year I issued a ministerial direction that Government Trading Enterprises needed to consider local businesses for works.

"We'll keep working to put WA first."

Comments attributed to Collie-Preston MLA Jodie Hanns:

"Collie has powered WA for generations, and the CEL - East expansion shows it will keep playing a vital role in our energy system for generations to come.

"The expansion of the Muja and Shotts terminals and the new 330kV transmission lines from both sites will keep Collie at the heart of the South West Interconnected System.

"As more renewable energy comes online, Collie will continue to play its part in powering homes, businesses and industry across WA."

title: PESP at Climate Week 2026: Private Equity and AI
description:
For the Private Equity Stakeholder Project (PESP), Climate Week reinforced the urgency of bringing private markets into that conversation.
Just before Climate Week, PESP, Americans for Financial Reform Education Fund, and Global Energy Monitor released the 2026 Private Equity Climate Risks Scorecard, the most comprehensive edition of the Scorecard to date.
PESP brought a cross-sectoral lens connecting AI infrastructure, private capital, fossil fuel generation, utility ownership, affordability, workers, and frontline communities.
The 2026 Private Equity Climate Risk analysis examined 145 private equity oil and gas funds that have largely completed their investment lifecycles.
Bringing ownership into the Climate Week conversation PESP’s experience at Climate Week reinforced the value of connecting conversations that are often happening separately.
text:
New York Climate Week and the high-level week of the 81st United Nations General Assembly took place amid an increasingly fractured geopolitical landscape. Conflict, energy and food security, tensions between major powers, and growing concern about artificial intelligence competed with the climate crisis for global attention.

Yet across the week, one reality was difficult to miss: the systems powering the global economy are changing rapidly, and decisions being made today about who finances, owns, and controls new energy infrastructure will shape climate outcomes for decades.

For the Private Equity Stakeholder Project (PESP), Climate Week reinforced the urgency of bringing private markets into that conversation.

Just before Climate Week, PESP, Americans for Financial Reform Education Fund, and Global Energy Monitor released the 2026 Private Equity Climate Risks Scorecard, the most comprehensive edition of the Scorecard to date. It examines the energy holdings and climate policies of 20 private equity firms managing a combined $7.3 trillion in assets and significantly expands previous analyses to include pipelines, LNG tankers, coal terminals, and oil- and gas-fired power generation.

The findings illustrate the scale of private equity’s role in the energy system: the firms back at least 244 energy companies operating more than 1,050 fossil fuel assets, including more than 250 oil and gas fields, 15,000 miles of pipelines, 35 LNG terminals, 13 coal terminals, and hundreds of fossil fuel power plants. Their energy portfolios produce an estimated 1.5 gigatons of greenhouse gas emissions annually. This footprint, if compared with countries’ fossil fuel emissions, would rank behind only China, the United States, India, and Russia.

Those findings provided an important backdrop to PESP’s conversations throughout Climate Week.

Climate remained urgent, even when it wasn’t always at the center.

Climate Week unfolded alongside a UN General Assembly dominated by conflict, geopolitical fragmentation, security concerns, and debates about the future of multilateral cooperation. At the close of the General Debate, the UN noted that peace had been the overriding theme across six days of speeches, with conflicts in the Middle East, Ukraine, Sudan, Myanmar, and elsewhere commanding substantial attention.

Climate nevertheless remained a significant part of outgoing UN Secretary-General António Guterres’ final General Assembly agenda. At a September 23 High-Level Event on Climate Action and Just Transition, the UN brought together governments, financial institutions, businesses, and civil society around accelerating climate action, clean energy, resilience, and a just transition.

Guterres also called on governments to develop national plans for transitioning away from fossil fuels aligned with 1.5°C, with timelines and protections for affected workers and communities, while arguing that those responsible for pollution should bear its costs

AI was everywhere.

If one issue seemed to cut across nearly every corner of Climate Week this year, it was artificial intelligence.

AI appeared in discussions about climate technology, grid reliability, electricity demand, energy security, financing, and economic growth. At the same time, advocates and communities raised concerns about the environmental consequences of the rapid data center buildout and the impacts to fenceline communities , including potential strains on local electricity and water systems and the potential for increased reliance on fossil fuels. Climate Week demonstrations in New York uplifted community concerns about the environmental footprint of AI and data center development and concerns about the use of AI in public schools.

The 2026 PECR Scorecard shows why private equity needs to be part of this discussion.

Private equity firms now back nearly half of the top 25 U.S. data center companies. Private equity investment in U.S. data centers reached $45.7 billion in 2025—approximately 72 percent of total investment in the sector.

But private equity’s role does not stop at the data center door.

Some firms are positioning themselves across multiple parts of the AI supply chain including data centers, utilities, power plants, pipelines, and other energy assets. The Scorecard notes that the AI buildout drives increased power demand while private equity and infrastructure firms race to acquire power assets and utilities and finance new generation.

That convergence was one of the central issues PESP brought to Climate Week.

AI infrastructure is Climate Infrastructure.

One message PESP emphasized throughout the week was straightforward: data centers cannot be understood simply as digital infrastructure. This issue is so much bigger and multifaceted than this.

AI facilities require enormous and continuous supplies of electricity. Meeting that demand can require new power generation, transmission, substations, pipelines, grid upgrades, and other infrastructure designed to operate for decades.

Depending on the decisions made today, that demand could support expanded clean energy deployment—or create new incentives to build gas generation and extend the operating lives of existing fossil fuel assets.

PESP’s research has already documented how the AI infrastructure boom is intersecting with private equity ownership across energy systems. The consequences of that intersection extend beyond greenhouse gas emissions to questions of electricity affordability, water consumption, land use, local air pollution, and the impacts on workers and communities living near data centers and related infrastructure.

This makes ownership a climate issue.

We need to understand who owns the infrastructure, who finances it, how investment decisions are being made, and with whom the financial and environmental risks ultimately land.

The Costs are Already Visible

The 2026 Scorecard also underscores why these questions cannot be reduced to emissions alone.

In the United States, air pollution associated with the private equity-backed extraction, coal, and LNG infrastructure analyzed by the consortium is linked to at least 1,000 premature deaths, 1,400 additional emergency room visits, 584,000 instances of asthma symptoms, 3,700 cases of asthma onset, and 27,000 lost workdays each year.

Those outcomes illustrate what is at stake when discussions about infrastructure development focus on capital deployment without equally considering impacts to the communities surrounding the assets.

That was an important theme in PESP’s Climate Week conversations, including discussions with organizations examining the consequences of the AI buildout. PESP brought a cross-sectoral lens connecting AI infrastructure, private capital, fossil fuel generation, utility ownership, affordability, workers, and frontline communities.

It is precisely this connection that can disappear when AI is discussed solely as a technology issue or electricity demand is discussed only as a grid-planning problem.

There is a financial accountability question, too.

The 2026 Private Equity Climate Risk analysis examined 145 private equity oil and gas funds that have largely completed their investment lifecycles. Investors contributed $190.4 billion to those funds and received $192.9 billion back. The median fund returned just 2 percent more than investors contributed, and after adjusting for inflation, investors lost money on average.

This matters because public pension funds and other institutional investors provide much of the capital flowing into private markets.

The question for those investors is therefore not only whether their private equity managers’ energy investments align with their climate commitments. It is also whether taking on long-term climate, transition, regulatory, and stranded-asset risks is delivering sufficient financial value for beneficiaries.

That question becomes increasingly important as private capital pours into AI infrastructure.

Data centers, power plants, pipelines, and utility infrastructure can have operating lives extending decades beyond a private equity fund’s typical ownership period. If expectations about future AI demand prove overly optimistic, institutional investors, utilities, customers, and communities could be left exposed to infrastructure built around assumptions that did not materialize.

Bringing ownership into the Climate Week conversation

PESP’s experience at Climate Week reinforced the value of connecting conversations that are often happening separately.

In discussions with environmental,climate, and community organizations and other environmental and climate focused organizations, we heard interest in examining the AI buildout as a cross-sectoral climate and environmental justice issue.

At New York Climate Week, PESP brought a private-markets and ownership lens to climate and energy conversations, connecting questions of emissions and infrastructure to who owns and finances these assets, who benefits, and who bears the risks and costs. We highlighted the growing role of private equity in utilities, energy infrastructure, and the AI and data center buildout, while emphasizing implications for energy affordability, fossil fuel dependence, environmental justice, and frontline communities. PESP also elevated the role of pension funds and other institutional investors in strengthening accountability and climate expectations for private-market managers. Overall, PESP helped connect climate, private capital, infrastructure, affordability, and community impacts in conversations where these issues are often considered separately.

That perspective also creates opportunities for deeper collaboration among organizations working on climate, financial accountability, environmental justice, energy affordability, labor, utility regulation, and technology policy.

The central questions are what gets built, what remains operating because of that investment, who controls the infrastructure, who receives the financial benefits, and who carries the risks.

The next phase of climate accountability must include private markets.

The 2026 Scorecard points toward several areas where greater accountability is needed: disclosure of fossil fuel holdings and emissions, science-based climate targets, portfolio-wide transition planning, attention to environmental justice impacts, and greater transparency around political spending and climate lobbying. It also calls for institutional investors and regulators to demand stronger disclosure and accountability from private fund managers.

Climate Week reinforced why those expectations matter.

Electrification is accelerating. AI is reshaping forecasts for electricity demand. Enormous amounts of private capital are flowing toward data centers, utilities, power generation, and other energy infrastructure. Meanwhile, communities are confronting questions about affordability, pollution, water, land, reliability, and whether they have a meaningful voice in decisions that will reshape their local economies and environments.

Private equity increasingly sits at the intersection of these trends.

PESP left Climate Week with strengthened relationships across the climate, environmental justice, investor, research, and policy communities—and with an even clearer case for making private markets accountability part of the broader climate conversation.

Climate accountability cannot stop at publicly traded companies. AI is not only a digital technology issue; it is also an energy, infrastructure, finance, affordability, and environmental justice issue. Energy policy cannot ignore financial ownership. And discussions about infrastructure investment cannot focus exclusively on how quickly capital can be deployed.

As trillions of dollars flow into the infrastructure that will power the coming decades, we need to follow the money as closely as we follow the emissions.

Because the future of AI and the energy transition is also a question of power: who owns it, who profits from it, who pays for it, and who gets a say in what comes next.

name: North Carolina American Energy
title: NC should see data centers as opportunity, not threat | Opinion - The Fayetteville Observer
description:
Unlike residential growth, data centers expand the tax base without a large influx of new residents straining public services.
Former President Donald Trump has advocated for building data centers responsibly, with developers addressing power, sound, and water impacts.
We should approach data centers with that same practical mindset — understanding both their benefits and their impacts and making decisions based on facts.
Data centers’ economic impact deserve attention The economic numbers deserve attention.
We should evaluate data centers on the facts of each project, not reject them because of misconceptions about the industry.
text:
Data centers are a significant economic driver in North Carolina, contributing billions to the state's GDP and tax revenue, John Szoka writes.

Unlike residential growth, data centers expand the tax base without a large influx of new residents straining public services.

Former President Donald Trump has advocated for building data centers responsibly, with developers addressing power, sound, and water impacts.

North Carolina can balance economic growth with responsible development by carefully planning data center locations and infrastructure needs.

Data centers have quickly become one of North Carolina's most misunderstood economic-development issues. Too often, the debate starts with what people fear instead of what these projects represent: enormous private investment, a substantial new tax base, construction and skilled-trade jobs, and the infrastructure required to compete in an increasingly digital economy. North Carolina has spent decades building a reputation as a state where companies want to invest, innovate and create jobs. We should approach data centers with that same practical mindset — understanding both their benefits and their impacts and making decisions based on facts.

Data centers’ economic impact deserve attention

The economic numbers deserve attention. According to the North Carolina Chamber, the data center industry contributed an estimated $18.45 billion to North Carolina's GDP in 2024 and generated approximately $1.39 billion in state and local tax revenue. These facilities also require enormous capital investment in land, buildings, electrical infrastructure, equipment and technology. Unlike residential growth, which can create immediate demand for additional classrooms, school buses, and other population-driven government services, a data center can add significant taxable property without bringing thousands of new residents. That distinction matters to counties trying to expand their tax base while continuing to provide quality services to existing residents.

President Donald Trump recently addressed this issue directly, making an important distinction between simply building data centers and building them properly. He argued that communities should want these investments when they are placed in appropriate locations and their impacts — including power, sound and water — are properly addressed. He also emphasized having large data center operators provide or finance the additional electricity infrastructure needed to serve their facilities, rather than simply shifting those costs onto existing ratepayers.

The administration's Ratepayer Protection Pledge similarly calls for participating technology companies to build, bring or buy new generation and pay for power-delivery upgrades associated with their facilities. That is the kind of approach North Carolina should examine carefully: growth that provides tangible benefits while requiring developers to address legitimate infrastructure concerns.

How to balance growth and responsibility

A much larger issue is also at stake. Artificial intelligence, cloud computing and advanced technology are becoming critical parts of the modern economy, and the physical infrastructure supporting those technologies must be located somewhere. President Trump made the point plainly: if one American community turns these investments away, other communities — and other countries, particularly China — would gladly take them. This is increasingly a question of American competitiveness. Data centers are the physical backbone supporting AI and cloud computing, and the Trump administration has described domestic data-center capacity as important to both economic and national security. America cannot expect to lead the next generation of technology while refusing to build the infrastructure that makes it possible.

North Carolina does not have to choose between responsible development and economic growth. We can demand appropriate locations, responsible water use, adequate setbacks, thoughtful land-use planning, and energy infrastructure that protects existing customers while still recognizing a tremendous economic opportunity. We should evaluate data centers on the facts of each project, not reject them because of misconceptions about the industry. North Carolina became one of America's strongest states for business because generations of leaders understood the importance of looking forward. As global competition for technology and investment accelerates, we should make sure North Carolina remains prepared to build, compete, and prosper.

text:
Madrid, October 14, 2026. Cox, the global integrated water and energy utility, has signed an agreement with the Government of the Republic of El Salvador to drive an investment program estimated at US$2.9 billion. The program will develop and modernize strategic water and energy infrastructure in the country.

The agreement was signed at Casa Presidencial by the President of the Republic of El Salvador, Nayib Bukele, and the Executive Chairman of Cox, Enrique Riquelme. It is built around four strategic partnerships in energy storage, solar photovoltaic generation, natural gas, and water and sanitation management.

The transaction is a further step in Cox’s growth strategy in Latin America. It also strengthens Cox’s model as an integrated company that can develop, finance, build, operate and maintain critical water and energy infrastructure. Through this partnership, Cox will put its industrial, technological and financial expertise at El Salvador’s service. The aim is to help strengthen energy security, increase the share of renewables, and improve the quality and coverage of water and sanitation services.

In the energy segment, the State is expected to take part as a partner. Subject to the relevant approvals and the execution of the specific agreements, Cox will structure the financing of the projects through project finance schemes. International financial institutions, multilateral organizations and export credit agencies will take part. The company will also develop, build, operate and maintain the projects.

The work will be carried out over the next three years. The relevant approvals are expected to be completed in the coming weeks, along with progress on the specific agreements.

Four strategic agreements

In energy storage, the agreement provides for battery systems connected to the national power grid. Their estimated initial capacity is between 440 and 500 MWh, expandable to 1,000 MWh. These facilities will help make the power system more stable and allow more renewable energy onto the grid.

The partnership also includes two solar photovoltaic plants, to be developed together with the Lempa River Hydroelectric Executive Commission (CEL). Their estimated initial capacity is 200 MW, expandable to 400 MW.

Plans also include a liquefied natural gas (LNG) regasification terminal and a combined-cycle power plant of approximately 380 MW. This infrastructure will increase generation capacity and help position El Salvador as a regional energy hub.

Finally, the agreement includes measures to improve water and sanitation management, expand coverage and raise service quality. In these areas, Cox will bring its experience as an international operator of water infrastructure.

A long-term strategic partnership

The agreement is part of the Government of El Salvador’s program to modernize the country’s energy and water infrastructure. The program also aims to establish El Salvador as an investment destination in the region.

“Our commitment to El Salvador and Latin America is a long-term one. We will put our experience as a water and energy utility at the country’s service to strengthen its power system, add more renewable energy and improve water service. With the natural gas terminal, El Salvador will become the region’s benchmark and its most important energy hub. We thank President Bukele and his Government for the trust they have placed in Cox,” said Enrique Riquelme, Executive Chairman of Cox.

For his part, Nayib Bukele said: “This agreement allows us to attract international investment for cleaner and more reliable energy, as well as the technical support needed to guarantee a quality water supply, without committing new public funds and with clear rules.”

Latin America, a strategic priority for Cox

The partnership with El Salvador strengthens Cox’s commitment to Latin America. The region accounts for approximately 95% of the company’s activity, and Cox has an investment plan there of more than US$7 billion in strategic water and energy projects.

The agreement adds to other major projects the company has recently launched in the region:

the Rosarito desalination plant

the acquisition of Iberdrola México

new renewable generation and storage projects in Central America

the expansion of its power transmission platform in Brazil

Cox runs its regional platform for the Americas from Panama, which brings management and decision-making closer to its main markets, projects, financial partners and institutions.

text:
Biofuels and agricultural stakeholders were pleased to see the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) propose reallocating 100 percent of the Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) volumes recently waived by the agency through Small Refinery Exemptions (SREs) for the 2025 compliance year. However, some also expressed reservations about the continuation of the exemption process going forward and its impact on increasing demand for biofuels.

“The integrity of the RFS depends on ensuring the volumes established under the program translate into real-world renewable fuel demand. Farmers and ethanol producers need certainty that RFS requirements will not be eroded after the fact by exemptions,” said American Coalition for Ethanol (ACE) CEO Brian Jennings. “While this proposed reallocation is an important step, the debate over SREs has held up adoption of year-round E15. Congress must act to provide greater certainty and expand opportunities for ethanol by passing nationwide E15 legislation before the end of the year.”

The proposal follows EPA’s August 31 announcement on 34 pending 2025 SRE petitions, which resulted in 1.76 billion RINs being exempted for 29 small refineries. EPA had previously projected approximately 990 million RINs would be exempted for 2025. EPA has proposed reallocating 100% of that difference to the 2026 and 2027 RFS obligations.

“We are pleased to see that the administration has kept its pledge to protect farmers and biofuel producers while administering this critical program, and we appreciate that biofuel producers will be kept whole with the reallocation of all waived volumes,” said National Corn Growers Association president Matt Frostic. “We hope that the Renewable Fuel Standard and the small refinery exemption program are managed with certainty in the years to come.”

Clean Fuels Alliance America Vice President of Federal Affairs Kurt Kovarik said, “Clean Fuels appreciates Administrator Lee Zeldin’s effort to keep the Renewable Fuel Standard volumes on track and to release this proposal earlier than originally promised. As a result of this year’s historic RFS proposal, the U.S. biodiesel, renewable diesel, and SAF industry has invested billions of dollars in rural America, created new job opportunities, and massively increased domestic production of fuel to secure America’s energy dominance.”

text:
Hyundai Motor(313,500 won ▼ 1,500 -0.48%) said on the 14th that it held a completion ceremony for its new Pune plant in India. It is the third foothold secured about 30 years after establishing its India subsidiary in May 1996. Hyundai Motor plans to make India a pillar of future growth by using the new plant as a base to convert locally produced models to electric vehicles, and by investing in Autonomous Driving and future mobility.

The new Pune plant was created by Hyundai Motor in 2023 through the acquisition and expansion of the General Motors (GM) plant in Talegaon, Maharashtra, in west-central India. The amount Hyundai Motor invested to rebuild the plant, which began operating in 2008, into a smart manufacturing hub comes to about 1 trillion won.

The site alone is 1.2 ㎢ (about 360,000 pyeong), with an annual production capacity of 170,000 vehicles. Hyundai Motor plans to increase capacity to 250,000 by 2028 and 320,000 by 2030. Hyundai Motor estimates that the number of employees who will work at the plant will reach more than 4,700, and that the employment effect, including partner companies, will be more than 12,400.

With the start-up of the new Pune plant, Hyundai Motor has secured an annual production capacity close to 1 million vehicles when combined with the Chennai Plants 1 and 2 (824,000 vehicles per year). Adding Kia's Anantapur plant's annual capacity (431,000 vehicles) brings Hyundai Motor Group's capacity this year to 1,425,000 vehicles per year. Hyundai Motor also set a goal of raising the India subsidiary's export share to 30% by 2030.

The first mass-produced model at the new Pune plant is the subcompact sport utility vehicle (SUV) All New Venue. In addition to domestic sales in India, it will also build units for export to more than 30 countries worldwide, including Mexico, Chile, South Africa and Saudi Arabia. Hyundai Motor plans to expand mass-produced models to include hybrid vehicles (HEV) and establish a flexible multi-model production system.

Hyundai Motor expects the expansion of its India business to translate into more business opportunities for partner companies in a new market. With the completion of the new Pune plant, the number of Korean parts suppliers that have entered India with Hyundai Motor and Kia has reached more than 120. That is 36 more than at the end of 2019, when Kia's Anantapur plant was completed. Partner companies' sales are also rising sharply, with Sungwoo Hitech and Seoyon E-Hwa posting India sales last year of 534.6 billion won and 592.5 billion won, up 54.6% and 97%, respectively, from 2019.

Following the Chennai Plants 1 and 2, Hyundai Motor's third production base in India, the new Pune plant, incorporates smart manufacturing technologies such as an artificial intelligence (AI)-based crack detection system and industrial welding robots. In addition to an automobile assembly plant, it also has an engine plant, a test track, and employee training facilities where Augmented Reality (AR)-based training is conducted.

Hyundai Motor plans to have the new Pune plant handle production of the local strategic model Venue, while pursuing a full electric vehicle (EV) transition at the existing Chennai plant. This aligns with the Indian government's production-linked incentive (PLI—subsidies paid to local EV manufacturers and parts procurement companies) policy under its goal to make 30% of new-vehicle sales electric by 2030.

Considering growing demand in India for electric vehicles and other future mobility, Hyundai Motor plans to launch a new small electric SUV—based on India's vehicle class standards—in the first quarter of next year, adding to the Ioniq 5 and Creta Electric currently on sale. It also plans to train top talent through its technology research center and equip newly launched models with Level 2 Autonomous Driving technology.

It will also invest in startups and new businesses, including collaborating with local two-wheeler maker TVS to develop and commercialize a prototype electric three-wheeler. The amount Hyundai Motor plans to invest by 2032 comes to 20.7 trillion won. To invest efficiently, it is also pushing to establish an investment-specialized corporation in India.

Hyundai Motor Group Chair Chung Eui-sun said at the completion ceremony, "From the first time we entered India 30 years ago, Hyundai Motor worked to earn the trust of local customers. Since launching our first local model, the Santro, India has become a key pillar in Hyundai Motor's global growth," and added, "The completion ceremony of the Pune plant will mark the opening of a new chapter for Hyundai Motor in India."

Attending the ceremony were Chair Chung; Vice Chair Chang Jae-hoon; Hyundai Motor CEO (president) José Muñoz; and Tarun Garg, CEO of Hyundai Motor India Ltd. (HMIL), among other top executives. Also present were Maharashtra Deputy Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis; Member of Parliament Shrirang Appa Barne; and Lee Seong-ho, Korea's ambassador to India, along with other political and government figures from both countries.

title: 'Not Even Free Money Worked' - The Brutal Truth About Why the Electric Truck Market Collapsed
description:
Here's why... Electric Pickup Sales Are In A Tailspin The numbers look catastrophic at first – but one outlier in this table quietly blows up the standard narrative about why EV sales collapsed.
With the sole exception of the Rivian R1T, every electric pickup has seen a dramatic fall-off into 2026.
EV credits helped to make a lot of new converts, but they haven't been the only factor in electric car adoption.
Exhibit B: incentives that match, or beat, the EV credits have failed to move the needle.
EV credits helped to expand the potential customer base a bit, but the growth was always going to be limited.
text:
In many ways, the end of the tax credits brought the EV segment's momentum to a screeching halt last year. They pulled the $7,500 bonus for qualifying electric vehicles and, seemingly overnight, countless battery-powered cars were discontinued or canceled, and sales plummeted.

We won't argue that there are fewer electric cars on the road today than there would be if those credits were still in place. But, we could argue that electric trucks like the Tesla Cybertruck and the Ford F-150 Lightning would be in essentially the same place they're in right now, with or without the credits. Here's why...

Electric Pickup Sales Are In A Tailspin

The numbers look catastrophic at first – but one outlier in this table quietly blows up the standard narrative about why EV sales collapsed. We're probably not telling you anything you don't know when we say that electric pickup sales have seen brighter days, but let's compare H1 sales for some leading models to see what we're talking about.

With the sole exception of the Rivian R1T, every electric pickup has seen a dramatic fall-off into 2026. Yes, the disappearance of EV credits plays a big part in this decline in sales numbers, but we don't think that's the only reason this has been such a bad year for the segment.

Ford Offered $8,000 Cash Back And Still Couldn't Move The Needle

Exhibit A: Declining sales have been a common, but not uniform, trend in the electric segment. Tesla sold around 1,000 more Model Ys in May and June than it did in the same months in 2025. EV credits helped to make a lot of new converts, but they haven't been the only factor in electric car adoption.

Exhibit B: incentives that match, or beat, the EV credits have failed to move the needle. Ford offered $8,000 cash back incentives on the F-150 Lightning in January this year, and only managed to sell 647 units that month. $8,000 more than makes up for the loss of the $7,500 incentive, and the brand still sold fewer than half as many electric pickups as it had a year prior. Not even free money worked.

These were regional offers, but they were being offered in major metropolitan areas. Additionally, Ford repeated the deal in various regions throughout the rest of H1, and still wound up selling around 16% as many units in H1 as it had in that same stretch of time in 2025.

The Early Adopters Are Gone – And There Aren't Many Buyers Left

We're not arguing that the evaporation of the EV tax credits has not had an impact on electric pickup sales, only that this is not nearly the only factor at play. But what does a market that's truly bottomed out look like? One data point stands out – and it's the one brand that didn't collapse.

The Rivian R1T Sales Numbers Look Better Because They're So Small

Our argument is that, once your early adopters have been taken care of, there aren't that many buyers left. EV credits helped to expand the potential customer base a bit, but the growth was always going to be limited. The Rivian R1T's 2026 sales are actually better than its 2025 sales, which we think helps to support our theory that it's not just the EV credits, and that we're looking at a very small potential market, with or without the credits.

With the sole exception of April, Rivian has been kicking its own butt every single month this year on sales. But, its sales numbers are very small. The R1T hasn't hit four figures in a month since September 2024, when it sold 3,541 units.

We can't tell you exactly what Rivian's sales goals are, or whether these numbers make the brand's investors happy; we can only tell you that 530 sales last June is an easy number to beat. Ford sold 2,200 Lightnings in that same stretch of time last year, an improvement over the year prior, and a number that the brand failed to match in June 2026, at just 491 units sold.

Our hypothesis? A handful of supply-chain hiccups over the years mean that not everyone who wants a Rivian R1T has one just yet. The brand will likely continue selling anywhere from 500 to 600 units a month until those buyers are covered.

While EVs Stall, Hybrid Pickups Are Setting Sales Records Every Month

EVs will likely continue to be a small, niche segment into the coming years, with expensive electric pickups being a niche within that niche. Hybrids, on the other hand, seem to set a new best month, every single month. Earlier this year, Ford sold 33,861 Maverick pickups in Q1, with 17,050 of those being hybrids, accounting for just over half of the total.

The i-Force Max Hybrid Toyota Tacoma only accounted for about 10% of Q1 Tacoma sales, but that comes out to 6,887 units in the first three months of 2026. That's more business than any electric pickup did in that same stretch.

We could go on for pages about why hybrids are more popular than EVs (and we have, more than once), but one key consideration is the fact that you don't need to plan your trips around charging stations.

There's Never Been A Better Time To Buy A Used Electric Pickup

If this all sounds very doom and gloom, the upside is that the auto industry's $1.2 trillion loss is your $42,100 gain. That's what you'll be saving on a 2022 Ford F-150 Lightning Platinum, according to our price tracker tool, which currently sees the top trim trending at just $48,774 from an MSRP of $90,874, representing a 46.3% drop in value after four years on the market.

EVs have been notoriously fast depreciators, thanks in large part to their steep initial costs and the fact that so many of these cars were leased rather than bought, meaning that dealer lots are now flooded with those first-year models. To round up some attractive used listings we were able to find...

A 42,380-mile 2022 Ford F-150 Lightning XLT is selling for $37,990 in Oklahoma.

A 43,692-mile 2023 Ford F-150 Lightning XLT is selling for $40,590 in Nevada.

An 18,072-mile 2023 Ford F-150 Lightning XLT is selling for $49,990 in Texas.

A 12,957-mile 2023 Ford F-150 Lightning XLT is selling for $48,990 in Massachusetts.

A 40,115-mile 2024 Ford F-150 Lightning Flash is selling for $49,990 in Virginia.

These numbers are just to give you an idea of what's out there, but the higher up the trim ladder you go, the more money you'll save, as the depreciation is steepest at the top.

Those who drive electric pickups tend to swear by them. But, Ford spent around $19.5 billion restructuring it's EV plans and getting these cars into production. A small-but-passionate fanbase simply isn't going to cut it at that price.

text:
Los Angeles, October 13, 2026 – Green SM officially launches its all-electric taxi service in Los Angeles, California, marking the company’s first entry into North America and its ninth global market. Green SM brings modern and safe mobility, professionally operated services and good fares to enhance the everyday travel experience for local residents.

Entering Los Angeles brings Green SM into one of the world’s most dynamic and demanding markets. It also marks another step in the international expansion of the Vietnamese mobility brand, following its rapid growth across markets in Asia and Europe.

Starting October 13, customers in Los Angeles can book Green SM rides through the Green SM app, by calling the company’s hotline or by hailing a vehicle on the street. With its growing service network, Green SM will cater to a wide range of mobility needs, from everyday trips and longer journeys to airport transfers.

Green SM is committed to delivering a high-quality customer experience through its 5 Good Promises: Good Cars, Good Drivers, Good Price, Good Experience and Good for the Environment. In Los Angeles, Green SM operates a 100% all-electric fleet of VinFast vehicles, featuring spacious, smooth and modern VinFast VF 8 models; a professional and courteous driver team carefully selected and thoroughly trained; transparent fare information and promotions; and attentive, reliable service designed to give customers rides that are not only greener, but also comfortable and dependable.

To celebrate the launch, new customers who sign up for Green SM will receive 50% off fares, up to USD 12 per ride, on their first five trips. In addition, customers can enjoy a complimentary Green Pass membership, which includes 10 discount vouchers per month, each offering 30% off fares, up to USD 10 per ride.

Ms. Hoang Thanh Hang, CEO of Green SM in the U.S., said: “The United States represents an important milestone in Green SM’s growth journey. We are not simply expanding into a new market. We aim to build trust with customers, drivers and local communities, one journey at a time. Our experience across international markets has shown us that the future of electric mobility is not defined by an all-electric fleet alone. It also depends on service quality, well-trained and reliable drivers, and genuine care in every customer interaction.”

Following the launch, Green SM will gradually build its local team and strengthen its operational capabilities, while recruiting and training local drivers. Through these efforts, Green SM aims not only to create new employment opportunities, but also to make a direct contribution to the transition toward greener mobility in Los Angeles and across the region.

Founded in Vietnam in 2023, Green SM currently operates a green mobility ecosystem across Vietnam, Laos, Indonesia, the Philippines, India, Kazakhstan, Denmark and the Netherlands. As part of its global expansion, Green SM has completed approximately 850 million rides, covering a total distance of nearly 6 billion kilometers, helping reduce more than 800,000 tons of CO₂ emissions, equivalent to the amount of carbon absorbed by approximately 36 million trees.

Green SM’s presence in the United States combines VinFast’s strengths in all-electric vehicles with Green SM’s operational expertise, giving customers an additional option for smooth, comfortable and zero-emission mobility. This also marks an important milestone in the global growth journey of the Vietnamese all-electric ride-hailing company. From Los Angeles, Green SM will continue investing in its fleet, technology, driver team and service quality, putting customer experience at the heart of its sustainable growth in the U.S. and international markets./.

name: Detroit and Evs
title: What a time to take the wheel - Auto retail faces disruption, but opportunity remains firmly ahead
authors: Lucas Malinowski, Ian Cruickshank, Duane Marino, Wolfgang Koehler, Blair Qualey, Canadian Auto Dealer, Perry Lefko
description:
The automotive industry has always been at the forefront of innovation and industrial imagination.
Cars are safer, faster, more reliable, luxurious and technologically advanced than ever before, all while maintaining affordability relative to inflation.
Looking across the river at GM’s Renaissance Centre and visiting my first North American International Auto Show in Detroit ensured that initial obsession would always be in the back of my mind, no matter what I ended up doing in life.
Another obsession with history and politics took me down a professional path of working in government, communications and public affairs.
The automotive industry has always been at the forefront of innovation and industrial imagination.
text:
One of my earliest childhood memories is walking through Nuremberg with my parents and my father challenging me to name the marque of every passing car on the busy streets.

Our family had recently escaped communist Poland, where the drab selection of Soviet-approved personal transportation didn’t quite spark the imagination of this fledgling car enthusiast in the same way the shiny and bright offerings of West Germany did toward the end of the Cold War.

I was hooked, and have always taken pride in being able to identify even the most obscure OEM badges and models wherever my travels took me.

Windsor was where my family initially called home in Canada, and for the first time in my life I actually met people who worked in the auto industry. For a living!

The automotive industry has always been at the forefront of innovation and industrial imagination. Cars are safer, faster, more reliable, luxurious and technologically advanced than ever before, all while maintaining affordability relative to inflation.

Looking across the river at GM’s Renaissance Centre and visiting my first North American International Auto Show in Detroit ensured that initial obsession would always be in the back of my mind, no matter what I ended up doing in life.

Another obsession with history and politics took me down a professional path of working in government, communications and public affairs. But the passion for all things automotive was always there, albeit in a personal rather than professional capacity.

That all changed in 2023 when I jumped at the chance to merge the two things that keep me up at night and join the team at Global Automakers of Canada. The past three years have provided a unique opportunity to grow from being passionate about cars to understanding the automotive industry, which for more than a century has sparked imaginations and obsessions around the world.

Now, the members of Global Automakers have given me the privilege and responsibility of representing the interests of an industry in the midst of truly profound change.

The automotive industry has always been at the forefront of innovation and industrial imagination. Cars are safer, faster, more reliable, luxurious and technologically advanced than ever before, all while maintaining affordability relative to inflation.

We have a history of meeting and exceeding challenges initially thought insurmountable, and have grown into a globally integrated industry where innovation knows few borders. But many of the underpinnings of the past century’s success are being stressed in new and multiple ways at once, particularly in Canada.

Automotive tariffs and a rupture in the highly integrated North American market are adding significant costs across the supply chain and impacting the competitiveness of the region’s manufacturing base. We need to get back to tariff-free auto trade to keep North America competitive for the dozens of Global Automakers who build cars in the region.

The transition to electrification requires new product development and production methods, along with significant capital investments from automakers.

It also requires outside players, such as charging providers, to do their part to support consumer demand, along with new consumer education.

EVs are getting better every day, but a significant percentage of drivers remain concerned that they’re not the right fit for their needs, particularly in North America.

A significant turn away from electrification in the United States could create a situation down the road where North American drivers don’t have access to the latest and greatest vehicle technologies deployed around the world — an unimaginable thought for a younger me calling out every single nameplate my father pointed at.

Either of these developments on their own would represent a generational shift in the history of the industry. But we also have to add the incredibly rapid rise of Chinese automotive manufacturing and significant export capacity that is making its impact on markets around the globe.

Automakers are competitors by nature and have always compared their own products against segment leaders to find ways they can improve the next generation. But there are serious and real questions about how competing with Chinese OEMs can be done on a level playing field.

As it looks to open our market to these new entrants, the Government of Canada will face a significant challenge in balancing fair competition that supports the benefits of our own domestic manufacturing with the need to address affordability for drivers.

I must admit that on a recent family vacation to a Central American country with significant Chinese imports, for the first time in my life I found myself passing cars with nameplates I’d never seen or heard of before. While humbling, it was also exciting to be reminded that there’s always something new to learn about automotive.

This is a daunting time for our industry, but we have shown over and over again our ability to adapt and thrive despite the roadblocks ahead. And as we all know, it’s the twisty roads that make for the best driving.

description:
“It’s not just a solar project when the sun shines or wind when the wind blows,” Oliver says.
“Now they’re starting to home in more on biomethane, which can go straight into the network.” Second life for solar panels Supply Solar founder Ali Zeerak’s biggest problem with Australia’s growing mountain of unwanted solar panels is simple: much of it still works.
Giving discarded Australian panels a second life could replace candles and other polluting energy sources while providing basic electricity.
Supply Solar added a retail arm in 2023, letting it collect panels directly from customers when they upgraded.
Santos funded its share through a $US150 million sustainable transition loan and a $15 million Australian federal government grant.
text:
ASX-listed Delorean’s earlier bioenergy facilities typically used biogas to generate electricity and heat. At Salisbury, it is upgrading the gas to biomethane, liquefying the separated carbon dioxide for industrial use, and recovering nutrients from leftover material to produce fertiliser.

Upgrading to biomethane extracts more energy from the fuel – about 95 per cent, against 87 per cent when the same gas is burned for electricity and heat.

The project is being delivered under a build-own-operate model, with six revenue streams including waste gate fees, renewable gas, electricity, liquid CO₂, biofertiliser and renewable-gas certificates.

Assembling the project took years as policy gradually shifted to support renewable gas, with rising fuel and fertiliser costs adding to the case for domestic alternatives.

Delorean bought the Salisbury land in 2019 and spent years developing the site, securing approvals, arranging feedstock and reaching financial close. Construction began in 2025, with total investment estimated at $40 million.

It was funded through Delorean equity, project debt from National Australia Bank and $7.74 million in support from the Australian Renewable Energy Agency.

“It’s not just a solar project when the sun shines or wind when the wind blows,” Oliver says. “This has got so many different moving parts.”

Delivery brought its own challenges, including shortages of skilled trades and specialist equipment, as well as the unusual task of putting gas into the distribution network rather than taking it out.

Now about 90 per cent complete, SA1 is close to delivering its first gas. Delorean has secured 10-year offtake arrangements with Origin for renewable gas and Supagas for liquefied CO₂.

The company sees SA1 as a proof of concept for a national roll-out, and five similar facilities are under consideration or development in NSW, Victoria and Queensland. The Salisbury site itself could eventually expand from 70,000 tonnes of annual feedstock capacity to 125,000 tonnes.

Oliver says the attention of the energy industry is shifting. “There was a lot of focus on hydrogen,” he says. “Now they’re starting to home in more on biomethane, which can go straight into the network.”

Second life for solar panels

Supply Solar founder Ali Zeerak’s biggest problem with Australia’s growing mountain of unwanted solar panels is simple: much of it still works.

Zeerak started the Save Energy Save Life initiative in 2021 after seeing panels discarded as households upgraded their solar systems. Many are only five to 10 years old, he says, leaving another decade or more of useful life.

His company collects, tests and refurbishes used panels before exporting them to communities in Afghanistan, Malaysia, Indonesia and parts of Africa. Supply Solar has repurposed about 9450 panels, representing 2.9 megawatts of capacity.

His motivation is personal. Zeerak grew up in Afghanistan, where his village had limited access to electricity. Giving discarded Australian panels a second life could replace candles and other polluting energy sources while providing basic electricity.

The initiative began as an export business and the company spent about eight months securing licences. It initially required Defence approval to export panels, before being allowed unlimited exports in 2024. Supply Solar added a retail arm in 2023, letting it collect panels directly from customers when they upgraded.

Logistics remain the biggest obstacle. Collecting panels from remote locations can cost more than the panels, making equipment unaffordable for overseas buyers. One recent enquiry involved about 1000 panels being decommissioned from 10 warehouses in Brisbane.

“You can’t really pay for a panel more than $1, or $2, or $3,” he says. “When you calculate the logistics, it’s going to cost you over $10.”

Supply Solar wants collection and storage facilities in every state, creating a national network for used panels, batteries and inverters.

Zeerak says the opportunity is both environmental and social: keeping usable equipment out of landfill while putting affordable renewable power within reach of communities that might otherwise struggle to access it.

Sustainable fuel gets off the ground

For sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) to become a meaningful part of Australia’s aviation market, airlines need more than access to the fuel itself. They also need proof that its environmental benefits are genuine, traceable and reportable.

That is the problem Viva Energy has addressed with a refurbished storage tank at its Pinkenba terminal, connected to Brisbane Airport’s existing fuel system.

The $4.9 million project, supported by $2.4 million from the Australian Renewable Energy Agency, allows Viva to receive, store, blend and supply SAF to the airport. It also includes an international certification and digital accounting system so customers can track and claim the fuel’s emissions benefits.

In July, Viva became the first Australian fuel supplier to supply SAF through an airport refuelling system with certified emissions certificates, after importing just over one megalitre of biogenic feedstock fuel from Malaysia. The fuel is blended into the existing supply chain and delivered through Brisbane Airport’s hydrant network.

Vanessa Lenihan, Viva’s head of decarbonisation and future fuels, says the project was conceived to bridge the gap between imported SAF available today and Australian production in the future.

“We could see there was a gap in the market of the infrastructure from the terminal to the airport,” she says. “What we want to do is be able to prove up that supply chain and get the market moving while domestic manufacturing is established in Australia.”

Cost remains a hurdle. SAF is three to five times more expensive than conventional jet fuel, making efficient shipping and logistics essential to building demand. Viva hopes to establish regular imports through Brisbane before domestic SAF becomes available, potentially in five to 10 years.

“Anything we can do to minimise those logistics costs is actually very important for reducing that barrier of uptake of SAF,” Lenihan says.

Carbon storage at scale

In South Australia’s Cooper Basin, Santos is using infrastructure that once produced gas to permanently store carbon underground.

The Moomba Carbon Capture and Storage project, Australia’s first large-scale onshore CCS facility, captures carbon dioxide from its gas processing operations and injects it into depleted gas reservoirs nearby.

Since it began operating in September 2024, it has stored 2.3 million tonnes of CO₂-equivalent. Santos says the project helped it reach its 2030 Scope 1 and 2 equity emissions-reduction target five years ahead of schedule.

The project represents an investment of about $US220 million ($316 million). Santos funded its share through a $US150 million sustainable transition loan and a $15 million Australian federal government grant. Reusing existing infrastructure and the Cooper Basin’s well-understood geology helped make Moomba one of the world’s lowest-cost CCS projects, Santos says.

Building it also meant developing the rules around it. Santos worked with the South Australian government and the Clean Energy Regulator to develop the approvals framework and methodology for generating Australian Carbon Credit Units.

The project uses former production wells to monitor the underground CO₂ plume rather than relying on more expensive 4D seismic testing. Moomba generated more than 1.4 million ACCUs in its first 12 months of operation.

For Santos, the project is also a test of whether carbon storage can become a larger business. The Cooper and Eromanga basins could store up to 20 million tonnes of CO₂ a year, and Santos is exploring infrastructure to import CO₂ for storage.

“CCS is an incredible opportunity for Australia to secure its standing as the region’s carbon storage powerhouse,” Santos managing director and CEO Kevin Gallagher says.

text:
Nuclear energy plays a significant role in the United States' efforts to build a stable and carbon-free electricity grid. It provides a consistent, reliable power source that complements intermittent renewable energy, ensuring electricity supply even when the sun isn't shining or the wind isn't blowing. Understanding its operational benefits, strict safety regulations, and economic implications is key to recognizing its contribution to the nation's energy future.

How Nuclear Energy Supports a Stable Grid

One of nuclear power's primary advantages is its unwavering reliability. Nuclear power plants operate continuously at full power more than 93% of the time, making them the most reliable energy source in the U.S. electric grid. This high capacity factor means these plants produce maximum power output for a higher percentage of hours in a year compared to any other energy source¹.

This consistent operation is crucial for grid stability. Nuclear facilities provide a constant baseload power supply, unaffected by weather conditions, which is essential for maintaining a steady flow of electricity¹. This stability is particularly important as the grid integrates more variable renewable sources like solar and wind power.

Nuclear power plants also have a minimal land footprint. They require relatively small amounts of land to generate large quantities of electricity compared to other energy sources¹. This reduces land disturbance and makes them efficient generators in terms of space.

Nuclear Energy's Role in Carbon Reduction

Nuclear energy is a cornerstone of the U.S.'s carbon-free electricity generation. In 2023, nuclear energy generated nearly half of the carbon-free electricity in the United States¹. This makes it a crucial component in achieving U.S. carbon reduction goals and combating climate change due to its carbon-free operation².

During operation, nuclear reactors do not produce carbon dioxide emissions or air pollution³. Annually, nuclear power avoids the emission of 437 million metric tons of carbon dioxide, equivalent to taking 95 million typical passenger vehicles off the road¹. This environmental benefit is a key driver for its continued support and development.

Nuclear power can effectively complement intermittent renewable energy sources, such as solar and wind. It provides a reliable, dispatchable power source that can operate 24/7, thereby ensuring grid stability when renewable output is low³. Combining nuclear and renewables can significantly lower the overall cost of achieving a carbon-free grid⁴.

Strict Safety and Regulation

Safety and security are paramount in the nuclear energy industry, overseen by the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC). The NRC is responsible for regulating commercial nuclear power plants and other uses of nuclear materials, ensuring their safe and secure operation⁵.

The NRC enforces stringent safety standards, licensing requirements, and continuous oversight through regular inspections to protect public health, safety, and the environment. Due to these strict regulations and protocols, major incidents in the U.S. nuclear industry are rare .

Reactor designs must meet a theoretical 1 in 10,000-year core damage frequency, with modern designs often exceeding this standard . Containment vessels are also designed to withstand extreme weather events and earthquakes. Each plant must have an NRC-approved cybersecurity plan to prevent attacks, and critical safety systems are isolated from the internet⁶.

Used nuclear fuel is stored securely on-site at nuclear power plants, primarily in dry casks or spent fuel pools. While the Department of Energy (DOE) is responsible for the long-term disposal of spent nuclear fuel, a permanent repository is still under development².

Economic Implications and Future Developments

The nuclear energy industry is a significant economic contributor in the United States. It directly employs about 73,800 workers in high-paying careers. For example, plant, system, and nuclear reactor operators earned around $120,000 annually on average as of May 2023².

In 2022, the nuclear industry supported approximately 256,849 jobs nationally and contributed roughly $63.8 billion to U.S. GDP². It also generated $15.9 billion in federal, state, and local tax revenue in the same year . Domestic nuclear fuel sources and a stable supply chain enhance U.S. energy independence and security¹.

The Cost of New Nuclear Plants

Building new traditional nuclear power plants involves very high upfront capital costs, long construction times, and significant financial risks⁵. For instance, the two AP1000 units at Georgia Power Co.'s Plant Vogtle cost approximately $35 billion for 2,234 MW, which comes out to about $15,700 per kilowatt (kW). This was significantly over its original certified cost. Government estimates for the next pair of AP1000 reactors are around $7,861/kW in 2023 dollars⁷.

Once built, nuclear power plants have relatively low and stable operating costs, primarily due to inexpensive fuel (uranium) and a long operational lifespan³.

Advanced Reactor Technologies

Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) are advanced reactor designs that aim for reduced capital investment, smaller physical footprints, and shorter construction schedules. SMRs are expected to have lower upfront capital costs and shorter construction schedules than traditional large-scale plants⁵. The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) actively supports SMR development, with deployment anticipated in the late 2020s to early 2030s⁸.

However, the path to SMR deployment is not without challenges. The first commercial SMR project in the U.S. by NuScale Power, the Carbon Free Power Project (CFPP), was canceled in November 2023 due to escalating costs and insufficient customer commitments. This cancellation highlights continued economic challenges for new nuclear builds, even for SMRs, with inflationary pressures and rising interest rates significantly impacting project costs⁶. Despite this, the DOE continues to support SMR development through various programs and funding initiatives, aiming to reduce costs and accelerate deployment .

Beyond SMRs, other advanced reactor designs, such as molten salt reactors and fast reactors, are being developed. These designs promise enhanced safety, efficiency, and potentially the ability to consume nuclear waste⁸.

Government Support and Future Investment

There is bipartisan support for nuclear energy within the U.S. government, driven by its benefits for climate change mitigation, energy security, and economic development. The Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 introduced the Zero-Emission Nuclear Power Production Credit (Section 45U). This credit offers a base of 0.3 cents/kWh (inflation-adjusted after 2024) for electricity produced at qualified nuclear power facilities for tax years 2024-2032¹.

In June 2026, the DOE announced a conditional loan commitment of up to $17.5 billion to support the deployment of 10 new large-scale nuclear reactors, with construction expected to begin by 2030 . This signifies a renewed federal commitment to expanding nuclear capacity. Furthermore, in October 2026, the DOE announced a conditional loan commitment of up to $4.2 billion to finance nuclear uprates and modernization across Vistra's nuclear fleet in Pennsylvania and Ohio. This financing aims to preserve existing baseload power and add 433 MW of new capacity⁹.

Rapidly increasing electricity demand, particularly from artificial intelligence infrastructure and large-scale data centers, is a key driver behind renewed investment in firm, reliable power sources like nuclear energy⁹. The ADVANCE Act, signed into law in 2024, aims to streamline regulatory processes and boost financing for nuclear energy . These legislative and financial actions underscore the strategic importance of nuclear power for the U.S. energy landscape.

To learn more about the broader discussion surrounding nuclear power, including its various advantages and disadvantages, you can refer to "The pros and cons of nuclear energy in 2025"¹(https://example.com/blog/nuclear-energy-pros-and-cons).

Conclusion

Nuclear energy is a critical asset for the U.S. power grid, providing a reliable, carbon-free baseload power source that enhances grid stability and energy independence. While new plant construction faces high upfront costs, advanced reactor designs and strong government support indicate a promising future. Its role in reducing carbon emissions, combined with strict safety regulations and significant economic contributions, positions nuclear energy as an indispensable component of the nation's clean energy transition.

text:
Swedish transport company Einride was an early pioneer in the development of autonomous electric trucks—the company has a cabless autonomous truck that has been running in pilots for several years. However, the company hasn’t put all its electric eggs in the autonomous basket—it operates a large heavy-duty EV charging site in California, and in August it placed an order for 500 Tesla Semis.

Now autonomous trucking is starting to happen. Einride has two of its cabless, driverless electric trucks running scheduled routes with EASE Logistics in Marysville, Ohio. The operations are part of the Truck Automation Corridor Project, a joint effort of the Ohio Department of Transportation (ODOT), DriveOhio, and the Indiana Department of Transportation. This is EASE’s third autonomous trucking deployment with DriveOhio.

“EASE believes in leading through action and putting innovation to work in real-world operations,” said Peter Coratola Jr, President and CEO of EASE Logistics. “This deployment builds on that commitment while helping advance the adoption of autonomous freight across the transportation industry.”

Einride’s vehicles are capable of SAE Level 4-autonomous mode, meaning that they operate without a human in the cab—a remote operator monitors each truck off-site and can intervene if needed. The trucks run on local public roads, carrying freight between EASE facilities. The deployment is generating operational data on safety, reliability and efficiency that will inform how autonomous freight scales beyond this initial route.

“This deployment reflects the maturity of our purpose-built autonomous stack, combining driverless operation with remote oversight to run safely in real-world operations,” said Henrik Green, CTO at Einride. “Daily operations in Marysville give us the proof points we need to keep expanding autonomous freight across the corridor and beyond.”
