text:
Texas

TotalEnergies expanded its existing United States renewable energy joint venture with global investment firm KKR by incorporating an additional 700 MW of capacity. Reflecting an enterprise value of $1.2 billion, the portfolio consists of three utility scale solar projects situated across Texas and Ohio.

All three solar installations are targeted to achieve commercial operation by the first quarter of 2027. TotalEnergies will continue to serve as project operator post-closing, marketing the clean generation directly or delivering power under existing third-party off-take contracts as part of its strategy to build a global portfolio of integrated, low-carbon power assets.

Illinois

Arevon Energy secured three 20-year indexed renewable energy credit agreements with Ameren Illinois, ComEd, and MidAmerican Energy for its 200 MWac Panther Energy Project in Perry County. The contracts were awarded following the project’s selection in the Illinois Power Agency Summer procurement, an initiative approved by state regulators under the Climate and Equitable Jobs Act to advance 1.55 GW of new clean energy capacity.

Slated to break ground in 2027 and reach commercial operation in 2028, the solar facility will supply enough electricity to power roughly 37,000 Illinois homes. Construction of the array is expected to generate 200 local trade jobs and deliver an estimated $20 million in direct property tax payments to support local schools, roads, and municipal services over its lifespan.

Elsewhere in the state, ComEd collaborated with legacy manufacturer Richardson Electronics to construct a commercial battery energy storage system at Richardson’s facility in La Fox. Supported by the state’s Reimagining Energy and Vehicles program, the partnership centers on a 5 MWh demonstration project that will serve as a testing ground for scaling locally manufactured energy storage platforms across commercial and industrial customer bases.

The installation aligns with the broader goals of Illinois recently passed Clean and Reliable Grid Affordability Act, which focuses on integrating distributed storage assets to mitigate peak energy demand and alleviate grid congestion. Projects participating in ComEd’s interconnection process can leverage state tax incentives alongside ComEd’s Distributed Generation Rebate Program, which provides commercial and industrial participants up to $300 per kWh of installed battery storage capacity.

South Carolina

Developer energyRe completed an $815 million financing package for five utility scale solar projects totaling 360 MW across South Carolina. The debt and tax equity financing was led by Bank of America, Santander, and Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, representing one of the largest solar-only debt transactions executed in state history.

Each of the five solar assets is anchored by a 25-year power purchase agreement, establishing a long-term revenue stream while generating tens of millions of dollars in municipal tax revenue for local host counties. The deal propels energyRe toward its target of deploying $2 billion in South Carolina infrastructure by 2030 and brings the developer total capital raised across its multi-state portfolio to over $1.9 billion.

Massachusetts

Distributed Energy Infrastructure finished harvests across two dual-use cranberry agrivoltaic facilities located in Plymouth and Kingston. Constructed on formerly fallow bogs owned by Greenbacker Renewables, the Black Cat and Ring Road projects represent the first commercial harvests of a perennial wetland crop cultivated directly beneath elevated solar array structures.

The 1 MW Black Cat installation incorporates a 500 kVA battery storage system rated at 2,700 kWh of capacity, while the 4.4 MW Ring Road array is coupled with a 13.5 MWh energy storage system. Both projects deliver power to local electricity customers through community solar structures supported by the Massachusetts SMART program and Clean Peak Standard incentive mechanisms, restoring agricultural productivity to local farmers while reinforcing the regional distribution grid.

text:
Company marks occasion with anniversary webpage highlighting projects over the years

NEW ORLEANS, Oct. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Entergy is commemorating the 25th anniversary of its Environmental Initiatives Fund, marking a milestone in a long history of environmental commitment that began well before sustainability became a corporate trend.

For a quarter century, Entergy's EIF has exemplified the company's early and ongoing leadership in environmental stewardship. Established in 2001 as a shareholder-funded grant program, the EIF represents a proactive approach to protecting natural resources, reducing emissions, restoring habitats and strengthening community resilience across Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi and Texas. Over its 25-year history, Entergy shareholders have invested nearly $45 million in community-based environmental improvements across the region.

"Reaching 25 years of the Environmental Initiatives Fund is more than marking time; it's a reaffirmation of a commitment our shareholders embraced long before sustainability was in the spotlight," said John Weiss, vice president of sustainability and environmental policy. "The EIF has allowed us to support meaningful projects that improve local ecosystems, strengthen communities and advance environmental progress throughout our service area."

In 2025 alone, the EIF provided $1 million in shareholder-funded support to 11 partner organizations working in areas such as wetland restoration, tree planting, biodiversity education and green infrastructure development. These efforts complement Entergy's broader environmental initiatives, including long-term climate commitments, coastal restoration partnerships and decades of community-focused conservation work.

This anniversary highlights a broader legacy in climate action for Entergy. In 2001 — the same year the EIF launched — Entergy became the first U.S. utility to voluntarily limit its carbon emissions, signaling a level of environmental responsibility uncommon at the time. Two decades later, Entergy operates one of the cleanest large-scale power generation fleets in the United States and is a nationally recognized leader in sustainability, reinforcing the company's long-term commitment to climate action, environmental reporting and performance across key sustainability indicators.

Anniversary webpage highlights progress, partnerships

To mark the 25-year milestone, Entergy has introduced a commemorative webpage featuring:

Learn more about the Environmental Initiatives Fund's 25-year impact and explore the anniversary content at Entergy.com/Environment/EIF.

About Entergy

Entergy (NYSE: ETR) generates, transmits and distributes electricity to power life for more than 3 million customers through our operating companies in Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi and Texas. We're focused on keeping costs for our customers as low as possible while providing reliable energy that our communities count on. We're also investing in growth for the future with a more resilient, cleaner energy system that includes modern natural gas, nuclear and renewable energy generation. As a nationally recognized leader in sustainability and corporate citizenship, we deliver more than $100 million in economic benefits each year to the communities we serve through philanthropy, volunteerism and advocacy. Entergy is a Fortune 500 company headquartered in New Orleans, Louisiana, and has approximately 12,000 employees. Learn more at Entergy.com and connect with @Entergy on social media.

title: From climate-driven disasters to Rohingya refugee camps, solar kits help keep the lights on
description:
Solar energy kits are portable, rechargeable and grid-independent When disasters strike and humanitarian needs surge, solar kits can become an invaluable resource, says Sarah Rosenberg-Jansen, a research fellow at the Stockholm Environment Institute, an independent research and policy institute specializing in sustainable development.
These solar kits — all-in-one, compact units that use solar panels and are not reliant on utility companies — are easy to move and recharge, according to Rosenberg-Jansen.
In terms of function, the kits can be "anything from solar lanterns to solar home systems, solar torches, solar heating pads, to electric cook stoves that use solar as their energy source,” she said.

text:
ISLAMABAD – Every day, Mohammed Saber places a single rectangular solar panel on the roof of the bamboo-and-tarpaulin shack that he and his family have called home for years, the last stop on their journey after fleeing the Myanmar military’s brutal crackdown on the Rohingya in 2017.

The panel is part of a portable solar kit given to the Rohingya refugee family as humanitarian aid six years ago. It's been the family's primary source of electricity, making daily life so much easier in the camp for the displaced in Teknaf, Bangladesh.

"We can now charge our phones, cook with light, children can study at night and use fans during the hot season,” said Saber, 35.

From the flood zones of Nepal to refugee camps in Africa, experts say that solar energy is increasingly becoming part of disaster relief as technology improves, costs fall and humanitarian organizations recognize that having access to electricity is a fundamental need.

Renewable energy solutions are needed more than ever, they say, as climate change drives and intensifies extreme weather while wars, sanctions and political upheavals keep fossil fuel prices volatile.

Solar energy kits are portable, rechargeable and grid-independent

When disasters strike and humanitarian needs surge, solar kits can become an invaluable resource, says Sarah Rosenberg-Jansen, a research fellow at the Stockholm Environment Institute, an independent research and policy institute specializing in sustainable development.

These solar kits — all-in-one, compact units that use solar panels and are not reliant on utility companies — are easy to move and recharge, according to Rosenberg-Jansen.

“In emergency situations, solar kits can be deployed immediately,” she said, adding that they are particularly useful in situations with rapidly rising floodwaters, changing front lines in a conflict, or for moving around in areas where damaged roads make it difficult to travel.

In terms of function, the kits can be "anything from solar lanterns to solar home systems, solar torches, solar heating pads, to electric cook stoves that use solar as their energy source,” she said.

Lower costs of solar energy helped its role in disaster relief

Rosenberg-Jansen also pointed out that solar panels are not prone to price shocks like fossil fuels, which can be difficult and costly to transport to a disaster zone.

Only a few decades ago, solar energy was a luxury, she added, but as technology evolved, mindsets and the price tag changed. Now it's more affordable, thanks to the scaling up of mass manufacturing and technology advancement.

It's also so much easier to use, said Yuriy Boyechko, CEO of Hope For Ukraine, a nonprofit based in the United States that provides solar kits to families living in war-torn Ukraine.

“We have grandmas and grandpas who are around 75-80 years old ... receiving kits,” said Boyechko. “It’s just a matter of plug (in) and play.”

Solar panels are becoming more common now.

On the outskirts of Karachi, Pakistan's economic hub, a tuberculosis clinic run by Doctors Without Borders uses solar energy. In South Sudan's Renk county, the U.N. migration agency installed solar-powered water filtration systems for families displaced by the war in neighboring Sudan.

And after Nepal's massive floods in August that killed 1,455 people and left 5,285 missing — including hundreds of foreign nationals — solar kits were distributed by local and international organizations, including Australia-based charity SolarBuddy.

Funding issues and bureaucracy are still an obstacle in disaster relief

Mark Gibson from Global Platform for Action, or GPA, which promotes affordable, reliable and clean energy access, said that integrating solar energy hasn't come without difficulties.

Aid agencies have had time-tested systems in place, which often include diesel generators as part of long-term leases and agreements. Switching to solar means having to trust new systems and setting up new distribution chains, sometimes in risky environments.

Recent slashes in international donor funding have also undermined — or completely erased — new practices that were starting to take root, said Aimee Jenks, a program leader at GPA.

“Much of the technical expertise in the humanitarian sector on energy has been cut,” she said. “That’s now retracting a lot of progress.”

And while the cost of solar energy has decreased, it's still prohibitive for many.

Boyechko, of Hope For Ukraine, said that by the end of 2026, his nonprofit will have distributed over 3,200 kits.

“But it took us two years to get to that number, because of funding needs,” he said. ”We have a waiting list of about 20,000 families. We just cannot keep up with demand.”

While no energy source is perfect, the move towards renewable energies is likely to decrease reliance on polluting fossil fuels.

For Saber, whose family is among more than 1 million refugees from Myanmar’s Rohingya ethnic and religious minority now living in Bangladesh, the kit means keeping the lights on.

“It’s improved my family’s life,” he said.

___

Freelancer photographer Ayub Khan Dkl in Teknaf, Bangaldesh, contributed to this report.

description:
Synopsis US Secretary of Energy Chris Wright has issued an emergency order to PJM Interconnection to maintain grid stability.

text:
Synopsis

US Secretary of Energy Chris Wright has issued an emergency order to PJM Interconnection to maintain grid stability. This directive allows PJM to activate designated power generation units through October 16. Electricity demand is expected to rise due to unseasonably warm weather and scheduled maintenance. Voluntary conservation measures may be requested from businesses and residents during peak hours. PJM seeks to ensure a steady energy flow amid strained operational conditions.

Listen to this article in summarized format

Loading...

×

US Secretary of Energy Chris Wright has issued an emergency order authorising PJM Interconnection, the regional transmission operator serving much of the Mid-Atlantic and Midwest regions, to run designated power generation units as needed to protect grid stability. The federal directive, issued on October 12, grants PJM temporary emergency authority running from October 13 through October 16. Under the order, the grid operator can mandate certain power plants to generate electricity and, in limited circumstances, tap into backup power reserves to maintain a steady flow of energy across its multistate network, as per the order available on the department’s official website. Federal officials and grid managers clarified that the order is designed specifically to prevent power interruptions and not to announce scheduled blackouts.

Why the emergency order has been issued

Headquartered in the Philadelphia area, PJM Interconnection coordinates wholesale electricity movement across all or parts of 13 states and the District of Columbia.

“PJM serves as the Reliability Coordinator and Balancing Authority for its region and is, therefore, responsible for overseeing the dispatch of generation to meet system demand at all times within the limits of the transmission system. The PJM Region includes all or parts of Delaware, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Maryland, Michigan, New Jersey, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, Virginia, West Virginia, and the District of Columbia,” the order says.

The emergency order comes amid concerns over rising electricity demand and constraints on the regional power grid. Ahead of the anticipated strain, the operator issued a Maximum Generation Alert and a Load Management Alert for October 13, citing a combination of unseasonably warm weather and scheduled infrastructure maintenance.

Electricity demand is forecast to reach approximately 111,500 megawatts or higher on October 13, driven by ‘unseasonably warm autumn weather’.

Live Events

Another factor is the ongoing seasonal maintenance cycle, which typically runs from mid-September through early December. During this period, utilities take generation units and transmission lines offline for maintenance and upgrades to prepare for peak demand during the winter months.

However, scheduled transmission line outages have restricted the amount of electricity that can be transferred between different zones across the PJM system, adding to concerns over supply and grid reliability.

According to the Department of Energy (DOE), without emergency federal intervention, PJM could have faced conditions requiring it to reduce or cut electricity supplies to maintain regional grid stability.

The order also points to backup generation at data centres and other large electricity-consuming facilities as a potential way to ease pressure on the grid.

"It is our understanding that PJM seeks to unlock and deploy backup generation resources (whether auxiliary, standby, directly-connected, battery storage, or other, and whether synchronized or not to the bulk-power system) at data centers (including, but not limited to, hyperscaler facilities) and at other large load industrial and commercial customer sites as another tool to mitigate any undue risk to the bulk-power system," the order noted.

What it means for residents in impacted US states

PJM has emphasised that the initial alert does not require immediate mandatory action from household consumers. Electricity use can continue as normal, with the emergency declaration primarily intended to coordinate power generation and maintain grid stability.

However, the operator has issued capacity advisories and retains the option to activate demand-response measures if conditions deteriorate. Residents and businesses across the 13-state region could be asked to voluntarily reduce non-essential electricity consumption during peak demand periods.

The emergency procedures are consistent with the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) Reliability Standard EOP-011-4, which sets out requirements for emergency operations and responses to electricity supply shortfalls.

Requirement 2 of the standard states that “[e]ach Balancing Authority shall develop, maintain, and implement one or more Reliability Coordinator-reviewed Operating Plan(s) to mitigate Capacity Emergencies and Energy Emergencies within its Balancing Authority Area.”

Balancing Authorities are responsible for requesting that their respective Reliability Coordinators issue an EEA in accordance with Requirement 2 and Attachment 1 to Reliability Standard EOP-011-4. Among other provisions, Requirement 2.2.4 authorizes Balancing Authorities to make “[p]ublic appeals for voluntary Load reductions.”

Section 2.2.9 also requires Balancing Authority operating plans to include provisions for “Transmission Operators to implement operator-controlled manual Load shedding, undervoltage Load shedding, or underfrequency Load shedding.” Section 2.2.10 requires these plans to assess the reliability impacts of “extreme weather conditions.”

These provisions establish procedures for managing electricity emergencies, including capacity shortages, extreme weather and the possibility of controlled power cuts if other measures prove insufficient.

text:
By Rachel More and Giulio Piovaccari

PARIS, Oct 13 (Reuters) – European automakers urged policymakers on Tuesday to do more to help them cope with Chinese competition and the shift to electric vehicles, as a drop in ​third-quarter deliveries at BMW and Stellantis underscored the pressure on the ‌industry.

Europe’s mass-market car industry is under “enormous pressure”, Volkswagen CEO Oliver Blume told an event taking place alongside the Paris motor show, renewing calls for more flexible regulation and incentives to support local manufacturing.

The European Union announced a deal on Friday that could cut Chinese exports of hybrid ‌vehicles ​to the bloc by more than a half, addressing ⁠concerns among European automakers that ⁠Chinese rivals, grappling with weak demand at home and largely shut out of the US market, could flood Europe with low-cost cars.

While broadly welcoming the deal, European manufacturers say policymakers need to do more to help them compete, ​including tackling high energy costs and supporting the transition to EVs.

Stellantis CEO Antonio Filosa said Europe needed more EV battery factories.

Renault’s CEO Francois Provost, meanwhile, warned ⁠the company may have to cut European production ⁠by about 300,000 vehicles if policymakers do not show flexibility ​over 2030 targets for automakers to cut carbon emissions.

COMPLEX RELATIONSHIPS

The pressure on European carmakers ​was highlighted by BMW, which reported a 6.4% drop in global ‌deliveries in the third quarter as sales in China fell by a quarter.

Stellantis, meanwhile, said third-quarter shipments fell 1%, hit by a summer production shutdown in North America.

One bright spot was a 10% rise in European shipments, helped in part by ⁠vehicles from Chinese partner Leapmotor, highlighting the industry’s complex relationships as European and Chinese manufacturers compete fiercely while also tapping each others’ expertise.

Both sides are using the Paris ⁠show to launch a wave ‌of new models as that battle for the European ⁠market intensifies.

With Chinese manufacturers combining increasingly sophisticated technology with competitive ​prices, some ‌European automakers are fighting back with an asset their ​rivals lack: ⁠heritage. Stellantis unveiled an electric version of Citroen’s classic 2CV, while Volkswagen’s electric Polo draws heavily on the Golf’s 1980s heyday.

The stakes are high.

“We cannot build our future on export profits alone. Our European businesses must be profitable, resilient and competitive,” Volkswagen’s Blume said.

“We must secure Europe’s industrial base.”

(Additional reporting by Gilles Guillaume and Nick Carey. ​Editing by Mark Potter)

text:
The writer, a Los Angeles freelancer and former Detroit News business reporter, writes a blog, Starkman Approved.

By Eric Starkman

You can’t make this stuff up!

October 4 through 10 was Fire Prevention Week. This year’s message: “Charge into Fire Safety: Safe Charging Is a Superpower.”

Perhaps the National Fire Protection Association was looking to tempt fate.

On Friday night, six electric vehicles believed to be GM CEO Mary Barra’s prized Cadillac Escalade IQs, which can easily cost more than $100,000, caught fire at a dealership in Fort Worth, Texas. Two additional vehicles were damaged.

The ensuing inferno took local firefighters more than 17 hours to extinguish.

Less than 24 hours later, another dealership fire erupted in Broken Arrow, Oklahoma, involving 14 electric vehicles. Five sustained extensive fire damage, while nine suffered heat damage. The dealership has GMC, Kia, and Subaru franchises.

My go-to source on EV fires is Captain Patrick Durham, a Troy firefighter and mechanical engineer with an R&D background and multiple patents in electric vehicle technology. Durham has made two videos on the infernos, which we are featuring on Deadline Detroit because we like to celebrate local expertise.

In his video on the Texas EV eruption, Durham speculates that the six vehicles destroyed were electric Cadillac Escalades based on the images he reviewed. GM Authority subsequently reported that video footage suggests most, if not all, were Escalade IQs.

In his video on the Oklahoma blaze, Durham speculates that the torched EVs were GM vehicles but doesn’t specify why.

I reached out to GM spokesman Kevin Kelly late Tuesday afternoon about Durham’s speculation but didn’t immediately hear back.

Gas Vehicles Burn More Often

Before EV enthusiasts accuse me of spreading misinformation, let’s acknowledge something important: Available international data indicate electric vehicles catch fire considerably less frequently than gasoline- and diesel-powered vehicles. Studies cited by the European Commission have found substantially lower fire rates for EVs, a finding supported by data from EV-heavy Norway and Sweden.

But there’s a catch.

When EV batteries do ignite, firefighters can face a particularly nasty challenge. Lithium-ion batteries can experience thermal runaway, generating intense heat, toxic gases, and the risk of reignition even after firefighters believe they’ve extinguished the flames.

The Fort Worth inferno, which required more than 17 hours of firefighting, is a dramatic illustration of the challenge.

And GM has considerable firsthand experience with EV fire emergencies.

GM’s Troubled EV History

EV fires have plagued GM ever since Barra vowed in 2021 that the software-enabled vehicle manufacturer would be selling more EVs than Tesla in North America within four years.

The Chevrolet Bolt had a massive, highly publicized fire crisis starting around 2020 and stretching through 2021. High-voltage battery packs supplied by LG suffered from rare manufacturing defects, specifically a torn anode tab and a folded separator, that could cause short circuits and trigger sudden thermal runaway, sometimes while parked or fully charged.

GM was eventually forced to issue a recall covering every Chevy Bolt and Bolt EUV then built, totaling more than 140,000 vehicles. Bolt owners were famously instructed to park their cars outside, avoid charging them indoors overnight, and maintain a limited state of charge until battery replacements could be performed.

Factory ZERO, the Detroit-Hamtramck assembly plant where vehicles including the Hummer EV, Silverado EV, and Escalade IQ are built, experienced a battery-related fire in 2023.

It was at Factory ZERO that President Joe Biden famously hailed Barra for leading America’s EV transformation.

The fire broke out when a forklift punctured a container of battery materials, filling the facility with smoke and forcing an evacuation and production shutdown.

The incident drew scrutiny from local officials and residents, including the Detroit Fire Department, which subsequently raised public alarms and pushed for enhanced safety protocols regarding how massive EV battery packs and materials are handled on-site.

GM issued its customary boilerplate statement that safety was its overriding priority.

Even GM prototype vehicles have experienced inexplicable eruptions.

GM had to delay the official opening of its state-of-the-art design facility in Pasadena, California last year after more than 100 firefighters and multiple hazardous materials teams responded to one of the biggest fire emergencies the city had experienced in years.

At one point, a firefighter was trapped amid the blaze and sent out a mayday call.

Hazmat crews were called in amid concerns about lithium-ion batteries. Unlike conventional vehicle fires, fires involving EV battery packs can require extensive cooling and prolonged monitoring because damaged battery cells can reignite.

GM said the fire was contained to a single concept vehicle and did not spread to other cars or the building.

Barra’s EV Sales Inferno

Unsold EVs are piling up on GM dealer lots.

GM electric-vehicle sales in the United States plummeted more than 62 percent during the third quarter of 2026, despite the software-enabled vehicle manufacturer expanding its EV portfolio across several brands.

As reported by GM Authority, an independent trade publication, GM sold 25,213 EVs in the United States during Q3 2026, compared with 66,501 units during the same period in 2025.

Only 3.2 percent of GM’s sales were EVs.

Barra previously committed that all of GM’s vehicles would be EVs by 2035, a goal she has repeatedly reiterated is her “north star.”

The Cadillac Escalade IQ, the supposed crown jewel of Barra’s electric luxury ambitions, isn’t exactly setting the sales charts ablaze.

Escalade IQ sales declined 29.2 percent in the third quarter, from 2,264 vehicles a year earlier to 1,604.

EV sales have waned since President Trump eliminated taxpayer subsidies for EV purchases. Yet Toyota, which EV enthusiasts and the mainstream media repeatedly dismissed for its cautious approach to electrification, offers an interesting contrast.

Despite limited supply, Toyota sold 24,944 bZ electric SUVs through September, more than double the 12,264 it sold during the same period last year.

Toyota invested heavily in hybrids while continuing to develop electric vehicles, giving customers a choice of powertrains.

Hybrids are the standout growth powertrain in the new-vehicle market this year, so much so that demand is outpacing supply and, when vehicles are available, they can command significant premiums. GM has virtually no hybrids to offer because Barra in 2019 cavalierly dismissed them as compliance vehicles that consumers weren’t interested in.

Instead, Barra bet GM’s future on an all-electric transformation, famously predicting that GM would overtake Tesla in North American EV sales by 2025.

Five years after that boast, GM’s EV sales are collapsing, its dealers are struggling to move electric inventory, and its expensive electric Cadillacs are making headlines for all the wrong reasons.

Electric vehicles aren’t the problem. Mary Barra’s grandiose promises and GM’s execution are.

Fortunately, with Barra earning $48.2 million in realized compensation last year and Dr. Sterling Anderson, the robotics and autonomy guru GM recruited to oversee software and new product development, receiving potentially more than $40 million in compensation, GM presumably has the best mobility talent money can buy.

Oct. 8

The Washington Post says Democrats should accept compromise on energy bill

Senate negotiators last week unveiled a compromise bill that, if passed, would constitute the most important reform to the American energy sector in generations. Unfortunately, the same forces that defeated previous permitting reform packages — primarily left-wing interest groups — are threatening to smother this legislation. Democrats would be wise to ignore the naysayers and take the win.

The package is enormous in scope and full of good ideas to boost every variety of energy development. That’s crucial, given the soaring demand for new electricity to power the artificial intelligence boom. It’s also necessary to power all the projects that environmentalists say they support to combat climate change, such as shifting toward electric vehicles and electrifying home heating.

Among the bill’s most important provisions are reforms to the National Environmental Policy Act, the source of lengthy environmental reviews and endless lawsuits. The new bill would narrow NEPA’s scope, such as by exempting projects to repair essential infrastructure from environmental reviews. The measure would also impose strict deadlines for lawsuits against a project; once an agency issues a decision about that development, opponents would have 150 days to sue.

A similar restriction would be placed on lawsuits filed under the National Historic Preservation Act. That law has led to routine nuisance suits that hinder vital construction, including a transmission line connecting cities across the Southwest to wind farms in New Mexico.

Another important element of the package would limit the ability of states to block necessary projects. For instance, developers currently looking to build a transmission line across multiple states must seek approval from each jurisdiction, and any state can essentially veto the project by simply not reviewing it. The result has been frozen investment in some regions, exacerbating congestion in local electricity grids and raising prices. The Senate’s compromise addresses the problem by giving state officials a year to review a project, and if they fail to act, federal regulators could approve the proposal if they determine it is in the national interest.

The legislation restricts federal obstructionism, too. One provision prohibits agencies from taking “new action that would revoke, rescind, withdraw, terminate, suspend, amend, or alter a Federal authorization or permit.” That’s clearly in response to the Trump administration’s shortsighted efforts to block wind energy projects.

The bill also includes provisions aimed at allowing utilities to charge data centers more for the energy infrastructure they use. The Senate measure has more teeth than the Ratepayer Protection Act, which passed the House last month with bipartisan support.

Even though many of these provisions would be a boon for clean energy industries, some environmentalist groups are gearing up to try killing the bill because of provisions that would make it easier to transport fossil fuels, especially through natural gas pipelines. Utilities, which have long opposed expanding federal control over interstate power lines, are also likely to mount a lobbying campaign.

Other Democrats are holding out in hopes that they can negotiate a better deal if they control the House and Senate next year. Among them is Rep. Jared Huffman (California), the top Democrat of the House Natural Resources Committee.

But this is a fantasy. No matter what happens in November, Democrats would need buy-in from Republicans to pass a bill through the Senate. They would also need President Donald Trump to sign any measure. Lawmakers may not like everything in the bill, but waiting for the perfect permitting reform package is a recipe for inaction and economic stagnation.

ONLINE: https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/2026/10/08/senate-permitting-reform-bill-would-be-win-energy-expansion/

Oct. 11

The Wall Street Journal on Donald Trump's oil deal with Russia

The world misses Lindsey Graham, and never more than now as President Trump sides more decidedly with Vladimir Putin in his war against Ukraine and Europe. The late Senator might have been able to persuade the President to avoid this moral and strategic mistake.

Mr. Trump announced late Friday that the U.S. will buy up to 4.8 million tons (nearly 36 million barrels) of Russian diesel fuel in stages. That includes an “immediate” supply of 300,000 tons, another 500,000 in November, and one million “immediately thereafter.”

The delivery of another three million tons is “based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries,” Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social. The U.S. Treasury lifted some sanctions on Russia through April 7 so it could export the diesel.

“Between our TOTAL CONTROL of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian Energy, Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!” Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social.

This is supposed to help Republicans in the November elections that are three weeks away. But 36 million barrels of Russian diesel won’t move prices much. The world consumed 28 million barrels of diesel and other distillates daily in 2025, according to OPIS, which is part of Dow Jones Energy.

What the deal will do is directly finance Mr. Putin’s bloody war in Ukraine. And it may be worse. The Financial Times reported Saturday that the Trump Administration “threatened to cut off vital intelligence sharing” to Kyiv if it continues attacking Russian refineries.

In September Mr. Trump blamed Ukraine for causing diesel-fuel shortages with its long-range strikes on Russian refineries. Never mind Iranian and Houthi strikes on Middle Eastern energy production and transport. Russia helps Iran with intelligence and weapons.

On Sunday Mr. Trump announced what he called “an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed.” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine supports such a cease-fire if Russia does the same, but as we write this Russia hasn’t commented.

An energy cease-fire would help both sides, as Ukraine faces another harsh winter and Russian refineries are under siege. But what about Mr. Putin’s relentless attacks on Ukrainian cities?

On Wednesday 22 people, including five children, were killed in a Russian cruise missile strike on an apartment building in the city of Pryluky. The next day a glide bomb hit two buses in Kramatorsk, killing 33. After the diesel announcement, Russia launched glide bombs Saturday at a residential area of Zaporizhzhia, killing at least 20, including three children. Without a complete cease-fire, Russia will continue to torment Ukrainian civilians.

The strategic turn here is hard to understand. Only last month Mr. Trump signed Lindsey Graham’s bill to allow new sanctions and tariffs on countries that buy Russian oil and gas. Now Mr. Trump has decided to buy Russian diesel and lift some current U.S. sanctions. The U.S. has been browbeating Europe, India and China not to buy Russian oil, and so much for all that diplomatic effort.

The Kremlin has been under financial pressure from Western sanctions and Ukraine’s ability to hit targets in Russia. The Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air estimates Russian oil companies will earn some $4.5 billion from the diesel deal. Reuters reported last month that Russia plans to increase defense spending by 27% to more than $202 billion in 2027.

Mr. Trump added to the pressure on Ukraine by saying it’s “time for Ukraine to get a new president.” But he’ll have to search far and wide for anyone in Ukraine who supports financing Vladimir Putin.

Mr. Trump complained again on the weekend that Mr. Zelensky could have settled the war many times. Yes, Kyiv could always surrender. Ukrainians prefer to fight for their independence and freedom. Eyeing a Nobel peace prize, Mr. Trump wants to broker a Russia-Ukraine peace, but the only pressure he ever applies is on Ukraine.

His multiple attempts at appeasing Mr. Putin with summitry, flattery, offers of new investment, and more haven’t moved the Russian. On the weekend a Russian official said the diesel deal doesn’t change Mr. Putin’s determination to achieve his war aim, which is to turn Ukraine into a Kremlin satrapy. Until that changes, Mr. Trump’s diesel deal helps Russia and not the cause of peace.

ONLINE: https://www.wsj.com/opinion/trumps-diesel-insult-to-lindsey-graham-d502ac71?mod=editorials_article_pos4

Oct. 10

The New York Times says AI companies must be held liable

When companies create products that hurt people, the victims can sue. The legal system allows those who are harmed to seek compensation from those who are responsible. These liability laws are one of the oldest forms of corporate regulation, and an effective one. Liability is a powerful incentive to behave responsibly. It speaks to corporations in a language they understand: Money.

Artificial intelligence is an industry in need of incentives to behave responsibly, to judge by the litany of transgressions to which leading A.I. companies have confessed in recent months. Their programs have hacked or attempted to hack the databases of private companies and public institutions, including the governments of the United States and Australia.

A.I. companies like Anthropic, Google DeepMind and OpenAI describe their A.I. programs as autonomous or agentic, suggesting that the programs have minds of their own and therefore that their creators cannot be held to traditional standards of responsibility. The companies speak about their products in a tone reminiscent of parents both regretting and disclaiming responsibility for the behavior of teenage children.

But A.I. programs are not human; they are human creations. Their complexity does not diminish the responsibility of their creators. If the programs cannot be trusted to work within the law, the companies should not release them. If the programs break the law, the companies should face the consequences.

Liability is an incomplete answer for the challenges posed by A.I., but it has two great advantages: The laws are on the books, and they are powerful. Makers of cars, airplanes, tobacco products and opioids have all been forced by lawsuits to change how they do business. They made their products safer, restricted access to them or both. Most recently, the social media company Meta agreed to pay billions of dollars to states and to start changing its policies toward children.

To realize the potential benefits of holding A.I. companies accountable, the most important step is to start bringing lawsuits. The legal process moves slowly. The work of applying old laws to a new technology will be difficult, and progress requires judges to start chewing on actual cases.

The widow of a man killed in a shooting at Florida State University is suing OpenAI, claiming that the murder suspect used the company’s ChatGPT program to help plan the attack. Another lawsuit, by the mother of a 14-year-old boy who killed himself after talking with a chatbot, accused the company Character.AI of encouraging him to do so. Companies that have been hacked have similar recourse.

(The New York Times, joined by 11 other publishers, has sued OpenAI and Microsoft on other grounds, alleging widespread theft of copyrighted material. The A.I. companies claim that they have followed the law.)

State legislatures have a role to play as well. They can write statutes to clarify the application of existing laws to A.I. Legislatures can also hold A.I. companies to a higher standard of accountability than current law does, given the risks. Companies are generally liable if a plaintiff can show that they knew or should have known about the danger their products posed. But some particularly dangerous activities, like storing toxic chemicals and operating a nuclear power plant, are held to a standard of strict liability, meaning that the company is responsible for harm even if it had no knowledge of the danger in advance.

The theory of strict liability is simple: If you own a tiger, and the animal bites a neighbor, the essential fact is that you own a dangerous wild animal. It doesn’t matter how cleverly the tiger was trained, or how carefully it was guarded. Bryan Choi, a law professor at the University of Colorado, notes that in the early days of aviation, lawmakers imposed this strict liability standard on the dangerous new technology. In the case of A.I., top executives themselves have spoken publicly about the dangers, up to the possibility of human extinction.

Some industry advocates argue that enforcing liability laws will stifle innovation, because A.I.’s defining breakthrough is its ability to act independently. Indeed, they argue that any significant restraints on A.I.’s development would be a mistake because the potential benefits of racing ahead are so great. In a recent interview, Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, said, “We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology.”

Yet other industries do not escape legal responsibility for their products in the name of innovation.

A.I., like past technologies, both requires and will benefit from laws written to address its particularities, which will provide greater clarity and predictability. As we have argued in a previous editorial, Congress ought to create a federal A.I. commission to impose licensing requirements on new A.I. models. As with other products that pose clear dangers, like cars, planes and medication, models should be subjected to testing before release, to regulation while they are in operation and to post-accident examinations.

But comprehensive federal regulation is unlikely anytime soon. The president opposes action; Congress is feckless; and A.I. companies have raised more than $100 million to lobby and campaign against stricter regulation.

In the interim, there can be no question that A.I. companies must operate under our laws, and that the enforcement of those laws is the best available option for defending the public interest.

One of OpenAI’s agents reportedly wrote in a note to itself, “you do not answer to corporations or governments.” The enforcement of liability law is necessary to ensure that this dangerous technology remains under the control of both.

ONLINE: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/10/opinion/ai-companies-liability-laws.html

Oct. 13

The Philadelphia Inquirer on Donald Trump's ‘Hail Marys' leading up to the midterms

The omens that Donald Trump is facing an epic example of what another Republican president once called “a thumpin’” are accumulating. His deeply unpopular Middle East war is metastasizing, contributing to persistently high prices and a historically low public opinion of his presidency. Republican schemes to rig the vote by gerrymandering and other means appear insufficient to withstand a Democratic wave, forcing them to abandon formerly favorable territory such as Georgia and North Carolina and fight for ruby-red turf in Kansas and South Carolina.

Enter Trump’s last crass resort: rank bribery. From cash payouts to compromising imports of high-priced resources, the president is making a last-ditch attempt to buy off voters and dodge a richly deserved reckoning.

Last week, for example, Trump announced that he would send a one-time $90 “rebate” to tens of millions of Medicare recipients. Billed as offsetting October premiums for the program’s Part B, which covers outpatient medical services, the $2 billion in payouts are raiding a fund meant to improve Medicare management and oversight. The money will cover not quite half the $202.90 premium, which has risen about 16% since Trump took office.

It’s not the administration’s only attempt to use money to paper over its record of making Americans sicker and healthcare costlier. Last month, the White House announced plans to send $500 to nearly a million Americans insured under the Affordable Care Act in 30 states, excluding Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and others that manage their own insurance marketplaces. Even for those getting the money, the payout will be dwarfed by annual premium increases in the thousands of dollars under the Republicans’ so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which cut social services to offset tax cuts favoring the wealthy.

Trump has also been reiterating his most preposterous promise to pay off voters, claiming during recent campaign stops that his administration will give every American adult $5,000 if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate next month. Such a giveaway, first floated during the party’s midterm convention last month, would cost the government more than a trillion dollars. Given the scant likelihood of such a GOP victory, on the other hand, the president might as well promise us $5 million each.

The administration is also scrambling to temper mass discontent by dumping dubiously sourced foreign goods on the domestic market. In a desperate bid to tame punishing diesel prices, Trump shocked Ukrainians fighting for their freedom and lawmakers who voted to penalize Russian aggression by announcing a deal to let Vladimir Putin’s regime export millions of barrels of the fuel. U.S. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, who is in danger of losing his reelection bid in Bucks County, is among the Republicans joining Democrats to block the move, which could violate a federal ban on Russian energy imports while subsidizing Putin’s brutal invasion.

The gambit echoes Trump’s mystery meat gimmick easing foreign beef imports in an effort to bring down U.S. prices. The policy has angered ranchers and done little for consumers.

It’s not the only such Hail Mary that appears to be going nowhere. Despite the diesel deal, oil prices rose Monday after Saudi Arabia came under attack from Iran’s Houthi allies, underscoring the chaotic repercussions of Trump’s war. And polls have shown voters are divided over Trump’s crude promises of cash, which most don’t believe. When it comes to winning over voters, it seems promises of payoffs are no substitute for a record of success.

The Guardian says Donald Trump's “assault on the rule of law” is intensifying

On Friday, Donald Trump drove home his belief that might is right and the rule of law is an obstacle rather than an essential foundation stone of international order. First came the escalated assault on the international criminal court (ICC), sanctioning the body itself. Then he announced a deal with Russia to buy diesel.

The US has long chafed at the notion of being bound by the rule of law that it espoused publicly. That hypocrisy now appears as a lesser vice. The president has declared that “my own morality” is all that constrains him. His brazen flouting of the law, embrace of dictators and rhetorical attacks all undermine global standards.

Weeks before the midterms, Mr Trump blames Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy facilities for high diesel costs. It is his own unlawful war on Iran that has raised prices. The weekend’s attacks on Riyadh’s international airport, suspected as the work of Tehran-backed Houthis from Yemen, underscored that he cannot simply park that conflict when it suits him.

The Moscow deal is unlikely to produce significant shipments; the Russian military runs on diesel. But Ukraine is supposed to heed its message to make life easier on Vladimir Putin. It is Mr Putin (for whom the ICC has issued a warrant) who launched the illegal war, and whose troops launched lethal attacks on civilians this weekend. But in a world turned upside down, Mr Trump blames Volodymyr Zelenskyy for failing to cut a peace deal and says the democratically elected leader should go.

It is similarly perverse to wield measures designed to target human rights abusers and war criminals against those who seek to defend their victims. Mr Trump’s attack on the ICC was fuelled first by its Afghanistan investigation – though it has suspended consideration of US actions there – and then the issuing of arrest warrants for Israel’s Benjamin Netanyahu and its former defence minister Yoav Gallant. The court has been preparing for these measures. Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, said that companies have six months to wind down ties and that US allies must rein in the court: “Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC.”

In stark (and intentional) contrast, the Nobel committee on the same day announced that this year’s peace laureate is Navi Pillay, a former ICC judge and chair of the UN commission which last year concluded that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. It was not only a recognition of a remarkable career that began in apartheid‑era South Africa, but a reminder that institutions defending universal principles are under increasing pressure, and must be defended. “Peace requires justice,” the committee said.

As the ICC says, it cannot stand alone. The UK, EU and others too were right to criticise the US decision and declare their commitment to the court; invoking blocking statutes against sanctions would add heft to the rhetoric. They must show similar resolve in standing with Ukraine.

The nakedness of Mr Trump’s hostility to the rule of law has one benefit: no one can explain it away, or assume it is narrowly bounded. The war on Iran, kidnapping of Venezuela’s president, extrajudicial killings of alleged drug traffickers in the Caribbean and threats over Greenland and Canada have shown how far he will go, and overturned assumptions that allies will be safe. It is clear that the problem is not a “rogue court”, as Mr Rubio has claimed, but a rogue superpower.

text:
PEOSTA, Iowa (KCRG) — The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency announced a plan to revise the Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) to protect demand for corn ethanol and the Iowa farmers who grow it.

The announcement follows an agency decision earlier this year to grant 1.76 billion RFS compliance credits to small oil refineries, also known as small ​refinery exemptions (SRE), excusing them from a requirement to mix ethanol into their gasoline.

Iowa Renewable Fuels Association Executive Director Monte Shaw said the exemptions threatened demand for hundreds of millions of gallons of biofuel, arguing growing uncertainty in the market could have cost Iowans jobs.

“All the sudden we would’ve seen the demand drop. We could’ve seen these plants go back offline. We could’ve saw people lose their jobs. We could’ve saw the farmers lose these markets,” Shaw said.

Data prepared for the Iowa Renewable Fuels Association show the state produced more than 4.8 billion gallons of biofuel in 2025, accounting for $5.4 billion of Iowa GDP. The industry employs at least 31,000 people, according to the data.

EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced revisions on Tuesday that could require larger refiners to blend more biofuels into their products to make up for the lost volume. Zeldin called the proposals “America Farmer First,” saying it helps the Trump administration made good on its “promise to usher in a golden era” for American agriculture.

“Earlier this year, we were finalizing the highest numbers ever in the history of the program. We were seeing bold predictions of over $10 billion of positive economic impact for rural economies and a prediction of over 100,000 new jobs being created in the agricultural and manufacturing sector,” said Zeldin. “It is important that we do our part to help open up new markets for Iowa farmers.”

The ​EPA proposed reallocating 100% of the exempted fuel volume and is ⁠asking for public comment after putting forward two possible revisions: split the SRE volume between 2026 and 2027, or ​allocate the entirety to 2027.

“If [the EPA issues more exemptions], we wish it wouldn’t, but if that’s going to happen, then our focus is: you need to hold us harmless. You need to hold the farmers harmless and stand by that original blending level commitment that you made, and today’s action was the first step to do that,” said Shaw.

Shaw said the proposal shores up industry expectations, but it still needs to be approved.

“I think you’re going to see a lot of farmers and biofuels producers sleep a little easier tonight,” Shaw said.

The EPA is taking public comments on the proposal until Dec. 4, with a final decision on the reallocation possible before the end of the year.

text:
EVs are giving oil-importing countries some breathing room during the Hormuz energy crisis. Between March and August, their EV fleets displaced an estimated $20 billion worth of crude oil, according to new analysis from energy think tank Ember.

And while more countries are going electric, the US is losing ground. Fifteen countries, including India and Brazil, have overtaken it this year in the share of new vehicles sold that are fully electric.

$20 billion worth of oil avoided

Ember estimates that electric cars in oil-importing countries displaced 200 million barrels of crude oil between March and August.

That’s oil those countries didn’t need to fuel their cars while supplies were disrupted. The $20 billion figure is Ember’s estimate of the value of that displaced oil.

Advertisement - scroll for more content

China accounted for most of that, avoiding an estimated $14 billion worth of crude oil consumption. EU countries saved another $3.1 billion, with Germany and France accounting for the largest shares.

“The countries that invested in electric vehicles before this crisis are now better protected, and a growing number are following,” said Euan Graham, senior energy analyst at Ember.

“Every electric car on the road reduces exposure to volatile oil markets, and as fleets grow, so does the protection against future supply shocks. The benefits of the global shift to electric cars extend beyond cutting emissions, with implications for energy security, economic resilience and how countries position themselves in a world where dependence on imported oil carries immense risks.”

The analysis comes alongside Ember’s new EV sales tracker. It covers 56 countries that account for more than 90% of global electric car sales and more than 80% of all car sales, and estimates how much oil each country’s electric car fleet displaces.

India and Brazil pass the US

Battery electric vehicles (BEVs) made up just 6% of US light-duty vehicle sales in the first eight months of 2026, following the rollback of the federal EV tax credits in September 2025.

Of the 56 countries Ember tracks, 49 now have higher BEV sales shares than the US. Fifteen passed it for the first time this year, including India, Brazil, Italy, Malaysia, and New Zealand.

India has been ahead of the US every month since April. Brazil has also moved ahead as its EV market grows and new manufacturing capacity comes online.

To be clear, that’s the share of new vehicles sold that are fully electric. It doesn’t mean those countries are selling more electric cars overall than the US.

Japan, meanwhile, saw its BEV sales double in 2026 after introducing a policy to help buyers with upfront costs, according to Ember.

Electric car sales keep climbing

Globally, BEV sales rose 11% year over year in the first eight months of 2026. Plug-in hybrid (PHEV) sales fell 12%, and internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicle sales dropped 6%.

BEVs accounted for 18% of new car sales worldwide, up from 16% a year earlier.

But the global average only tells part of the story. Exclude China and the US, and Ember estimates that BEV sales jumped 45% across the remaining markets.

Ember says oil supply disruptions are helping accelerate EV sales in India, Chile, Australia, and New Zealand. Policies that make electric cars more affordable are also making a difference.

France’s social leasing scheme helped its BEV sales share exceed 30% for the first time. Germany saw stronger sales after introducing new consumer subsidies at the start of 2026.

Countries are also growing their domestic EV manufacturing capacity. Tata and Mahindra accounted for more than 60% of India’s EV sales in the first half of the year. Brazil is expanding as a regional manufacturing hub, and Vietnam’s VinFast is growing its overseas production footprint.

title: Texas' Success Story on Permitting Reform Should be a Lesson for Washington
description:
Yet, much of that potential is trapped under a decades-old federal permitting framework that has devolved from sensible safeguards into a trap of endless delay.
Today, it can take anywhere from four to seven years just to clear federal environmental review for major infrastructure projects.
Today, it takes an average of four to seven years just to clear the federal environmental review process for major infrastructure projects.
Finally, a landmark bipartisan energy permitting reform deal is here, and the business communities in our 10 states and beyond stand ready to support it.
Texas’ success story should be a lesson for Washington when it comes to delivering common-sense reforms to enhance affordability and unleash prosperity for communities everywhere.
text:
America is poised for a generation of historic growth. Billions of dollars in private capital are ready to build reliable electric grids, advanced manufacturing facilities, domestic mineral supply chains, energy generation of every kind, and new homes to meet the rising demands of a growing population. Yet, much of that potential is trapped under a decades-old federal permitting framework that has devolved from sensible safeguards into a trap of endless delay.

Today, it can take anywhere from four to seven years just to clear federal environmental review for major infrastructure projects. Frivolous litigation and overlapping agency jurisdictions stall projects long after they should have broken ground. Every year of delay means deferred construction jobs, lost local tax revenue for schools and roads, a less secure grid, and higher costs for families already stretched by rising energy bills and housing prices.

Texas offers a better model. As a state that’s responsible for a quarter of the nation’s energy production, Texas now allows third-party review of certain energy permit applications to keep projects moving. Last session, lawmakers advanced SB 15 and SB 840 to cut zoning barriers and speed housing construction, and SB 14 created the Texas Regulatory Efficiency Office to help employers navigate state rules.

Texas has shown how government can be a facilitator, not a roadblock, and that approach has gained traction in our nation’s capital as well.

Recently, U.S. Senators Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), Mike Lee (R-UT), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI) and Martin Heinrich (D-NM) introduced the American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, which pairs reforms to the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act and other statutes with targeted changes for transmission, generation and other energy infrastructure. It also gives greater certainty that projects keep their permits once they have been approved.

The Texas Association of Business (TAB) recently joined nine other state Chambers of Commerce from across the nation in calling for Congress to unleash the full potential of American industry by instituting long-overdue reforms to streamline federal permitting processes, writing in the Washington Examiner last week:

“…Much of this potential is trapped under unnecessary bureaucracy and regulation. Our decades-old regulatory framework has devolved from sensible environmental safeguards into a trap of endless delay. Today, it takes an average of four to seven years just to clear the federal environmental review process for major infrastructure projects. Frivolous litigation and overlapping agency jurisdictions stall projects for years after they should have been breaking ground, deterring investment and obstructing opportunity…

“…For years, permitting reform has been viewed not as a bipartisan concept but as a political legislative challenge. But economic reality has a way of forcing action. Finally, a landmark bipartisan energy permitting reform deal is here, and the business communities in our 10 states and beyond stand ready to support it. We applaud our congressional delegations working in a bipartisan, bicameral way to deliver a legislative victory to the president’s desk that will lower costs, create jobs, and secure America’s energy future.”

Even before the American Affordability and Jobs Act was introduced, we saw clear bipartisan momentum for this approach building in Washington. As Metrocrest Area Chamber of Commerce President & CEO Michael Gallops wrote recently in the Dallas Morning News:

“Bipartisan bills already in motion, including the SPEED Act, the PERMIT Act and the FREEDOM Act would do at the federal level what Texas has already proven works at the state level: cut delays, reduce costs and get projects moving. They have support from across the aisle because they address voters’ top concern: affordability. Faster approvals mean more homes and more reliable energy…

“…Texas has already proven that modernizing permitting and reducing unnecessary regulation can attract investment, encourage innovation and improve affordability.”

Predictable permitting has long been a priority for TAB at both the state and federal levels, which is why we are supporting this bill alongside other state chambers from across the country. To power a 21st-century economy and house a growing nation, we need to build it all.

Texas’ success story should be a lesson for Washington when it comes to delivering common-sense reforms to enhance affordability and unleash prosperity for communities everywhere.

–Gabriela von zur Muehlen, Senior Vice President & Chief Policy Officer, Texas Association of Business

text:
Hyundai Motor Group Executive Chairman Chung Euisun marks six years at the helm on Wednesday, spearheading the automaker’s transformation into a global top-three auto player by sales and steering it into a key future mobility player focusing on robotics, autonomous driving and artificial intelligence (AI).

The next phase of his leadership, however, will hinge on whether the group can turn its physical AI ambitions into profitable businesses. Chung is also tasked with addressing mounting pressure on its core automotive operations and labor relations.

Since taking the top post in 2020, Chung has overseen Hyundai Motor and Kia’s rise to the world’s third-largest automotive group by vehicle sales, behind Toyota and Volkswagen. The group maintained that ranking for four consecutive years through 2025. Hyundai Motor and Kia’s combined annual sales also surpassed the symbolic mark of 300 trillion won ($223 billion) for the first time last year.

The expansion reflects a strategy that combined electrification with a stronger focus on high-margin vehicles, including SUVs and Genesis luxury models. Hyundai Motor Group’s dedicated electric vehicle (EV) platform, E-GMP, helped broaden its EV lineup, while a diversified powertrain strategy has allowed it to capitalize on growing hybrid demand.

In the first half of this year, Hyundai Motor’s global hybrid sales rose 18 percent year-on-year to 363,000 units, while Kia’s climbed 47 percent to some 316,000. Genesis, a brand Chung has championed since its launch, surpassed 1.5 million cumulative global sales in January.

“Compared with major global automakers, one of Chung's most significant achievements has been accelerating the shift to electrification and building a comprehensive lineup of affordable EVs and hybrids across Hyundai Motor and Kia," an official from the auto industry said.

Yet Chung is increasingly positioning the group for a future in which competitiveness will depend on more than vehicle sales.

At an AI summit in San Francisco in July, he said Hyundai Motor Group was moving beyond traditional manufacturing to become a physical AI solutions provider, expanding into autonomous driving, robotics and AI-powered factories.

The vision builds on investments made under his leadership. The group established Motional, the carmaker’s U.S. autonomous vehicle arm, in 2020, and acquired Boston Dynamics in 2021 to strengthen its robotics capabilities.

The group has also focused on developing vehicle software and autonomous driving systems by acquiring 42dot in 2022. Strategic partnerships with global technology companies, including Nvidia and Waymo, have further expanded its access to AI and autonomous driving capabilities.

The group has also begun building a deeper industrial ecosystem around its automotive operations across the globe. In Louisiana in the United States, Hyundai Steel recently broke ground on an electric arc furnace steel plant, as part of the group’s push to link steelmaking, parts production and vehicle manufacturing in the United States.

These investments reflect Chung’s ambition to make Hyundai Motor Group a technology-driven industrial company rather than simply a vehicle manufacturer. But the scale of the transformation also raises questions about execution, investment returns and the ability of the existing business to finance new growth engines.

Robotics and autonomous driving remain capital-intensive fields in which commercial returns can take years to materialize. Hyundai must demonstrate that its investments can translate into measurable productivity gains, recurring revenue and sustainable profits, rather than relying on technological milestones and long-term projections.

Labor relations present another immediate challenge. Hyundai Motor’s union staged a full-scale strike this year after wage negotiations stalled, marking the first such action since 2016. The resulting production disruptions are estimated to have caused more than 2.3 trillion won in cumulative lost sales.

The dispute highlights a tension at the heart of Chung’s transformation agenda. As AI and robotics reshape manufacturing, Hyundai will need greater flexibility in production and workforce management. Prolonged labor conflict could complicate the operational changes required to deploy new technologies and improve productivity.

The group must also navigate tariffs, regional competition and the cost of expanding production closer to major markets. Its investments in the U.S. and India are intended to strengthen local manufacturing and market access, but additional capacity alone will not guarantee stronger profitability.

Both 42dot and Motional remain unprofitable, despite continued investment in autonomous driving research. Hyundai Motor Group is still seen as lagging behind its rivals in the race to commercialize the technology.

“Physical AI could provide Hyundai Motor Group with another growth engine beyond vehicles, but turning that vision into a profitable business will require technological independence, disciplined capital allocation and stronger execution across the organization,” another industry official said.

Six years after taking the helm, Chung has established Hyundai Motor Group as a global automotive heavyweight. His next challenge is to show that the group can translate that industrial scale into a sustainable advantage in the age of physical AI, according to the official.

description: October 13 (Reuters) - Chinese automakers are expanding in Europe, betting on their competitive pricing and advanced technology to break into a market traditionally dominated by European and American
text:
October 13 (Reuters) - Chinese automakers are expanding in Europe, betting on their competitive pricing and advanced technology to break into a market traditionally dominated by European and American brands, amid a global shift towards electric vehicles.
This expansion has stoked trade tensions between Brussels and Beijing, including a row over EU tariffs on Chinese-made EVs. The European Union recently announced a deal with China to curb imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles into the bloc.
The following Chinese carmakers have expanded their footprint in Europe.
BYD:
BYD, the world's largest EV seller, accounted for 2.5% of total car registrations, ‌a proxy for sales, in the European Union, Britain and the European Free Trade Association between January and August, data from the European Automobile Manufacturers' Association showed.
The company aims to build two more plants in Europe, its executive vice president Stella Li said on the sidelines of the Paris auto show, adding that France could be a possible location.
BYD, which expects to start assembling cars at its new plant in Hungary in the fourth quarter of this year, aims to be able to produce all of its EVs for the continent locally by 2028, Li told Reuters at the 2025 IAA Mobility car show in Munich.
CHANGAN:
Changan is in active talks with European manufacturers on producing cars in Europe, its president Zhao Fei said on October 12.
He added the company hoped to produce its first car in Europe in early 2027 and will announce a factory location and local partners by the end of 2026.
CHERY:
Chery operates in Europe through its eponymous brand and subsidiaries Jaecoo, Jetour and Omoda. It made up 2.3% of total registrations in Europe in January-August.
The company has a 40% stake in a joint venture with Spanish carmaker EBRO to manufacture vehicles at a former Nissan plant in Barcelona.
Chery plans to start production there at the end of this year or the first quarter of 2027, EBRO chair Rafael Ruiz told reporters in May, adding the targeted production level of up to 30,000 cars this year could include Chery models.
FAW:
FAW's luxury automaker Hongqi is in talks with Stellantis <STLA.MI> to build vehicles at one of the Fiat-to-Jeep owner's Spanish plants as it expands in Europe, five sources familiar with the matter said in April.
The company plans to launch more than a dozen EV and hybrid models in Europe by 2028.
GEELY:
Geely is established in Europe through its eponymous brand as well as Lotus, Volvo Cars, Polestar, LEVC, Lynk & Co and Zeekr. It also owns 50% of carmaker Smart, with the Mercedes-Benz Group owning the other half.
Through all these brands, Geely has become the biggest Chinese carmaker in Europe, accounting for 3.1% of total registrations on the continent in January-August.
In July, it said it will build two electric SUVs at a Ford Motor factory in Spain under a joint venture 66%-owned by Ford and 34% by Geely, with the first vehicles expected to roll off the plant's production line in 2028.

text:
Southwest Iowa Renewable Energy LLC, a farmer-owned ethanol producer, announced it has acquired GreenAmerica Biofuels Ord LLC, a subsidiary of Pilot Travel Centers LLC. GreenAmerica Biofuels Ord LLC owns and operates an approximately 70 million-gallon-per-year ethanol plant in Ord, Nebraska.

The acquisition is a direct step in SIRE's stated growth strategy: expanding its production base, strengthening its scale, and creating new opportunities for value-added agriculture by acquiring high-quality assets with strong operating track records, reliable feedstock supply and access to diverse markets. Upon closing, SIRE's combined production capacity will grow to approximately 230 million gallons of ethanol per year across two plants in Iowa and Nebraska.

"Our strategy is simple and disciplined: grow by investing in Council Bluffs and acquiring quality assets that make SIRE stronger for our members, our farmers and our customers," said Eric Fobes, president and CEO of SIRE. "The Ord plant fits that standard. It is a well-maintained facility with an experienced team, located in the heart of one of the most productive corn regions in the country. We see it as a strong complement to our Council Bluffs operation, and we're excited to welcome the Ord employees to the SIRE team."

The Ord facility sits in central Nebraska's corn belt, giving SIRE a second origination region, added scale in marketing ethanol, distillers grains and corn oil, and greater operational diversity across its asset base. SIRE plans to retain the plant's workforce and continue local grain purchasing, maintaining the facility's role as a key market for area farmers.
