title: A 5-megawatt reactor sealed in a 1,000-ton steel vault on a Texas university campus got ...
description:
On October 7, Last Energy announced that the Department of Energy had approved that document for the pilot reactor the company’s building on Texas A&M’s RELLIS campus in Bryan, Texas.
DOE’s nuclear safety rules say a DSA has to describe the facility, identify every hazard it could face, natural or man-made, and work through normal operation, abnormal conditions, and accidents.
Except this house has a reactor core in it.
The pilot uses the commercial reactor’s full-size core Last Energy calls the reactor the PWR-5.
In early July, a company spokesperson told the American Nuclear Society’s Nuclear News that the building was complete and that critical reactor components had been installed.
text:
Nuclear power has a reputation for paperwork, and there’s a reason for it.

Before a new reactor in this country gets switched on, somebody has to spell out exactly what could go wrong with it, what’s in place to stop each of those things, and who’s trained to deal with them if they happen anyway. Feel bad for whoever has that job.

On October 7, Last Energy announced that the Department of Energy had approved that document for the pilot reactor the company’s building on Texas A&M’s RELLIS campus in Bryan, Texas. It’s called a Documented Safety Analysis, or DSA, and the announcement describes it as “the final and most comprehensive safety analysis in the DOE authorization process.”

DOE has one step left. Next up is what the department calls a readiness review, and once that’s done, it can issue the authorization that lets the reactor start up and go critical.

I’ll admit a safety document isn’t the most exciting thing I’ve ever written about. The reactor’s arguably a lot more interesting, though, mostly because of the steel box it’s sealed in.

So what’s in a Documented Safety Analysis?

Basically, it’s the rulebook for running the place safely. DOE’s nuclear safety rules say a DSA has to describe the facility, identify every hazard it could face, natural or man-made, and work through normal operation, abnormal conditions, and accidents. It then has to lay out the controls that keep workers, the public, and the surrounding environment safe, as well as the programs for training, maintenance, fire protection, and emergency planning.

DOE approved a preliminary version, the PDSA, back in May. The October approval covers the finished one.

The readiness review is a different animal. It’s basically DOE checking that the hardware, the procedures and the crew match what’s on paper before anything starts up, kind of like the final walkthrough before you close on a house. Except this house has a reactor core in it. I couldn’t find a timeline for that review anywhere.

The pilot uses the commercial reactor’s full-size core

Last Energy calls the reactor the PWR-5. Not the catchiest name, but there’s a very scientific and number-y reason. It’s a pressurized water reactor, the same basic type as most of the big reactors already running in the US, and it’s rated at 5 megawatts of electricity, against 20 for its commercial sibling, the PWR-20.

For comparison, the Unity reactor we covered after it went critical in Idaho and the Kaleidos that rode a flatbed out of the Los Angeles area this summer are both 1-megawatt machines.

So why give a 5-megawatt pilot a full-size 20-megawatt core?

Because it’s pretty much the same reactor. The PWR-5 shares the PWR-20’s physical geometry and full-scale core, according to Last Energy, and the difference is in the fuel. The pilot’s uranium is enriched less, enough for 5 megawatts instead of 20.

If enrichment isn’t something you think about much, it’s the share of uranium-235 in the fuel, the kind of uranium that splits easily and gives off heat. Lowering that share for the pilot sets the core up for a quarter of the power.

Frankly, that’s a pretty sensible way to run a pilot. You get to test the real hardware rather than a shrunken model, and the company’s argument is that a full-size core in Bryan demonstrates how the commercial version will perform. Last Energy hasn’t said exactly how far it reduced enrichment, though. Its commercial design runs on standard low-enriched uranium, kept under 5%.

So the pilot’s fuel sits somewhere below that, and that’s as precise as I can get.

The reactor’s sealed inside 1,000 tons of steel

Most nuclear plants you’ve seen in photos have a containment building, often that big concrete dome. Its job is to prevent radioactive material from leaking in an accident.

Last Energy went a different way. Its containment is a steel vault that weighs 1,000 tons and gets sealed airtight, with the reactor and its primary systems inside, which basically means everything the core’s cooling water touches. According to the company’s spec page, it has a double seal and maintenance-free parts, because the whole idea is that nobody goes in there.

The commercial PWR-20 isn’t designed to be refueled either. Last Energy’s FAQ says each one’s fueled for about six years, and then a replacement unit gets installed next to the old one.

I’ll admit a reactor nobody’s supposed to walk into sounds a little strange at first. But if nothing in there needs a wrench, you can probably skip designing the inside around somebody holding one, and I’d say that’s the cleverest idea in the whole design.

It doesn’t take up much ground, either. The reactor module would fit in a single parking space, according to the spec page, which puts it at 114 square feet. That figure’s for the PWR-20, but Last Energy has described the pilot as physically identical to it.

What I couldn’t find anywhere is how tall or how wide that vault is. As far as I can tell, they haven’t been made public.

The commercial plant is designed to be made in a factory, hauled on regular roads and assembled on site, according to the October announcement. The vault alone weighs as much as 25 semis loaded right up to the 80,000-pound federal limit on interstates, so I’d assume it makes the trip in pieces.

Figures: Last Energy.

So when does it go critical?

The October 7 announcement doesn’t put a date on it. And the deadline a lot of these reactor startups were racing this summer has already come and gone.

A presidential executive order set a goal for DOE to achieve at least three new test reactors to criticality by July 4, 2026, the country’s 250th birthday, and DOE says four made it. Last Energy wasn’t one of them, even though the company aimed to go critical by mid-2026 when it announced the RELLIS project, according to Nuclear Engineering International.

Honestly, a few months late barely counts as late in nuclear. Construction at RELLIS only started in January, and Texas A&M says the whole project is privately financed. In early July, a company spokesperson told the American Nuclear Society’s Nuclear News that the building was complete and that critical reactor components had been installed.

For what it’s worth, DOE approved the DSA for Aalo Atomics’ reactor in April, according to Nuclear News, and that reactor went critical on the Fourth of July. I wouldn’t treat that as a schedule for Texas, though, since every one of these projects is different. (They have one thing in common, though: there’s always a long wait, and often a delay…)

The fuel’s the other open question. Last Energy said in May that its fuel had been manufactured, and that the DSA was what it needed to get DOE’s authorization to receive it on site. Whether that uranium’s in Bryan yet, I can’t tell you. The October announcement doesn’t mention a delivery.

And if “going critical” sounds alarming, it really isn’t. It just means the chain reaction keeps itself going, with each round of splitting uranium atoms setting off the next. A reactor’s built to do exactly that, and the plan for the PWR-5 starts with a low-power run before it moves on to making electricity.

Adam Lenarz, Last Energy’s vice president of development, told a crowd at a community open house at RELLIS in September that the company intended to get DOE’s final authorization within a couple of months, KBTX reported. With the DSA approved on October 7, the readiness review is the only DOE step left before startup authorization for the PWR-5.

description:

text:
While the industry awaits information on the remaining $2.3 billion available through the EPA Clean School Bus Program, three U.S. representatives hope to extend the program through 2031, reauthorizing another $1 billion in funding annually for five more years.

To date, the CSBP has awarded $2.7 billion to replace more than 8,500 school buses, reaching nearly every U.S. state. More than 5,200 electric school buses funded through the program have already been delivered to schools. Ninety-one percent of the new school buses applied for were electric. The remaining 9 percent consisted mostly of propane with a small number of CNG also awarded. No new CNG-powered school bus models are being manufactured.

The Clean School Bus Reauthorization Act builds on the Clean School Bus Program funding included in the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, signed into law in 2021. The program was expected to award $5 billion over five years, through competitive grants and rebates. However, following President Donald Trump’s return to office, the funding has reached a standstill. The last funding opportunity from the EPA was the 2024 Clean School Bus Rebate Program, which opened September 2024. However, the EPA canceled the rebate and no organizations received awarded funds. The last round of distributed funds was the 2023 rebate program.

The new legislation would amend the Energy Policy Act of 2005 by replacing the program’s current authorization period of fiscal years 2022 through 2026 with fiscal years 2027 through 2031. Under the existing statute, the program is authorized to receive $1 billion annually, totaling $5 billion. Rep. Jahana Hays, D-Conn., introduced the bill Oct. 9 and was joined by Reps. Greg Landsman, D-Ohio, and Buddy Carter, R-Ga.

“Since I came to Congress in 2019, I have advocated for clean school bus funding. As an educator with over a decade of classroom experience, I know how damaging diesel exhaust can be for student well-being and learning. The consequences of diesel emissions extend to our environment, exacerbating the effects of greenhouse gas emissions,” Hayes said in a statement. “The Clean School Bus Reauthorization Act will help to provide cleaner and healthier air for school children in Connecticut and across the country, support clean energy jobs, and protect our environment for decades to come.”

The legislation would maintain the existing funding structure, which allocates $500 million annually for clean and zero-emission school buses and another $500 million exclusively for zero-emission school buses. Funding supports the replacement of older school buses with cleaner alternatives.

It does not establish new grant requirements or change program eligibility. Rather, it extends the existing authorization for five additional years.

According to a press release, The Clean School Bus Reauthorization Act is endorsed by the American School Bus Industry Coalition which includes Blue Bird, First Student, Beacon Mobility, National Express, Highland, Greenpower Motor Company, National School Transportation, Student Transportation of America, and IC Bus. Additional endorsers include the American Bus Association, American Asthma and Allergy Foundation (AAFA), League of Conservation Voters, Moms Clean Air Force, Sierra Club, Union of Concerned Scientists, and World Resources Institute’s (WRI) Electric School Bus Initiative.

Sue Gander, director of WRI’s Electric School Bus Initiative, stated that children’s health is not a partisan issue.

“As this bill shows, there’s real enthusiasm on both sides of the aisle to give children the clean ride to school they deserve,” she said. “This bipartisan support is no surprise, as 51 percent of school districts with electric school buses on the road or coming soon are in Congressional districts represented by Republicans.

Related: EPA Opens $180 Million in 2026 Diesel Emissions Reduction Act Grants

Related: Oregon School Districts Make Case for Propane at STN EXPO West

Related: School Buses as Power Plants? Real-World V2G Journey Offers Roadmap

Related: Updated: EPA Seeks to Expand Fuel Scope of Clean School Bus Program

“The Clean School Bus Program has been a game-changer, answering school districts’ call to replace aging diesel buses with clean, zero-emissions vehicles in rural, suburban and urban communities alike,” Gander continued. “Replacing diesel buses with electric buses protects children from the dangers of diesel exhaust pollution, which disproportionately impacts low-income and Black communities.”

She added that electric school buses are popular with school districts that use them, especially the drivers behind the wheel. The number of ESBs on the road today is 12 times higher than it was five years ago, she noted.

“With diesel prices at record highs, Congress has a chance to help school districts save big on fuel costs and improve children’s health at the same time,” she said.

Meanwhile, First Student posted on Facebook that it welcomes the bipartisan introduction of the legislation.

“As the program’s largest recipient of funding, First Student has seen firsthand its importance in helping bring zero-emission school buses to our customers students and communities we serve,” the post reads. “Continued bipartisan support for this program is important to helping school districts and communities access funding for cleaner school bus technologies, including electric school buses.”

The school bus contractor added that reauthorizing the program would help preserve a pathway for Congress to continue supporting ESBs.

name: Clean Energy
title: Expecting Clean Energy Credits? Know Your Supply Chain - Aprio
authors: Aprio Publisher, Shazan Rizvi, Esq. Director, Federal Credits
description:
Summary: New rules under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) change how businesses evaluate clean energy tax credits.
For years, clean energy tax incentives have helped businesses offset the cost of investing in renewable energy projects, advanced manufacturing, battery production, hydrogen technologies, and other strategic initiatives.
Recent changes under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) introduce new Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) restrictions that significantly affect major clean energy tax credits.
Decisions that may have seemed operational before now directly affect the qualification of federal clean energy tax incentives.
Those deeper supply chain connections may now have tax consequences, presenting additional challenges to businesses pursuing clean energy incentives.
text:
Summary: New rules under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) change how businesses evaluate clean energy tax credits. In addition to meeting traditional project performance and qualifying expenditure requirements, companies must now consider the origin of project materials throughout their supply chains. For organizations accustomed to using clean energy incentives to offset project costs and improve returns, sourcing decisions have become a new and critical eligibility consideration.

For years, clean energy tax incentives have helped businesses offset the cost of investing in renewable energy projects, advanced manufacturing, battery production, hydrogen technologies, and other strategic initiatives. Eligibility for clean energy credits has largely depended on factors such as whether a project met the statutory requirements of the applicable credit, generated qualifying investment or production activity (e.g., building eligible energy property, producing clean electricity, or manufacturing qualifying components), and was properly documented and substantiated.

As a result, companies evaluating these opportunities often focus on project economics, technical and engineering requirements, and qualifying expenditures or production metrics to determine project eligibility and the calculation of the anticipated tax benefit. However, another factor is predominantly more likely to determine whether a project qualifies for these tax credits: where critical components, materials, and technologies come from.

Recent changes under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) introduce new Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) restrictions that significantly affect major clean energy tax credits. These rules are intended to prevent entities connected to certain foreign adversaries, including China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea, from benefitting from U.S. clean energy incentives. The legislation also includes “material assistance” rules that can deny credits when too much of a project’s supply chain relies on specified foreign adversaries.

By adding a new dimension to eligibility that examines who supplied the materials, components, and technologies that made the project possible, supply chain sourcing now plays an important role as well. Businesses pursuing clean energy credits must spend more time and resources assessing the origin of project material, components, and suppliers.

A change in perspective: supply chain visibility as a tax issue

Historically, companies pursuing clean energy incentives focused primarily on whether a project satisfied the requirements of the applicable credit and generated sufficient qualifying investment or production activity to support the expected tax benefit. While documentation and substantiation remained important, relatively little attention was paid to where materials, components, and technologies originated. The FEOC rules change that equation by making supply chain sourcing a critical factor in determining credit eligibility.

Under the new framework, eligibility depends not only on what a company builds or manufactures, but also on ownership structures, financing arrangements, supplier relationships, sourcing decisions, and contractual agreements throughout the supply chain. For many businesses, this means tax, procurement, legal, manufacturing, supply chain, and finance teams must work together earlier in the project lifecycle. Decisions that may have seemed operational before now directly affect the qualification of federal clean energy tax incentives.

Why supply chains matter

The FEOC provisions are designed to strengthen domestic energy production and reduce reliance on countries viewed as posing strategic risks to U.S. economic and national security interests. The rules target entities that are owned, controlled, or significantly influenced by organizations linked to certain foreign governments.

This reflects a broader policy shift already visible across multiple industries. Federal incentives are becoming more intertwined with domestic production, domestic content requirements, critical mineral sourcing, and supply chain resiliency. The clean energy sector is no exception. As companies expand manufacturing operations, invest in clean energy facilities, or develop energy storage technologies, policymakers want incentive dollars to support supply chains that align with these objectives.

Consequently, a project that appears eligible based on its technology or investment alone may still face qualification challenges if its supply chain does not satisfy the applicable sourcing requirements.

The hidden risk in material assistance

One of the most important concepts introduced by the OBBBA is the material assistance rule, in which a project must demonstrate that a sufficient percentage of its direct costs are not attributable to foreign adversaries. This is measured using the Material Assistance Cost Ratio (MACR), which calculates the percentage of qualifying costs that are not attributable to prohibited foreign entities.

Simply put, the calculation measures how much of a project’s direct costs come from acceptable sources versus prohibited foreign entities. For certain credits, including those available through Sections 45X, 45Y, and 48E, projects can lose eligibility if too much of its materials or components originate from foreign adversaries. The credit may also be denied if the percentage of costs attributable to acceptable sources falls below the required threshold. Because clean energy incentives can represent a significant portion of a project’s financial return, losing eligibility due to sourcing issues may materially affect project economics.

While companies may know the identity of their primary suppliers, they often have less visibility into second- and third-tier sourcing relationships. Those deeper supply chain connections may now have tax consequences, presenting additional challenges to businesses pursuing clean energy incentives.

The reason companies may be unprepared

Modern manufacturing and energy supply chains are global by nature. Components frequently move through multiple countries and providers before arriving at their final destination. For instance, developers may source inverters from one supplier, battery components from another, and raw materials from several additional vendors.

As a result, some organizations may struggle to answer fundamental questions such as:

Where are critical components manufactured?

Who ultimately owns or controls the supplier?

What percentage of project costs originate from potentially restricted sources?

Do supplier contracts provide sufficient sourcing transparency?

Can suppliers substantiate their certifications if challenged?

These questions were not historically part of many companies’ tax credit planning processes, though they may be essential now. Waiting until tax return preparation to investigate sourcing details can create significant challenges, given procurement decisions have often been finalized, contracts executed, and equipment installed.

Businesses that intend to pursue clean energy tax credits should evaluate sourcing considerations early in the project lifecycle to help ensure supply chain decisions do not inadvertently jeopardize eligibility for available incentives.

Clean energy credits may require new due diligence

As sourcing becomes more important, organizations should consider building credit eligibility reviews into existing procurement and vendor management processes. That does not mean every company needs to become a supply chain forensic investigator, however, companies expecting significant clean energy incentives should establish reasonable procedures to evaluate sourcing risks before major purchasing decisions are made.

The earlier these reviews occur, the greater the flexibility to address potential issues. For example, identifying a problematic supplier during project planning provides the opportunity to explore alternative sourcing options. Discovering the same issue after construction begins could be considerably more costly.

Best practices for protecting credit eligibility

1. Map your supply chain early

Many businesses understand their direct vendor relationships but have limited visibility beyond the first tier. Companies planning significant clean energy investments should consider mapping critical components and materials before contracts are finalized.

The goal is not necessarily to achieve perfect visibility, but rather to identify areas where sourcing concentration or ownership concerns may exist. Understanding where key products originate can help organizations identify risks before they affect project economics.

2. Strengthen supplier documentation requirements

The new rules place more emphasis on documentation and certifications. Many companies already retain supplier certifications but should evaluate how supplier information is collected, maintained, and periodically refreshed to ensure all documentation is updated and meets new requirements.

Questions worth considering include:

Are sourcing certifications obtained consistently?

Is supporting documentation retained?

Who is responsible for validating supplier representations?

Are there procedures for updating information if supply chains change?

A proactive documentation strategy can make future compliance efforts significantly easier.

3. Bring tax into procurement conversations earlier

Procurement, operations, and engineering teams often make purchasing decisions based on cost, availability, performance, and delivery timelines. While those considerations remain important, companies pursuing clean energy incentives should also evaluate whether sourcing decisions could affect anticipated tax benefits.

A component that appears less expensive initially may become more costly if it jeopardizes eligibility for a substantial tax credit. Cross functional collaboration can help ensure procurement decisions align with broader financial objectives.

4. Monitor regulatory developments

The FEOC framework remains an evolving area as Treasury guidance, safe harbor provisions, certifications, and compliance procedures continue to develop over time. Companies with long project timelines should monitor these developments regularly and stay informed to adapt sourcing strategies before they become compliance challenges.

Final thoughts: Credits are earned longed before the tax return is filed

Many businesses think of tax credits as the final step in a project. In reality, clean energy credit eligibility is increasingly being determined throughout the project’s lifecycle. Supplier selection, component sourcing, ownership structures, financing agreements, and contractual relationships can all influence whether a project ultimately qualifies for the incentives it expects to receive.

The new FEOC and material assistance rules reinforce the reality that tax planning can no longer operate independently from supply chain planning. Organizations that treat credit eligibility as an enterprise-wide consideration, rather than a year-end tax exercise, will be more likely to successfully maximize clean energy incentives. Enlist the help of an experienced tax credit advisor to help evaluate sourcing risks, address compliance considerations, and plan proactively to preserve valuable tax benefits.

These kinds of facilities do not generate any power on their own.

As part of hours of deliberation, Nat Drucker with Jupiter Power addressed several concerns from residents – like capping the number of total batteries, draining water to an independent system, and taking precautions against fire.

“We hope that all of this shows and demonstrates that we are absolutely willing to work with people.” Drucker said. “And we’re working to do this better, and to provide this very important piece of infrastructure that is going to help keep this county, and this part of Indiana, moving forward.”

The rezoning was proposed last month with the planning commission, but Jupiter Power developers at that meeting requested a continuance to better respond to concerns and questions.

Despite that new information, members of the public remained firmly against the battery storage facility.

Former Madison County Council member Ben Gale was among them.

“So the numbers we’re seeing up here, I don’t buy them,” he said. “I’ve been through the process before, I see how it works, and the promises made up front are never what ends up working.”

Officials with Jupiter Power say neither project involves a large building. The sites instead feature “container-based” energy storage.

After the unfavorable recommendation, the project will now move to the county commissioners to consider and vote on the rezoning request.

If it were to be approved in Madison County, Jupiter Power says the first site, Liberty 1, would start construction in 2027 and be operational in 2028. Indiana Michigan Power has an agreement with Jupiter Power to purchase the battery storage facility upon its completion.

The second site, Liberty 2, is significantly bigger, and has a longer development time. No long-term ownership of the site has been determined yet.

title: What are data centers, and why do they need so much power? - EPIC
description:
One of the problems is that large data center companies have been pursuing aggressive business tactics.
Data centers don’t have to be built next door.
So, data centers don’t have to be anyplace that people don’t want them.
It should be organized and planned to concentrate the data centers in “industrial” areas with power and networking infrastructure.
Further, data center companies should REALLY cover the cost of new infrastructure—for its full lifetime of 15 to 30 years.
text:
We also pioneered an approach we call “Middlebox.” The idea is to build a little energy station next to the data center. This means the data center itself gets highly reliable power (and doesn’t have to be flexible about when it runs computations). The combined data center + power station can also now actually reduce peak loads overall on the grid, in addition to supporting renewable energy by increasing consumption when there is excess energy from wind or solar.

Remarkably, we did a study on this and showed that in the majority of cases, the data center companies would actually make money from doing this, because they can get better prices for energy and they don’t get charged extra for drawing power during peak usage times.

So technically and economically, it’s absolutely clear that this is the right thing to do. All the technology is there. But the companies are not taking these steps. In fact, several of them are bringing lawsuits against attempts to regulate them.

Are data centers good for a community?

One thing to keep in mind is that data centers don’t employ a lot of people, relative to say, an automotive factory, or even a store of similar square footage. Once the initial construction is done, communities often see very little positive economic impact.

One of the problems is that large data center companies have been pursuing aggressive business tactics. But they do so at the cost of alienating the local community and causing a backlash.

For example, a common tactic is to come into a small town or county and tell the mayor, “We want to build a data center,” and the first thing they do is make the mayor sign a non-disclosure agreement about the discussions. When the deal is done, then the citizens hear about it—often with surprise and dismay.

Worse, some of these deals carry NDAs into their operating stage—where the concessions or permits granted may not be known for many years—or ever.

I think it’s a good idea to ban companies requesting or public officials signing such NDAs and require all such deals to be shared openly. This would decrease the information and power asymmetry, and force the data center companies to compete for community support!

“If it’s really that important that data centers be built, let’s solve the problem in a way that works for everybody.” —Prof. Andrew A. Chien

What do you think more people should know about data centers?

Data centers don’t have to be built next door. With the modern fiber-optic internet, communication can travel across the country in less than 15 milliseconds. So, data centers don’t have to be anyplace that people don’t want them. They can be anywhere in the USA and serve AI to the entire population, businesses, etc.

How do you recommend we solve the problem?

National and state government needs to organize infrastructure for data centers. Coordinated regulation is needed because the companies are so powerful. It should be organized and planned to concentrate the data centers in “industrial” areas with power and networking infrastructure. If it’s zoned properly, it will reduce the impact on local community.

Further, data center companies should REALLY cover the cost of new infrastructure—for its full lifetime of 15 to 30 years. They have plenty of profit. If it’s really that important that data centers be built, let’s solve the problem in a way that works for everybody.

I think sometimes people feel that governments can’t force companies to change. But I don’t really believe that’s true. When I was at Intel, my experience was that if public policy changes, the companies change. The auto companies complied with the Inflation reduction act quickly. American tech companies comply with European policies in order to sell there.

We should expect that companies will fight every step of the way to get more profit, but I still believe people can win that battle in the U.S. to reach a balanced solution where we can have the AI computing power we need, but the communities that host data centers get valuable training, community contribution, and good jobs.

Original post by UChicago News.

text:
Researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) have found that renewable portfolio standards (RPS) and utility-scale renewables are not associated with higher residential electricity prices in the United States, while rooftop solar is associated with higher prices.

Fischer J. Espiritu Argosino and Christopher R. Knittel of the MIT Center for Energy and Environmental Policy Research (CEEPR) built a state-utility panel covering 1998 to 2023. It links residential prices, RPS stringency, generation mixes and utility spending, using data from the US Energy Information Administration (EIA), the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL).

“Using a two way fixed effects regression model that controls for unobserved differences across years and between states, we find that RPSs and utility scale renewables are not associated with higher residential electricity prices,” the researchers said in a summary of the paper. “Instead, RPSs have virtually zero impact on prices and utility scale renewables are modestly associated with lower prices; in particular, utility-scale solar is strongly linked with lower prices.”

Based on the paper’s regression coefficients, which measure generation shares relative to coal, a 10-percentage-point rise in utility-scale solar’s share of generation is associated with residential prices just over 8% lower. A 5-percentage-point rise in rooftop solar’s share is associated with prices roughly 16% higher. The authors cautioned that the results are correlations and said further work will apply “more rigorous econometric techniques to further strengthen the causal interpretation of these estimates.”

“One explanation is that large solar plants may reduce network congestion and place downward pressure on overall generation costs because they do not require fuel inputs,” the researchers said. A second model, which also controls for differences between utilities, found utility-scale solar strongly associated with lower transmission, distribution and total operation and maintenance (O&M) costs.

The researchers suggested tariff design may partly explain the rooftop solar result.

“One possible reason for this is that current rate structures in some states shift fixed costs associated with rooftop solar from the owners onto other ratepayers,” they said. “In effect, this means that those without rooftop solar often fund those who do through an additional volumetric rate.”

Distribution strain

Rooftop solar was also strongly correlated with higher distribution O&M costs.

“One reason for this is that the distribution network was not designed for bidirectional power flows,” the researchers said.

CEEPR does not peer-review working papers before posting them.

“Policymakers can secure an affordable energy future by improving the integration of low-cost renewables while implementing more equitable cost recovery strategies,” the researchers said.

A June 2025 LBNL study led by Ryan Wiser reached a similar conclusion on utility-scale renewables. It found that the roughly 75% of US utility-scale wind and solar built outside RPS programs had no broadly discernible upward effect on retail prices.

The rooftop solar finding feeds into a long-running dispute over cost-shifting in California. The California Public Utilities Commission’s Public Advocates Office has estimated an $8.5 billion cost shift from rooftop solar customers to other ratepayers. A 2025 report by M.Cubed Consulting and the California Solar and Storage Association found instead that rooftop solar delivered a $1.5 billion net benefit to all California ratepayers. Solar advocates have also argued that rising transmission and distribution spending is a larger driver of rate increases.

description:

text:
"Congress must reject this cynical industry-backed effort to force data centers on America and get to work on protecting the public, not the tech billionaires.”

WASHINGTON — Nearly 200 community, labor, climate and environmental justice organizations today urged Congressional leaders to oppose anti-environmental permitting reform legislation.

The groups’ letter opposes this “back-door deal” to drive a massive buildout of hyperscale AI data centers and the fossil fuel infrastructure to power them.

Jim Walsh, Policy Director at Food & Water Watch said:

“Communities are fighting AI data centers because they see first-hand the impacts these monstrosities are having on utility bills, quality of life and precious water resources they depend on. Instead of helping, this bill will further harm families by facilitating a Big Tech power grab while limiting the power of states’ and local communities to protect the public. Congress must reject this cynical industry-backed effort to force data centers on America and get to work on protecting the public, not the tech billionaires.”

“This legislation is a golden ticket for huge AI data centers and tech billionaires. Gutting environmental safeguards means we’ll see a lot more gas-powered data centers draining communities’ water supplies,” said Camden Weber, senior climate and energy policy specialist at the Center for Biological Diversity. “This trillion-dollar industry is ravaging neighborhoods and making Americans pay more for their electricity. This bill silences communities who have been crystal clear that they don’t want more data centers.”

The “Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026” rolls back the Clean Water Act, National Environmental Policy Act, and Endangered Species Act. It will turn federal approvals into a rubber-stamp for both data centers and the fossil fuel infrastructure that powers them, all but ensuring each project will be approved regardless of community opposition.

Gas generation being developed specifically to serve data centers has increased from roughly 4 gigawatts in early 2024 to more than 189 gigawatts today.

Today’s letter explains that permitting reform will not accelerate the much-needed transition to clean energy. Instead, it will drive up electricity demand by data centers that use gas and other fossil fuels, requiring the following:

Narrowing state and Tribal authority under the Clean Water Act to protect waterways

Exempting pipelines in existing rights-of-way from NEPA review

Capping NEPA reviews at one to two years

Giving communities only 150 days to challenge federal permits in court

Creating a new right for gas pipeline and power plant developers to sue for taxpayer money over permit denials and delays.

Bill McKibben, Co-founder of Third Act: “It would be highly ironic if the first action Congress took after an election largely defined by opposition to data centers would be to make it easier to build them.”

Lorne Stockman, Research Director at Oil Change International: “This bill will make it virtually impossible for communities and individuals to challenge infrastructure projects that threaten their air and water. It comes as communities across the U.S. face an unprecedented buildout of gas power plants currently being planned to fuel the AI data center boom. If the current slate of data centers and associated gas power plants move ahead, the power sector’s gas consumption could rise by 50 percent, the equivalent of the gas consumption of Central and South America combined. This would be disastrous for our climate and the communities whose air and water would be poisoned. We urge senators to reject this bill.”

Mar Zepeda Salazar, Legislative Director at Climate Justice Alliance: “Six years, the same message from frontline communities: listen to us, protect our health, and build solutions with us. Instead, each version of this backroom deal gets worse, and now, rather than listening to their own constituents, politicians are trying to force through legislation that will allow data centers to explode at an even faster pace, even as families across the political spectrum are saying enough is enough. Announcing a deal before the public can even see the bill is simply undemocratic. They may call it affordability, but affordable for whom and at what cost? You don’t make energy cheaper by sacrificing our health, our neighborhoods, and our children’s future. We’ve offered common-sense solutions. We’ve helped craft better policy. And once again, communities are being sidelined for industry gain under the very risky assumption that we won’t make our voices heard at the ballot box.”

Andrea Marpillero-Colomina, PhD., Policy Advisor at GreenLatinos: “Latino communities know the cost of fossil fuel expansion. We breathe it, drink it and pay for it with our wallets and our health. More than 1.8 million Latinos already live within half a mile of oil and gas facilities. This bill would bring even more gas plants and pipelines into our neighborhoods to power data centers for some of the richest companies on earth, at further health and likely economic costs to us. Many of these projects are going up in the Southwest, where water is already scarce, near sacred ancestral lands, while our families struggle with rising electricity bills, energy monopolies, and serious and valid concerns about the consequences of these new data centers. This bill does not address affordability. It’s asking working families to give up their health, their water and their voice so Big Tech and the fossil fuel industry can build faster and with less oversight. We urge Congress to reject this deal, and to remember that their job is to protect and serve the communities who will live with the consequences

Jenna Ruddock, Advocacy Director at Free Press Action: “Across the country, communities couldn’t be clearer about their demands in the face of the frenzied data center build-out: more public oversight and community control, not less. From Tennessee to Texas, people already have too little time and systematically restricted access to information when confronted with massive industrial projects targeting their communities, including hyperscale data centers and the largely fossil-fueled energy infrastructure being built to power them. Our communities deserve more information about and opportunities to both influence and challenge decisions that will profoundly impact our public health, our quality of life, and our environment for generations to come – not less.

Paige Knappenberger, Environment & Health Program Director at Physicians for Social Responsibility: “The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 does anything but advance the priorities of its title. Supporting the proliferation of data centers, most of which are or plan to be powered by fossil fuels, is unacceptable in the face of community-led opposition. Polluting facilities are being constructed in places where residents are already subjected to health, environmental, and economic burdens. These are not sacrifice zones for big oil and big tech; they are communities being denied the opportunity to thrive. Research on the health impacts of data centers has not even had time to catch up to the AI boom, but the breadth of research available on the harms of exposure to fossil fuel emissions could not be more clear. Advancement of this bill would be reckless. The Senate should go back to the drawing board and this time listen to their constituents about what equitable permitting reform can look like.”

Alli Finn, Director of Community Partnerships at AI Now Institute: The toxic tech industry is forcing data center expansion down the throats of communities across the US—selling us a false narrative of AI inevitability while taking our water, land, energy, public health, and economic futures for their profit. This deregulatory agenda will only accelerate the harms of Big Tech’s data centers, and simultaneously dismantle some of the few tools the public has to hold them accountable. Our elected leaders must enact policies that ensure communities—not the wealthiest corporations in the world—decide our own futures, and continuously work to wrest power from the tech industry back into the hands of the public.

Jai Dulani, Senior Research Specialist at MediaJustice: “This bill signals that the Senate is happy to let Big Tech and Big Oil move fast and break things at a level of irreparable damage to public health. Giving corporations more legal power than states and Tribes in order to poison clean air and clean water is shameful. The Senate must reject this bill that is a blatant handout to Big Tech and Big Oil and a blatant betrayal to Black, brown and Indigenous communities who will bear the brunt of this massive scaling of environmental racism.”

Today’s letter is led by AI Now Institute, Center for Biological Diversity, Climate Justice Alliance, Food & Water Watch, Free Press Action, GreenLatinos, Indigenous Environmental Network, MediaJustice, Oil Change International, Our Revolution, Physicians for Social Responsibility, Science Environmental Health Network and Third Act.

WASHINGTON—The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) today announced plans to lower electricity costs and strengthen grid reliability by supporting the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) in funding 84 transmission and distribution projects across eight states. The projects are expected to add approximately 2.5 gigawatts (GW) of grid capacity to help mitigate outages and create greater grid resilience. The TVA award is for approximately $581 million in total, including $250 million in federal funding and about $331 million in applicant cost-share funding.

As part of the Resilience Amplified: Multi-Market Grid Interconnection Initiative funding award under the Grid Resilience and Innovation Partnerships (GRIP) project, the investments will help ensure 2.58 million families and businesses have access to the affordable, reliable, and secure power they need. The project is estimated to support about 800 jobs.

“Since day one, President Trump has recognized that years of misguided energy policies under the previous administration left our bulk power system less robust than it should be,” said U.S. Deputy Secretary of Energy James P. Danly. “America is blessed with an abundance of natural resources and some of the most advanced technology in the world, but we must have the generation and transmission infrastructure necessary to support our rapidly growing economy and its electricity needs. These investments with TVA will help reduce congestion, improve efficiency, and make better use of our existing transmission system to lower costs for ratepayers while delivering affordable, reliable, and secure energy essential to American prosperity.”

“America's electric grid cannot become a roadblock to economic growth,” said Office of Electricity (OE) Assistant Secretary Katie Jereza. “By bringing TVA and local utilities together, we're helping reduce costly outages and deliver more power where it's needed. That means fewer disruptions for families, more opportunities for businesses, and a stronger foundation for American jobs.”

The award builds on DOE's selection of TVA for the Speed to Power through Accelerated Reconductoring and other Key Advanced Transmission Technology Upgrades (SPARK) program. Together, the GRIP and SPARK projects for TVA represent nearly $741 million in planned grid investment, including approximately $329.8 million in federal support, and are expected to add more than 4,300 MW of additional grid capacity.

Under SPARK, TVA plans to upgrade about 125 miles of existing transmission lines across Tennessee, Alabama, and North Carolina using advanced conductors and grid-management technology. The $159.7 million project is expected to add approximately 1,900 MW of transmission capacity and reduce congestion.

Final federal funding, project scope, schedules, and other award conditions remain subject to executed DOE agreements and applicable environmental, permitting, regulatory, and Tribal reviews.

text:
Report shows that an additional 25 GW of residential demand flexibility can be turned on quickly and could generate between $4 and $7 billion per year in financial benefits for US households.

BOSTON, Oct. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- A new report from The Brattle Group finds that rapidly scaling residential virtual power plants (VPPs) could reduce expected household electricity bill increases by more than half over the next five years (in inflation-adjusted terms), while providing utilities with hundreds of megawatts of dependable capacity.

The report, The Affordability Advantage: How Virtual Power Plants Can Alleviate Household Electricity Bill Pressure, was prepared by Brattle experts Ryan Hledik and Kailin Graham for Everyday Electric (formerly Renew Home). The analysis evaluates how aggregating flexible household technologies – including smart thermostats, electric vehicles, and behind-the-meter batteries – could both reduce system costs and translate those savings into lower electricity bills for customers.

Available National Scale

The analysis comes as the cost of expanding the conventional power system has risen substantially. The authors note that forecasts for new gas-fired generation costs have increased sharply in recent years amid equipment shortages, supply-chain constraints, and rapid electricity demand growth. The report finds that VPPs can dependably offset a portion of these rising costs by reducing demand during periods when the system is most constrained. VPP capacity value is planning grade, remaining robust across 10 years of historical load and weather conditions considered in the analysis.

The report also shows substantial opportunity to expand residential demand flexibility nationally. Residential demand response currently represents approximately 1.1% of utility system peak demand on average, or about 10 GW nationwide. By contrast, the top 10% of utilities have achieved approximately 4% system-peak contribution.

If utilities nationwide reached that level, Brattle estimates residential VPP capacity could more than triple, from approximately 10 GW to 35 GW. Extrapolating the report's modeling nationally, that additional 25 GW of residential demand flexibility could generate $4 billion to $7 billion annually in financial benefits for US households, including approximately $1.8 billion to $5.5 billion benefiting all ratepayers and another $1.9 billion paid directly to participating customers. This report comes on the heels of a March 2026 Brattle analysis which showed how better utilization of the existing US power system could save consumers more than $100 billion over the next decade.

Drilling Down to the Utility Level

For a representative utility serving one million residential customers, Brattle finds that making it simple for consumers to participate could allow a residential VPP to grow to more than 300 MW within five years, equivalent to approximately 4% of that utility's total coincident peak demand. As a result, the report estimates that the utility could avoid $65 million per year in generation capacity, energy, and distribution upgrade costs by its first year of full-scale operation. Brattle estimates that $56 million of those annual savings would benefit consumers through a combination of lower system costs shared across ratepayers and direct performance payments to participating households.

"Electricity affordability has become one of the most pressing challenges facing the industry, at the same time that utilities are confronting sharply higher costs for new infrastructure," said Mr. Hledik, a Brattle Principal and report coauthor. "Our analysis shows that there is a significant amount of untapped flexible capacity already sitting in customers' homes. If utilities and technology providers can activate that capacity at scale, VPPs can provide a meaningful source of near-term bill relief while also helping meet emerging system needs."

What It Means for American Households

Those savings could have a significant impact on monthly household electricity bills. Under the report's modeled rate-growth scenario, without expanded VPP deployment, the average household's annual electricity cost is projected to increase by $98 in inflation-adjusted terms after five years. The VPP reduces that increase by $56, or 57% on average across all households served by the utility. The savings are greater for households enrolled in the utility's VPP, who are predicted to nearly eliminate the projected inflation-adjusted bill increase. Non-participating households will reduce the increase by more than a third ($34 annually).

The analysis incorporates emerging evidence on how easy-to-use features embedded directly in home energy products can dramatically simplify potential bill savings. Everyday Electric has found that four times as many customers choose to turn on flexible energy shifting features compared to traditional demand response programs, which are built around more noticeable adjustments.

"This report makes clear just how significant the opportunity is: Virtual power plants that make it easy for customers to save can help households that enable VPP features offset nearly all of their projected electricity bill increases within five years," said Ben Brown, CEO of Everyday Electric. "And even the households that don't take part in a VPP stand to benefit. When the grid has access to more flexible capacity, electricity bills can be more affordable for all homes."

The full report is available at The Affordability Advantage | Brattle.

About The Brattle Group

The Brattle Group is a global consulting firm specializing in economics and finance. With 550+ professionals across North America, Europe, and Asia-Pacific, Brattle provides independent analysis in litigation, energy and financial markets, and regulatory and strategic advisory settings.

Our Electricity Practice serves utilities, grid operators, power producers, customers, regulators, developers, investors, law firms, and policymakers. For more than three decades, our experts have been recognized as trusted advisors and thought leaders in the planning, regulation, litigation, and operation of electricity grids and markets. Our clients collectively serve more than 90% of North American electricity customers, and our experts have testified before courts and regulatory agencies worldwide.

For more information, please visit www.brattle.com.

text:
Global electricity demand from data centers is on track to more than double by 2030, with AI as the single largest driver of that growth, according to the International Energy Agency. Less discussed is what that growth means for backup power. Every new data center campus adds not just servers and cooling systems but a fleet of diesel generators standing by to keep operations running through grid outages, and each one is a source of regulated air emissions.

“Backup generators aren’t an afterthought at a data center, they’re required infrastructure,” said Anoosheh Oskouian, CEO of Ship & Shore Environmental, a global provider of industrial air pollution control solutions. “As more of these facilities come online, the emissions from that backup power fleet grow right along with them, and that’s a problem our industry already knows how to solve.” Anoosheh Oskouian, Ship & Shore Environmental

A Fast-Growing Fleet with a Real Footprint

Northern Virginia alone has more than 9,000 backup generators available to supply emergency power to data centers, according to Virginia Mercury. In Texas, a July 2026 analysis by the Environmental Integrity Project, reported by The Texas Tribune, found 32 new natural gas plants planned specifically to power data centers, are projected to emit more than 287 million metric tons of greenhouse gases annually. A separate National Bureau of Economic Research analysis found that Texas and Virginia together account for roughly 30% of the national economic damage tied to data center emissions, underscoring how concentrated the impact already is in the regions building the fastest.

That concentration is starting to show up in how these generators are actually used, not just how many exist. In spring and summer 2026, the U.S. Department of Energy issued a series of emergency orders directing data centers in several regions to run their backup generators during periods of extreme grid stress, a shift the EPA now treats as emergency operation exempt from the usual hourly limits on non-emergency use. Oskouian said that trend is worth watching closely.

“When backup power starts getting called on for grid support and not just outages, the emissions conversation changes,” Oskouian said. “That is exactly why the control technology needs to be built in from the start, not treated as something to revisit later.”

Regulators and Communities are Paying Closer Attention

Virginia, home to the country’s densest cluster of data centers, passed legislation this year requiring new data center air permits submitted after July 1, 2026 to meet emissions limits at least as strict as Tier 4 generator standards. Separately, the EPA's Office of Air and Radiation launched a Clean Air Act Resources for Data Centers webpage to help developers navigate permitting requirements for backup power fleets.

“Regulators and communities are asking sharper questions about backup power than they were even a year ago,” Oskouian said. “That’s not a reason to slow down data center development. It’s a reason to bring emissions control into the design conversation from the start.”

Technology that Already Exists

Proven emissions control technologies, including selective catalytic reduction, diesel oxidation catalysts, diesel particulate filters, cleaner fuels and battery storage, can be combined to cut regulated pollutants from backup generators without compromising the reliability data centers depend on. Ship & Shore Environmental designs and engineers these systems for industrial clients across North America, Europe and Asia, tailoring the combination to each facility’s generator fleet, fuel source and local regulatory requirements.

“There is no single solution for every project,” Oskouian said. “The right combination depends on how a facility is built and what its permits require. What matters is treating emissions control as part of the engineering from day one, not something addressed after the fact.”

Early Planning is the Biggest Lever

Oskouian, a chemical engineer with nearly three decades of industrial environmental experience, points to early-stage collaboration between environmental engineers, permitting specialists and developers as the single biggest opportunity to avoid costly redesigns and permitting delays down the line.

“When environmental engineers, permitting specialists and developers work together during facility design, projects can evaluate emissions control strategies, improve permitting certainty and avoid costly redesigns,” Oskouian said. “Responsible environmental planning is not a barrier to innovation. It is part of building resilient infrastructure.”

Community Trust Matters as much as Compliance

Beyond regulatory compliance, Oskouian said developers who engage nearby communities early, and can speak plainly about how new facilities may affect air quality and noise, are more likely to build trust and avoid project delays.

“Communities deserve transparency,” Oskouian said. “Developers who engage communities early and demonstrate a commitment to responsible engineering are more likely to earn trust while avoiding unnecessary project delays.”

A Pattern with Precedent

Oskouian frames the moment as a familiar one in industrial history. Cleaner manufacturing, cleaner vehicles and cleaner power generation all became possible once engineers treated environmental performance as a design problem to solve rather than a trade-off to accept.

“The question is not whether we should build more data centers,” Oskouian said. “The question is whether we will build them responsibly. By integrating environmental planning, emissions mitigation and engineering excellence into every project from the outset, we can support AI innovation while protecting the communities where these facilities operate.”

title: EPA Proposes Reallocating Refinery Exemptions to Preserve Biofuel Demand
description:
Under Tuesday's proposed rule, EPA would reallocate 770 million RINs that haven't been accounted for.
"With this proposal, EPA would deliver on the full potential of historic RVOs and fulfill its promise to make American farmers and biofuel producers whole," said Growth Energy CEO Emily Skor.
He credited the Trump administration for recognizing "this is no time to undermine domestic biofuels" with small refinery exemptions.
Still, Cooper also said RFA continues to call for reforms to small refinery exemptions.
"As soon as we got into office, American farmers asked the Trump EPA not to give them handouts but create avenues for them to enter additional markets.
text:
OMAHA (DTN) -- In a move aimed at protecting demand for ethanol and biodiesel, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin used a trip to Iowa on Tuesday to announce a proposal to reallocate 770 million renewable fuel blending credits granted to small refiners by adding them to volume obligations for refiners either this year or next year.

The proposal, which dives into the weeds of the Renewable Fuels Standard, would essentially protect the equivalent of 770 million gallons of ethanol from being waived from refiners' blending requirements.

Zeldin announced proposed revisions to the Renewable Fuels Standard (RFS) to ensure 100% of the blending volumes granted by EPA through 29 small refinery exemptions in August won't reduce the overall renewable fuel blending requirements for the country's petroleum refiners.

While meant to boost markets, the proposed rule didn't lead to any immediate reactions in the corn and soybean markets on Tuesday. Corn futures were essentially flat at midday while soybean futures were down 3 to 3.5 cents.

EPA granted 18 full exemptions and 11 partial exemptions to small refineries in August, totaling 1.76 billion in exempted Renewable Identification Numbers (RINs), which serve as compliance credits under the RFS. EPA had already factored 990 million RINs into its "Set 2" rule that set the RFS blending requirements for 2026 and 2027.

Under Tuesday's proposed rule, EPA would reallocate 770 million RINs that haven't been accounted for. Those RINs go back to the 2025 RFS renewable volume obligations. Under Tuesday's announcement, EPA will reallocate 100% of those RINs to refiners under the 2026 and 2027 RFS volume requirements.

EPA is proposing two options to revise its Set 2 rule. Under one option, EPA would split the exempted RINs and add them to 2026 and 2027. Under the second option, the agency would add the entire volume to 2027 requirements.

Growth Energy and the Renewable Fuels Association (RFA), which represent the biofuels industry, both praised EPA for the proposal.

"With this proposal, EPA would deliver on the full potential of historic RVOs and fulfill its promise to make American farmers and biofuel producers whole," said Growth Energy CEO Emily Skor. "Reallocating lost gallons would strengthen the rural economy and provide relief to farmers looking for reliable new markets that won't be destroyed by costly exemptions.

Geoff Cooper, president and CEO of RFA, said his members believe the small refinery exemptions were unjustified, but the reallocation plan – if finalized – would help offset the demand loss for ethanol producers and farmers.

Cooper added that refiners are "enjoying record profit margins" while gasoline supplies are tightening and consumers are paying higher fuel prices. He credited the Trump administration for recognizing "this is no time to undermine domestic biofuels" with small refinery exemptions. Still, Cooper also said RFA continues to call for reforms to small refinery exemptions.

"These exemptions were always meant to be a temporary measure to give truly small, independent refiners a little more time to come into compliance with the RFS program," Cooper said. "Unfortunately, many so-called small refiners have viewed SREs as an entitlement program and have exploited this loophole for two decades, putting American consumers, farmers, and biofuel producers on the losing end."

The American Petroleum Institute (API) criticized EPA's announcement, arguing that the reallocation would make it harder for refiners to plan and invest in fuel supplies.

"U.S. refiners are running all out to meet demand and keep fuel flowing to American consumers," said Kristin Whitman, senior vice president of federal relations for API. "Reallocating small refinery exemptions, particularly at historically high renewable volume obligation levels, would add new uncertainty to an already strained fuels market, making it harder for refiners to plan and invest in the reliable fuel supplies consumers depend on. We are continuing to review EPA's proposed rule and remain committed to working with the administration and Congress on durable solutions that strengthen market stability and help keep fuel affordable."

Dave Walton, an Iowa farmer and president of the American Soybean Association (ASA), said the proposal would help maintain the historic renewable fuel volumes in the 2026-2027 Set 2 rule and protect domestic biofuel demand. Walton urged EPA to finalize the rule and reallocate the biofuel volumes as quickly as possible.

"Soybean farmers are navigating a tough farm economy, and the administration's strong domestic biofuel policies will continue to drive much-needed market demand in the U.S.," Walton said. "We are encouraged by today's proposal and urge EPA to get it across the finish line quickly."

EPA stated, "The Trump EPA understands the importance of providing a predictable and stable market for farmers, refiners, and American consumers to help maintain economic competitiveness and keep energy prices low. The proposal reflects the Trump administration's commitment to have a robust and growing market for their crops while also unleashing American energy."

The rule would help protect and expand markets for farmers, Zeldin said in a news release.

"As soon as we got into office, American farmers asked the Trump EPA not to give them handouts but create avenues for them to enter additional markets. As our farmers continue to harvest their crops, today's proposal is working to maintain a strong and durable market for them to sell to," Zeldin said.

Zeldin made the announcement at an event in Peosta, Iowa, as the Trump administration looks to boost support for Republicans in the state ahead of the November election. Zeldin maintained his visit was official and not a campaign event. EPA's news release included comments from Iowa's congressional delegation, including two House members in competitive re-election races and a House member running for U.S. Senate.

EPA will take public comments on its proposed rule until Dec. 4.

Also see, "EPA Waives 1.76B Gallons From 2025 RFS, Pledges Full Reallocation in 2026, 2027," https://www.dtnpf.com/…

title: Badland Batteries Expands U.S. Battery Manufacturing with New Cell Production Facility
description:
Badland Batteries Manufacturing Facility Opens in North Dakota The new Fargo facility is designed to manufacture lithium-ion pouch battery cells for defense, aerospace and autonomous systems applications.
According to Badland Batteries, the facility is intended to support domestic battery production while providing greater control over materials, manufacturing quality and supply chain traceability.
Badland Batteries is positioning its domestic production capabilities to support growing demand from U.S. defense and commercial customers.
Badland Batteries describes its Fargo operation as the first UAS-specific battery manufacturing facility designed to control the complete manufacturing process, beginning with raw material sourcing and qualification.
Badland Batteries Expands American Energy Manufacturing The Fargo facility represents a significant expansion of Badland Batteries’ manufacturing capabilities and its role in the domestic UAS supply chain.
text:
Badland Batteries has officially opened a new 80,000-square-foot lithium-ion battery cell manufacturing facility in Fargo, North Dakota, expanding domestic production capabilities for unmanned aircraft systems, defense platforms, robotics and other autonomous technologies.

The Badland Batteries manufacturing facility, which celebrated its grand opening on October 8, 2026, represents an investment in rebuilding the U.S. battery supply chain and reducing dependence on overseas manufacturers for critical energy storage technologies.

The facility combines automated and operator-controlled manufacturing equipment to produce lithium-ion pouch cells, with the capacity to manufacture more than 15,000 battery cells per day as production scales.

Badland Batteries Manufacturing Facility Opens in North Dakota

The new Fargo facility is designed to manufacture lithium-ion pouch battery cells for defense, aerospace and autonomous systems applications.

The 80,000-square-foot plant incorporates a combination of automated manufacturing processes and equipment operated by personnel.

According to Badland Batteries, the facility is intended to support domestic battery production while providing greater control over materials, manufacturing quality and supply chain traceability.

“Opening this facility marks an important step forward in building a secure and resilient battery supply chain here in the United States,” said Terri Zimmerman, CEO of Badland Batteries and Packet Digital.

“Simply put, we believe that America should build its own batteries, and this facility represents years of work towards that goal and demonstrates our unwavering commitment to supporting our nation’s defense.”

New Facility Targets Drone and Autonomous Systems Batteries

The manufacturing operation is focused on producing battery cells for technologies that require reliable and domestically sourced power systems.

Target applications include:

Unmanned aircraft systems

Military and defense platforms

Autonomous vehicles

Robotics

Aerospace technologies

Commercial autonomous systems

Battery technology is a critical component of electric unmanned aircraft, affecting flight endurance, payload capacity and operational reliability.

Badland Batteries is positioning its domestic production capabilities to support growing demand from U.S. defense and commercial customers.

“These battery cells will help power today’s and tomorrow’s cutting-edge autonomous and UAS systems, which are critical to our nation’s security,” Zimmerman said.

Domestic Battery Supply Chain Reduces Foreign Dependence

According to Badland Batteries, more than 80% of batteries and critical materials used in autonomous systems are manufactured overseas.

The company identifies this dependence as a significant supply chain vulnerability for U.S. defense and advanced technology programs.

Badland Batteries describes its Fargo operation as the first UAS-specific battery manufacturing facility designed to control the complete manufacturing process, beginning with raw material sourcing and qualification.

The company plans to use domestic or allied-sourced raw materials with full traceability.

This approach is intended to strengthen supply chain security while giving customers greater visibility into the origins and production of critical battery components.

Integrated Battery Cell and Pack Manufacturing

The new facility will handle lithium-ion pouch cell production, beginning with raw material sourcing and in-house material qualification.

Once cells are manufactured, they can be transported to Badland Batteries’ existing manufacturing and assembly facility located approximately one mile away.

That second facility provides the capability to assemble completed cells into customer-ready battery packs.

The combined operations create a manufacturing workflow covering:

Raw material sourcing

Material qualification

Lithium-ion cell production

Battery cell manufacturing

Battery pack assembly

Customer-ready power systems

The company said this integrated approach is intended to provide a reliable domestic source of batteries for UAS and other autonomous platforms.

Production Capacity Exceeds 15,000 Battery Cells Per Day

Badland Batteries said the new facility has the ability to produce more than 15,000 lithium-ion battery cells per day.

The company also designed the manufacturing operation with the flexibility to increase production as demand grows.

The announced figure represents the facility’s production capacity rather than a confirmed current daily output.

Actual production volumes, battery cell specifications and customer delivery schedules were not disclosed in the announcement.

The manufacturing capacity is intended to support growing demand for domestically produced energy storage technologies across defense, aerospace and autonomous systems markets.

Federal Investment Supports North Dakota Battery Industry

The facility opening brought together federal, state, local, industry and military representatives.

U.S. Senator John Hoeven highlighted the importance of domestic battery manufacturing for national security and economic competitiveness.

“Building a strong domestic battery ecosystem is critical to our nation’s economic competitiveness and national security,” Hoeven said.

“That’s why we’ve worked over the last six years to secure more than $50 million in federal funding to advance these efforts in North Dakota.”

Hoeven said the Badland Batteries investment supports efforts to expand American manufacturing, create skilled employment opportunities and reduce reliance on foreign suppliers.

The announcement does not specify how much of the referenced federal funding was awarded directly to Badland Batteries.

U.S. Drone Industry Requires Secure Battery Manufacturing

As unmanned aircraft and autonomous systems become increasingly important to defense and commercial operations, the availability of reliable battery technology is a growing industrial consideration.

Domestic battery cell manufacturing can provide additional supply chain options for U.S. drone manufacturers and defense contractors seeking greater control over component sourcing.

Badland Batteries is focusing on lithium-ion pouch cells and integrated battery pack production for these markets.

The company’s approach combines U.S.-based manufacturing with domestic and allied raw material sourcing, aiming to reduce exposure to overseas supply chain disruptions.

Badland Batteries Expands American Energy Manufacturing

The Fargo facility represents a significant expansion of Badland Batteries’ manufacturing capabilities and its role in the domestic UAS supply chain.

“This facility is more than a manufacturing plant,” Zimmerman said. “It is a statement that America can reshore critical industries, create meaningful careers and develop the technologies that will power the future.”

With an 80,000-square-foot production facility, capacity exceeding 15,000 cells per day and a nearby battery pack assembly operation, Badland Batteries is establishing an integrated U.S. manufacturing capability focused on the power requirements of defense, aerospace and autonomous systems.

The Badland Batteries manufacturing facility adds domestic lithium-ion cell production capacity at a time when the U.S. unmanned systems industry is seeking more secure and traceable sources of critical components.

Source: Press release from Badland Batteries, October 8, 2026.

Regional convenience-store chain and ice cream maker United Dairy Farmers is installing Seattle-based Electric Era Level 3 DC fast chargers at six locations in the Cincinnati and Columbus, Ohio, areas, the two companies announced Oct. 6.

The initiative represents the first deployment of Level 3 EV charging in Cincinnati-based UDF’s history and “reflects the family-owned company’s strategy of evolving its stores to meet the changing needs of the communities and customers it serves,” the companies said.

United Dairy Farmers is No. 47 on CSP’s 2026 Top 202 ranking of U.S. c-store chains by store count.

UDF applied for six locations and was awarded all six, strategically selecting stores based on charging demand, proximity to major highways, accessibility and the overall customer experience each location can provide.
