Columbus: 5171 Riggins Road, Hilliard

Cincinnati: 890 Columbus Ave., Lebanon

Cincinnati: 5261 Kings Mills Road, Mason

Cincinnati: 6643 OH-48, Maineville

Cincinnati: 11610 Lebanon Road, Cincinnati

Cincinnati: 5275 Beechmont Ave., Cincinnati

UDF anticipates chargers will begin coming online in early 2027. Installation and launch timing for each location will be announced as chargers become operational.

Level 3 chargers, alternatively known as DC fast chargers, are the quickest chargers, according to Car and Driver. “Level 3 chargers are especially useful during long trips that necessitate charges between destinations, as this sort of charging can add around 100–250 miles of range in 30–45 minutes,” the magazine said. “Unlike Level 1 and Level 2 charging, Level 3 setups connect to the vehicle by way of a socket with additional pins for handling the higher voltage (typically 400 or 800 volts).”

Unlike a traditional fueling stop designed for a few minutes, EV charging creates a need for expanded amenities for customers who will spend, on average, 20 to 30 minutes at a UDF location, the companies said. UDF intentionally selected some of its newest stores to better meet those needs, with expanded food and beverage options, comfortable indoor and outdoor seating areas, and clear sightlines to the charging area.

‘The fuel of the future’

“We’ve always believed UDF should evolve alongside our guests, and this is another step in doing that,” said Jim Dwenger, UDF's head of retail. “For more than 85 years, we’ve focused on making everyday life more convenient for the communities we serve. Adding fast EV charging allows us to provide the fuel of the future while giving guests a welcoming place to recharge themselves—whether that’s with a scoop of their favorite ice cream, a meal, a snack or a drink from our wide selection of offerings. It’s another way we’re meeting guests where they are and helping them fuel up for wherever they're headed.”

The Electric Era chargers utilize battery-backed charging technology and are designed to provide reliable, high-speed charging while helping manage the demands placed on the electric grid, the companies said. Electric Era technology combines grid power with on-site battery storage and proprietary software to optimize power delivery, reducing peak demand and maintaining charging performance even when grid capacity is constrained. Electric Era guarantees industry leading 98%+ per-port uptime and 85%+ first plug-in success reliability.

The technology also lets UDF create a seamless, branded experience for EV drivers, the companies said. Charging stations will integrate with UDF’s U-Drive Plus loyalty program, giving members access to credits off charging just as they receive cents off gasoline. As with UDF’s existing loyalty members, customers will be able to earn additional charging credits with qualifying purchases inside UDF stores.

The charger loyalty integration also will provide opportunities for UDF to offer personalized loyalty rewards, including food and beverage promotions and other offers through both the U-Drive Plus app and the charging stations themselves, creating a direct connection between the charging experience and the UDF store, the companies said.

Making stores destinations

The move also builds on UDF’s broader strategy to ensure stores are more than transactional stops, transforming its next-gen stores into destinations where customers can comfortably spend time, the companies said.

“With comfortable indoor and outdoor seating at its newest locations, expanded food and beverage offerings and the added utility of public Wi-Fi, UDF sees EV charging as another opportunity to develop its stores into a community-oriented ‘third place’—a convenient place to stop, recharge your car and yourself, and spend time,” they said.

“We’re thinking beyond the charger itself and about how we can make those 20 to 30 minute charge times convenient, valuable and enjoyable for our guests,” said Rob Lindner, UDF’s corporate head of initiatives. “Whether they’re commuting, running errands or traveling through the region, we want UDF to be a place that works well for them.”

UDF will monitor charging demand, customer behavior, store visits and engagement with UDF amenities and loyalty offers to determine how EV charging can best serve customers and what future expansion might look like, the companies said.

Founded in 1940, United Dairy Farmers is a regional convenience-store chain and ice cream parlor with more than 170 locations across Ohio, Kentucky and Indiana.

text:
U.S. Senators represent all citizens of North Carolina at the federal level for six-year terms. They vote on federal legislation, confirm presidential appointments, ratify treaties and secure federal funding for state priorities. North Carolina's 11 million residents would be represented by this senator. The U.S. Senate currently has 53 Republicans and 45 Democrats, as well as two independents who caucus with Democrats.

Former Gov. Roy Cooper faces Republican Michael Whatley. The seat is currently held by Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, who decided not to seek reelection because of the “political theater and partisan gridlock” in D.C. Democrats have not won a Senate election in North Carolina since 2008. North Carolina’s junior senator, Republican Ted Budd, was elected in 2022; that seat will be up for reelection in 2028.

Two other candidates, Libertarian Shannon Bray and the Green Party's Michael Dublin, will also appear on this ballot.

Key issues in the race are affordability, the cost of healthcare, crime and the recovery of western North Carolina following Hurricane Helene.

As of June 2026, Cooper has raised over $26 million while Whatley has raised over $8 million. SuperPACs have also spent approximately $735,000 against Cooper. Dublin has raised $25,000. To date, Bray has not filed any campaign finance reports for this race.

Michael Dublin

Party: Green

Incumbent: No

Age: 69

Previous experience in elected office: None; ran unsuccessfully for U.S. House in 2024

Occupation: Retired public school teacher

Description:

Dublin's four pillars include government reform ("end gerrymandering"), environmental justice ("a Green New Deal for North Carolina"), social and racial equity, and peace. He wants to tax the wealthy and increase the minimum wage to $25/hour. He says that "ICE is a scam" and that the arrest of immigrants is activity that benefits private prisons. He says he is "the only candidate in the race who refuses all corporate donations." Dublin's Green Party was granted official status in North Carolina in 2025 with the support of Republicans on the state Board of Elections and over the objections of Democrats.

Dublin is from Raleigh and lives in Garner, N.C. He describes himself as a retired public school educator and a former leader in a prison ministry. He was a former DJ and rapper, which he says helps him "speak truth in rhythm." He was a U.S. Marine and has a bachelor's degree from N.C. State University.

Description:

Cooper has been an elected official in North Carolina politics for nearly four decades, most recently as governor and attorney general. Cooper's bio says that as governor he "focused on boosting public education, tackling the opioid crisis, revitalizing rural communities and making sure North Carolinians have the training to fill better paying jobs that require more skills." In his eight years as governor, Cooper led a state that grew quickly and attracted economic investment, although he faced criticism from Republicans over Covid shutdowns and his opposition to their plans for tax cuts and private-school vouchers. title: National Critical Minerals Council Act Introduced in Congress - environment coastal & offshore
description:
“Our bill establishes a National Critical Minerals Council to unite all federal investment, research, and development on critical minerals under a single national strategy.
“That’s why I’m proud to join my colleagues in introducing the bipartisan, bicameral National Critical Minerals Council Act.
“I am proud to co-lead the National Critical Minerals Council Act with my colleague, Congresswoman Lee.
Specifically, the council would: Develop a national critical minerals strategy to reduce our reliance on foreign adversaries.
Hickenlooper has introduced several bills that boost the supply of critical minerals: Critical Materials Future Act, which would establish a pilot program for the Department of Energy to financially support domestic critical material processing projects.
text:
Critical minerals power our modern way of life, including vehicles, smartphones, defense systems, medical equipment, AI, and clean energy. Yet, China dominates the market, processing or refining about 70% of the world’s critical minerals. The US is fully reliant on imports for 16 critical minerals. Given the scale of the challenge, our federal response remains fragmented, with more than 15 federal agencies and departments working on critical minerals issues. Absent a unified effort, the US risks falling behind in securing the minerals essential to our competitiveness and leadership in energy security and national defense.

“China doesn’t need to fire a shot. It just needs to stop a shipment,” said Hickenlooper. “We need a national strategy on critical minerals now. Otherwise, Beijing decides who gets the supply—and who doesn’t.”

“The United States can no longer afford to take a piecemeal approach to address our critical minerals needs,” said Tillis. “I am proud to reintroduce this bipartisan legislation to establish a comprehensive and unified strategy to secure the minerals that are essential to our national security and economic stability.”

“As the world races to acquire and leverage the critical minerals that power the modern economy, the United States needs an efficient and effective plan to secure these important resources,” said Rosen. “I am proud to help introduce this bipartisan bill to ensure the United States has the infrastructure it needs to secure critical minerals and remain at the forefront of modern development.”

“It’s common sense: we cannot continue to rely on adversaries like China, which dominates the world’s critical minerals processing, for our critical mineral needs because it puts America’s national security at risk and threatens our competitive edge,” said Sheehy. “This crucial legislation reduces our dependence on others and bolsters America’s critical mineral supply chains by centralizing federal coordination, strategy, and research, making our nation more secure and self-reliant. I’m proud to cosponsor this legislation as we work to ensure America’s needs can be securely met.”

“We cannot afford to become more dependent on other countries for the critical minerals needed to power our economy and strengthen our national security,” said Cramer. “Our bill establishes a National Critical Minerals Council to unite all federal investment, research, and development on critical minerals under a single national strategy. The demand for critical minerals is growing every single day, and we need to seize every opportunity to jumpstart domestic production.”

“Critical minerals are used in everything from our phones to solar panels and aircraft used by the Department of Defense. It’s essential we develop our domestic critical mineral supply chains and reduce our dependence on foreign countries for rare earths,” said Lee. “That’s why I’m proud to join my colleagues in introducing the bipartisan, bicameral National Critical Minerals Council Act. This commonsense legislation will ensure the United States continues to grow our domestic supply of critical minerals, strengthening our national security and energy grid.”

“For far too long, our country has depended on foreign adversaries for vital minerals that support many of our defense capabilities and energy systems. This legislation will establish important structures for mineral development and help build critical partnerships,” said Fulcher. “I am proud to co-lead the National Critical Minerals Council Act with my colleague, Congresswoman Lee. By securing the critical minerals we have here at home today, we can build stronger energy security for tomorrow.”

The Secretary of the Interior, the National Security Adviser, and the Director of the National Economic Council would co-chair the council. They would appoint a Chief Minerals Adviser to oversee the Council’s operations and collaborate with experts from universities, industry, national labs, governments, Tribes, non-profits, and civil society.

Specifically, the council would:

Develop a national critical minerals strategy to reduce our reliance on foreign adversaries.

Work with allied nations and private entities to make the US the partner of choice on critical minerals projects.

Track foreign investments in global critical mineral projects.

Coordinate education and workforce development.

Oversee the responsible development of domestic resources.

Hickenlooper has introduced several bills that boost the supply of critical minerals:

Critical Materials Future Act, which would establish a pilot program for the Department of Energy to financially support domestic critical material processing projects.

Unearth Innovation Act, which would create a Mining and Mineral Innovation Program within the Department of Energy to drive the responsible production of domestic critical minerals, with a focus on minimizing the environmental impact of mining.

Critical Minerals Security Act, which would direct the Department of the Interior to evaluate the global supply and ownership of critical minerals and make it easier for the US to establish stable supply chains with international allies.

name: American Energy
title: While Black Families Pay More for Power, Some Attorneys General Fight to Save High-Cost Coal
description:
At the same time, demand for power is climbing fast as the nation adds data centers, factories, and other large energy users.
The attorneys general argue this restricted coal supply, raised coal prices and, in the end, raised electricity prices for consumers.
Paxton and his colleagues have presented the case as a way to bring down power bills.
Too many of our neighborhoods carry both burdens at once: high energy bills and a greater share of the pollution.
But government should be just as cautious about using its power to guarantee coal a permanent place in the market.
text:
Families across the country are opening their monthly utility bills with a growing sense of dread. Groceries cost more. Rent costs more. Now electricity has become one more expense pushing household budgets to the breaking point, and for many in the Black community – as usual – the squeeze is being felt hardest of all.

Residential electricity prices are expected to average more than 18 cents per kilowatt-hour in 2026, about 5 percent higher than last year, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. At the same time, demand for power is climbing fast as the nation adds data centers, factories, and other large energy users. And consumers remain exposed to a market rattled by global conflict and swings in fuel prices.

These costs do not land on everyone equally. For a family with little left over at the end of the month, even a modest jump in the light bill means less for food, transportation or medicine. Low-income households spend three times more of their income on energy than other households, and Black households spend 43 percent more than white households, according to the American Council for an Energy-Efficient Economy.

The question every public official should be asking, then, is simple: How does America add the reliable electricity it needs while keeping costs down for the families least able to absorb them?

Instead, a group of state attorneys general has chosen a very different fight.

In November 2024, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton sued three of the nation’s largest asset managers, BlackRock, State Street and Vanguard, and was joined by a coalition of other states. The lawsuit claims the firms bought up large stakes in major coal producers and then used their influence as shareholders to pressure those companies to cut production in pursuit of climate goals. The attorneys general argue this restricted coal supply, raised coal prices and, in the end, raised electricity prices for consumers.

Paxton and his colleagues have presented the case as a way to bring down power bills. But when Paxton’s office announced its settlement with Vanguard, it billed the deal as an agreement “to protect the coal industry.” That wording tells us a great deal about whose interests are really at the center of this case.

Attorneys general have only so much time, staff, and money. Every hour spent on litigation against investment firms is an hour not spent on the problems that actually drive up household energy costs: transmission bottlenecks, permitting delays, an aging grid, energy efficiency and the shortage of new power generation.

There is actually an even deeper problem with making coal the centerpiece of an affordability strategy. Coal has been losing ground in the marketplace for decades.

Around 1990, coal supplied more than half of the nation’s electricity. By 2025, its share had fallen to about 17 percent. Most of that decline came from competition, chiefly cheaper natural gas, along with the growth of renewable energy and tougher environmental rules. In the first three months of 2026 alone, coal plant output fell 11 percent from a year earlier, while renewable generation grew. And this summer, Lazard’s annual analysis found renewables remain the lowest-cost option for new power plants, even as existing plants have become more competitive and continue to provide real value to the grid.

Coal’s decline did not begin with Wall Street, investment policies or the climate movement. It is the result of decades of change in America’s energy economy. Where a coal plant remains affordable and necessary to keep the lights on, utilities should keep running it. But keeping a useful plant open is very different from treating the survival of an entire industry as public policy. If other sources can provide power more cheaply, government has no business shielding coal from that competition.

For Black communities, the cost of coal does not stop at the utility bill. Burning coal produces air pollution and coal ash that must be managed, and the Environmental Protection Agency notes that coal ash contains contaminants like mercury, cadmium, and arsenic. A landmark NAACP study found that the roughly 6 million people living near coal plants had lower average incomes than the nation as a whole, and that people of color made up a majority of those living near the worst polluters. Too many of our neighborhoods carry both burdens at once: high energy bills and a greater share of the pollution. Any policy that claims to help consumers should account for both sides of that ledger.

The truth is that families do not much care whether the power running their refrigerator comes from a coal plant, a natural gas facility, or a wind farm. They care that it is there when they need it and that they can afford to pay for it.

Critics of environmental policy often complain that government should not pick winners and losers in energy markets. That principle should apply evenly. Financial firms should not be allowed to break antitrust laws in pursuit of climate goals. But government should be just as cautious about using its power to guarantee coal a permanent place in the market. Coal, natural gas, nuclear, wind, solar, battery storage, and new technologies should all compete on cost, reliability, and what the grid needs.

The real challenge before the nation is building enough reliable power, and building it quickly. Clinging to coal’s past, especially through the courts, does nothing to solve that.

At a time when so many Americans are struggling just to pay bills, it is fair to ask why state officials are pouring so much energy into protecting one industry. Attorneys general should be working to make power more plentiful and more affordable. Families facing economic hardships deserve more than to be invoked as props in a political fight between government officials and some of the world’s largest financial institutions.

text:
Texas Border Business

BROWNSVILLE, Texas – Brownsville Public Utilities Board (BPUB) Senior Key Accounts Representative, Mirta Vasquez, was selected to serve on a statewide advisory council supporting the development of Texas’ HOMES (Home Efficiency Rebates) and HEAR (Home Electrification and Appliance Rebate) residential energy-efficiency rebate programs.

As a member of the HOMES and HEAR Rebate Programs Advisory Council, Vasquez will provide subject matter expertise and input to the program implemented during the planning period and after the programs launch. Council members will participate in meetings during the planning period, with ongoing participation anticipated quarterly following launch.

Vasquez said her participation will help BPUB build a deeper understanding of the programs, so the utility can provide customers with accurate information about available rebates and how to take advantage of them. It will also give BPUB an opportunity to bring customer needs and questions to the program.

“Mirta understands the importance of making energy efficiency practical and accessible for the people we serve,” BPUB General Manager and CEO Marilyn D. Gilbert said. “Her experience will bring a valuable perspective to this statewide effort and help ensure the needs of communities like Brownsville are part of the conversation.”

The HOMES and HEAR programs are authorized by the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022, with $690 million allocated to Texas through the U.S. Department of Energy’s State Energy Conservation Office. The programs are currently under development, and rebates are not yet available. SECO is gathering public feedback as it develops the programs, with a future launch date to be established after approval from the U.S. Department of Energy.

HOMES will provide rebates for comprehensive energy-saving home improvements, while HEAR will provide rebates for eligible energy-efficient electric appliances and supporting upgrades for income-qualified households.

SECO will host a virtual community event about the Texas HOMES and HEAR programs on Oct. 20 at 6:30 p.m. The event will cover anticipated program benefits and the expected launch timeline and provide an opportunity for the public to share feedback. For more information about the programs and the event, visit the SECO website.

For more information on BPUB’s team of experts and their efforts to serve the Brownsville community, visit www.bpub.com.

description:
EPA proposes restoring 770 million biofuel credits, potentially boosting U.S. corn, soybean oil and ethanol demand while reshaping refinery obligations.
Under the Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS), refiners and fuel importers must meet federally established renewable fuel obligations, although qualifying small refineries can receive exemptions.
The final decision could influence the timing of renewable fuel purchases, the availability and pricing of compliance credits, and expectations across the U.S. agricultural supply chain.
Why the EPA Biofuel Decision Matters for Corn, Soybeans and U.S. Agriculture For American corn growers, the proposal could reinforce one of the most important domestic markets for their crop.
EPA Biofuel Policy Faces a Critical Decision Before 2027 The timing of the announcement carries political significance.
text:
EPA proposes restoring 770 million biofuel credits, potentially boosting U.S. corn, soybean oil and ethanol demand while reshaping refinery obligations.

Emily Trask is a U.S.-based journalist covering agricultural trade, policy, and agri-food markets, with a focus on U.S.-Latin America relations and their impact on global agribusiness.

Fuente: AgroLatam.com

Autor: AgroLatam.com

On October 13, 2026, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) proposed reallocating 100% of additional renewable fuel obligations waived for small oil refineries, potentially strengthening demand for American corn, soybean oil, ethanol and renewable diesel. The announcement, reported by Reuters, follows exemptions granted to 29 small refineries for the 2025 compliance year. The proposed rule matters because it could restore approximately 770 million Renewable Identification Numbers (RINs) to the federal biofuel program, influencing agricultural commodity markets, refinery compliance costs and renewable fuel demand during 2026 and 2027.

The proposal comes as U.S. farmers face continued uncertainty over commodity prices, production expenses and agricultural profitability. Under the Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS), refiners and fuel importers must meet federally established renewable fuel obligations, although qualifying small refineries can receive exemptions. According to EPA decisions announced on August 31, the agency granted 18 full exemptions and 11 partial exemptions, representing approximately 1.76 billion RINs for the 2025 compliance year. The new proposal addresses the additional exemptions beyond volumes already anticipated in federal regulations.

Reuters reported that the EPA is considering two alternatives for redistributing the additional obligations. The first would divide approximately 770 million RINs equally between 2026 and 2027, adding roughly 385 million credits to each compliance year. The second would assign the entire additional volume to 2027. The agency has opened a public consultation period, with comments due by December 4, 2026. The final decision could influence the timing of renewable fuel purchases, the availability and pricing of compliance credits, and expectations across the U.S. agricultural supply chain.

Why the EPA Biofuel Decision Matters for Corn, Soybeans and U.S. Agriculture

For American corn growers, the proposal could reinforce one of the most important domestic markets for their crop. Ethanol production consumes a substantial share of U.S. corn supplies, connecting farm revenues to gasoline demand, federal blending requirements and renewable fuel policy. Restoring previously waived obligations could provide additional support for ethanol consumption, potentially benefiting producers across the Midwest. However, higher RIN requirements do not automatically translate into equivalent increases in physical ethanol production, because obligated parties may also satisfy requirements by purchasing eligible compliance credits.

The soybean industry is another potential beneficiary. Soybean oil is a key feedstock for biodiesel and renewable diesel, making the sector particularly sensitive to changes in federal biofuel obligations. Stronger demand for eligible renewable fuels could improve opportunities for soybean processors, crushing facilities and agricultural cooperatives. The American Soybean Association welcomed the EPA announcement, emphasizing the importance of domestic biofuel demand for producers navigating difficult market conditions. Nevertheless, the actual effect on soybean prices will depend on feedstock competition, fuel production economics and how refiners fulfill their obligations.

The proposal also adds another layer to the ongoing debate between agricultural interests and petroleum refiners. Renewable fuel organizations argue that small refinery exemptions can weaken mandated demand for ethanol and other biofuels. Refiners, meanwhile, have expressed concerns about the financial burden of compliance and potential volatility in RIN markets. RINs are tradable credits used to demonstrate compliance with the Renewable Fuel Standard, and their prices can respond to regulatory changes, fuel blending economics and credit availability. The ultimate effects on fuel costs and agricultural commodity prices remain uncertain.

The Renewable Fuels Association expressed support for the EPA's proposed action, arguing that restoring waived obligations would help protect demand for renewable fuels and agricultural feedstocks. The development also follows the agency's March 2026 renewable fuel regulations, which established total obligations of approximately 26.81 billion RINs for 2026 and 27.02 billion RINs for 2027, including previously planned reallocations. The additional 770 million credits under consideration would supplement those requirements rather than replace them, potentially strengthening the effective mandate depending on the final compliance schedule.

EPA Biofuel Policy Faces a Critical Decision Before 2027

The timing of the announcement carries political significance. Reuters reported that the proposal comes ahead of the November congressional elections, when agricultural policy remains an important issue in major farm-producing states. Lawmakers from agricultural districts have pressed federal regulators to preserve renewable fuel demand while balancing the concerns of independent refiners. A bipartisan group of House lawmakers also urged EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin to follow through on refinery exemption reallocations. The administration's decision could influence both agricultural market expectations and the broader debate over U.S. energy policy.

For producers planning their 2027 operations, the proposed changes deserve attention alongside USDA supply and demand forecasts, crop insurance decisions, input costs and international trade developments. Higher renewable fuel obligations could improve domestic demand expectations, but they cannot independently guarantee stronger corn or soybean prices. Global grain supplies, weather conditions, export competitiveness, processing margins and energy markets will continue to shape farm profitability. The most important question is whether the restored RIN obligations will generate additional physical biofuel demand or primarily affect compliance credit trading.

The EPA's final decision will determine whether the additional obligations are spread across two years or concentrated in 2027. That distinction could affect refinery purchasing strategies, renewable fuel production planning and short-term market sentiment. For farmers, agronomists, agricultural investors and policymakers, the proposal represents a potentially important development in the relationship between U.S. energy regulation and agricultural economics. Until the rule is finalized, the potential benefits for corn, soybean oil and renewable fuel producers remain prospective rather than guaranteed, making the December 4 comment deadline a key milestone for the industry.

title: The US is fighting over data centers. China is building them fast | CNN
description:
Nearly 90 data centers are slated to be built in this city of fewer than two million people.
As of last year, the US had roughly 10 times more AI data centers than China, according to Stanford University research – and vastly more computing power, other estimates show.
And, crucially, throughout the Communist Party-run country, public opposition to the mass construction of data centers – the kind that is making headlines in the US – is non-existent.
But that is still less than one-fifth of the $800 billion in AI data center investment from their US peers.
Water is another key resource that’s sparked backlash against data centers in America, but Zheng says it’s not an issue here.
text:
The area appears like a high-tech mirage. Block after block of hulking data centers – both new and under construction – rise up seemingly out of nowhere from rolling plains and fields of sunflowers and sorghum.

On their sides are some of the biggest names in Chinese tech – hardware giant Huawei, social media platform Kuaishou, service provider VNET – all packed into a zone thrumming with bustle and movement.

This is Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia, a Chinese city on the edge of the Gobi desert. It’s fast becoming one of the data hubs fueling a massive AI boom in China that’s made the country the only serious rival to the US’ ambitions to dominate the technology. Nearly 90 data centers are slated to be built in this city of fewer than two million people.

As of last year, the US had roughly 10 times more AI data centers than China, according to Stanford University research – and vastly more computing power, other estimates show. American tech firms have something China’s don’t: access to the most advanced chips, the single most important ingredient for developing AI.

But Ulanqab – with its growing number of AI and big-data centers – showcases the advantages on China’s side in the race for the technology that could define the 21st century.

The towering units here were constructed at breakneck speed, with most of the densely packed Bayin Big Data Industrial Park taking shape in just two years, testament to China’s capacity to build fast.

Heavy winds, beating sun and wide, open spaces give the area plentiful access to cheap green energy and land.

And, crucially, throughout the Communist Party-run country, public opposition to the mass construction of data centers – the kind that is making headlines in the US – is non-existent.

‘With open arms’

At Ulanqab’s Bayin industrial park on a recent weekday, a steady stream of construction workers had their faces scanned as they filed past guards to enter building sites, while trucks rumbled along, feeding supplies to the facilities taking shape within. Outside their perimeters, vendors hawked noodles and cigarettes from makeshift stalls.

The din of construction didn’t appear unwelcome to locals living nearby. Some who spoke to CNN said they were benefiting from the projects – and the influx of migrant construction workers that came with them to an area whose economy was otherwise largely reliant on agriculture.

“Before, we’d just sit there and wait for customers. Now we’re constantly busy – picking up orders, doing this and that. We barely get a break,” said Ma Rong, 56, who has run a grocery store and guest house in the area for the past 30 years. “Our business has gotten much better than before,” he said.

Some have been uprooted by changes sweeping the region, like restaurant owner Liu Baoping, 58, who said he had to leave his original business location due to the demolition of a highway. But he describes his daily clientele as doubling alongside the data-center buildout. “The environment isn’t as clean as before, but people’s incomes and the economy – it’s way better,” he said.

Ulanqab is part of Beijing’s vision to rapidly scale up data infrastructure – a key priority for a government that sees AI as a crucial engine of growth for the country’s slowing economy with its shrinking population.

“China has embraced AI with open arms,” Chinese leader Xi Jinping told a global artificial intelligence conference in Shanghai this past July. He pointed to China’s initiative to inject AI into sectors from health to home goods and hailed its push to embed AI in manufacturing as a “shining hallmark of Chinese modernization.”

Already more than 700 million people use AI in China, according to official statistics. And the plan to weave AI across manufacturing, industry and daily life also requires massive amounts of compute.

Beijing last month announced a $560 billion plan to rapidly scale up information infrastructure, including computing facilities, over the next five years. Private tech companies are also ramping up investment in AI infrastructure, though they still trail their Silicon Valley peers by a longshot.

Such investment from listed Chinese companies will double this year to around $139 billion, according to research firm Rhodium Group. But that is still less than one-fifth of the $800 billion in AI data center investment from their US peers.

And that’s not the only bottleneck.

Chinese firms face another critical challenge: limits on the amount of high-end hardware available to fill these centers. Washington’s export bans restrict their access to the best AI chips, like certain models from Nvidia and AMD, while Beijing has restricted imports of some less powerful options. Domestic chipmakers are racing to catch up, but their tech still lags the US – and supplies of their cutting-edge models are tight.

“If you look at the overall production cost of building a data center, chips are the most important factor, and they just don’t have enough,” said Nick Corvino, a researcher at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

But what China lacks in chips and capital, it’s trying make up for with an advantage: ample, affordable power, much of it green.

Excess energy

While energy-hungry data centers are straining an aging US grid that’s not expanded significantly in decades, China between 2022 and 2025 added capacity equivalent to that of industrial power sources across the entire US as of the end of 2025.

And it has more green power than it can use: the country wasted enough excess green energy in the first six months of 2026 to power the entire country of Mexico for a year, findings from independent research organizations the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air and Global Energy Monitor suggest.

Beijing wants data centers to sop up that excess – much of it in western, rural areas where sun, wind and land are plentiful – while boosting business for its green tech sector, under a plan known as “Eastern data, Western compute.”

Under that strategy, first launched in 2022, China has designated eight national computing hubs – including several in its west – and 10 national data center clusters. Its latest five-year national economic blueprint elevated the linkage further, calling for pairing the build-out of computing infrastructure and green energy.

“China’s trying to take advantage of the fact that it has this muscle memory for building energy (infrastructure) quickly,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution. “Whereas for the US, we haven’t done this kind of grid buildout in a long time and so we are struggling on the power generation and grid connection front.”

Abundant power can also help China make up for its less powerful domestic chips. Chinese chip designers like Huawei are combining clusters of chips to create the computing power of superior tech. The fix can be effective for some tasks, analysts say, but uses significantly more electricity.

Observers say that even with ample power, Beijing’s vision has its limits.

Some computing hubs in the west are too far away to handle certain tasks at the speeds needed for urban hubs in the densely-populated east. There’s also concern about so-called “ghost data centers” or ill-conceived projects in rural areas, built to fit a topline government initiative, yet lacking the hardware or users to justify the investment.

But in hubs in Inner Mongolia, where optical cables can transmit data to Beijing – some 200 miles away – faster than the blink of an eye, and top players are pouring major resources, China’s vision appears to be taking shape.

‘Get prepared’

Long one of China’s top coal producers, the wind-swept region bordering Russia and Mongolia has more recently become a hub for green energy.

Fields of solar panels blanket parts of Inner Mongolia, while the slender silhouettes of wind turbines spin above grazing sheep. Along some stretches of highway unused turbine blades line the roadsides like giant, fiberglass elephant tusks.

In Ulanqab, which falls within one of China’s 10 national data center clusters, nearly half the grid draws from wind and solar – and some data center providers are finding ways to rely even more heavily on clean sources.

Several miles from the thrumming construction of Ulanqab’s Bayin industrial park, the Envision “Galaxy Campus” is running one such model.

Spanning more than 20 football fields and slated to be among the world’s largest by area when completed, this data center will be home to servers and chips from tech companies, used to handle queries users input into AI apps in places like Beijing.

Upwards of 80% of the power for the facility will come directly from wind farms operated by the company, bypassing the grid completely, Envision says.

Battery systems then store wind power, while a cutting-edge solid-state transformer can rapidly adjust how much power is feeding the servers, based on demand, according to Ricky Zheng, the facility’s general manager, who showed CNN around the under-construction campus on a recent day.

Water is another key resource that’s sparked backlash against data centers in America, but Zheng says it’s not an issue here. The chilly climate in Ulanqab reduces the need for cooling overall, while the facility is running a so-called “zero-water” system that uses industrial alcohol as coolant, he says.

Zheng also seemed optimistic when it comes to demand from tech companies for their facilities – and those clients’ ability to kit out server racks with needed hardware.

The first phase of the planned total 2GW facility was already fully booked, he said, and the company was building additional phases, both for AI and cloud services.

AI chips and servers “are owned by our off-takers,” he said. “When they give us the order to build such a big data center … they were confident to have enough infrastructure to be installed in these (server) racks.”

And this company, like Ulanqab itself, is planning to be ready for an expected surge in AI demand in the coming years.

“We designed this for the next 10 years,” said Zheng. “You need to get prepared for the future.”

text:
PEOSTA, Iowa – The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has proposed adding back all of the additional renewable fuel volume that was waived through 2025 small refinery exemptions (SREs). The proposal, announced by EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin at an event on Tuesday in Peosta, Iowa, aims to keep the Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) “Set 2” volumes intact.

Zeldin said farmers asked the agency “not to give them handouts but create avenues” into additional markets, and called the proposal an effort to maintain a “strong and durable market” as harvest continues. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said she was pleased to see “a path forward to 100% reallocation by 2027.” She noted that the biofuel industry supports more than 100,000 jobs and generates over $100 billion in economic activity.

Iowa’s congressional delegation also weighed in. Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-IA) said he worked with the White House, Sen. Joni Ernst and Reps. Ashley Hinson, Mariannette Miller-Meeks, Zach Nunn and Randy Feenstra to secure full reallocation. He said the biofuels industry directly employs 31,000 Iowans. In a statement, Grassley said in part that “today’s decision is a major boost for Iowa’s rural economy and the 31,000 Iowa jobs that biofuels directly employ.” Ernst said reallocating the volumes into 2026 and 2027 will “strengthen our farm economy” and lower consumer prices. Hinson said the proposal reflects a 100% reallocation agreement she helped secure in August. She added that farmers are facing difficult conditions, and that finishing the rule is “a big deal.”

What EPA Is Proposing

When EPA finalized the Set 2 rule, it estimated how many hardship exemptions small refineries would receive for their 2025 obligations. The agency’s August 31 decisions on 34 pending petitions came in well above that estimate. EPA had projected roughly 990 million RINs would be exempted for 2025. The actual total was 1.76 billion RINs across 29 small refineries, according to the American Coalition for Ethanol (ACE). The Renewable Fuels Association (RFA) says 18 refiners received full exemptions and 11 received partial ones, making it the second-highest annual SRE volume EPA has ever granted.

The 770 million RIN gap between projection and reality is the volume at issue. EPA is proposing two ways to reallocate 100% of it:

Approach one: Divide the additional volume equally between the 2026 and 2027 compliance years.

Approach two: Place all of the additional volume in the 2027 compliance year.

EPA will take public comment through December 4, 2026. The agency also said the revision to the 2026 standards may extend the existing March 31, 2027 compliance reporting deadline for 2026.

Industry Groups Applaud, With Caveats

Biofuel trade groups welcomed the proposal, though several used the moment to press for more. Renewable Fuels Association President and CEO Geoff Cooper thanked Zeldin and the White House for honoring their commitment, but said the group believes most of the exemptions were unjustified. He called for reform of what he described as a broken SRE program.

“While we believe most of the exemptions were unjustified, EPA’s reallocation plan—if finalized as proposed—will help offset the demand loss for ethanol producers and farmers,” according to Cooper. “We look forward to this proposal being swiftly finalized so that renewable fuel producers, refiners, and our partners in agriculture have the certainty they need heading into 2027. With refiners enjoying record-high profit margins, gasoline supplies tightening, and drivers still paying too much at the pump, the Trump administration understands this is no time to undermine domestic biofuels with SREs. The administration should be expanding access to affordable American-made ethanol—not giving the oil industry another break.”

Cooper said SREs were meant as a temporary measure for truly small, independent refiners, but that many have treated them as an entitlement. He also cited EPA analyses showing that RIN costs are passed along at the wholesale level and offset when lower-cost renewable fuels are blended. RFA also cited Morning Consult polling it commissioned, which found that more than three-quarters of respondents with an opinion want oil companies required to meet their blending requirements.

Clean Fuels Alliance America said EPA released the proposal earlier than originally promised. Kurt Kovarik, the group’s vice president of federal affairs, urged EPA to finalize supplemental volumes in both 2026 and 2027 so the market signal is “clear and immediate.” He said the biodiesel, renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel industry has invested billions in rural America and is supplying lower-cost diesel. Kovarik added that “The clean fuels industry is delivering on the goals for the RFS and providing a critical supply of lower-cost diesel fuels right now. That contribution is important to control diesel prices and associated consumer costs. We urge EPA to finalize the proposal to add supplemental volumes to both 2026 and 2027 to ensure that the market signal from the robust RFS volumes is clear and immediate.”

Growth Energy CEO Emily Skor said the proposal would let EPA “deliver on the full potential” of the Set 2 volumes and make farmers and biofuel producers whole. “With this proposal, EPA would deliver on the full potential of historic RVOs and fulfill its promise to make American farmers and biofuel producers whole,” said Growth Energy CEO Emily Skor. “Reallocating lost gallons would strengthen the rural economy and provide relief to farmers looking for reliable new markets that won’t be destroyed by costly exemptions. We applaud our champions in Congress for fighting tirelessly on behalf of homegrown biofuels, USDA Secretary Rollins for advocating for the nation’s rural communities, and EPA for continuing to deliver markets for America’s farmers and supporting growth and investment in liquid fuels across the country.” The group noted that EPA had pledged in August to account for lost demand before the end of October.

American Coalition for Ethanol CEO Brian Jennings called the proposal an important step. He said every gallon displaced by an exemption is lost demand for ethanol and lost value for farmers. He also tied the issue to year-round E15, saying the SRE debate has held up adoption and urging Congress to pass nationwide E15 legislation before the end of the year.

“The integrity of the RFS depends on ensuring the volumes established under the program translate into real-world renewable fuel demand,” according to Jennings. “Farmers and ethanol producers need certainty that RFS requirements will not be eroded after the fact by exemptions. While this proposed reallocation is an important step, the debate over SREs has held up adoption of year-round E15. Congress must act to provide greater certainty and expand opportunities for ethanol by passing nationwide E15 legislation before the end of the year.” ACE said it will keep urging EPA to set strong volumes in the upcoming Set 3 rule and to account for any impact if SRE gallons are not fully reallocated.

The American Soybean Association also welcomed Tuesday’s EPA proposal to fully reallocate renewable fuel volumes lost to 2025 small refinery exemptions under the Renewable Fuel Standard. “ASA applauds Administrator Zeldin and the Trump Administration for keeping their commitment to farmers and proposing to restore 100% of biofuel volume impacted by 2025 small refinery exemption actions,” said ASA Vice President Dave Walton, an Iowa soybean farmer. “Soybean farmers are navigating a tough farm economy, and the administration’s strong domestic biofuel policies will continue to drive much-needed market demand in the U.S. We are encouraged by today’s proposal and urge EPA to get it across the finish line quickly.”

Background and What’s Next

EPA’s Set 2 rule, announced March 27, 2026, set the highest renewable fuel volumes in the RFS program’s history. The agency estimated it would generate more than $10 billion for rural economies and more than 100,000 new jobs in agriculture and manufacturing. Producers and industry groups will now watch the comment period and whether EPA settles on a split or a single-year reallocation. Several groups, including Clean Fuels, ASA and RFA, have asked that the rule be finalized quickly so the market has clarity heading into 2027.

text:
JOHANNESBURG (AP) — Climate activists picketed outside the African Energy Week conference in Cape Town, South Africa, on Tuesday, calling for an end to new oil and gas exploration across the continent and accusing energy companies of prioritizing profits over people and the environment.

Greenpeace Africa and Extinction Rebellion campaigners challenged efforts to position Africa as a new frontier for fossil fuel development, arguing that further investment would worsen climate change and threaten communities already grappling with its effects.

“Oil companies from overseas have made billions in profits this year alone at the expense of people’s lives, at the expense of ecosystems, at the expense of African lives,” Siya Myeza, a climate and energy campaigner with Greenpeace Africa, told The Associated Press.

Myeza branded the gathering “Africa Exploitation Week,” accusing the industry of driving environmental destruction and poverty. Police removed the protesters, who wore T-shirts bearing the slogan “Make polluters pay.”

The protests come as South Africa seeks to expand oil and gas development to attract investment and bolster energy security. The government presents natural gas as a complement to renewable energy, saying gas-fired plants could provide electricity when wind and solar output drops.

Despite legal setbacks, British energy giant Shell plans to drill up to five deepwater wells in the Northern Cape Ultra Deep block off South Africa’s west coast to explore for and assess oil and gas deposits. The project’s environmental approval has drawn appeals.

Protesters say such plans risk prolonging dependence on fossil fuels at a time when countries should be cutting emissions.

Judy Scott-Goldman, a representative of Extinction Rebellion in Cape Town, acknowledged that renewable energy would feature at the conference but said campaigners opposed promoting new oil and gas exploration.

She said expanding fossil fuel use would run counter to commitments under the Paris climate agreement to reduce emissions.

“We’re here to say we don’t want to see any exploration of oil and gas on this continent,” she told the AP.

She pointed to fires, floods and rising food prices as consequences of climate change, warning that its effects could also drive migration and social unrest.

title: AI data centers are coming for federal land. They're roiling the Nevada governor's race

He recently signed an agreement with Trump's Republican administration to streamline infrastructure projects, which could include data centers on federal lands.
Data centers have quickly become a “catalyzing issue” in the midterms, catching many politicians flat-footed, said David Damore, a political science professor at the University of Nevada Las Vegas.
In September, Lombardo, who has said data centers provide enormous economic opportunity for Nevada, signed an executive order placing more guardrails on data centers and requiring them to pay more taxes to support schools.
text:
BOULDER CITY, Nev. (AP) — Janelle Sorenson loves the clear night skies in Boulder City, less than an hour's drive from the bright lights of the Las Vegas Strip. It’s a small, quiet town, and she thinks an artificial intelligence data center would ruin the community and scar the desert landscape.

So over the summer, she joined with other residents to successfully oppose plans for one of the giant computing warehouses that have popped up around the country.

But their victory was short-lived. The developers withdrew their application and instead sought adjacent land owned by the federal government — and the U.S. Bureau of Land Management signed off.

“Not only did we not get to decide anything or have a say,” Sorenson said, “we were just really kept in the dark.”

The Townsite data center was the first in the country to be approved on federal public land, though construction is stalled after a judge ruled that the government couldn’t use an old environmental review from when the project was intended to be a solar farm.

Tech companies are eager for vast tracts to build data centers that can be as large as 70 football fields, and Townsite could set a precedent for similar projects on federal property with more than a dozen others in the planning stages. President Donald Trump has been a steadfast supporter of the artificial intelligence industry, which he views as a source of economic growth and part of a global competition with China.

However, data centers have been unpopular in many communities as voters worry about higher electricity bills, declining water supplies and other impacts. In Nevada, where 80% of the land is owned by the federal government, Townsite and other projects have become a dominant issue in the battleground state's closely watched governor's race.

Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo, one of his party's most vulnerable incumbents, doesn't outright oppose building data centers on public lands, as long as they have community support. He recently signed an agreement with Trump's Republican administration to streamline infrastructure projects, which could include data centers on federal lands.

Democratic nominee Aaron Ford, the state attorney general, has pledged to oppose data centers on public lands, saying affordable housing should be the priority.

Both say the projects, whether on public or private land, must follow state rules, such as requiring data centers to cover their own energy costs and protecting water supplies, or they would lose eligibility for state tax abatements.

Voters across the political spectrum unite against data centers

Sorenson, the Boulder City resident, considers herself to be liberal, but she said her conservative neighbors are on the same page as she is.

“We’re all aligned on this,” she said.

Autumn McGrath-Shook, who lives in the same town, said she recently left the Republican Party and registered with the Green Party over data centers, though she still identifies as conservative. Worried about the environmental impact on wildlife, she joined forces with “these crazy libs” to oppose the project.

Data centers have quickly become a “catalyzing issue” in the midterms, catching many politicians flat-footed, said David Damore, a political science professor at the University of Nevada Las Vegas.

Some state leaders who were previously supportive of data centers have rushed to respond. For example, Republican Texas Gov. Greg Abbott paused data center approvals until audits are completed, and Democratic Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro signed an executive order removing data center proposals from a fast-track permitting process and requiring them to receive local approval before seeking state approval.

In August, Ford announced his plan to pause new tax abatements for data centers while an audit is conducted to see if the projects have fulfilled promises about producing tax revenue and economic benefits.

In September, Lombardo, who has said data centers provide enormous economic opportunity for Nevada, signed an executive order placing more guardrails on data centers and requiring them to pay more taxes to support schools.

The two have successfully “muddied the waters” on their data center positions, Damore said.

Lombardo criticized Ford for co-sponsoring 2015 legislation that created the state’s tax abatement program for data centers, a measure that received bipartisan support. Ford criticized Lombardo for giving more than $200 million in tax breaks to data centers, which is connected to the legislation that Ford co-sponsored.

Ford told The Associated Press that he would use “every tool” at his disposal to prevent data centers from skirting state guardrails, including withholding tax abatements and pursuing litigation.

Lombardo, whose campaign declined to make him available for an interview, has a similar pitch. His office said he would not hesitate to confront the federal government to advocate for Nevadans.

But that's not good enough for McGrath-Shook, who is on the fence in the governor's race. She thinks Ford is soft on crime, but she views Lombardo as more pro-data centers.

“I would much rather vote for Lombardo than Aaron Ford in a normal world,” she said. “But with the looming data centers, it really changes the landscape — and literally.”

Data centers on public lands are the latest effort in AI race

Last year, Trump signed an executive order to accelerate permitting for artificial intelligence data centers, and his administration has rolled back the National Environmental Policy Act, saying the bedrock law needlessly delays federal approval for energy and infrastructure projects.

Dan Diorio, executive vice president of state policy and government affairs for the Data Center Coalition, said the industry wants to be a part of the conversation regarding responsible development on federal lands.

“The good-faith actors in this space are going to be approaching that development responsibly,” he said, “ensuring that it’s going to do no harm on important federal lands.”

But environmentalists are concerned about data centers developing on federal lands to skirt environmental protections and laws and circumvent permitting processes. They're generally opposed to using public lands for the projects in the first place.

“We believe that public lands are reserved for public good and should be protected and kept in trust for future generations,” said Olivia Tanager, director of the Sierra Club’s Toiyabe Chapter. “And the idea of using public lands for data center construction totally flies in the face of that set of values.”

She said Congress should pass legislation with new standards for environmental reviews and public engagement that could slow development.

“Short of some type of legislation to that effect," Tanager said, “we’re staring down the barrel of having many data centers move forward on public lands over the next few years.”

text:
LANSING – Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer has declared a statewide energy emergency this week in an effort to reduce the “unprecedented” financial strain on Michigan’s farmers and loggers as a result of “record-high diesel prices, tight margins, and significant market volatility.”

The executive order signed Monday will temporarily allow farm and wood harvester vehicles to use “dyed diesel” on public roads without penalty.

Dyed diesel refers to “red dye diesel,” which is dyed red to signify its exemption from state and federal motor fuel taxes. Under the Michigan Motor Fuel Tax Act, the use of dyed diesel is restricted to off-road vehicles only, such as farm and construction vehicles.

Whitmer said Monday the executive order was issued in response to the soaring fuel costs as a result of the Iran War, which she says “continues to raise the price of everything.”

“Exorbitant diesel prices are hitting Michigan’s farmers and loggers hard right in the middle of harvest season,” she said.. “This order will allow farm and logging vehicles to use dyed diesel on our highways without risk of penalty. We need to keep work moving and reduce pressure on the people who keep our state’s ag economy running.”

The move by Whitmer follows an executive order signed last week by President Donald Trump, which temporarily allows “anyone to purchase tax-free red dye diesel for any reason” and defers the federal diesel tax on that fuel through the end of the year, without interest or penalties.

According to the White House, the federal diesel tax is 24.4 cents per gallon, or about $60 on a 250-gallon fill-up. The Trump administration says savings would top $100 per fill-up in states that match the federal executive order.

Whitmer’s order will end no later than Dec. 31, 2026.

text:
Democrat Callie Barr is trying a second time to unseat incumbent US Rep. Jack Bergman, R-Watersmeet in Michigan’s 1st Congressional District.

In 2024, Barr earned 38% of the vote to Bergman’s 59% in a four-way race.

This time, Barr’s part of a seven-way race for the seat representing the northern Lower Peninsula and all of the Upper Peninsula in Congress. In addition to Barr, Bergman also faces Libertarian Arnett Satterla, independent candidate Zebulon Featherly, Green Party candidate LaVeta Davenport, US Taxpayers Party candidate Doc Kovaly and Working Class Party candidate Liz Hakola.

Barr spoke with WCMU about her goals for the district.

David Nicholas: Callie Barr, thank you very much for joining us.

Callie Barr: Thank you so much for having me.

DN: First question is, how would you define yourself politically?

CB: You know, I'm a patriot. I believe in representing the people of upper and northern Michigan to deliver what we need here. I often say this isn't a seat for Republicans or Democrats, it's a seat for the people of upper and northern Michigan, and being a fifth-generation Michigander from Cheboygan, Michigan, I'm deeply, deeply rooted here.

And so right now, to me, it's about returning this seat to the people who live and work here and just want a shot to be able to afford life.

DN: And what specific ideas or plans do you have to address affordability?

CB: Yeah, well, right now I'm running against an incumbent, Jack Bergman, who's done nothing but increase our costs while actually costing the taxpayer. I mean, he's the number-one spender, number-one out of 435 members of Congress, the number-one spending on lodging. I mean, even during COVID, when members were getting reimbursed like $600, he was reimbursed over $61,000. And along with that, he's done things like vote to cut Medicaid.

I would not do that, right? Medicaid funds our rural hospitals. He didn't extend the (Affordable Care Act) subsidies. I would not have done that, right? Because that is something that has increased our insurance premiums across this district.

He supports the war in Iran. That has increased the cost of gas and diesel, which has increased the cost of our food and our groceries and the things that we buy at the store.

He supports the tariffs, which has increased our costs for our small businesses and also for us, the consumer, and damaged our relationship with Canada.

So, when we think about decreasing costs, what we need to do is get someone out of Congress right now who is at every point increasing our cost of living here, while also at the same time using our taxpayer dollars to live a pretty lavish lifestyle.

And so, enough's enough. And so, I support policies that will decrease our costs, which means tackling insurance, making sure we can negotiate every drug price, making sure our rural hospitals are fully funded, not supporting a war right now that is driving up the cost of gas and everything else.

DN: And what is your position on US foreign policy specifically in Iran?

CB: So, no one's crying that we fight terrorism, right? And I want to be clear about that. The problem is, though, is when you go into a country and you have no plan, and when you are, like I said, increasing, the cost for us, right?

We're spending billions of dollars there. We don't have a plan. It's increasing our gas prices.

The other thing is, we're not at full military readiness. You know, I come from a military family. My husband is a Marine for 15 years. He served in Iraq and Afghanistan. And what concerns me is that we fired inspector generals. We fired JAG officers. We fired military leaders and commanders who had decades of knowledge and experience in the Middle East because they weren't yes men and yes women.

And so, that is also very concerning that we don't have a military that's at its full capacity and full military readiness to do the job that they're over there being asked to do. And frankly, I don't even know that they know what the plan is because there isn't a plan.

And so all of that, we need leaders in Congress right now, leaders in Congress that are going to have to take a look at this and figure out how we work to negotiate so that we're not in an endless conflict in the Middle East again, like my family was a part of for 20 years.

DN: What is your position then on tariffs and trade wars, specifically with Canada?

CB: I mean, this is ridiculous. Canada is a friend of ours and has been. We have been so damaged, not just with our friendships, but economically as well.

When we look at our Canadian friends coming across and sue Canada, they're not coming anymore.

We've seen just significant declines and it has resulted in the loss of millions and millions of dollars of economic benefit to us. These tariffs have not … these were not thoughtful. They’re chaotic. They've damaged our relationship with Canada. They've damaged our own economy. They were thoughtless and stupid. And we should not be supporting something that not only hurts one of our closest relationships, but also just hurts us too.

DN: And what is your position specifically on the construction of data centers in Michigan?

CB: We are the Great Lakes State and we have to do everything we can to protect our water. And we need regulation to protect our water.

We also need to make sure that there is strong local control that means something, that local communities can make decisions and have voice to actually realize that.

And that also means that we need absolute transparency. We need to know what risks are. We need to know what the impact on the environment is. And the other thing is that our local communities in no way are paying for any kind of energy infrastructure upgrades or costs associated with data centers.

DN: And finally, how would you address the ongoing debate over the Line 5 pipeline running under the Straits of Mackinac?

CB: Yeah, as a congressional representative, I think about, what are the things that you can actually do as a congressional representative? Because, of course, a representative is not going to, cannot by law, overturn a federal permit, a state permit, a state court decision, which is where that line is right now.

But what you can do is help to advance towards a clean energy future.

We had tax incentives and subsidies to do exactly that, to help us have the jobs of the future when it comes to working towards a cleaner energy future.

And this was supported by environmentalists. It was supported by our businesses. It was supported by labor because it was a way to have jobs and training and to start thinking about how we can diversify our energy sources, because we want to have reliable and affordable energy.

And of course, we want to continue to move towards energy sources that help protect this wonderful environment that we live in and that we are stewards over of.

And so, to me, that's really important, that we revitalize that effort, which this administration has pulled us back years in that kind of progress.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency on Tuesday released a draft rule that would fully reallocate renewable fuel volumes lost through small refinery exemptions under the Renewable Fuel Standard.

EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said the proposal is intended to provide more certainty for farmers and biofuel producers while preserving the integrity of the federal renewable fuel program.

In August, EPA issued decisions on 34 small refinery exemption petitions for the 2025 compliance year. The agency granted full exemptions to 18 petitions and partial exemptions to 11 others, exempting 29 refineries from some or all of their renewable fuel obligations.

The agency said it would propose reallocating 100% of the difference between projected and actual exempted volumes into renewable volume obligations for 2026 and 2027.

The proposal could be significant for Iowa’s ethanol and biodiesel industries, which have long pushed federal officials to restore renewable fuel demand lost through refinery exemptions.

The draft rule has not been finalized.

text:
The project count, capacity and puchase agreement terms match the portfolio announced in February, but energyRe has not confirmed to ENR that the two announcements cover the same projects and did not immediately respond to additional project questions.

“This financing secures the capital to advance these projects and demonstrates energyRe's ability to finance its development portfolio at scale,” Surya Mohan, energyRe senior vice president of mergers and acquisitions and capital markets, said in a statement.

The transaction also advances energyRe's stated goal of investing $2 billion in South Carolina by 2030, according to Chief Financial Officer Pedro Pereira.

Construction Begins on Culpepper Grid Connection

Duke Energy crews work at a substation in North Carolina. The utility has begun below-grade work on a separate $10.1-million grid connection serving energyRe’s Culpepper Solar project in South Carolina.

Photo courtesy Duke Energy

Duke Energy Progress, a subsidiary of Duke Energy, told the South Carolina Public Service Commission Sept. 30 that below-grade work had started on the planned Byrdtown Road 230-kV substation needed to connect Culpepper Solar to its system in Darlington County. The utility's quarterly construction update said the land transfer for the substation site was still being processed.

Duke's plans also call for a Culpepper Solar 230-kV switching station and an approximately 370-ft generation tie line connecting it with the Byrdtown Road substation. The utility will reconfigure its existing Robinson Plant-Florence 230-kV line to connect with the new substation and replace four existing transmission structures with five new structures.

Each substation is planned on about seven acres provided by Culpepper Solar. Duke estimated the work at $10.1 million, with Culpepper Solar responsible for the cost. Its February filing projected completion in April 2029 and said the improvements are necessary for the generating facility to deliver power to Duke's system.

The filing documents construction of associated utility infrastructure, not the Culpepper solar array itself.

Darlington County Tightens Solar Siting Rules

Darlington County, where three of energyRe's previously announced projects are planned, has adopted tighter development standards for utility-scale solar facilities following a debate over the industry's expanding footprint.

County officials reported about 622 acres of tax parcels already dedicated to solar generation and another 12,553 acres in various stages of development when they proposed a nine-month moratorium on new solar and wind projects.

The county council rejected the moratorium Sept. 10 in a 5-3 vote, allowing development applications to continue through the permitting process. The council subsequently adopted Ordinance 26-06, amending the county's renewable-energy development standards.

The county Planning Commission recommended 100-ft setbacks from neighboring property boundaries and 600 ft from residences, along with continuous vegetative screening and financial assurance of at least $50,000 or 125% of estimated decommissioning costs, whichever is greater.

Residents near a separate proposed solar development around Deer Run Drive and Clyde Road have pushed for larger setbacks, stronger decommissioning requirements and restrictions on new development. “Simply put, a utility-scale solar facility does not belong in the middle of a neighborhood,” residents Earl and Trena McElveen told county officials in a written statement.

A petition seeking stronger solar siting protections and opposing the neighborhood project had collected 115 verified signatures. The opposition concerns a different project, and ENR has identified no opposition specifically targeting energyRe's Culpepper, Rollins or Ross developments.

EnergyRe says it broke ground on about 450 MW of solar projects over the past year, but has not named contractors or construction schedules for the five projects in its latest financing. It remains unclear how much of the $815 million will fund new construction versus projects already underway.

text:
By Siddharth Cavale

CHICAGO, Oct 13 (Reuters) - The US Environmental Protection Agency proposed on Tuesday to make larger refiners blend more biofuels into their products over ‌the next two years, a move that will likely appeal to farm-state voters ‌ahead of November's congressional elections.

The proposal would help offset concerns about lost demand for ethanol producers and farmers ​after the EPA announced in August it would waive renewable fuel volume obligations for 29 small refineries that argued the requirements would cause economic hardship.

The EPA proposed reallocating 100% of those waived fuel volume obligations and is seeking public comment after putting forward two ‌approaches. One would split the ⁠additional 2025 small refinery exemption volume evenly between the 2026 and 2027 compliance years, while the other would allocate all of it to ⁠2027.

Comments are due by December 4, 2026, the EPA said in a statement.

Renewable credit prices for biodiesel and ethanol fell slightly on the news, according to a refinery trader at ​the OPIS ​biofuels conference in Chicago.

The EPA in August decided ​to grant 1.76 billion RINs worth ‌of small refinery exemptions for the 2025 compliance year, including full exemptions for 18 refineries and partial waivers for 11 others. At the time, the agency said it would seek to reallocate the exempted volumes to other refiners in future years to preserve overall biofuel blending requirements.

The exemptions, the largest ever issued under the Renewable Fuel Standard, ‌drew sharp criticism from biofuel producers and farm groups, ​which argued they would reduce demand for ethanol and ​biodiesel and undermine markets for agricultural ​feedstocks.

Refiners said compliance costs and elevated RIN prices justified relief for ‌facilities facing economic hardship.

"While we believe most ​of the exemptions ​were unjustified, EPA's reallocation plan, if finalized as proposed, will help offset the demand loss for ethanol producers and farmers," said Geoff Cooper, CEO of the Renewable ​Fuels Association, which represents ‌ethanol producers.

The EPA also said reallocating the waived obligations could require extending the 2026 ​compliance year deadline of March 31, 2027.

(Reporting by Siddharth Cavale in Chicago, ​Editing by Franklin Paul and Nia Williams)
